Heterogeneity in the Marginal Propensity to Consume among U.S. Households
Aditya Aladangady, Jesse Bricker, Andrew C. Chang, Sarena Goodman, and Gina Li, with assistance from Payton Crawford1
Introduction

Precise estimates of marginal propensities to consume (MPCs) are central to understanding economic activity and the effects of economic shocks on households. However, the literature does not yield a consensus on either an aggregate MPC or the extent to which MPCs vary across the population.

To advance this literature, we, along with other members of the Federal Reserve staff, introduced a new question to the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) that directly elicits households' MPCs. Specifically, after respondents provide a detailed accounting of their income over the previous calendar year, they are asked how they would allocate, over the next year, a hypothetical windfall equal to one month of their normal income between spending (their MPC), saving, and paying down debt. The SCF includes high-income and high-wealth households often missing from other data sources, meaning that MPCs can be evaluated across the entire income and wealth distribution, including, importantly, at the top. The breadth of the SCF also enables heterogeneity analysis across household types emphasized in the literature, including those varying in liquidity, income uncertainty, and financial literacy. This note previews key results that will be expanded upon in a subsequent working paper.

On average, households spend 22 percent of this hypothetical windfall, save 47 percent, and use 30 percent to pay down debt. The estimated spending response of 22 percent falls well within, though toward the lower end of, the broad range of MPC estimates in the empirical literature. MPCs decline gradually over much of both the income and wealth distributions (moving from around 25 percent to 20 percent) before ticking down sharply at the top of both distributions.2 As a result, relative to other households, households in the top 1 percent of the income and wealth distributions have substantially lower MPCs—about 14 percent and 15 percent, respectively.3 In addition, MPCs are higher for households with less liquidity, for households with greater income uncertainty, and for less-financially knowledgeable households, in line with theoretical predictions from standard models.

Windfall question in the 2025 SCF

The SCF is a triennial cross-sectional survey that has been conducted in its current form since 1989, capturing detailed information on household income, wealth, demographics, and many other household financial characteristics and attitudes. Notably, it oversamples wealthy households to capture the full distribution of income and wealth.4

We, along with other staff working on the 2025 SCF, introduced a new hypothetical windfall question that allows us to measure a household's MPC.5 Specifically, a respondent is asked:

Imagine you unexpectedly receive a sum of money equal to one month of your family's normal annual income. Thinking over the next 12 months, please indicate the percent of this money that you would save, the percent that you would spend, and the percent that you would use to pay down debts.6

Four features of this question are relevant for interpretation, particularly when placing our estimate within the empirical literature.

First, the question elicits responses to a hypothetical windfall rather than an observed transfer, though there is evidence that hypothetical responses align fairly well with real-world behavior.7

Second, the windfall is defined relative to normal annual income.8 Holding constant the share of a household's cash flow that's at stake, rather than fixing the dollar amount, ensures that the relative size of the shock is uniform across respondents.9 Scaling by normal income, as opposed to income in a given calendar year, removes transitory income fluctuations from this baseline. The windfall question appears shortly after respondents are asked to characterize normal annual income, so this concept is both meaningful to and fresh in the minds of respondents. Based on households' normal income, the median implied windfall is $7,000, and the mean implied windfall is $11,800.

Third, debt repayment is offered as an explicit third choice for allocating the windfall alongside spending and saving. Although economists classify debt reduction as saving, households may consider it an outlay and lump it together with spending. Delineating it explicitly reduces ambiguity, preventing MPCs from being artificially inflated.

Fourth, the question asks about allocations over a twelve-month horizon to allow households a broad time frame to respond to the shock and to align with reference periods elsewhere in the survey. Spending responses likely build over time, such that our MPCs would expectedly be larger than those measured over shorter horizons.

Overall spending responses

On average, households in the 2025 SCF would spend 22 percent of a one-month windfall of income within the next year, save 47 percent into assets, and use 30 percent to pay down debt (Figure 1). Underneath these averages, responses are quite varied but bunch heavily at round numbers (Figure 2). Roughly 47 percent of households would not spend any of the windfall, and most of the remaining households would spend between 20 and 35 percent of it.10

Notably, only a small share of households—around 4 percent—would spend all of the windfall, which could partly reflect its large size (one month of a household's normal income). Even the group with the smallest implied windfalls—households in the bottom decile of earners—are basing their responses on $1,500, on average; for context, the maximum Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act stimulus payment was $1,200 for single filers and $2,400 for joint filers.11

Due to the importance of the question, many empirical studies are devoted to recovering MPCs, producing a wide range of estimates generally falling between 0.1 and 0.5. Much of the literature recovers MPCs indirectly, either through natural experiments—such as tax rebates, stimulus payments, lottery winnings, or randomized cash transfers—or randomized controlled trials (e.g., Johnson, Parker, and Souleles, 2006; Fagereng, Holm, and Natvik, 2021; Bartik, Rhodes, Broockman, Krause, Miller, and Vivalt, 2024).12 In all of these approaches, the resulting estimates are setting-specific and may not generalize to the behavior of households in other settings or those unexposed to the shock being studied. Another approach, which has gained traction in recent years and which we leverage here, elicits MPCs within surveys using hypothetical scenarios (e.g., Japelli and Pistaferri, 2014; Christelis, Georgarakos, Japelli, Pistaferri, and van Rooij, 2019; Coibion, Gorodnichenko, and Weber, 2020; Drechsler, Fessler, and Lindner, 2020; Koşar and Melcangi, 2025). To the extent hypothetical responses mirror real-world choices (which existing evidence supports, as noted above), these estimates are generated over wider populations, though they might still be sensitive to sample composition and question framing, particularly with respect to the features noted above. The estimates from hypothetical scenarios also vary quite a bit, with several clustering near 0.35-0.4 and others falling on the lower end near 0.15-0.2. Broadly, our estimated MPC of 0.22 falls toward the lower end of the literature, but it is notably close to consensus estimates from the 2001 and 2008 stimulus payments as well as the directly elicited average MPC over U.S. households in Koşar and Melcangi (2025).13

MPC heterogeneity across households

A major advantage of eliciting MPCs within the SCF is that it allows us to study variation across households of different types, which is relevant for policy design as well as testing theoretical models. This section previews MPC heterogeneity across key dimensions emphasized by the literature—income, wealth, liquidity, income uncertainty, and financial knowledgeability—presenting simple comparisons along each dimension. These initial cuts do not isolate specific dimensions from other relevant factors and should not be interpreted as such.

Income and wealth
The left panel of Figure 3 shows how responses vary over the normal income distribution, which, relative to sorting by a single year of income, ranks households according to a more stable income position. In general, the share of the windfall that households spend is lower than the share they save and declines gradually with income for much of the distribution, dropping off more notably at the top.14 MPCs peak at 28 percent in the bottom decile and reach their lowest point of 14 percent in the top 1 percent. The saved share of the windfall is the largest of the three options across all income groups, but this share is relatively flat over the bottom two-thirds of the distribution—hovering between 41 and 48 percent of the windfall—and then rises dramatically from there, reaching 67 percent in the 95–99th percentile and 78 percent for the top percent. The share applied to deleveraging essentially coincides with the distribution of household debt in the SCF, rising gradually over the bottom two-thirds of the distribution but declining sharply from there, falling below 10 percent for the top percent of earners.

Figure 3. Mean allocation by income and wealth group

Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026).

Accessible version

Allocations across the wealth distribution are similar in magnitude to income, though sorting by wealth concentrates net debtors at the bottom and net savers at the top more aggressively than sorting by income (right panel). MPCs are little changed over the bottom two deciles of wealth (rather than edging down) and drop more sharply at the very top of the distribution. Across the remainder of the distribution, the decline in MPCs is relatively similar for wealth and income.

Altogether, the SCF reveals that average MPCs decline gradually with both income and wealth—from around 25 percent to 20 percent—before dropping off in the upper segments. Average MPCs among households in the top percent of the income and wealth distributions are about 14 percent and 15 percent, respectively. While notably lower than the rest of the distribution, removing these households (a group uniquely captured by the SCF) leaves the aggregate average MPC virtually unchanged; thus, their inclusion does not affect the placement of our estimate with respect to other estimates in the literature. Shifting focus to the bottom of the distribution, the share of the windfall applied to deleveraging is perhaps surprisingly high in light of their presumably high immediate spending needs, which is consistent with these households facing competing demands for limited resources. Reflecting these distributional patterns, the remaining comparisons in this note are based on regression-adjusted MPC estimates that hold (log) normal income constant.

Liquidity
Many leading theories in the literature posit liquidity as a key determinant of MPCs. Standard saving models assume that households draw on liquid assets to buffer against shocks, making their spending relatively insensitive to transitory income changes. Conversely, spending among households with limited liquid holdings ("hand-to-mouth households") is highly sensitive to such changes. Because of its comprehensive balance sheet detail, the SCF is uniquely well-positioned to examine whether MPCs behave according to these models.

Following the literature, we characterize a household's liquidity according to the number of months of normal income held in liquid assets, classifying households as "hand-to-mouth" if they hold less than one-half month of normal income in such assets (e.g., Kaplan and Violante, 2014).15 Hand-to-mouth households spend 22.9 percent of their windfall, compared with 20.3 percent among households with more liquidity (Figure 4), which is directionally consistent with theoretical predictions but somewhat smaller than one might expect.16

Figure 4. Conditional MPC by hand-to-mouth status

Note: Figure plots the conditional marginal propensity to consume (MPC) based on whether a household does or does not have one-half month of normal income in liquid assets (“not hand-to-mouth” or “hand-to-mouth,” respectively), adjusting for normal income.

Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026).

Accessible version

A household's total wealth is likely particularly material to how sensitive their spending is to their liquid wealth position. Thus, we estimate slightly more elaborate regression-adjusted MPCs by hand-to-mouth status, allowing the relationship between hand-to-mouth status and MPCs to vary according to whether the household is low or higher wealth.17 Households whose wealth is below the 30th percentile of the wealth distribution are considered low wealth.

Figure 5 displays the resulting differences by hand-to-mouth status (within panels) and wealth group (across panels). Comparing the side-by-side bars in each panel, differences between hand-to-mouth and non-hand-to-mouth households remain substantial. Across panels, hand-to-mouth status generates larger MPC differentials among lower-wealth households, but notably, differences persist among higher-wealth households who hold most of their assets in illiquid forms. Specifically, among low-wealth households, hand-to-mouth status increases the spending response by 2.9 percentage points relative to non-hand-to-mouth households, compared with a 1.8 percentage point increase among higher-wealth households. These results are consistent with liquidity constraints among "wealthy hand-to-mouth" households binding at higher wealth levels than they do for poor hand-to-mouth households. While our broader results suggest liquidity is a relevant factor in aggregate macroeconomic dynamics (Kaplan, Violante, and Weidner, 2014), the MPC among hand-to-mouth households is smaller than what models generally imply. Nonetheless, our results are quite in line with some estimates from the empirical literature using actual shocks. For example, recent work by Boehm, Fize, and Jaravel (2025) runs a randomized controlled trial and finds average MPCs of 0.23, very close to our baseline estimates. Their study, like ours, recovers higher MPCs among liquidity constrained households with differences smaller than is implied by theoretical models.

Figure 5. Conditional MPC by hand-to-mouth status and wealth group

Note: Figure plots the conditional marginal propensity to consume (MPC) based on whether a household does or does not have one-half month of normal income in liquid assets (“not hand-to-mouth” or “hand-to-mouth,” respectively) and whether a household’s wealth is below the 30th percentile of the household wealth distribution (“low-wealth”). Conditional MPCs are obtained by regressing MPC on hand-to-mouth status, low wealth status, log normal income, log wealth, and the interaction of hand-to-mouth status with low-wealth status. The key from top to bottom identifies bars within each wealth group in order from left to right.

Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026).

Accessible version

Beyond asset holdings, we can also examine variation over households differing in liquidity using a qualitative question regarding budget shortfalls over the past year, which provides a more dynamic view of whether households are operating at their budget constraint. Specifically, households are asked whether their spending exceeded, matched, or fell below their income. Households operating at (or beyond) their budget constraint over the past year would spend 21.6 percent of a windfall, compared with 19.7 percent among those operating within their budget constraint (Figure 6).

Figure 6. Conditional MPC by whether a household spent within its budget constraint last year

Note: Figure plots the conditional marginal propensity to consume (MPC) based on whether a household’s spending was below its income last year (“below budget constraint”) or a household’s spending exceeded or matched its income last year (“at or above budget constraint”), adjusting for normal income.

Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026).

Accessible version

Income uncertainty and financial literacy
Beyond economic capacity and liquidity, MPCs might reflect both a household's perceived budgetary risk and its capacity to optimize over complex choices.

Figure 7 evaluates differences by perceived budgetary risk through the lens of precautionary motives based on whether households have a good idea of what their income will be in the coming year. While households facing greater income uncertainty generally favor saving to defend against future volatility, the arrival of a windfall alters this dynamic. Buffer stock models predict that at a given level of wealth, a "certain" windfall alleviates some of that risk, providing households that have greater income uncertainty a sharper relief in financial anxiety that translates into a higher MPC (Carroll and Kimball, 1996). Consistent with this prediction, holding normal income constant, households who are more uncertain of their income would spend a larger share of their windfall than those who are more certain (21.7 percent versus 20.1 percent, respectively). Indeed, our results directionally align with Koşar and Melcangi (2025), who find that MPCs are increasing and concave in subjective earnings growth uncertainty within the Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE), which holds within quartiles of net liquid wealth. The estimated difference is smaller in our setting, potentially due to the coarseness of our measure.

Figure 7. Conditional MPC by income uncertainty

Note: Figure plots the conditional marginal propensity to consume (MPC) based on whether a household has a good idea of next year’s income (“more certain”) or a household does not have a good idea of next year’s income (“less certain”), adjusting for normal income.

Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026).

Accessible version

Figure 8 evaluates differences in households' underlying capacity to optimize based on their financial knowledgeability (e.g., Lusardi, Michaud, and Mitchell, 2017). In a basic intertemporal framework, financially knowledgeable households can better optimize over time and would generally save more of their windfall. (Still, a higher MPC among less financially knowledgeable households does not necessarily imply suboptimal behavior.) Respondents that answer all three financial literacy questions in the SCF correctly—constituting roughly half of households—are classified as "more financially knowledgeable." The MPC among such households is lower than less knowledgeable ones—19.9 percent versus 21.4 percent, respectively—consistent with this framework.18

Figure 8. Conditional MPC by financial knowledgeability

Note: Figure plots the conditional marginal propensity to consume (MPC) based on whether a household answered all three financial literacy questions in the SCF correctly (“more financially knowledgeable”) or a household answered any of the three financial literacy questions incorrectly (“less financially knowledgeable”), adjusting for normal income.

Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026).

Accessible version

Conclusion

The new SCF question provides a novel insight into MPCs across the distribution of households in the United States. The survey captures MPCs across the full breadth of income and wealth in the country and also provides detailed information about households that allow us to understand how MPCs may vary across household characteristics.

Measuring MPCs inside the SCF has broader value, as many quantitative macroeconomic models are calibrated to income and wealth distributions taken from the survey. Having an internal measure of MPCs (or of spending levels, see the companion note: Aladangady, Bricker, Chang, Goodman, and Li, 2026b) allows researchers to discipline the joint distribution of spending responses and balance sheets within a single dataset rather than combining moments across surveys with different sampling frames and different wealth concepts.

Finally, the survey—which has been continuously run in its current form since 1989—will provide a means to track changes in household spending behavior in the future. Insights into the distribution of MPCs will provide a dynamic view of how households manage shocks over time and across different points in the business cycle.

Figure A1 in the appendix shows MPC estimates from a group of selected studies, breaking out estimates for studies that use a hypothetical windfall versus not and showing over what time horizon the studies estimate their MPCs over. The MPC estimate of 0.22 in the 2025 SCF is consistent with retrospective surveys of stimulus, such as Sahm, Shapiro, and Slemrod (2012) and Shapiro and Slemrod (2003), who find 21.8 percent of households would "mostly spend" their stimulus. Difference-in-differences estimates from Johnson, Parker and, Souleles (2006) range from 0.2 to a high upper-bound of 0.4, but more modern difference-in-differences estimates in Orchard, Ramey, and Wieland (2025), which they combine with macro counterfactuals, place estimates on the lower end of this range. Among survey-based estimates, ours is closest to Koşar and Melcangi (2025) who use a similar question in the Survey of Consumer Expectations, but somewhat lower than 1-year horizon estimates by Colarieti, Mei, and Stantcheva (2024) or European studies (Japelli and Pistaferri, 2014 and 2020; Drechsler, Fessler, Lindner, 2020). 14. This gradient over income is consistent with most of the literature. Jappelli and Pistaferri (2014, 2020), Johnson, Parker, and Souleles (2006), Coibion, Gorodnichenko, and Weber (2020), and Christelis, Georgarakos, Jappelli, Pistaferri, and van Rooij (2019) all find larger responses lower down the distribution, although Shapiro and Slemrod (2003), Sahm, Shapiro, and Slemrod (2012), and Fuster, Kaplan, and Zafar (2021) do not. Several of those studies use fixed-dollar windfalls whose economic significance falls as income rises, which may flatten the measured gradient. A notable exception is Kueng (2018), who finds MPCs remain high for higher income households, which is attributed to higher income households having lower welfare losses from small "mistakes" from optimal spending. Welcome back to Market Matters, October edition.
It been about 2 months since we had the US Treasury/Bessent announcement with respect long end bond liquidity support, which begin September 9th. Since then, yields have continued marching higher, with the 10Y surging through 5% to levels last seen in 2007. This was compounded by the Fed’s decision to increase the target rate by 25bps at the last FOMC meeting.
The Iran War continues to be a thorn in the side of markets, specifically oil. Oil prices have resumed their upward trajectory, continuing to put pressure on governments and markets alike.
Gold has sold off and given up most of it’s gains from the last few months.
Equities remain resilient and continue grinding towards all time highs, even as breadth continues to narrow.
Crypto markets have shown a patch of relative strength with BTC almost pushing into the $90K region. We have also seen a resurgence in overall risk appetite among crypto participants since the August US Treasury announcement. Over the last few weeks, however, crypto markets and risk appetite appear to be waning.
In this month’s episode, we highlight our updated Delphi Unified Macro Regime Model, which no incorporates drivers of liquidity, growth, and inflation while taking into account positioning. We lay out the backdrop as we move into year end. We then dive deeper into crypto markets to look under the hood and discuss crypto’s recent weakness and what it means going forward.
Are we back? Is there still room to run? Or is the party ending? You wont want to miss this month’s episode.
We will see you again in a month to recap the November Midterm Election results and what that means for our views as we close out the year!

articles.title: Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

October 16, 2026
Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States
Katie Brinkman, Christine Dobridge, Tim Dore, Simon Glossner, Elizabeth Holmquist, Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek, and Irina Stefanescu1
Section 1: Introduction

Over the past decade, private credit has played an increasingly important role in providing funding to middle-market businesses. While there are several definitions of private credit, here we define it as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds rather than by traditional financial intermediaries such as banks.

Until now, private credit loans and the financial vehicles that originate them have not been separately identified in the Financial Accounts of the United States, largely due to the private nature of these transactions and limited available data. We now address this gap using confidential SEC Form PF data along with other data sources to compile balance sheets for private debt funds and other private credit vehicles.

Beginning with the September 2026 release, we have integrated private credit into the Financial Accounts by adding new sectors for private credit vehicles and new financial instrument tables for private credit loans and shares of private debt funds.2 Integrating private credit into the comprehensive Financial Accounts framework—rather than producing standalone tables—helps users to trace the full intermediation chain from investors through private credit vehicles to borrowers, facilitating analysis of its effects on business leverage and financial stability.

This note explains how we have incorporated private credit into the Financial Accounts and discusses implications for key balance sheet measures for businesses and households. Section 2 provides a brief overview of the U.S. private credit market. Section 3 reviews the previous treatment of private credit in the Financial Accounts. Section 4 describes the integration approach, including data sources and methodology for each private credit vehicle and new financial instrument. Section 5 discusses implications for nonfinancial business leverage and household net worth. Section 6 concludes.

Section 2: Background

The private credit market has grown rapidly over the past decade. As shown in Figure 1, assets under management in private credit vehicles have grown from approximately $350 billion in 2012 to over $2.6 trillion as of 2025:Q4, with outstanding private credit loans to U.S. businesses totaling approximately $1.5 trillion.

Figure 1. Assets of Private Credit Vehicles and Private Credit Loans to U.S. Borrowers3

Note: Data as of Q4 each year. The key identifies bars in order from top to bottom.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, SEC Form PF.

Accessible version

Private credit is primarily provided through private debt (PD) funds and business development companies (BDCs), though private credit provided through middle-market collateralized loan obligations (MM CLOs) and interval and tender offer funds has also grown substantially in recent years.4 Most borrowers are middle-market nonfinancial firms seeking funding for acquisitions, growth capital, or refinancing. Given the scale and growth of private credit, its integration into the Financial Accounts is essential for comprehensive measurement of credit flows to nonfinancial businesses and for understanding the role of private credit in the financial system.

Section 3: Previous Treatment in the Financial Accounts

Prior to the September 2026 release, most private credit loans from domestically domiciled private credit vehicles were included as liabilities on nonfinancial corporate business balance sheets but were not identified as debt instruments, and the intermediation activities of private credit vehicles were largely excluded from the Financial Accounts. This section describes the previous treatment of private credit and explains why integrating these vehicles has effects that extend beyond the private credit sectors themselves.

The previous treatment of private credit vehicles in the Financial Accounts varied depending on whether the originating vehicle was domiciled in the United States or abroad. We already captured foreign private funds lending to U.S. businesses in the Rest of the World (ROW) sector. Therefore, we only added U.S.-based private credit vehicles as new sectors in the Financial Accounts to complete the picture.

U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles
U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles were not identified as separate sectors in the Financial Accounts. As a result, their balance sheet assets and liabilities were either missing entirely or incorrectly attributed to other sectors.

For the most part, loans originated by U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles were not recorded as loan assets of a financial sector, however, the corresponding loan liabilities of U.S. businesses, were not entirely absent.5 Private credit loans to nonfinancial corporate businesses were generally recorded as miscellaneous liabilities, while loans to noncorporate businesses were generally classified as depository institution loans. As a result, the previous treatment obscured the composition of business borrowing and understated measures of nonfinancial business debt captured by the Financial Accounts' debt instruments.

Depository institution loans issued to U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles were incorrectly attributed to foreign nondepository financial institutions. In addition, debt securities issued by business development companies (BDCs) and U.S.-domiciled MM CLOs were not previously recorded and therefore represent additions to financial sector debt outstanding in the Financial Accounts.

Similarly, equity shares issued by U.S.-domiciled private debt funds, closely held BDCs, interval funds, and tender offer funds were previously omitted from the Financial Accounts. Equity issued by publicly listed BDCs, by contrast, was already included in corporate equity issues but was attributed to the other financial business sector.

Because the Financial Accounts comprise an integrated set of sectoral balance sheets, the omission of U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles also affected the measurement of assets and liabilities in other sectors. These effects are particularly important for the household sector, for which many asset holdings are calculated residually.6 For example, when private credit vehicles hold instruments that are also held directly by households—such as checkable deposits and corporate equities—the absence of private credit vehicles from the accounts caused some of these assets to be residually attributed to households, thereby overstating measured household assets and net worth. Conversely, household net worth was understated by the omission of directly held equity shares in private debt funds, closely held BDCs, interval funds, and tender offer funds. Incorporating private credit vehicles therefore both reallocates existing financial assets and liabilities across sectors and introduces instruments that were previously absent from the Financial Accounts.

Foreign-domiciled private credit vehicles
Foreign-domiciled private debt funds and middle-market CLOs have not been introduced as separate sectors in the Financial Accounts because their transactions and positions with U.S. residents were already captured in the ROW sector. In particular, private credit loans extended by foreign-domiciled vehicles to U.S. businesses were recorded as foreign loans to U.S. corporate businesses within the "other loans and advances" instrument category but are now separately identified. Similarly, U.S. financial assets held by foreign private credit vehicles are recorded as ROW assets, with holdings of private debt fund shares now separately identified. Private credit loans extended to foreign businesses by domestic private credit vehicles are a new addition to rest of the world loan liabilities. Equity issued by foreign private credit vehicles and held by U.S. residents is included among U.S. holdings of foreign corporate equities, with private debt fund shares now shown separately.

Section 4: Integration of Private Credit into the Financial Accounts

This section describes how we integrate private credit into the Financial Accounts framework. We begin with an overall summary of the private credit market followed by a description of each new sector and financial instrument added to the accounts.

4.1 Summary of Private Credit Market
Table 1 provides a snapshot of balance sheet assets and liabilities for all vehicles that make up the U.S. private credit market. As of the end of 2025, U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles had assets under management of $1.9 trillion. At the same time, there were $1.5 trillion in private credit loans extended to U.S. businesses, including $335 billion from foreign-domiciled funds. Private debt funds and BDCs have the largest shares of the market, with each holding just under half of total private credit loans outstanding. These private credit vehicles also hold substantial amounts of corporate equity in their portfolios, including equity stakes taken in connection with lending arrangements.

U.S. private credit vehicles are primarily funded through equity issuance ($1.1 trillion), although they also access funding though bank loans ($349 billion), and debt securities ($135 billion). Foreign-domiciled private debt funds also provide a substantial share of credit in the market. We estimate that the portfolios and capital structures of these foreign funds are similar to those of U.S.-domiciled private debt funds.

As noted in Section 3, we have added U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles to the Financial Accounts. The following subsections describe each new sector and the associated financial instruments.

4.2 New Financial Sectors
Private debt funds: tables S.124.8.t and S124.8.s
Private debt funds are privately offered, closed-end investment vehicles that are typically organized as limited partnerships and managed by an affiliated investment adviser. These funds are "private funds" and thus exempted from the regulations of the 1940 Investment Act. PD funds cover different private credit strategies with various mandates and risk profiles, including direct lending, mezzanine and junior capital, distressed and special situations, asset-based and specialty finance, private real estate debt, and infrastructure debt. Capital is raised through commitments from qualified investors—such as pension funds and insurance companies—and drawn over time through capital calls to fund loan originations and acquisitions. Investors do not typically have the right to redeem fund shares before the termination of the fund.

Our primary data source for private debt funds is confidential SEC Form PF, which provides detailed balance sheet information for private funds. These Form PF data translate well into the Financial Accounts structure, as funds report levels of assets and liabilities, which we use for the balance sheet table, as well as holders of private fund shares, which we use for the instrument table.7

However, there are some measurement challenges associated with compiling these balance sheets. First, PD funds are not explicitly identified in Form PF data, so to classify funds as private debt funds, we use signals from fund strategies, fund names, and classifications that are provided in other databases, including Preqin, PitchBook, and Moody's. We merge Form PF data with fund-level information from these sources to construct comprehensive sector-level balance sheets.

Second, not all funds file Form PF on a quarterly basis; some file only annually and provide more limited information. For funds that file quarterly, we are able to estimate quarterly balance sheets. For funds that file only annually, we impute annual balance sheet data using portfolio shares from quarterly filers with similar investment strategies, then interpolate quarterly values between the annual estimates.8

The Z.1 includes data on transactions and stocks for U.S. private debt funds in tables S.124.8.t and S.124.8.s (see Table 2). U.S-domiciled private debt fund AUM have grown over time, from $180 billion in 2012 to about $940 billion as of 2025:Q4.9 Private credit loans account for about 60 percent of assets, and corporate equities account for about 18 percent.10

These shares are added as a new financial instrument "private debt fund shares" in the Financial Accounts and are shown in table F522.3.s of the release, discussed in more detail in Section 4.3.

Business development companies (BDCs): tables S.124.5.t and S.124.5.s
Business development companies are closed-end investment companies created by Congress in 1980 to channel capital to small and mid-sized U.S. businesses. BDCs elect to be regulated under Section 2(a)(48) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 and must invest at least 70 percent of their total assets in eligible portfolio companies—primarily domestic unlisted companies or certain small-cap companies. Unlike traditional investment companies, BDCs can employ substantially higher leverage, with statutory limits allowing up to 2:1 debt-to-equity ratios.

BDCs can be structured as publicly traded companies (with shares listed on exchanges), public non-traded companies (offering shares directly to investors meeting certain suitability criteria with periodic redemptions), or private companies (offering securities to either accredited or qualified investors through private placements, similar to private debt funds). All three types of BDCs are included in the Financial Accounts.

Our primary data source is BDC Collateral, a proprietary financial analytics platform and data aggregator developed by LSEG LPC. The platform extracts data from BDCs' 10-Qs and 10-Ks, which we use to estimate equity investments, private credit loans, syndicated loans, cash positions, and miscellaneous assets. The dataset includes both cost and fair value for BDCs' investments, enabling us to decompose changes in asset levels into transactions and revaluations. The BDC table includes memo items showing the breakdown of assets across the three BDC types.

As shown on table S.124.5.s (see Table 3), BDCs have AUM of about $570 billion as of 2025:Q4, up from less than $40 billion in 2012 (see Figure 1). Private credit loans account for 80 percent of assets, while syndicated loans and corporate equities each account for about 7 percent.

On the liability side, we distinguish between debt securities, bank loans, and miscellaneous liabilities. Bank loans (line 11) account for about 2/3 of the total, while debt securities (line 10) account for most of the remainder.

BDCs also issue public and private equity that is classified in the Financial Accounts as corporate equity and included on the corporate equity financial instrument table F51.1.s. Equity shares issued by BDCs (line 13) were valued at $287 billion in 2025:Q4.

Interval funds and tender offer funds: tables S124.6.s and S124.6.t
Interval funds and tender offer funds are closed-end investment vehicles designed to invest in illiquid asset classes (e.g., private credit) while providing investors with limited, periodic liquidity through scheduled repurchase mechanisms. The fundamental distinction between the two structures lies in the mandatory versus discretionary nature of their repurchase obligations, with interval funds being required to redeem a certain number of shares at specified intervals while tender offer funds have more discretion over the timing, frequency, and offer size.

Registered interval and tender offer funds are regulated under the 1940 Act. Regulatory requirements include enhanced disclosure through Form N-2 registration statements and Form N-PORT reporting of portfolio holdings, adherence to leverage limitations, and independent board oversight. We use data from Morningstar and SEC Form N-PORT to construct the balance sheet.11

Balance sheet data for interval and tender offer funds appear in table S124.6.s (see Table 4), which shows combined assets of $292 billion as of 2025:Q4, up from $100 billion in 2021 (the beginning of our series). Together, private credit loans and syndicated loans (lines 7 and 8) account for nearly 30 percent of assets, while corporate equities (line 9) account for 44 percent.

Middle-market CLOs: Added to tables S125s1.3.s and S125s1.3.t
Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) are financial vehicles that issue securities backed by pools of loans. Middle-market (MM) CLOs are backed specifically by loans to middle-market companies. The loans underlying MM CLOs are often originated by direct lenders such as PD funds, BDCs, and asset managers affiliated with life insurers. These lenders, or their affiliates, also commonly serve as the CLO managers.

To estimate the outstanding value of private credit loans held by MM CLOs, we use data from Moody's Analytics Inc., Global CLO database, which includes information on CLO assets, performance of CLO tranches, and attributes of the underlying loans and loan obligors.12 We identify MM CLOs by filtering for deals and tranches identified as small and middle-market CLOs that are denominated in U.S. dollars and are backed by loans to U.S. businesses. We then calculate total quarterly MM CLO assets under management (AUM) using data on the outstanding deal value of all CLO tranches meeting these criteria.

Unlike the other private credit vehicles described above, MM CLOs are not added as a new sector but are instead incorporated into the existing issuers of asset-backed securities (ABS) sector, which captures private-label securitization activity collateralized by a variety of financial assets, most notably mortgages and syndicated loans. To do this, we added private credit loans held by U.S.-domiciled MM CLOs to the asset side of the ABS balance sheet and the same amount of corporate bonds to the liability side (shown in lines 7 and 18 of table S125s1.3.s, see Table 5). In 2025:Q4, domestic MM CLOs held $54 billion in private credit loans. MM CLOs domiciled abroad (primarily in the Cayman Islands) are included in the ROW sector.

4.3 New Financial Instruments
The private credit integration introduces two new financial instruments into the Financial Accounts: private credit loans (the loans originated by private credit vehicles) and shares of private debt funds (ownership stakes in private debt funds).

Private credit loans: table F4.4.s
As noted in the introduction, private credit loans are defined here as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds. This definition encompasses corporate direct lending, asset-based and specialty finance, real estate debt, infrastructure debt, and other privately negotiated loans. It therefore does not depend on the identity of the borrower, the purpose of the loan, or the assets supporting repayment. These loans span the full range of seniority levels: some are senior secured with first claim on collateral, others are unsecured or junior claims that absorb losses earlier but expect to earn higher returns, and still others are hybrid instruments blending debt and equity characteristics.

Private credit loans originated by all private credit vehicles are reported on a new financial instrument table. This table shows both the holders (lenders) and issuers (borrowers) of the loans, providing a complete picture of U.S. private credit market activity.

As of 2025:Q4, total private credit loans outstanding across all vehicles amounted to approximately $1.5 trillion. U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles—primarily PD funds and BDCs—account for about $1 trillion, or roughly two-thirds of the total, while foreign-domiciled vehicles (mainly PD funds) account for $376 billion in loans to U.S. businesses (see Table 6).

Section 5. Effects on Financial Accounts Measures of Debt, Leverage, and Household Wealth

Nonfinancial business debt and leverage
This section examines how adding private credit loans to the Financial Accounts affects measures of aggregate nonfinancial business debt and leverage. Private credit now makes up a substantial fraction of total business debt. As shown in Table 8, which presents components of total debt of the nonfinancial business sector as of 2025:Q4, private credit loans accounted for about 6 percent of total business debt, up from around one percent in 2012 (Figure 4).

Debt positions of nonfinancial businesses have been identified as important metrics of financial health and systemic financial risk. Measures of nonfinancial leverage based on Financial Accounts data are also used to evaluate financial stability risks in the Federal Reserve's biannual Financial Stability Report.13 Prior to incorporating private credit loans as a component of debt in the Financial Accounts, aggregate debt positions of nonfinancial businesses were understated. It is useful, therefore, to evaluate whether debt trends are meaningfully different with the inclusion of private credit in aggregate measures of U.S. business debt.

Despite the strong growth in private credit loans in the U.S. economy since 2018, the addition of private credit loans to the Financial Accounts does not substantially change the trends in business debt overall. Panel A of Figure 5 presents the ratio of nonfinancial business debt-to-GDP with and without private credit loans included in the measure of debt. The debt-to-GDP ratio is around 5 percentage points higher in recent years when private credit is included, but the ratio remains below the median as measured since 2012 and has been on a declining trend since 2020. Panel B of Figure 5 shows debt growth with and without private credit included in the measure of total business debt. Annual debt growth since 2018 is somewhat higher when private credit is incorporated but the trend is not substantially different.

Figure 5. Debt Trends for the Nonfinancial Business Sector, with and without Private Credit Loans

Household net worth
The integration of private credit also directly and indirectly affects measures of household net worth. As discussed in Section 3, the previous treatment of private credit led to the misattribution (directly or indirectly) of certain financial assets on the household balance sheet. The integration of private credit vehicles and instruments results in more accurate measurement of household balance sheets. Additionally, we now show households' direct exposures to private credit through investment in private debt fund shares as well as their indirect exposures through important household assets such as pension entitlements.

Section 6. Conclusion

Beginning with the September 2026 release, the Financial Accounts of the United States fully integrate private credit by adding new sectors for private credit vehicles and new financial instrument tables for private credit loans and shares of private debt funds. Using confidential SEC Form PF data along with other sources, we construct comprehensive balance sheets for approximately $1.1 trillion in private credit loan activity by U.S.-domiciled vehicles. The integration helps users track the intermediation chain from investors through private credit vehicles to borrowers, with detailed data available on private credit loans across sectors.14

This integration substantially improves measurement of nonfinancial business leverage and provides more accurate measurement of household balance sheets and exposures to private credit markets. The comprehensive framework facilitates analysis of the connections between private credit and the broader financial system, enhancing the Financial Accounts' utility for assessing financial stability risks. For more detail on the institutional features of private credit vehicles and the growing role of private credit in financial markets, see the forthcoming companion FEDS note "U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets." For complete methodological details on the construction of these series, see the Guide to the Financial Accounts of the United States.

INTERNATIONAL CORPORATE BANKING

3 trends driving new capital flows to Lloyd’s of London insurance marketplace

Contributor: Gavin Westmoreland

09 Oct 2026

After a period of lagging behind lighter-regulated markets, new capital and entrants are driving change as Lloyd’s of London marketplace modernises. Growth has been aided by favourable underwriting conditions, but structural changes are also reshaping the market, according to our International Corporate Banking expert, Gavin Westmoreland, Head of UK Insurance.

Key takeaways

Modernisation and underwriting discipline are drawing capital back to Lloyd's of London marketplace
Alternative investors are expanding the pool of insurance capital
More complex capital structures are reshaping syndicates' banking needs

Parsys 2

Double click here to edit Go To Section component

GO TO SECTION

1. Market evolution drives growth 2. New players are invigorating the marketplace 3. Insurance syndicates seek greater treasury efficiency

Parsys 3

1. Market evolution drives growth
The Lloyd’s of London marketplace – which accounts for around 10% of global insurance and reinsurance businessi – has begun a modernisation of the market and placed an increased emphasis on underwriting discipline. It’s a notable change of direction, given that for some years, the marketplace was perceived to be falling behind jurisdictions with lighter-touch regulation and a more agile approach to innovation, technology and bureaucracy.
These efforts appear to be delivering growth and bolstering financial strength. Gross written premium rose to £57.9 billion in 2025 from £55.56 billion a year earlier while return on capital reached 22% according to Lloyd’s FY2025 results. It is important to note benign underwriting conditions and price increases in 2023 and 2024, particularly in the property-catastrophe market, also provided a valuable tailwind.
While Lloyd’s marketplace performance has improved and the market is growing, this has been accompanied by restraint among market participants. In previous market cycles favourable conditions led to a flood of capital that ultimately pushed down prices and created a soft insurance market. However, while considerably softer on particular lines of business compared to the highs of 2023 and 2024, rates through 2025 and into 2026 have still been considered adequate in most classes, although Lloyd’s is laser focused on ensuring that market participants retain underwriting discipline heading into 2027, which it believes is likely to experience a further acceleration in rate reduction.
Not all capital entering the Lloyd’s marketplace is aimed at expanding existing underwriting capacity. Much of it supports the transfer of risk into Lloyd’s or meets rising demand in areas such as cyber, where premiums are growing faster than inflation. These dynamics help balance supply and demand rather than drive prices down.
Although modernisation is welcomed, there is also broad support to retain the characteristics that make Lloyd’s distinctive, including its syndicate model. This model allows diverse underwriting views to coexist and enables the separation of underwriting from capital provision. As a result, third-party investors can access returns without managing underwriters directly, making it easier to scale business and diversify risk.
i. Financial Times, 2025

2. New players are invigorating the marketplace
In recent years, Lloyd’s marketplace has attracted increased interest from both traditional and non-traditional market players, drawn by double-digit returns on capitalii and low correlation with other asset classes.iii After the crises of the 1980s and 1990s, so-called Names – usually high net worth individuals – have returned to the market.
A key innovation supporting this growth has been the second phase of the London Bridge risk transformation platform, which allows institutional capital to enter the marketplace more efficiently and addresses previous tax and structural barriers. Lloyd’s marketplace members and managing agents can use London Bridge and the expanded London Bridge 2 programme to meet their capital and risk management needs by bringing in new sources of funding and reinsurance protection. London Bridge 2 enables the funding of reinsurance contracts through insurance-linked securities, such as catastrophe bonds.
Originally launched in 2021, London Bridge doubled in size to $2.9 billion of deployed capital at the end of 2024, with $2.55 billion committed from institutional investorsv. Notable recent successes include the structure deployed by Blackstone's Syndicate 2478, which underwrites a portion of AIG’s reinsurance portfolio (allowing AIG to cede risk and capital requirements while continuing to write the business).Such structures have often been domiciled in Bermuda in the past, so Syndicate 2478 indicates the potential for London Bridge 2 to win new business.
iii. Lloyd's, 2025
iv. Financial Times, 2025
v Lloyd's, 2025

3. Insurance syndicates seek greater treasury efficiency
While the core banking needs of Lloyd’s syndicates have remained largely consistent, the sophistication and expectations of market participants have grown. Managing Agents are increasingly focused on reducing the costs, with improved treasury efficiency being one route to achieving this. Underwriters and investors are more focused on underwriting performance and underwriting/asset return respectively. Costs are a feature of the market but Managing Agents would implement efficiencies at Syndicate level.
Syndicates typically require a broad suite of treasury services, including cash management, syndicate-level overdrafts or shock loss credit lines, foreign exchange both for regular transactions and larger ‘dealt’ trades and may also require investment management services to enhance returns on assets backing liabilities.
Members, including private equity funds, family offices and other institutional investors, may benefit from gaining additional leverage within their Funds at Lloyd’s (FAL) structure. FAL represents the capital that backs underwriting activity and is held in trust and forms part of Lloyd’s Chain of Security. If a member’s FAL is fully exhausted, policyholders have final recourse to the Lloyd’s Central Fund. FAL is divided into Tier 1 (cash and highly liquid securities) and Tier 2 (less liquid assets). Facilities that help optimise leverage can also be valuable to syndicates in relation to FAL: letters of credit are used to support syndicates in meeting Tier 2 capital requirements. Members may also look to access loan markets and will typically elect to use investment managers to optimise return on capital.
Alternative asset managers who have entered the Lloyd’s market typically provide capital but do not influence underwriting. Their focus is primarily on using insurance liabilities to support their broader asset management strategies with the goal of building a stable – and ideally growing – pool of liabilities that can be invested. In some cases, non-life insurers’ strategies now more closely resemble life insurers, using a barbell strategy of highly liquid, low-yield assets (such as bond and gilts) on one end, and illiquid, higher-yield assets like private credit on the other.

articles.title: A low transaction, stagnant price housing market will continue next year
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

14 Oct 2026

A low transaction, stagnant price housing market will continue next year

The UK housing market faces stagnation with low transactions and flat prices,
while borrowers may see rising mortgage costs ahead. Discover more insights.

Our new home buyer affordability index shows that UK house prices are roughly 11% overvalued based on the affordability of mortgage payments, up from 4% before the conflict between the US and Iran began. This reflects a sharp increase in mortgage interest rates. Other affordability metrics have been stable , but weaker mortgage affordability has been the decisive factor in pushing down mortgage approvals.

Though we think the Bank of England will ultimately tighten policy by less than market pricing implies, it’s likely to be some time before swap rates drop back. We expect wage growth will stay subdued, so mortgage affordability will remain stretched and this will keep residential transactions low in 2027.

There’s no evidence that higher interest rates are increasing levels of financial stress among existing borrowers. A lack of forced sales, less trading up, and low levels of housebuilding will reinforce the downward pressure on transactions. Low supply will also mitigate the impact of subdued demand on house prices, and we expect prices to remain broadly flat in cash terms over the coming year.

Caspian upstream: 5 things to look for in 2024

View Craig Saunders 's full profile

As the war in Iran pushes energy security ever higher on government agendas, importing countries want to diversify their sources of oil and gas. For IOCs and NOCs scanning the globe for upstream investments, resource holding countries are in pole position. Geopolitically stable contenders in the Caspian region include Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. These producers have a great opportunity to collaborate and elevate the region to play a bigger role as a reliable supplier of energy and natural resources.  
Malcolm Forbes-Cable and Ian Simm from our Consulting team have spearheaded WoodMac’s engagement in the region, along with Craig Saunders from Upstream Research and, on occasion, me. They shared their thoughts on the prospects for future regional autonomy.  
Azerbaijan’s strategic position to access global markets  
Azerbaijan not only ranks as a sizeable oil and gas producer in global terms but, importantly, is ahead of the game having invested in critical infrastructure to export its oil and gas from the landlocked Caspian Sea. Its upstream industry, more than a century old, rose to global significance early this millennium with the development of BP’s giant offshore ACG and Shah Deniz projects.  
These fields propelled total production to 1.2 million boe/d by 2010, with 80% of that oil. Output has held this level ever since, and on our forecasts will stay there through to the late 2030s helped by Phase 2 of TotalEnergies’ Absheron gas project which FID’d last month. Gas has become the growth story, comprising about 60% of production in 2026.  
The NOC SOCAR is a significant investor in all upstream projects. The government is also aiming to attract more investment offshore as well as onshore where ExxonMobil has a licence to explore a large unproven shale play. Azerbaijan’s refining capacity is focused on meeting domestic fuel demand.  
The construction of major export pipelines opened the ‘Southern Corridor,’ connecting Azerbaijan’s oil and gas supplies to wider markets beyond the Caspian. The 1.2 million b/d BTC oil pipeline (2005) transports mainly Azerbaijani crude to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan. Even topped up with volumes shipped across the Caspian from Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, BTC is substantially underutilised. The TANAP (2018) and TAP (2020) gas pipelines carry Azerbaijani gas through Georgia and Turkey and on to the European gas network via Greece and Italy.  
New pipeline connectivity – the ‘Middle Corridor’ 
Energy connectivity and diversification of export routes were big themes last week at the KIOGE conference in Almaty, Kazakhstan. A possible East-West ‘Green Corridor’ linking renewable power supply to Azerbaijan via an interconnector across the Caspian Sea was much discussed.  
It is future oil and gas connectivity, however, that could be game changing for the region. NOC KazMunaiGas is the biggest resource holder in Kazakhstan, but the scale of resources has attracted IOC investors for decades. Key players include Chevron, ExxonMobil, Eni, Shell, TotalEnergies, CNPC, Lukoil and Inpex. Kazakhstan currently produces 2.2 million b/d of liquids, with over 1.5 million b/d exported through the CPC pipeline to a port near Novorossiysk on Russia’s Black Sea coast. Flows have, however, been seriously disrupted by attacks on the pipeline and port facilities related to the Russia/Ukraine war. There is potential to lift export volumes by more than 0.2 million b/d if the next phase of the giant Kashagan project goes ahead. 
Turkmenistan’s situation as a substantial gas producer is different. The giant Galkynysh is the second largest gas field in the world, with exports contributing up to a third of the country’s GDP. The exports, 34Bcm/year sold exclusively to China, are well below half of Qatar’s larger North field gas exports in 2025. While the two countries have discussed additional sales there’s been little progress. Turkmenistan needs to cultivate alternative export options if it is to commercialise Galkynysh’s vast reserves. The main gas producers in Turkmenistan are NOC Turkmengaz, CNPC, Petronas and XRG. 
A logical solution for the region is obvious – build new pipelines across the Caspian Sea to link Kazakhstan’s oil and Turkmenistan’s gas to the existing export routes through Azerbaijan to the Mediterranean and European gas network respectively. Filling in the missing links, cross-Caspian oil and gas pipelines, would complete the ‘Middle Corridor,’ a new Silk Road for molecules.  
The Middle Corridor would give Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan the export optionality they seek, allow them to accelerate investment in their resource, and boost the availability of supply and energy security importing countries need. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, would capture valuable tariff revenues, and strengthen its position as a strategic linchpin all along the corridor. 
Realisation of the concept is far from straight forward. Progress awaits answers to big questions, these three among them. How to gain support from multiple governments with varied, individual and vested interests, not only Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan but others not least Russia and China? Is Europe keen to commit to long-term gas contracts? And who finances the large-scale cross-border infrastructure – governments or the oil and gas industry?  
The Caspian – an emerging source of critical minerals 
Beyond oil and gas the Central Asian countries are rich in critical minerals. Efforts to attract foreign investment are ramping up as countries focus on developing their mining and processing industries to capitalise on the current dash for these vital resources. China’s insatiable appetite is an obvious market but the pull from the west has also surged with the recognition of the strategic importance of these resources.

articles.title: View from the markets: A critical earnings season approaches - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

As the third quarter earnings season kicks off, investors are nervous given the recent sharp rise in bond yields, which have so far had only a modest impact on equities. While the MOVE index, which measures expected bond market volatility, has returned to levels last seen with the start of the Iran war, the VIX index of equity volatility is not far from the lows for the year.

The dominance of technology hardware in driving earnings growth and equity price appreciation means that any disappointing announcements from these companies will likely be keenly felt. Expectations are high, with the sector globally forecast to see a doubling of earnings compared to the same quarter a year ago. For emerging markets, it is twice that.

These growth rates are substantially higher than those for other sectors, leading some to see the concentration of earnings growth this quarter as a sign of the market’s fragility. It is true that tech earnings will likely dominate the season. They account for nearly two-thirds of the increase in profits for equities globally, followed by energy stocks at 20% (see Exhibit 1).

The dominance of tech earnings, however, is not inherently bad if the other sectors are themselves generating sufficiently positive growth in profits, even if the absolute increase in profits is far less than for technology. For this quarter, however, that is only partly the case.

The median earnings growth for the remaining sectors (that is, excluding tech and energy) is 7%, which is not particularly high. The materials sector is the one expected to see the strongest growth, but most of the forecasts for the other sectors are comparatively low (see Exhibit 2). If this pattern were to continue into the quarters ahead, one would indeed expect the market to be vulnerable as technology would be practically the sole source of profit expansion.

For 2027, however, the pattern is forecast to be different. Earnings growth for the energy sector turns negative, while it moderates for the tech sector. The growth rate for the remaining sectors rises to 12%, spread more evenly across the sectors. That should be sufficient to support ongoing market appreciation.

Third quarter forecasts

The importance of the tech and energy sectors for earnings is reflected in the third quarter forecasts for country and regional indices. Growth rates for indices with a large share of tech or energy stocks are high, while excluding these sectors results in lower figures. For example, we noted that emerging market tech stocks earnings are expected to increase more than four-fold, but for the remaining sectors the forecast is just 11%. In Europe, the 29% gain expected for the index this quarter is reliant on the energy sector; if we exclude it, the growth rate drops to 17% (which is still good; see exhibit 3).

EM tech volatility

Despite the renewed increase in oil prices over the last week, and the higher-than-expected US CPI (consumer price index) inflation data, Treasury yields have dropped by more than 20 basis points from their recent peak. This has prompted a modest rebound in non-tech equities globally. The tech hardware sector, however, has seen another wave of selling, concentrated in South Korea, as it was last July.

We have always expected above-average volatility in the tech sector because of the newness and significance of the artificial intelligence phenomenon. Price gains have been so large, and earnings expectations so high, that any marginal change in sentiment has a commensurately bigger impact.

We remain positive on the medium-term outlook and see volatility along a rising trend. Nonetheless, the impact of AI investment should continue to broaden to other sectors, notably in the US, allowing for the wider breadth of earnings, as shown in Exhibit 2.

articles.text:
