By Karen Karniol-Tambour

At the Milken Institute's 2026 Global Conference, Co-CIO Karen Karniol-Tambour joined a panel moderated by Stephanie Ruhle of MS NOW on the shifting macro landscape facing investors today. Karen addressed topics central to how investors should be thinking right now, including:Modern mercantilism is a structural, not cyclical, force—every country spending to close its vulnerabilities is inherently inflationary.Portfolio concentration leaves most investors overweight US equities, underweight real assets, and poorly positioned for the environment ahead.The AI capex boom is driving US growth today, with markets still largely living on the buildout phase rather than the adoption phase that follows.Geographic fragmentation is creating distinct investable ecosystems as industrial policy supports national champions, warranting exposure across regions.This content is provided by the Milken Institute and originally appeared as programming during the 2026 Milken Institute Global Conference.Please see important disclosures and other information.

articles.title: A sea change in regulatory investigations and enforcement − speech by David Chaplin
articles.text:
A sea change in regulatory investigations and enforcement − speech by David Chaplin

Given at the 5th Conference on Financial Law and Regulation, University of Leeds School of Law, 24 June 2026

In this speech, David Chaplin, Head of Enforcement and Litigation, examines how behaviour in regulatory investigations is evolving. Drawing on recent PRA and Bank enforcement cases, he discusses a shift towards earlier engagement and candour, and considers how this can support faster, more efficient enforcement while maintaining appropriate and effective regulatory outcomes.

Speech
It is a real pleasure to be in Leeds for the Fifth Conference on Financial Law and Regulation.
Leeds is an important base for the Bank of England as we build a stronger national presence and deepen our engagement with institutions, practitioners and scholars across the UK. The Bank first opened a Leeds branch in 1827,footnote [1] and our growing presence here reflects a commitment: not only to operate from different locations, but to engage across the country with the professional and intellectual communities that shape our financial system.
It is therefore particularly fitting to be here at the University of Leeds, contributing to a conference that brings together legal, regulatory and academic perspectives on some of the most challenging questions facing financial law and regulation today.
Some of these questions arise in the context of investigations and enforcement. And that’s what I am going to talk about.
Introduction
For a long time, there was a relatively settled picture of what a regulatory enforcement investigation looks like: how it begins, how it proceeds, and when (where appropriate) responsibility for regulatory breaches is acknowledged and action taken. That model has served an important purpose, and in many cases, it continues to do so.
What I want to discuss today though is how, in a growing number of PRA and Bank enforcement cases, that familiar pattern is changing. I’ll explore how that change has come about, what it entails, and why we think it matters.
Recently, we have seen a clear and consistent shift in how the subjects of our investigations are engaging with us. This is a change we have championed and will continue to encourage because of the benefits it brings for all concerned.
What is that trend? Put simply, it is that subjects of investigations are engaging with us earlier in the investigations and enforcement process and proactively identifying, acknowledging and remediating breaches.
This is not something isolated to a small number of cases. It is not behaviour confined to exceptional or isolated circumstances. Rather, what we are seeing is a sustained change in approach, which we see as having the potential to become the new default: a shift in how responsibility and candour are being understood and acted upon in regulatory enforcement.
We believe this represents a genuine sea change in how a growing number of enforcement cases are now being approached.
The focus here is not on the launch of a new policy, but on how a policy we have already introduced is playing out in practice and the impact it is having on behaviour in live enforcement cases.
Our remit
As a reminder, the PRA is responsible for the supervision of approximately 1,300 banks, building societies, credit unions, insurers and major investment firms. In addition to this, the Bank of England has broader regulatory responsibilities, including the supervision of certain financial market infrastructures in the UK.
In the enforcement space, we have powers to discipline firms, including through financial sanctions, public censures and the temporary suspension of permissions. We also continue to pursue individual accountability and to publish outcomes in appropriate cases, including, where necessary, prohibiting individuals who are not fit and proper in order to protect the wider regulated community.
Before going further, it is worth stepping back and making a broader point about the character of PRA and Bank enforcement.
The PRA is a supervision-led rather than an enforcement-led regulator. Our investigations and enforcement resource has always been precision-focused, and used in a targeted way to support supervisory aims. This reflects a need to look back and understand what has gone wrong, as well as a need to look forward and positively influence future behaviour, including in relation to matters where there may be shortcomings apparent, but (perhaps just by good fortune) crystallised harm has not yet arisen. While the enforcement division works closely with supervisors and supports their aims, we are functionally independent from supervision, which helps ensure that we approach matters objectively and with fresh eyes. Our enforcement activity stretches across the entire gamut of PRA-authorised firms: large and small deposit-takers, designated investment firms, insurers, reinsurers and credit unions.
Enforcement action is brought to support specific supervisory objectives, strategies, and outcomes. In the PRA context, this is guided by its primary statutory objectives: to promote the safety and soundness of PRA‑authorised firms and to secure an appropriate degree of protection for policyholders.
That approach has resulted in a steady number of public outcomes each year, and we expect that to continue. Our focus is on cases that deliver appropriate outcomes while sending clear deterrent signals to the wider community of PRA-authorised firms, individuals and Bank regulated entities.
But what is changing, against that steady position, is how those cases are conducted and resolved, and how efficiently and constructively accountability is achieved.
‘Contentious regulatory work’ - the investigations and enforcement orthodoxy
To understand why this matters, let’s briefly consider the orthodox model that has traditionally shaped regulatory enforcement cases. That model typically followed a familiar pattern:
The regulator opens an investigation and gathers evidence, perhaps over a significant period. The evidence is analysed and tested. Once a settled regulatory view has formed, if the regulator considers that breaches have been identified and action is appropriate, a proposal for action is put to the subject. This may be treated as a case to answer and engagement often becomes, at least in the first instance, defensive: the subject, and their counsel, often adopt a defensive posture, with initial engagement focused on minimising exposure by challenging the regulator’s conclusions. Admissions may eventually come as part of a settlement, but often late on in the process.
This approach has driven a set of familiar conventions, on the part of investigation subjects and those advising them, including caution about taking early positions; the labelling of learning and remediation as “enhancements” rather than corrections; careful avoidance of any acknowledgement of rule breaches until the regulator’s view is known; and a tendency to approach enforcement as “quasi‑litigation" rather than as a process of regulatory accountability.
It is important to say that this approach may not be wrong or improper. In some cases (particularly where facts are contested or responsibility is genuinely unclear) it may be entirely appropriate.
But it is not the only model, and it is not the best model for every situation. If it is treated as the only model, we risk losing the opportunity, in appropriate cases, to do something better — better not only for the regulator but also better, undoubtedly, for the subject of investigations and the wider regulated community.
And it bears pausing here to note that, every (not the majority, but every) enforcement case where we have made findings of breaches of rules by a firm to date has been resolved by settlement (that’s 21 cases in total).footnote [2] To date, no firm cases have been contested at our Enforcement Decision Making Committee or the Upper Tribunal (Tax and Chancery Chamber).
We do not open investigations unless the statutory thresholds for doing so are met and our investigation opening criteriafootnote [3] are engaged. But we do not think the fact that all our actions against firms have settled is a function of the PRA only pursuing cases where breaches are clear and obvious at the point of opening an investigation. Rather, it reflects the fact that firms, by the time we reach a settlement proposal, have understood the nature of the case against them and internally acknowledged the weaknesses and failings within their systems, controls and governance frameworks. Firms typically recognise the value in the certainty of a settlement and the opportunity to demonstrate contrition and move on from past wrongdoing or failures.
This might be taken to suggest that the approach followed historically where an investigation may be treated as a contentious or adversarial endeavour may be misplaced and unnecessary in many cases.
Not all investigations result in enforcement action. It remains the case, that some investigations are closed with no action taken, and that will inevitably continue.
We do not open investigations lightly, but the fact that some investigations conclude without findings of breach reflects an important feature of how we approach enforcement. We do not open investigations with a predetermined outcome, nor do we focus only on the most straightforward or easily provable cases. This also demonstrates a central point that PRA and Bank investigations are conducted with an open mind; something that will not change.
But I am talking about a different, yet substantial, category of investigations: cases where there is often a realistic and shared understanding at an early stage that a regulatory breach is very likely to have occurred. Such scenarios are not uncommon and often arise as a result of independent reports firms may have commissioned, section 166 “skilled person” reviews,footnote [4] root cause analysis exercises or post incident reports. Such work is often sufficient to enable a firm to understand what went wrong, why and how; and who is accountable for this.
In cases such as these, the traditional orthodoxy can lead to unnecessarily slow, resource intensive, and expensive processes.
The consequence, which we have seen many times, can be investigations that take much longer than they need to. This increases cost, uncertainty, and strain for firms, individuals, and, yes, for regulators alike. It can also introduce significant delay between the events which may have prompted an investigation and the publishing of a settled enforcement outcome.
It needn’t be like this.
Efficiency, speed and regulatory burden
Efficiency and speed are not abstract virtues in enforcement.
They matter because quick and efficient investigations reduce prolonged uncertainty for firms and individuals, as well as allowing regulatory resources to be deployed where they add most value and where they enable the regulator to be most effective. Quick and effective investigations also enable lessons from enforcement outcomes to reach the wider market more quickly, with the aim of improving understanding and therefore behaviours, to the benefit of firms, individuals and the regulator.
This also connects to a broader discussion about efficiency and regulatory burden on firms.
Some of that regulatory burden arises directly from the need to comply with rules. Regulators should, of course, keep their rules under review and look to reform them where appropriate to reduce burden in a way which is proportionate to risk. There are rightly many recent examples of regulators, including the PRA, seeking to do this.
In an enforcement context, reducing regulatory burden does not, however, mean reducing enforcement activity such that the incentive to properly and fully comply with the letter and spirit of rules diminishes.
But regulatory burden does not arise only from compliance with rules. It can also be driven by the conduct and behaviour of parties and unnecessary procedural friction.
Where enforcement can be carried out in a way that uncovers the facts and delivers accountability more quickly, without compromising deterrence, and without unnecessary duplication of effort, that is a real and meaningful reduction in regulatory burden.
From the Bank’s perspective, efficient enforcement is not about rushing. It is about doing the right work meticulously, in the right order, without unnecessary delay, to ensure an appropriate regulatory outcome is achieved.
Over recent years, we have focused on how enforcement policy design can support that aim with clear architecture and incentives which promote efficiency and candour.
Incentives
A helpful analogy here is civil justice.
In civil litigation, early engagement is not just encouraged; it is structurally incentivised. Under the Civil Procedure Rules, the overriding objective, costs rules, and judicial expectations all push parties towards narrowing issues, accepting responsibility where appropriate, and resolving disputes proportionately.
Accordingly, a party that resists the obvious, or prolongs proceedings unnecessarily, does so at real risk.
I referred earlier to a tendency to treat investigations and enforcement as “quasi litigation” – investigations and enforcement are not civil litigation, quasi or otherwise. This has been affirmed at the Court of Appeal: a regulator is not an “ordinary litigant” and the conduct of cases is not to be treated as “ordinary litigation”.footnote [5] But the underlying insight holds: behaviour follows incentives.
And what we have sought to do in our enforcement policy is rebalance incentives, without compromising rigour or fairness.
The Early Account Scheme as a signal
That brings me to the Early Account Scheme — the “EAS”.
The EAS was introduced as part of an enforcement policy update we made in 2024.footnote [6] It is available to subjects under investigation in appropriate cases, and it is best understood as a signal to subjects of PRA and Bank investigations about how we expect mature regulatory engagement to work in appropriate cases.
It signals that: early, high quality internal investigation is valued; comprehensive and accurate factual accounts matter; early admissions of regulatory breaches made well in advance of settlement are meaningful; and proactive candour can materially affect the efficiency and outcome of an investigation.
The EAS is available to both firms and individuals, and gives subjects a mechanism to adapt their approach to regulatory engagement, in effect an architecture for co-operation with appropriate checks and balances.
Specifically, it gives a subject an opportunity to produce a candid Account (with an expectation that this will be done in six months or less) which is comprehensive, accurate and timely, supported with relevant material, and arrived at through an appropriately rigorous process.
This is not a process that relies on the subject simply providing an account in isolation. It is a collaborative and iterative endeavour, with the PRA actively engaging, testing and, where necessary, challenging the content of the Account as it is developed. Our existing investigative tools remain fully available, including the use of compulsory powers where appropriate, and an Account produced under the EAS sits alongside the broader evidential picture, including documentation and information already held by Supervision. In addition, senior management accountability is built into the process, through attestation as to the accuracy and completeness of the Account. We also retain the ability to pursue any lines of enquiry that are not adequately reflected in an Account. Taken together, these features are designed to ensure that early candour is accompanied by rigour, not at the expense of it.
Where a subject produces an Account in this way, and makes early admissions, providing they have ceased the behaviour giving rise to the breaches, and carried out necessary remediation, they may be entitled to an enhanced discount of up to 50% on any regulatory penalty.
What do we mean by “early admissions”? This is an area where precision matters.
”Early admissions” do not mean general expressions of regret, tactical concessions made once settlement parameters are already clear, or pure factual acknowledgements distinguished from regulatory breaches.
What we mean by early admissions in PRA and Bank cases is the acceptance of relevant facts and regulatory breaches which are made significantly in advance of any settlement proposal and at a stage where those admissions genuinely shape the scope, direction, and duration of the investigation.
In other words, open and candid regulatory engagement in good faith. This mirrors what comprises one of our fundamental expectations as to firm engagements with the regulator more generally: to be open and co-operative.footnote [7]
What the lived experience shows so far
We recognise that this may demand an adjustment in mindset and requires an element of trust. That includes confidence that subjects who come forward early will be treated fairly, in line with the framework we have set out.
But what has been striking is how these signals have already translated into real behavioural change. We welcome this change.
Across a growing number of our enforcement investigations, we are now seeing earlier without prejudice engagement, investigation subjects volunteering structured factual accounts, and admissions being made months, and in some cases years, earlier than would previously have been typical.
This is evident if you look at our cases since the EAS policy was published in early 2024 with admissions as to rule breaches now regularly being proactively made early on and, in one case, with a firm even making clear that it would, in light of the facts and matters, be appropriate for a financial sanction to be imposed (crucially, this was before any such proposal had been put before the firm).
A number of these cases were already in progress when the EAS policy was published so were not formally on the “EAS track”. However, the way that these outcomes were arrived at represents a response to the policy signal the EAS policy sent upon publication.
And in March this year we published our first outcome in a firm case in which the EAS policy was formally applied.
This was action in respect of U K Insurance Limited, a subsidiary of Direct Line Insurance Group plc (now owned by Aviva).footnote [8] It proved to be a successful pilot case. We were impressed with how the subject engaged and the commitment the firm demonstrated to self-reflection and contrition which was completely in tune with what we are hoping to achieve with the scheme. The firm engaged proactively and candidly with our investigation team during the EAS process and provided a comprehensive, timely, accurate and fulsome Account. Shortly following production of the Account, and (critically) significantly in advance of any settlement proposal being put to the firm by the PRA, the firm made admissions, both as to relevant facts and regulatory rule breaches. This meant our investigation could proceed efficiently and quickly and we recognised this by giving the firm the maximum discount.
Collectively these recent examples represent a break with our past actions. They represent a pattern of change in how subjects are choosing to engage with enforcement.
It’s one we hope will continue and why we would describe what is happening as genuinely significant. It is grounded not just in policy language, but already in observable behaviour across our cases.
For the PRA and the Bank, it means more focused and efficient investigations, better use of specialist resources, and outcomes delivered closer to the underlying events.
For firms and individuals under investigation, it means shorter periods of uncertainty, reduced cost and disruption (an opportunity to acknowledge, reflect and move on from breaches) and stronger incentives for governance, escalation, and remediation.
Bringing this together
Enforcement works best when it is understood not as a contest, but as a disciplined process for accountability, learning and rebuilding trust, with responsibility recognised early enough for it to do its job properly.
The approach I have described today is new and may take some getting used to. It will sit alongside more traditional approaches rather than replace them entirely.
But the destination, an appropriate regulatory outcome, has not changed. What is changing, in many cases, is the route taken to get there and the pace at which we arrive.
Together, these developments represent a sea change in how regulatory investigations and enforcement are conducted. They bring new optionality and scope for faster outcomes. They mark not just a change in form, but in substance, in how subjects of investigations engage with us and how accountability is achieved.
I would like to thank Edward Aldred, Tara Connolly, Geoff Egerton and Ossie Fikret for their help in preparing this speech. And to colleagues across the Bank, including in particular Olie Dearie, Rob Price and Aaron Schroeder-Willis, for their helpful comments.

articles.title: The Fruit Of Tariffs Is Fraud
articles.text:
The Fruit Of Tariffs Is Fraud

Thomas Gatley

Gavekal Dragonomics | 16 Oct 2026

Trade tensions between China and the US seem to have eased a bit recently, with the two sides agreeing on a mutual reduction of tariffs on some goods after their presidential summit. Yet the environment remains hostile: the US has another Section 301 investigation underway on “structural excess capacity.” The reality, though, is that tariffs are not working very well at keeping out Chinese goods. While on the surface it appears that eight years of tariffs has led to a material decoupling of US-China trade, this is a fiction. The US continues to import huge quantities of Chinese goods, but these imports are obfuscated by widespread fraud and re-routing.According to US Customs, imports from China and Hong Kong totaled US$276bn over the past 12 months, down by half from US$550bn in late 2018. This is well below the total of imports from Canada, Mexico, Asean, or the EU, all of which used to be smaller sources of US imports than China. If this trade data was accurate, it would represent a major, rapid and historic decoupling of the world’s two largest economies. But it is not accurate. China’s exporters and US importers have found two important ways to minimize the amount of tariffs they pay, which combine to massively distort US trade statistics. The true value of Chinese-made goods flowing into the US is likely in excess of US$600bn annually, more than twice as much as US Customs reports.

articles.title: El Niño heating up inflation
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

12 Oct 2026

El Niño heating up inflation

El Niño’s impact on agricultural production raises concerns over food price inflation and economic stability across Africa, particularly in the east and the south of the continent.

The intensifying El Niño weather event is projected to be the worst on record. This phenomenon, combined with the Subtropical Indian Ocean Dipole, poses severe risks to agricultural output, livelihoods, external balances, and energy markets.

Food carries a substantial weight in many African CPI baskets, exceeding 50% in Ethiopia and Zambia. As a result, rising food prices could have a greater inflationary effect than this year’s oil shock. Most major African markets are expected to see higher inflation in 2027 than in 2026.

Encouragingly, numerous countries across sub-Saharan Africa have already tabled disaster preparedness and response strategies encompassing physical strategic food reserves and emergency financing options.

Committing $50M to USHP: The Product Bringing U.S. Home Prices Onchain

Worth roughly $55 trillion and comparable in size to the entire S&P 500, U.S. residential housing is one of the world’s largest asset classes. Yet unlike equities, Treasuries, or gold, investors have lacked a simple, liquid way to hold index-level exposure to U.S. home prices. Benchmarks such as the FHFA House Price Index and the Case-Shiller Index exist, but the benchmarks themselves are not investable products. The usual alternatives – homebuilder stocks and public or private REITs – bury home price exposure under operating leverage, management decisions, and equity-market beta. As a result, the largest store of household wealth in America has remained one of the hardest asset classes to own.Galaxy is excited to announce our $50M commitment to USHP, the first digital asset referencing a U.S. home price index, through USHP Limited’s pre-launch institutional round.
The Onchain Efficient FrontierOur thesis at Galaxy is that capital markets are moving onchain, and that an Onchain Efficient Frontier is forming across the full spectrum of risk and return profiles. To date, that frontier has been built largely on crypto-native sources of yield: basis trades, rehypothecation, leverage, and token incentives. Meanwhile, roughly $300 billion of stablecoin supply sits idle, generating little or no yield while quietly losing ground to inflation. We believe the next chapter of onchain asset management will connect that capital to real-world assets with durable, exogenous yield. The strongest candidates are large, historically difficult-to-access asset classes, backed by genuine economic activity rather than reflexive incentives. Few asset classes fit that description better than U.S. housing.U.S. housing is one of the deepest, most stable sources of long-term returns in global markets, yet it has remained largely inaccessible as a simple, liquid index investment. USHP is designed to change that.
A New Way to Access the World's Largest Asset ClassFor generations, U.S. real estate has been one of the most dependable engines of household wealth, and also one of the least accessible. Investing has traditionally required a substantial down payment, a mortgage, local market expertise, and the ongoing responsibilities of property ownership. USHP changes that. It will launch on Ethereum and provide eligible participants liquid, indexed exposure to U.S. home prices without the burdens of owning or managing physical property.We believe the asset class’s historically low volatility, relatively low correlation with other financial assets, and its backing by dollar-denominated real assets will appeal to a range of eligible (non-U.S.) investors. Beyond traditional real estate investors, we believe crypto-native institutions that hold stablecoins, tokenized Treasuries, and other cryptoassets may also value the combination of yield and index-linked exposure that USHP is designed to provide.Over time, we expect that the blockchain and tokenization infrastructure underpinning USHP will be used to support an entirely new category of investment products designed for U.S. homebuyers, creating new ways for households to access, manage, and participate in the economics of residential real estate.
Why We Are InvestingAt Galaxy, we invest in companies that are working to build the financial infrastructure of the future. Throughout the history of capital markets, some of the most impactful innovations have made large, valuable asset classes easier to access, own, and trade. We believe tokenization will do the same for many of the world's largest markets, and U.S. residential real estate is among the most compelling opportunities.Our experience backing companies such as Ethena and Ornn has reinforced our belief that when novel financial products solve a real market need and are designed to scale, adoption can accelerate quickly. We believe USHP has the potential to become another important building block in the onchain economy.We are thrilled to partner with the founding team of the platform that powers USHP. They pair deep crypto-native investing and operating experience with Blackstone Real Estate pedigree and a track record scaling a cutting-edge institutional real estate investment platform. articles.title: The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland

Speech at the Intergraf Currency & Identity Conference, Denmark

Published on
15 October 2026

Maintaining trust in banknotes is crucial to their continued demand and relevance. This requires more than robust security features and resilient infrastructure. Victoria Cleland explores how communications and public engagement can help build and maintain confidence and trust in cash.

Speech
Trust is essential to everything the Bank of England (the Bank) does. It underpins all our activities, from setting Bank Rate to operating payment settlement systems and much in between. And banknotes are among the most visible manifestations of that trust.
The Bank is the second oldest central bank in the world and issuing banknotes (originally promissory notes) was one of its earliest functions. Historically, confidence in banknotes was linked to their convertibility into gold. You can still see the words ‘I promise to pay the bearer on demand’ on our banknotes. While the nature of that promise has evolved over time and our notes are now indirectly backed by UK government bonds,footnote [1] the principle remains the same: banknotes derive their value from trust, and that trust must be maintained.
Every time someone accepts a banknote, they trust that it is authentic and worth the value stated. They have to be confident that it can be used again in the future: whether to spend it, save it or bank it. Without that trust, a banknote is simply an object, albeit with a beautiful design. With it, households spend, businesses trade and economies function.
Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining this trust in banknotes. We do so by ensuring banknotes are available, that the cash industry remains effective, resilient and sustainable, and that banknotes remain a secure method of payment.
Communicating openly with businesses and the public so that they can recognise and easily authenticate banknotes is also an essential part of maintaining this security. The Bank has engaged extensively with the UK public on the imagery for our next series of banknotes to ensure our banknotes remain recognisable as national symbols. This culminated in last week’s announcement that the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will feature as the central imagery on our next series of banknotes.
I will now dive deeper into the Bank’s work to ensure this essential trust in our banknotes through availability, secure design and public engagement.
Ensuring trust through availability
The public need to trust that banknotes will be available when required. The Bank does not, and cannot, do this in isolation. Just as a beehive depends on its community of different bees performing complementary roles, maintaining trust in banknotes requires organisations across the cash ecosystem to work together.
Central banks, printers, cash centre operators, cash-in-transit companies, financial institutions and retailers are all important members of this ecosystem. They all play crucial and complementary roles in ensuring that the public can continue to access and use banknotes so that cash remains a trusted source of payments. At the Banknote Conference earlier this year,footnote [2] I spoke about the importance of preserving choice in payments and the role of cash in preserving choice. Ensuring that choice remains requires the whole industry to work together like an efficient beehive.
For the Bank, this includes issuing banknotes to meet public demand. The use of cash for transactions has declined over recent years, accounting for 8% of all transactions in the UK in 2025, down from 45% a decade earlier.footnote [3] But according to our research, cash is still the preferred payment method for one in seven people and, is used at least once a week by almost a quarter of the public. It is essential for some people and is seen as an important contingency by many.
And the value of Bank of England notes in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5 billion at the end of February 2026. This demonstrates the enduring importance of cash to our economy and our society.
We are committed to meet the demand for our banknotes and to ensure that the right banknotes are available, in the right places at the right time. It is important to us that people and businesses who want to use cash can continue to do so. We do this by monitoring payment trends and a range of economic factors to inform demand forecasts and contingency requirements, and to help us decide how many banknotes we need our printer De La Rue to produce.
Authorities and industry must work closely together to ensure the cash cycle as a whole remains effective, resilient and sustainable. The wholesale cash distribution market is the underlying “plumbing” that gets cash to where it is needed, via cash centres through to ATMs and retailers. Last year, the Bank took on a new role to supervise firms in the wholesale cash industry who operate cash centres and their backing FIs.footnote [4] In addition, the Financial Conduct Authority has powers to protect retail access to cash for consumers. Together, these regimes will help ensure that cash will be available and accessible.
Ensuring trust through design
Another key component of trust in banknotes is counterfeit resilience: the public and businesses must be confident that the banknotes they receive are genuine. We do this by incorporating sophisticated security features into the design: these need to be both hard to counterfeit and easy to authenticate. For trust in the security of banknotes to endure, it is important that central banks change the design from time to time to incorporate the latest security features. This requires suppliers and manufacturers to innovate and invest in developing new technology and more resilient features. To maintain trust in banknotes, it is essential that this innovation continues.
When you picture a puffin, you may think of its distinct colouring including its bright orange beak. Did you know their beaks glow under UV light, just like our banknotes? These markings and photoluminescence are not purely about aesthetic appeal but also serve a functional purpose in helping puffins lure prey, deter predators and attract mates. Similarly, at the Bank, we need to design banknotes that are not only attractive but also designed with function, particularly security, at their heart.
Our next series of banknotes (Series H) is currently being designed. The driver, as with any new series, is to further enhance counterfeit resilience. And following public consultation, the new notes will celebrate UK wildlife. Images of wildlife will also support resilience, enabling us to incorporate intuitive movements into the security features which are engaging and easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Trust also stems from our notes being accessible to all. We are continuing to invest in banknote accessibility, running research on how people with disabilities use cash today and including tactile features to help people with visual impairments differentiate between denominations.
Ensuring trust through communication and engagement
Trust in banknotes is founded on availability and effective design, but sustaining it requires engagement – with businesses, law enforcement and the public. Even the most sophisticated security feature is only effective if people know how to use it to verify a banknote. And so public engagement and communication are a pivotal part of our anticounterfeiting strategy.
The Bank provides free educational materials, such as booklets and posters to help businesses and the public to authenticate banknotes. We also provide online training and run a free Banknote Checking Scheme to help businesses keep a watchful eye out for counterfeits: a vigilance one could compare to the barn owl which will feature on our next series. This Scheme has grown considerably, now covering over 50,000 business locations.
Recently, we have supplemented this by launching a communications campaign aimed at businesses. This campaign shows business owners talking about their own experiences and how using best practice banknote checking has enhanced their trust in banknotes. We also engage closely with law enforcement, including the National Crime Agency and local police forces, to help them investigate and prosecute potential counterfeiters.
Incorporating images that resonate strongly with the public and which they can easily recognise is also a key part of banknote authentication and maintaining trust. So last year, we launched a two-stage process to engage the public in the choice of imagery for the next series of banknotes.
In July 2025, we announced that we would introduce a new series of banknotes with even more robust security features. A new series necessitates changes to the imagery, so we launched a consultation asking the UK public which theme they wanted to see featured in the design. The Bank has been celebrating historic figures on our banknotes since 1970. However there are many ways to represent the UK so we wanted to hear the views of the public, the users of our banknotes.
Around 60% of respondents chose nature as one of the themes they wanted to see featured with many nominating specific native animals. And this March, we announced that in the light of feedback from the consultation, images of UK wildlife would feature on the next series of our banknotes. We worked closely with a panel of wildlife experts to create a shortlist of native UK animals and in June we launched a second consultation asking the public to help us choose which of the shortlisted animals to feature as the central imagery on the next series. We were delighted by the scale of the response, with almost half a million people participating.
The Bank’s overarching objective is to increase counterfeit resilience through secure design, and for this to be effective, it is also important that the new series represents the UK and resonates with the users. After all, banknotes are not just a means of payment, but also a shared symbol of national identity. This helps to promote trust and security, as familiar imagery which resonates with the public will mean they look more closely at their banknotes.
The importance of awareness and familiarity is not new. In 1797, when the Bank rushed to issue new £1 and £2 banknotes following gold shortages, counterfeiting surged as counterfeiters took advantage of people’s unfamiliarity with new banknotes. The lesson remains relevant today: when introducing a new series, issuers must bring the public along on the journey to ensure they can recognise and authenticate the notes.
To do this successfully and inclusively, central banks need to engage people through different methods including the platforms they use every day. To help publicise our most recent consultation, the Bank used an integrated communication strategy which included press, social media, engagement with schools and visiting local communities around the UK. We also collaborated with influencers to help us reach young people and audiences who may not have engaged with the Bank’s work in the past.
We opened the consultation with a launch event at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) London Wetland Centre to celebrate the shortlisted animals and give journalists an opportunity to ask questions – both to me and the wildlife Expert Panel who helped us develop the shortlist of animals. This provided an engaging backdrop to create content about wildlife to help raise awareness and encourage participation in the consultation.
To sustain momentum, we produced a variety of engaging and accessible content with the aim to appeal to different audience groups and help convey our broader message. This included factsheets on each of the animals and educational posts showing how banknotes have evolved over time, as well as some more fun posts.
Alongside the formal consultation, we also visited schools and ran a design challenge for children across the country to give young people a voice in shaping our next generation of banknotes. And we held a number of in-person Youth and Citizens’ panels in communities including Llandudno and Devon. These were a great opportunity for the Bank to learn directly from people about the role that cash continues to play in society as well as their views on the shortlisted wildlife.
Conclusion
Trust in banknotes begins with secure design but only endures if banknotes are available and recognised. Keeping banknotes trusted and relevant requires innovation and strong collaboration across the whole of the cash industry. And this must be coupled with communication and engagement to enable businesses and the public to understand, recognise and trust the banknotes they use.
Our recent consultation gave people a voice, helping them connect with the banknotes they use and have a meaningful say about their future design. There will now be a quieter period in our communications about the next series, while our design work continues in the background, with security at its heart. Like the hedgehog emerging after its winter retreat, we will return when we are ready to unveil the first denomination.
I would like to thank Elijah Lee, Zahra Damji, Nick McLaren, Ellen Caswell, Stuart Cooper, Lauren Murphy, Kiran Keer, Millie Rettie and Lisa Young.

articles.title: AI poses uneven opportunities and risks across APAC cities
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

16 Oct 2026

AI poses uneven opportunities and risks across APAC cities

Investment and expansion in professional services have propelled Asia’s major cities into the ranks of the world’s most influential economic hubs. AI advances have the potential to reinforce these trends, but there are also clear risks ahead.

Investment and expansion in professional services have propelled Asia’s major cities into the ranks of the world’s most influential economic hubs. Since 2000, gross value added in these sectors has grown on average by 7.9% each year across all our Asia Pacific cities, boosting incomes and living standards. AI advances have the potential to reinforce these trends, but there are also clear risks ahead.

Cities that cater to AI-related demand have seen robust gains. Reputation, strategic policies, and a skilled and abundant workforce have supported Asia’s specialisation in producing the electronic components needed for AI systems. With AI-related exports set to boom across Asia this year, we expect strong manufacturing growth for key cities such as Hsinchu (Taiwan), Georgetown (Malaysia), and Hai Phong (Vietnam).

As AI adoption rates rise, service-centric cities will be the key beneficiaries, reinforcing the strength of the region’s major hubs like Singapore, Beijing, and Tokyo. This is because service sectors like IT and finance are the most likely to receive productivity and income gains, given their ability to leverage the technology.

However, city-level labour market responses will be complex. Although we do not expect widespread job losses from AI adoption, there will be greater exposure for specific low value-added occupations in ICT and administrative activities, which heightens the risk for outsourcing economies like Manila and Bengaluru. Developments are also likely to widen regional inequalities as more rural and industrial regions fall behind.

Global Markets and EconomyOngoing Developments in Financial Services Regulation in the EU and UK – Part IIGlobal Regulatory Impacts Series • Article • October 08, 2026KEY HIGHLIGHTSBoth the UK and EU are rewriting the rules on what information must be given to retail investors before they buy investment products — with the goal of making that information clearer and easier to understand. The UK is moving first: its new retail disclosure regime (called "Consumer Composite Investments") will be fully in place by mid-2027. The EU's equivalent reforms for PRIIPs will follow roughly one to two years later.Although the UK and EU are legislating separately, both are heading in the same direction: ensuring customers get good value and fair treatment. The UK has had its "Consumer Duty" in place since 2023. The EU is now introducing similar requirements — firms will need to justify their fees and charges and prove that any payments or commissions they receive genuinely benefit the client.Both regions are jointly working toward a major infrastructure change: shortening the time it takes to settle securities trades from two days to one ("T+1"), targeted for October 2027. This is a coordinated effort, with UK and EU regulators aligned on timing even though each is legislating independently. Separately, the EU has introduced a rule requiring certain derivatives trading to route through EU-based clearing houses.A year has passed since we last compared developments in financial services regulation in both the European Union (EU) and the United Kingdom (UK). This included where the respective jurisdictions were diverging and where they were progressing towards similar policy objectives, albeit with different approaches (for example, prescription versus outcomes-based regulatory regimes).This year, as we revisit these evolving topics, and cover the latest policy developments, we have split our update into three complementary articles. In this, our second article, we look at topics including retail disclosure frameworks, the EU’s Retail Investment Strategy, the FCA’s Consumer Duty and more. Global Markets and Economy Capital Market Harmonization: The EU's Market Integration and Supervision PackageOver a decade in the making, the journey toward fully integrated EU capital markets began with the Capital Markets Union Action Plan in 2015. Despite significant legislative progress, fragmentation, regulatory divergence, and cross-border barriers have persisted. Renewed calls for action followed in 2019, 2020, 2023, and 2024 — culminating in the launch of the Savings and Investments Union (SIU) in March 2025 and the EU’s Market Integration and Supervision Package (EU MISP) in December 2025 (which is a cornerstone of the SIU).Global Markets and EconomyContinental Drift: Financial Services Regulation in the EU and UKPost the UK’s departure from the European Union (EU), we entered a realm of UK/EU financial services regulation, which has lost its harmonised nature, which included relying on passporting rights across EU Member States. Blackstone on hedge funds: Why multi-strats are back
[Music]
Voiceover: This podcast is intended for institutional and professional investors, not for retail use.
Kumar Panja: Welcome to the J.P. Morgan Making Sense channel. I'm Kumar Panja and I'm excited to be joined by two very knowledgeable leaders from Blackstone. Joe Dowling, who is a Senior Managing Director and Global Head of Blackstone's multi-asset investing business called BXMA, and Riad Abrahams, who is a Senior Managing Director in BXMA as well, where he serves as Head of Strategy, Risk and Quant Analytics. Welcome, gents.
Joe Dowling: Kumar, thanks for having us.
Riad Abrahams: Thanks, Kumar.
Kumar: Today, we're going to be focusing on the multi-strategy hedge fund space and the way in which investors are increasingly using multi-strats, multi-strategy as a powerful tool within their alternatives portfolio. And Blackstone have been investing in this space for 29 years, am I right?
Joe Dowling: You are.
Kumar Panja: And are both investors in multi-strategy hedge funds as well as having their own multi-strategy solutions, so I'm really keen for them to share their views on the segment. But first, let me set the scene with some numbers and my colleague Katie Crawley in the Capital Advisory Group published a report on multi-strats. And according to which the space in terms of size as we see it expressed in assets under management is estimated to be $595 billion at the end of 2025. That number will have gone up already this year substantially. That is a year-on-year increase of $92 billion, which is up 18%. And that AUM growth can be broken down into $61 billion of performance and $31 billion of new inflows. And that is the highest that we've observed since we started to track the data in 2020. Performance for full year 25 across our group of multi-strats that we track was 11% last year. It was 11.8 at the end of 24. But interestingly, larger funds outperformed. So the AUM weighted return was in fact closer to 12.5% last year. The spread of returns between cost pass-through firms and non-pass-through firms narrowed last year. And we'll get into those terms and the significance of that a little bit later. Needless to say, the team here has seen a lot of interest in this space from our conversations with the full spectrum of investors. It's also a popular discussion topic for a number of reasons that we're going to get into. So, Joe, kick us off. Why do you like multi-strategy funds?
Joe Dowling: I think fundamentally that the demand for multi-strats and the demand for multi-strat solutions stems from the underlying problem, which is that stocks and bonds are correlated a lot more than investors think. If you look back over 50 years, it's 62%. And that has risen since 2022. And obviously, we know we live in a world that is very volatile, a world where deglobalization is happening. And that has resulted in a lot of winners and losers and a lot of volatility. And that's just the perfect weather for these strategies. And as an allocator, people are looking for something that's completely uncorrelated to stocks and bonds. And multi-strats are the solution. So, yeah, I'm not surprised by your statistics.
Kumar Panja: And as investors rethink this traditional 60-40 portfolios, what's the nature of the demand that you're seeing from your investors for multi-strategy solutions?
Joe Dowling: The demand is across the board for hedge funds in general. It's the number one asset class in 2026 for allocators, which I can never remember a time where that was the case. Can you, Riad?
Riad Abrahams: Yeah, I think it's actually the second year in a row that hedge funds are the most sought-after asset class. And within that, multi-strats are obviously in huge demand. I mean you quoted the growth over the last 12 months. If you zoom out, I think over the last five years
Joe Dowling: 16%.
Riad Abrahams: Yes. And that's compared to the rest of the industry at around 4%. So, I think this problem that traditional portfolios face given the shift in the correlation regime, institutions recognize it and they're gravitating towards multi-strategy solutions as the answer.
Kumar Panja: How should investors be thinking about using multi-strategy funds in their portfolio? Should they be using more of it? Do you think they are underweight currently?
Joe Dowling: I definitely think people in general are underweight, the asset class. You can see some of the Ivy League endowments are actually now at 20% in their portfolios across the board. They're using it as a fixed income substitute in most cases. But if you look at allocations to multi-strat, they're quite low. And I think people have a host of reasons to not like them. But the reality is that these firms have been delivering, especially the top ones, year after year after year, an uncorrelated double-digit return with a high sharp. That is nirvana for investors.
Riad Abrahams: Yeah, just to put some numbers around the long span of performance for multi-strat. So, the longest index is the pivotal path multi-strategy index. It goes back almost 30 years. And so, if you think about multi-strats over that period, they've delivered 9% returns with less than 5% volatility.
Joe Dowling: It goes back 30 years, Riad? Is Millennium the only fund at that point?
Riad Abrahams: It's a more limited index back then for sure. But if you compare it, that's actually ahead of equity returns. Over that same time period, equities have generated an 8% return with 15 vol. And bonds have only generated a 3% return with 6 vol. So, multi-strats are delivering you equity-like returns with a fraction of the risk. And so, if you think about that as your portfolio objective and what can be realized, multi-strat should be a core holding in any institutional portfolio, any individual's portfolio. And I think that's why, as Joe mentioned, you see that the most sophisticated pensions, sovereign wealth, endowments, their absolute return allocation is around, I think it's 20%.
Kumar Panja: So, multi-strategy funds often come with perceived challenges, Joe, as you mentioned. And these are things like closed to new money, i.e. capacity. They have high fees or pass-through fee structures. They have increased their terms in terms of their liquidity. There is a question around the level of transparency that is sometimes provided. And there are increasing correlations between multi-strategy firms as well. How do you think about these trade-offs, particularly when building a platform? And how do you differentiate? How does Blackstone differentiate its approach to investing in multi-strategy funds?
Riad Abrahams: So, look, I think the top institutions here have done a phenomenal job. I mean, they have delivered, right? We talked about some of the returns over time. But that prevailing model, broadly, it includes running maybe 100 or 200 individual teams. But most of those teams are doing something quite similar, which is they're running some version of an equity long-short strategy. If you look at those individual teams through the use of kind of the risk models and leverage, what they do is they basically have each pod generate a low return on assets that they then apply a lot of leverage to to get a very high return on equity. And that helps fund the compensation for the PMs through a structure called the pass-through fee structure. That sort of describes the prevailing model.
Joe Dowling: I would emphasize people underestimate how big a moat the top players have created in not only their recruiting, and this is a big recruiting business, in their information technology, in their policies around using the center book, using leverage. It is formidable. And we've seen many sophisticated people try to come into this industry with the hopes of creating a firm and failing. Very talented people.
Kumar Panja: That's a good segue into the question. What do you think are the barriers to entry in this space? And more broadly then, because I guess there might be two sides of the same coin, what makes a good multi-strategy firm?
Joe Dowling: Well, again, I think we talked about it. It all comes down to the durability of the return, the consistency of the return, how high quality is it. Does it stand the test of time? And markets test you. I mean, if you look at just at a 60-40 over the last five years, there have been seven quarters where it's been down. And it's during these periods or the big macro dislocations like 2008 where these firms have come through and protected capital. It is a very, very hard thing to do.
Riad Abrahams: Yeah. The really great ones, as Joe mentioned, they excel at attracting talent, right? And they're constantly filling the funnel of new potential PMs. They are able, through their infrastructure, to arm those PMs with access to data and very formidable trading operations. And then I think that one of the key, key things that the best ones do…
Joe Dowling: …risk management
Riad Abrahams: Is they manage risk very well, right? And there are different variants of how they do it, but broadly, they're able to factor neutralize their portfolios. They employ different stop-loss approaches. And that is what has really reduced their correlation, reduced their volatility, and allowed you to create this compounding stream through time. So, I think, again, that that prevailing model, the guys at the top have done an incredible job at it. But as you say, Kumar, a lot of them are also now closed and so a bit more difficult to access.
Kumar Panja: So Riyad, you've talked about some of the challenges to the traditional way that largest managers deliver on the promise of multi-strategy returns. Is there an alternative approach and what is that approach?
Riad Abrahams: Well Kumar, just to summarize again, I think those challenges are high fees, high leverage and challenging investor liquidity. And I would say an alternative approach would be one that uses a centralized team that deploys capital across multiple internal strategies as opposed to many teams effectively running the same strategy. That in turn could enable a portfolio construction approach that can really de-emphasize leverage as the primary means of risk control and instead capitalize on the power of something that we like to call stacking structurally uncorrelated alphas together across asset classes. It's a model that can probably plug into a broader ecosystem of proprietary data, insights, idea generation, obviously tech infrastructure that will effectively reduce the operating expense burden and compensation burden of the prevailing kind of platform approach. And that really allows you to pass along the savings that come with scale economies to the end customer and investor. And then finally, I think it can be one that achieves a better balance between investor liquidity and business risk by really building upon the benefits of deep duration, of longevity, institutionalization that large scaled firms enjoy.
Kumar Panja: OK, Riad, and I think I know the answer to this question, but does Blackstone adopt this approach and have this ecosystem you talk about?
Riad Abrahams: Well, naturally, Kumar, I'm going to say yes. And when it comes to liquid markets in particular, it is our multi-asset investing division, BXMA. You know, Joe mentioned this earlier, but across BXMA alongside our absolute return business, which largely deploys capital through external manager partnerships. We also have a direct investment business that today manages 18 billion dollars and runs 11 internal strategies that really span the spectrum of asset classes. And historically, that platform has really served institutional investors, but the same capabilities are increasingly supporting the needs of high net worth investors and families where access to this type of return and risk stream has historically been limited.
Kumar Panja: That's great. That makes a lot of sense, Riad. Thank you. So, as we're talking about the challenges, one of the things we constantly have a debate with our investors in conversations is the level of fees for multi-strategy funds. We tell them that you focus on the net return and that's what you should care about. But nevertheless, fees and the level of fees and more importantly, the share of Alpha that they receive as LPs seems to be a sticking point. What do you say to that, Joe?
Joe Dowling: Absolutely. It's the biggest objection that we hear from investors. But if you think about it, these are limited capacity strategies. And whenever something is limited, you have pricing power. And the demand for these multi-strats is really exceptional. Every time they open, they can immediately fund tens of billions of dollars and they've earned it because they've outperformed as Riad said earlier in the statistics. So, I like to focus on the net return and its consistency. Yes, the fees are high but the best performers deserve those fees.
Riad Abrahams: Yeah. And I think that at a high level, it's consistent, right? Generally, the funds that have performed the best through time, they do have the highest fees. And so, you shouldn't be necessarily uncomfortable with high fees. But high fees do create a high burden when you look at those net returns. And I think a lot of platforms, not the top ones, but some platforms have adopted this pass-through fee structure and it's compromised the net investor's experience because there's a big hole you got to climb out of. We like there to be just a lot of alignment between the manager as well as the investor.
Kumar Panja: Okay. So, where are you seeing the most innovation within the multi-strategy space today?
Riad Abrahams: Yeah, I would say two areas. Number one, and I think this is a derivative of their growth and how investors have flocked to them, but you see more external allocations. And so, if you looked back in 2022, just over the last three years, 50% of multi-strats were doing some form of external allocation. That has grown to 75%. A big way they do that is through the use of external SMAs. That has grown from 25% a few years ago to nearly 40% today. So, I do think that they are in some ways moving towards that more traditional…
Joe Dowling: Towards our business.
Riad Abrahams: Yeah the portfolio of funds approach, and I think there is a bit of convergence there. Number two, I think they are in some ways beginning to live up to their name as multi-strats as opposed to just multi-PMs. You see them expanding into other asset classes. I think everyone has read about the expansion into commodities. There are some that are now expanding into private credit. So, I think they are trying to put more arrows in the quiver. That's something that we applaud. I think that's a hallmark of what we're able to do because of our access to all of the different strategies that we run internally across the firm.
Joe Dowling: I think investors underestimate the amount of innovation that's happening at these firms, especially around the center book, the use of AI, and isolating super alpha performers and amplifying those performers overall in the portfolio construction.
Kumar Panja: Riad, we mentioned earlier cost pass-through funds and non-cost pass-through funds. Can you spend a minute or so just talking about what pass-through actually means? Yeah.
Riad Abrahams: Yeah, so if you rewind the clock, I think back when sort of we were all initially in the business, the traditional hedge fund model was a 2 and 20 model. So, 2% management fee, a 20% incentive fee, and then the GP, the actual hedge fund manager, used that compensation to compensate all the underlying investors on the team, to pay for the research cost, to pay for the data, to pay for the offices, to pay for all of the various inputs into the investment strategy and running a complex business. Today, there's something called the pass-through fee structure, where before that incentive fee is even charged, all of the underlying costs of the hedge fund itself are passed through to the end investor. And so, those data costs, those research costs, and very, very importantly, the direct compensation for the underlying investors, for the PMs, all of that actually goes to the end investor. So, what does that all mean at the end of the day? You know a traditional hedge fund model of old, the LPGP share was probably something around 70-30. If you look at the platforms today, and you've written on this, other banks have written on it, the LP on average is keeping about 40 cents of every dollar. So, there is an enormous burden that investors now have to bear to access that traditional multi-strategy model.
Joe Dowling: But Riad, it has a fixed component and a variable component. So, when you were implying the 42, that's based on quite a high return. So, let's remember that.
Riad Abrahams: That's true. And I think in-
Kumar Panja: Or should be.
Riad Abrahams: 100%.
Joe Dowling: It is.
Riad Abrahams: If you look at it, that's for funds that are netting around a low double-digit return.
Joe Dowling: Right.
Riad Abrahams: I think what you also have to think through is because of the war for talent, some of that compensation has become semi-fixed. Because you hear about the payouts all the time, these guaranteed payouts. And so, the traditional pass-through model was 100% variable. So, it was in some ways fully aligned. Now, there is a little bit of this semi-fixed nature to it. So, you have operating leverage alongside financial leverage.
Joe Dowling: Right. But there's always been a fixed component though in terms of your trading costs and those base necessities.
Riad Abrahams: Yes. But the compensation has become-
Joe Dowling: Correct.
Riad Abrahams: Semi-fixed.
Joe Dowling: But your point is more subtle, which is when you're paying for people in the war of talent, they get to put that through the pass-through. So, it increases effectively your fixed component of the pass-through.
Riad Abrahams: Yes.
Kumar Panja: And so what will distinguish successful multi-strategy platforms in the future? Will it be this use of continued investment in technology?
Riad Abrahams: Yes, I think technology and risk management and AI. I think one of the challenges with their success and their very large footprints today is it becomes naturally harder to make sure you're doing something differently than the others. Because you're in some ways, as we were just describing, you're becoming the market, at least in terms of kind of hedge fund trading. And so those that are able to continue to evolve the way that they deploy the capital, the strategies in which they invest, and importantly, the way they use data and leverage AI, that will really, I think, allow some to separate further from the pack.
Joe Dowling: If you think about it, because of the strong demand for this type of investing and their limited capacity, what they've been able to do is lengthen up the lockups around that capital. So the logical thing for me, for them to do, is to start expanding away from purely liquid strategies into a giant TAM of what I would call semi-liquid strategies or less liquid strategies. And so that's probably what you're going to see them do as they move forward.
Kumar Panja: So there's plenty going on in this space.
Joe Dowling: Plenty of addressable market. It's going to be very interesting to see, because they're going to bring their sophisticated risk management and their incredible technology advantages to these sectors, and they will eat up a lot of alpha.
Kumar Panja: All for the benefit of investors.
Riad Abrahams: As it should be.
Kumar Panja: Excellent. Thank you. One last important question that I think our listeners want to hear about. Do you know what the theme this year will be of your holiday video?
Joe Dowling: No one ever knows except for John Gray, who actually writes the holiday video himself, which is a little known fact. And even Kumar, when they film it, and they film it in the fall, we will never know the plot until the whole movie is shown to us, because they compartmentalize everything. So when you go to do your part, they give you your two lines, but when you ask about the plot line, they say, we can't tell you. And they put together, so a lot of us will be talking, and we still can't figure out what the plot is. So we'll all find out at the same time.
Kumar Panja: Amazing. Well, we look forward to that as well. Okay, I think we're at time. That was excellent. Thank you so much, Joe and Riyad, for speaking with us today.
Riad Abrahams: Thank you.
Joe Dowling: Thank you for having us. Thanks to our listeners. Stay tuned for the next episode. In the meantime, stay well.

articles.title: What’s driving the municipal market’s remarkable growth? | RBCCM
articles.text:
The following conversation was recorded on September 29th, 2026.
Despite recent volatility, what is the outlook for U.S. Municipal Finance?
Bob Spangler: Rates are obviously up pretty dramatically but, fundamentally, the market remains strong.
We’re currently at $476 billion of issuance in our market. About $125 billion of that is refundings, which leaves new money at around $340 billion, and I think we will reach around $585 billion for the calendar year.
So, we're in a market now that's grown quite a bit. Part of that is a reflection of state and local governments’ responsibility in building infrastructure in the U.S, and part of it is inflationary.
Will rising rates slow refunding activity?
Spangler: 30% of the issuance year to date has been refunding. That compares to 25% on average over the last five years. We’ve had a run-up in refundings up through September but, with rates having risen as much as they have, we’re not anticipating that level of refundings going forward.
Do you expect new issuance to continue to grow?
Spangler: This is a $4.2 trillion market with more than 50,000 municipal issuers in the U.S.
Local governments continue to face ongoing funding needs for schools, roads, water and sewer systems, and other essential projects.
Local governments set out capital expenditures and project out what they need for three, five, 10 years out. So many of those capital needs will have to get funded no matter what. With that as a backdrop, the notion of us being in a market where we have elevated issuance for the next three to five years, if not beyond, is very real.

"The notion of us being in a market where we have elevated issuance for the next three to five years, if not beyond, is very real."
Bob Spangler, Head of U.S. Municipal Finance, RBC Capital Markets

Where are issuers deploying capital today and looking beyond traditional structures?
Spangler: In the current environment, issuers that compete against the taxable market are likely to be among the most active. We continue to see strength in single-family mortgage revenue bond issuance as the spread between tax-exempt and taxable funding has widened. Affordable housing, workforce housing and first-time homebuyer programs are all areas of continued focus.
We're also seeing significant activity in power and prepaid energy financing. Growing electricity demand from data centers is increasing the need for new generation capacity, while prepaid energy structures can help deliver meaningful savings directly to consumers. Prepaid gas deals now total more than $33 billion year to date, representing roughly 7% of the municipal market and already exceeding last year's volume.
Healthcare is another area of growth. Issuance is already running ahead of last year as providers look to improve efficiency and invest in their operations. We are also seeing growing interest in energy efficiency projects and industrial development bonds tied to reshoring and other public policy priorities.

"We’re also seeing a lot of focus on power. With all the data center buildout, this country needs every electron it can find."
Bob Spangler, Head of U.S. Municipal Finance RBC Capital Markets

Why has the market absorbed record issuance so well?
Keith Solomon: Despite increasing supply, the municipal market has benefited from a healthy supply-demand dynamic for several years.
Reinvestment cash continues to flow back into the market, while municipals have remained attractive to investors relative to other asset classes.
More recently, rising Treasury yields, inflation concerns and heavier new-issue supply have put pressure on municipal valuations. Yet that has also created opportunity.
As yields have moved higher, municipal bonds have become increasingly attractive to retail investors and crossover buyers evaluating relative value versus Treasuries. The result is renewed investor interest despite recent market volatility.

"Despite record supply, the muni market has remained remarkably resilient — reinvestment cash and steady inflows continue to support demand."
Keith Solomon, Head of Municipal Products, RBC Capital Markets

Has anything changed in relation to borrowers and their approach to capital?
Spangler: Our bread and butter remains state and local governments – schools, water and sewer, a lot of local transportation. Those will stay as long-term fixed-rate 20-, 25-, and 30-year bonds.
But what we’re starting to see is that those with a more dynamic revenue stream and cost basis are looking to be as creative as they can in finding products and reaching different investors.
How are investor expectations evolving?
Solomon: Investors are increasingly looking to get involved earlier in the process and seeking more customized opportunities.
Particularly within private capital, investors are looking for structures that better suit their needs while helping issuers access financing more effectively. That trend is creating greater flexibility in how deals are brought to market and funded.
How are we adding strategic value for issuers and investors?
Spangler: We’ve maintained a presence in the local markets where we've historically had strength.
That includes Texas, where we're currently the number one underwriter and represent roughly 15% of the market year to date.
We've continued investing in our core markets, including Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico, California, Illinois, Ohio and New Jersey, while combining that local presence with national sector expertise.
Our bank commitment to the municipal market, whether it be investors on third-party TOBs or directly as issuers, will exceed $25 billion by the end of this year.
This bank appreciates the market, appreciates the infrastructure and the vital nature of what we're funding, and appreciates that it is really the backbone of the U.S.
Solomon: We've maintained market share north of 10% in the new-issue market and have worked over the last three years to strengthen our position in the secondary market as well. By allocating more balance sheet to sales and trading, we've become a larger liquidity provider and a more meaningful counterparty for investors.
We've also expanded our high-yield capabilities, allowing us to pursue opportunities where other firms have pulled back or reallocated resources. As investors look for yield and more specialized opportunities, that part of the market has become increasingly important.
What is the outlook for municipal finance?
Solomon: While recent volatility has pressured the market, municipal bonds have historically proven resilient. Higher yields are attracting investor attention, and the market continues to benefit from strong long-term demand fundamentals.
Spangler: While refunding issuance may slow, the underlying need for capital remains. Infrastructure investment, housing, healthcare and other essential services will continue to require funding, supporting elevated issuance levels in the years ahead.

articles.title: Another Leg Up In US Inflation?
articles.text:
Another Leg Up In US Inflation?

Tan Kai Xian

Gavekal Research | 15 Oct 2026

US inflation accelerated in September, with the headline consumer price index rising 3.7% year-on-year, up from 3.4% in August. This was hardly surprising given elevated energy prices, which were bound to feed through to consumer prices (see No Good Outcomes For Energy Inflation). Looking ahead, geopolitics and energy prices will, of course, remain key swing factors for inflation. But beyond energy, the question for investors and policymakers is whether price pressures will spread through the economy, pushing up long-term inflation expectations, as some Federal Reserve officials fear. Two scenarios are worth considering.First, US inflation moves higher in the coming months, but long-term survey and market-based inflation expectations remain well anchored. This is the status quo, and it is likely to persist as long as rising inflation is largely driven by energy supply disruptions and markets remain confident in the Fed’s commitment to its inflation target. The disruption could prove temporary, whether because of peace deals or adjustments in supply chains and demand. Meanwhile, real borrowing costs in the US have risen across the board this year, increasing the risk of an economic slowdown. The widening of US high-yield corporate credit spreads, and perhaps yesterday’s -15% plunge in CoreWeave’s share price, point to growing financial strains. If energy prices and/or economic growth moderate, the rise in US inflation will likely be short-lived.

articles.title: Mapping the AI trade boom
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

13 Oct 2026

Mapping the AI trade boom

The global build-out of AI capacity is fuelling a trade boom in the goods needed to deliver it.

The global build-out of AI capacity is fuelling a trade boom in the goods needed to deliver it. We track 104 AI-related products, spanning semiconductors, servers, computing equipment, and other inputs and capital goods, and use them to construct an AI export index.

What you will learn:

Our basket of 104 AI-related products reveals a supply chain centred on Asia and dominated by intermediate goods (inputs such as chips and components), with the characteristics and geography of production creating distinct air, container, and overland freight networks.

Semiconductors account for around 34% of AI-related trade, with the rest spread across computers, networking equipment, power infrastructure, and other inputs. Intermediate goods account for around 60% of the basket, showing how far the AI investment boom reaches upstream into global supply chains.

Asia sits at the centre of AI-related trade, but economies play different roles within the supply chain. China is the largest exporter, while Taiwan is considerably more exposed to shifts in AI investment. The US is the largest importer, with its import mix weighted further downstream.

Air freight is the largest transport mode for AI-related trade, but freight networks differ sharply by mode.

This means a supply chain that spans several economies can still depend on a common regional freight network, leaving freight exposure less diversified than the geography of the supply chain might suggest.
