Motoring along: how Chinese EV production is powering the battery sector

View Milan Thakore's full profile

High fuel prices are good news for electric vehicle (EV) sales, a theme we’ve been monitoring closely since the start of the Iran war. France, UK, Sweden, Australia, Norway and China are among those reporting record EV penetration in September, while sales in Southeast Asia and Latin America are also surging.
But the global picture of switching from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric is far from uniform. I asked Milan Thakore, Principal Analyst in our Electric Vehicle and Battery Supply Chain team, how he sees things playing out.
Where have EV sales surged?
The global trend is up, with global EV (including battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle) sales increasing 14% year-on-year to end August. EVs now represent nearly one in three new car sales globally. However, at a regional level, the picture is patchy. In Europe and most emerging markets, Chinese EVs have set the benchmark in terms of affordability, and this is reflected in strong sales numbers in those markets.
The US has still not recovered from the withdrawal of supportive policy and EV penetration is down. Even ‘difficult-to-electrify’ markets like India are now overtaking the US in percentage terms. The surprise is China’s own domestic sales. Despite EV penetration approaching 70%, EV sales are down by nearly 1 million units from last year’s peak of 9 million.
What’s holding EVs back in China?
The entire vehicle market in China is tanking, with light vehicle sales across all power trains falling by 3.6 million units year-on-year. ICE vehicles account for the biggest share of the drop – more than double the hit to EVs – with the main factors high fuel costs, a shrinking pool of legacy replacement buyers and a weaker macroeconomic outlook. This twist has unexpectedly lifted EVs’ penetration rate almost to the country’s 2030 EV target four years ahead of time. High fuel costs are also changing consumer behaviour – owners with two vehicles are unsurprisingly favouring their EV and leaving the ICE car at home.
Will Chinese EVs manufacturers ramp up exports?
Big time, as they look to offset slowing growth domestically. More Chinese brands are coming to the market, with ever-improving vehicle designs and performance. Critically, they are priced very competitively to entice customers to often unheard-of brands. One such brand is Leapmotor, which has partnered with Stellantis, the world’s fifth-largest automaker.
Leapmotor’s B05 model sells at around €30,000 for which the buyer gets up to a 300-mile range and a wide array of features as standard, including ventilated seats, panoramic sunroof and the whole suite of safety features. A comparable German ICE model could cost up to €5,000 more once you’ve added on all the ‘extras’.
Could ‘NextGen’ batteries be transformational?
Yes. The latest LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries will hit international markets at the end of 2026. The largest battery makers, CATL and BYD, are amongst those pushing the technology, and others will follow. These will dramatically speed up charging from up to 30 minutes today to below 10 minutes. Charging infrastructure will have to move from kilowatts to the megawatt-level to achieve ‘flash’ charging. BYD doesn’t see this as a challenge.
Is Europe about to be swamped by Chinese exports?
Europe has the highest EV penetration outside China, with sales pushing towards 40%. Sustained subsidy support, abundant model availability, and high retail gasoline and diesel prices drove record September sales in most European countries.
Policymakers need to balance climate goals with defending European manufacturing and employment by supporting a local EV and battery manufacturing value chain. Chinese automative companies are already building manufacturing capacity and battery supply chains in Europe so European-made Chinese EVs will eventually replace imports. European OEMs are also investing heavily but will need to keep advancing to protect market share.  
Where else are EVs flourishing?
Sales in South America and Southeast Asia have all but doubled, driven primarily by a flood of imports from China. As in Europe, these regions want to keep manufacturing local, and Chinese automakers are already building out that capacity. East Asian BEV growth has also doubled as South Korean manufacturer Hyundai-Kia attempts to offset the drop off in US EV demand with sales into its home market.
Are we at an inflection point for EVs? There’s a good chance we are for two reasons. First, the evolving attractiveness of EVs as a product, particularly the quality of vehicles on offer, longer battery range and speed of charging all of which will continue to improve into the future. Secondly, the soaring cost of gasoline and diesel fuel in 2026 has shifted running costs massively in favour of EVs in all markets.
Our sense is that the Iran war will be seen as an inflection point, accelerating a trend already well underway, with EVs eating into ICE vehicles’ market share in many markets. The duration of both the conflict and high pump prices will determine how soon it unfolds – and how much road fuel demand is eroded. 
It’s possible that Wood Mackenzie’s base case assumption that global passenger EV penetration hits 50% by 2035 arrives a few years earlier.

articles.title: New Insurer Start-up Unit
articles.text:
New Insurer Start-up Unit

The New Insurer Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new insurer in the UK.

Thinking of becoming an insurerBeing an insurer means undertaking the regulated activities of effecting or carrying out contracts of insurance. Any firm that wants to be an insurer must be authorised to undertake these activities by the PRA with consent from the FCA. Before going through the new insurer authorisation process, firms will need to consider what functions they will carry out as an insurer and submit a regulatory business plan to outline their strategy and how it meets our threshold conditions. When you are ready to start the process, you should contact the NISU team by emailing NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk. Upon receipt of an enquiry with the regulatory business plan, we will arrange a meeting with you to get started with the pre-application and application phases. The NISU team are ready to help you become a UK authorised insurer, and please expand the headings below to find out more.

From a regulatory perspective, an insurer is a firm with a ‘Part 4A permission’ that includes the activities of effecting contracts of insurance or carrying out contracts of insurance. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 sets out a list of relevant regulated activities (see Chapter III Insurance) but does not attempt an exhaustive definition of a contract of insurance. Potential applicants should refer to section 6 of the FCA’s Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG 6 - FCA Handbook Opens in a new window) for Guidance on the identification of contracts of insurance. The section Guidance on insurance mediation activities in section 5 may also be helpful (PERG 5 - FCA Handbook Opens in a new window).
The UK insurance market covers various lines of business, to list a few:
Non-life class of business:
• Accident and sickness
• Motor vehicle liability and other motor vehicle insurance
• Fire and other damage to property
• Marine, aviation and railway rolling sock
• General Liability
• Credit and suretyship
• Other classes
Life class of business:
• Life and annuity
• Marriage and birth
• Linked long term
• Permanent health
• Capital redemption
• Pension fund management
• Collective insurance
Depending on the area of the insurance market you plan to enter, there may be alternatives which allow you to offer similar products through another insurer without becoming a direct insurer yourself. For example, if you are interested in working in a niche area of the market or perhaps prefer to test your product first, operating as an intermediary under some form of delegated authority from an existing insurer e.g. as a managing general agent (MGA) may be more appropriate. There are a range of intermediaries, and the most appropriate route will depend on a number of factors, e.g. through which sales channels the insurance will be sold. Information on how to apply for intermediary activities can be accessed via the following link to the FCA website: apply to become a consumer investments firm Opens in a new window.
A firm wanting to sell regulated products but not wishing to become directly authorised can also agree with a PRA and/or FCA authorised firm to become its appointed representative (AR). Insurance mediation activities that an appointed representative can carry out are set out in the FCA handbook Opens in a new window, however, the AR is limited to only carrying out the regulated activities the authorised firm has permission to undertake. A prospective AR will undergo fitness and propriety checks and will have to follow the rules and procedures as set by the authorised firm. Rules relating to appointed representatives are set out in SUP 12 of the FCA Handbook and applicants can also get further information about the application process via the following link to the FCA website: become an appointed representative Opens in a new window.
Will my firm be subject to the Solvency II Directive?
Within the United Kingdom, newly authorised insurers and reinsurers will be subject to the Solvency II regime if they meet all the conditions stated in PRA Rulebook. Insurance General Application | Prudential Regulation Authority Handbook & Rulebook Opens in a new window.
Firms that are not subject to the Solvency II regime are known as ‘Non-Directive Firms Opens in a new window’ and are subject to different rules around key areas such as capital requirements, governance requirements, and reporting requirements. Applicants should consider whether their firm will be subject to the Solvency II regime when preparing any application and plan accordingly.
What business will your insurer carry out?
Before contacting us, you should familiarise yourself with the PRA’s expectations around key topics such as governance and financial resources. Further information on financial planning may be found in SS4/18 Opens in a new window, while the PRA’s expectations regarding governance are detailed in SS5/16 Opens in a new window. The full range of PRA publications containing guidance on a broad range of topics may be found at Prudential regulation publications Opens in a new window.
It is important that you consider the following key areas, as these are things we will initially want to focus on in our review.
• Regulatory business plan
• Senior management, the board and governance
• Financial resources
• IT strategy
• Reinsurance
• Resolution
• Outsourcing
What if your firm is already authorised?
If your firm is already authorised by the FCA, e.g. as an intermediary, you will need to apply to the PRA and FCA to vary your permissions to add insurance activities. While this is legally a different regulatory transaction to a new authorisation, you will need to follow the same process as a new firm applying to be an insurer (because of the substantive change to your business model) and we encourage you to start pre-application with us as normal to help the process of varying your permissions run smoothly.
When can I call myself an Insurer?
A firm cannot call itself an insurer until it has been authorised. The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘Insurance’ and ‘Insurer’, ‘reassurer, ‘reinsurance’, ‘reassurance’, ’reinsurer’, ‘underwriter’ and ‘underwriting’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation in order to prevent the public from being misled. You should seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words, checking the guidance found at sensitive business names Opens in a new window.
What are the next steps?
As mentioned earlier, when you are ready to start the process, you should contact the NISU team by emailing NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk to discuss your application and we will arrange an initial pre-application meeting. The NISU team are ready to help you become a UK authorised insurer.

The pre-application stage helps the firm to:

Meet the NISU team
Understand how the authorisation process works
Understand regulatory expectations of the firm, in particular, the PRA and FCA Threshold Conditions
Submit an application that is as complete as possible when the firm is ready to formally apply for authorisation
Identify any particular concerns that we might have early on and help you to decide whether you want to spend time and money on an application that may not progress further

It helps the NISU Team to:

Meet the firm and understand their business proposal
Identify any concerns, which will be communicated quickly to the firm and gives the firm the opportunity to resolve them before submitting an application
Deal with the firm’s application quickly once it has been submitted

The table below outlines what we expect from firms during the pre-application process and what you can expect from the NISU team.

Firm’s Responsibilities

NISU Team’s Responsibilities

Be open, honest and collaborate with us.

Be open, honest and give clear feedback on your proposals.

Develop your plans, complete the necessary work, prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us.

The PRA and FCA will attend all meetings unless we advise you otherwise.

Ensure key individuals at your firm who will drive the proposition forward are involved throughout the process and attend the pre-application meetings.

Ensure the pre-application meeting is productive, and the authorisation process is clearly explained.

Provide all information that you think we should be aware of. Be ready, willing and organised.

Hold the appropriate number of meetings for your application (maximum of 3) giving due consideration to the proposals in the business plan.

Address and incorporate any feedback provided by us into your Business Plan before moving to the next stage.

Ensure feedback letter is sent to the Firm within a maximum of 10 working days after each meeting.

Please note that the NISU team do not provide a consultancy service or legal advice.
We offer a maximum of three meetings for standard applications. However, additional meetings may be arranged if a firm’s proposal involves innovative or particularly complex IT systems. These meetings include the initial meeting, feedback meeting, and challenge session. Established firms, such as those seeking to open new branches or subsidiaries in the UK, may require fewer meetings.

Initial meeting
The initial meeting is held after the submission of a high-level business plan summarising your plans. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 10 working days before we meet. Once you have sent us your materials, we will arrange the meeting at a mutually convenient time and agree on the agenda for the meeting.

The business plan should not be a ‘sales pitch’ as the regulators will have a different focus, and you should aim to provide an explanation of why you want to be an insurer and your business strategy including:

Business plan – products, target market, customer types
Sources of funding – how will the business be funded and details of any investors and/or funding in place
Project plan – an overview and timeline of your plan to set up the new insurer. (This is particularly important if new IT systems are required)
Owner and controllers – details of proposed owners and controllers
Corporate governance – details of structure, board, senior management and governance arrangements

The initial meeting provides an opportunity for firms to discuss their plans with us and ask questions about the authorisation process. It provides the NISU team with the opportunity to raise any concerns with the proposed business at an early stage.

The NISU team will then provide written feedback to the firm within 10 working days of the meeting to enable the firm to respond to and resolve any issues. You should continue to develop your business proposition and incorporate responses to our feedback into the next version

Feedback meeting
The feedback meeting will be held after the firm has submitted, and we have reviewed, a more detailed business plan, which includes the firm’s response to the feedback from the initial meeting. This meeting provides an opportunity to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the firm’s proposed business model. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 10 working days before we meet. After the meeting, the NISU team will provide written feedback to the firm which we expect the firm to address in their subsequent business plan.

At the end of the feedback meeting, we will discuss the actions you will need to complete if you want to progress to the next stage. Within 10 working days of the meeting, we will send you our formal feedback in a letter. You should continue to develop your business plan and incorporate responses to our feedback into the next version.

Challenge session
The challenge session are the culmination of the pre-application application process. This final meeting is held just before a firm submits an application. The aim of the meeting is to discuss your proposals in depth and provide detailed challenge on the content of the final business plan. At this stage, your business plan should be fully developed and will form the basis of the discussion at the challenge session where we will offer an honest and open assessment of your plans. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 15 working days before we meet. Once you have sent us your materials, we will arrange the meetings at a mutually convenient time.

Firms can expect rigorous challenge on their proposed business model. The aim is to identify any remaining issues that need to be addressed before you submit your application. The challenge session will be attended by your case officers along with senior representatives and specialists from both regulators. We expect several of your executives and, where possible, non-executives to attend. You should expect the meeting to last about two hours.

At the end of the challenge session, we will discuss next steps and actions with you and within 10 working days of the meeting, we will send you our formal feedback in a letter. If you go on to submit an application, you should finalise your business plan and incorporate responses to our feedback from the challenge session.

The meetings will typically be held at the PRA’s office in London. The meetings can be held in person or virtual. We will send you an agenda before all meetings which will centre on your explanation of the materials that you have sent us and the attendees from each regulator.

Our aim is that the pre-application process will give the firm a clearer understanding of our regulatory expectations, and the opportunity to resolve any potential problems before an application is submitted. Once the application is submitted, it is expected to be of sufficiently high quality to enable the NISU team to reach a decision more quickly.

Pre-application timeframes
The pace at which a firm progresses through the pre-application stage is up to the firm. Please read through the application forms and supporting notes as you may find them helpful when preparing for the meetings.

The NISU team expect to be kept up to date on your progress and will endeavour to hold pre-application meetings in a timely manner. If, however, we do not hear from a firm for six months after a meeting we will assume that you do not want to proceed with your application and close our file.

Please contact the NISU inbox at NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk and submit a high-level regulatory business plan along with your request for a pre-application meeting. We will then organise the meeting with you. The firm’s advisors or consultants are welcome to attend the pre-application meetings, but we do not expect them to speak on the firm’s behalf.

Please note that the pre-application stage is optional. If you choose not to use it, you can send your application directly to the NISU inbox at NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk. We will then use our statutory powers as set out in FSMA to reach a decision on your application. If you have any questions about the pre-application process, please contact the NISU team, and we will be happy to assist.

Your Business Plan should cover the following points as a minimum:

business plan – details of products, delivery channels and target market
business viability – competitive advantage, market research and how your firm will make money
financial resources – financial projections (for three years), capital management strategy (as appropriate)
sources of funding – proposed funding model
owners and controllers – proposed owners and controllers
corporate governance – structure, board, senior management and governance arrangements
risk management – risk management and control framework
customer journey – products, pricing, complaint handling and on-boarding arrangements (including Anti-Money Laundering/Know Your Customer processes)
outsourcing - details of key outsourcing arrangements
IT infrastructure and systems and timescales for implementation and testing recovery and resolution plans (if appropriate)
policies and procedures – operational and regulatory policies and procedures
business continuity – business continuity plans (if appropriate)
scope of permissions – details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake reinsurance arrangements
project plan – project plan for setting up the insurer

Background to NISUThe New Insurer Start-Up Unit (NISU) is a joint initiative by the UK’s financial regulators, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), set up in 2018.NISU is a team of experts across the PRA and FCA that provides necessary information and support to prospective insurers, aiding their progression to become authorised UK insurers. Our joint assessment process ensures any firm wishing to be an insurer is authorised by both the PRA and FCA.NISU’s objective is to guide firms through the authorisation process by leading efficient pre-application engagement and formalising the application process. We frequently explore initiatives to improve our process and contribute to the PRA’s and FCA’s secondary competitiveness objectives.This NISU guidance serves as a reference tool covering key supervisory topics. While it provides valuable information, it is not exhaustive and does not encompass all applicable UK laws and regulations. Prospective firms should use this webpage to aid their business planning and ensure compliance with all relevant regulatory requirements in the UK. Before commencing the new insurer authorisation process, firms should also consider whether setting up an insurer is right for them and what functions they will carry out. The regulatory business plan (RBP) they develop must outline their strategy and how they will meet and comply with PRA and FCA threshold conditions.We also encourage prospective UK insurers to take advantage of our PRA and FCA pre-application meetings as they can be extremely beneficial for all parties.

Authorisation process and regulatory expectationsTo achieve their objective of setting up an insurer, firms should be ready, willing and organised. It is important for firms to understand the authorisation process and regulatory expectations before submitting an application to us. This will ensure that the application submitted is of high-quality and as complete as possible. Read the New insurer authorisation process and regulatory expectations.
This section clarifies why submitting a complete application is important and gives an indication of what happens during our assessment process, including decision timelines.
Please be aware that authorisation is only the start of a new insurer’s journey to being established. In our guidance below, we have outlined some of our key regulatory expectations, but firms are responsible for considering in detail and complying with all the applicable laws, rules and regulatory policies.Mobilisation regime for new insurersThe PRA created a ‘mobilisation’ regime, effective from 31 December 2024, to facilitate new insurer expansion and entry into the UK market. We welcome discussions with potential new applicants who are applying for authorisation and considering using this new mobilisation phase.

The regime offers an optional stage, beginning at the point of authorisation, during which a new firm can operate with business restrictions while it completes the final development aspects of its insurer. These newly authorised insurers-in-mobilisation are given a period up of 12 months to finish building out their business, including securing additional funding, if required, while operating with business restrictions and proportionate regulatory requirements, as well as adhering to lower minimum capital requirements. Read the mobilisation regime for insurers webpage for further information.For more details on the mobilisation framework for new insurers, refer to:
CP12/23 - Review of Solvency II: Adapting to the UK insurance market
PS2/24 – Review of Solvency II: Adapting to the UK insurance market

Other pathwaysAs well as the formal new insurer authorisations process guidance above, there are other pathways available for firms to consider.

Insurance special purpose vehicles (ISPVs)As part of our amendments to allow the UK non-life insurance sector to play a bigger role in the global ILS market, we have created an accelerated pathway for ISPVs that meet certain defined criteria to gain approval. In such cases, the PRA will undertake rapid assessment of applications and, where satisfied, issue approvals within 10 working days of a 'complete' application submission.We recommend early engagement with the NISU team at the PRA, to assist with ensuring completeness of your ISPV application. Email us at ISPVMailbox@bankofengland.co.uk if you are interested in this accelerated route.The specific criteria for the accelerated 10 working day ISPV process can be found here: PRA's approach to authorising and supervising UK Insurance Special Purpose Vehicles Opens in a new window.For more information, visit insurance special purpose vehicles (ISPVs) Opens in a new window, where you can also find applicable application forms for ISPVs, to be submitted to ISPVMailbox@bankofengland.co.uk.

Wholesale insurance accelerated authorisation pathwayThrough the Wholesale Insurance Accelerated Authorisation Pathway (The Pathway), developed jointly by the PRA and FCA, we aim to provide an accelerated route to authorisation for a sub-set of London Market wholesale applicants.Read our wholesale insurance accelerated authorisation pathway Opens in a new window webpage for more information.

Submitting an applicationThis section lists the relevant application forms and provides details about applicable fees once you are ready to submit an application.

Application feesThe PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with the PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and the FCA Handbook Opens in a new window. It is your responsibility to cross-check the fees against the PRA Rulebook and FCA guidelines before making any payment. If you are unsure what fees are applicable to your firm, please email us at NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:Account name: FCA Collection account
Bank name: Lloyds Bank
Account number: 00828179
Sort code: 30-00-02
Swift code: LOYD GB 2LCTY
Iban code: GB68 LOYD 3000 0200 8281 79.When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to:fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.If you cannot make payment to the FCA using BACS. Please contact NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk for instructions on how to pay by cheque.

Applications forms

Full authorisation application form (DOCX) Opens in a new window

Authorisation with restriction (mobilisation) application form (DOCX) Opens in a new window
Branch application/re-domiciliation form (DOCX) Opens in a new window
Supplement for Lloyd's managing agents - notes (DOC) Opens in a new window
Supplement for Lloyd's managing agents (DOC) Opens in a new window

Corporate controller form (docx) Opens in a new window
Partnership controller form (docx) Opens in a new window
Individual controller form (docx) Opens in a new window
Trust controller form (docx) Opens in a new window

IT self-assessment questionnaire: insurers (xlsm)
Detailed IT controls form: insurers (xlsm)

Waivers and modifications applications (pdf)
Application form: Solvency II approval (pdf)

Form A – Long: Application to perform controlled functions (long) (pdf) Opens in a new window
Form A – Short: Application to perform controlled functions (short) (pdf) Opens in a new window
SOR: Statement of responsibilities (pdf) Opens in a new window
Form M: Notification of non-executive director or key function holder (pdf) Opens in a new window

Being an authorised insurerAuthorisation is only the start of the journey to becoming an established insurer. Insurers must continue to meet our threshold conditions at all times, as well as ongoing regulatory requirements under both PRA and FCA Supervision.

Insurers must submit regular financial, risk, and conduct reports, and ensure frameworks and policies are continually reviewed to align with risks and business growth.

As supervision evolves over time, the PRA and FCA adopt a risk-based approach, adjusting oversight based on an insurer’s size, complexity and risk profile. As staying informed is essential, the PRA and FCA provide ongoing industry guidance, thematic reviews, and policy updates that insurers must follow to ensure compliance.

Read Being an authorised insurer for further information.

FAQsVisit our Frequently asked questions page for common queries regarding the application process.

Authorised insurersVisit Which firms does the PRA regulate? for a list of authorised insurers regulated by the PRA.

Contact usIf you have any queries about becoming a new insurer, email us:NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk.The NISU is part of the regulators’ ongoing work to improve the authorisation process for prospective new insurers in the UK. We want the process, information and materials to be helpful for potential applicants so that we can have an effective and efficient way of working together, and lead to an improved quality of application when the time comes. It’s really important that we hear from you, the users of the NISU, about what is working well and what we can improve.As our consideration of further developments relating to the authorisation of new insurers continues, we are also interested to hear views on challengers faced by the firm in the insurance industry and possible measures to address them. Please email NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk with your feedback and input.

In Europa, dem Nahen Osten und Afrika sowie im asiatisch-pazifischen Raum gilt dieses Material als Marketingmaterial, in den USA ist dies jedoch nicht der Fall. Es kann keine Zusicherung gegeben werden, dass Prognosen oder Ziele erreicht werden können. Prognosen basieren auf Annahmen, Schätzungen, Meinungen und hypothetischen Modellen, die sich als falsch erweisen können. Die Wertentwicklung in der Vergangenheit ist kein Hinweis auf zukünftige Renditen. Die Wertentwicklung bezieht sich auf einen Nominalwert, der auf Kursgewinnen/-verlusten beruht und die Inflation nicht berücksichtigt. Die Inflation wirkt sich negativ auf die Kaufkraft dieses nominalen Geldwerts aus. Je nach aktuellem Inflationsniveau kann dies zu einem realen Wertverlust führen, selbst wenn die nominale Wertentwicklung der Anlage positiv ist. Investitionen sind mit Risiken verbunden. Der Wert einer Anlage kann sowohl fallen als auch steigen, und Sie erhalten möglicherweise zu keinem Zeitpunkt den ursprünglich investierten Betrag zurück. Ihr Kapital kann gefährdet sein.

Die Inhalte und Materialien auf dieser Website können als Marketingmaterial betrachtet werden. Der Marktpreis einer Anlage kann sowohl fallen als auch steigen, und Sie erhalten möglicherweise nicht den ursprünglich investierten Betrag zurück.Die auf diesen Webseiten enthaltenen Produkte, Dienstleistungen, Informationen und/oder Materialien sind möglicherweise nicht für Einwohner bestimmter Gerichtsbarkeiten verfügbar. Hedging US Growth Stocks

Tan Kai Xian

Gavekal Research | 12 Oct 2026

US growth stocks have proved remarkably resilient, with the MSCI US growth index generally outperforming its value counterpart since 2007. The surge in bond yields in 2022 briefly reversed this trend, but growth stocks regained the upper hand in 2023. Given the jump in oil prices and US bond yields this year, one might have expected a repeat of 2022. Not so. The MSCI US growth index has lagged the value index by just 3.7pp so far this year. But when everything is going well, prudent investors look for potential pitfalls. So, what could derail the strength of US growth stocks, and how can one hedge against these risks?

articles.title: ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
European UCITS ETFs (EU regulated exchange-traded funds) attracted a record €125 billion in the third quarter, taking year-to-date inflows to almost €350 billion. Global equities led the way, Europe rebounded and emerging markets recovered, while Chinese equity ETFs continued to see outflows.

As Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research, explains to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, fixed-income ETFs also attracted strong inflows, particularly into government bonds and ultra-short-duration products, despite rising yields. “Active ETFs also continued their rapid growth, which we believe highlights investors’ appetite for new strategies.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into the forces shaping ETF flows and investor positioning.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Daniel Dornel

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing the latest ETF (exchange-traded fund) fund flows. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research. Welcome, Daniel, and thanks for joining me.

Daniel Dornel: Thank you, Daniel. I’m very happy to be here.

DM: As always, Daniel, it’s been an eventful quarter. One of the key surprises has been the resilience of equity markets. When you’ve seen the big increase in yields for government bonds, typically a rise in interest rates goes with the decline in equity markets but, so far, they seem to have shrugged that off. In terms of ETF flows, what are the dynamics you’ve seen in the third quarter?

DD: It has been a remarkable period. Q3 was the strongest quarter ever, with inflows around €125 billion. What’s really impressive is that we are seeing a pattern of breaking records one quarter after another. If we look closer at the monthly breakdown, July and August were the two largest months ever recorded in the UC[ITS] ETF landscape, with July alone bringing in over €50 billion.

This momentum is carrying us into an historic year. Year to date, we have already seen almost €350 billion inflows into UC[ITS] ETF[s], which means we have already surpassed the total full-year figure from last year, €327 billion.

While the growth is broad, equity projects dominated the landscape this quarter, capturing almost €100 billion of those €125 billion of total inflows.

DM: It’s interesting that you say that because there’s been a long discussion about cash on the sidelines and whether or not investors are willing to put that cash to work. And it seems from the figures you cite for ETF flows, maybe they are. We also see the strong performance of equity markets being followed by flows into ETFs. Clearly that’s a strong support for the market. Are there any particular categories or products that stand out?

DD: Without doubt, global equities have been standing out. In Q3, they attracted just under €55 billion. This isn’t a sudden spike; it is a sustained trend we have been seeing from last year.

Just to give a few figures, the year-to-date figure for global equities is already €145 billion compared to just under €100 billion for last year. So global equities now represent about a third of all equity flows.

What is particularly interesting is the acceleration in all-country exposures – a blend between developed and emerging market equities. Historically, they have been behind developed-only global equities. But on this particular sub-category, we have seen a jump from €40 billion last year to €83 billion on a year-to-date basis. This suggests investors are looking for the more diversified product[s] they can find these days.

DM: I would imagine these inflows into global ETFs, including emerging markets, probably has something to do with the strong performance we’ve seen, particularly in Taiwan and [South] Korea, around semiconductors and tech hardware. I think investors are looking to try to tap into that dynamic. Speaking of dynamics, is there anything else that you see across equity markets?

DD: Let’s start with the US. After a very strong acceleration in Q2, the appetite for US equity remained, with €23 billion in flows in Q3, again mostly concentrated in core exposures.

Moving on to Europe, we saw an interesting rebound in Q3, with €9 billion inflows. This suggests a return in confidence from investors after a very difficult Q2 where we had around €5 billion [of] outflows. We also saw an acceleration in emerging markets, bringing in €6.8 billion, a recovery from a quiet second quarter on emerging markets.

However, it hasn’t been positive everywhere. China continues to be a challenge, and we saw another difficult quarter with €1.5 billion outflows from Chinese equity product.

Looking at sub-asset classes, sector and thematic ETF[s] brought in €15 billion, the lion’s share driven by IT and tech-related themes. But there were two interesting additional trends, with healthcare – we saw €1.5 billion inflows there – and Eurozone banks, with €1.3 billion inflows.

DM: That is encouraging that you’re starting to see inflows again into Europe. We’re seeing that all the investment that the region is putting towards strategic autonomy, defence and so on is starting to bear some fruit. It’s also interesting that, despite the inflows into emerging markets, you still see outflows from Chinese ETFs. And we appreciate that tech is a big driver for the interest in emerging markets.

I started out saying we’ve had [a] surprisingly strong performance for equity markets despite the big increase in [bond] yields. I’m curious if that increase in government bond yields has had an impact on flows for fixed-income ETFs?

DD: Fixed income had a very strong quarter as well, bringing in €27 billion. The primary engine was government bonds, with €10 billion inflows. It was a mix of all maturity exposures, especially on global and euro bonds, as well as short-term maturities, especially on US, but also on European exposures.

We also saw a significant interest in ultra-short instruments, which brought €8 billion. Roughly half of that was on overnight euro exposures and 25% in US Treasuries with a maturity from zero to one year on corporate investment grade.

We also see some flows there with €4 billion, a split between US all-maturity product and euro short term. The only area of weakness was a yield with a significant slowdown, only €500 million inflows over the quarter, primarily because of the September figures where we had very negative flows on euro high yield.

DM: The outflows for high yield are relevant, as I’ve heard from our portfolio managers. That was one of the key drivers behind the increase in yields and spreads that you saw for high yield, particularly in September. Last word on ETF flows for the quarter?

DD: I’d like to highlight the rise of active ETFs again. This is where things are moving quite rapidly. In Q3 alone we saw €11 billion of inflows. This brings us on a year-to-date basis to €34 billion, so roughly 10% of the flows and it’s already ahead of [the] 2025 figure, which was just under 30 billion.

So, the dynamic is very impressive, especially on enhanced strategies and equity income strategies. But it’s not just about the flows, it’s also about the product innovation. If you look at all the ETFs launched in Europe year-to-date, 40% were active ETF[s] – that’s already over 100 new funds this year.

DM: If I can summarise some of the key points, you said not only was the third quarter the strongest ever in terms of ETF flows, but recently almost every quarter is the strongest, so it really does seem there’s a lot of momentum behind ETFs.

You highlighted that flows are going more towards global equities, conceivably as investors are looking to tap into the tech dynamic in emerging markets. That said, you also saw a rebound of flows into Europe, so another renewed bout of optimism.

And finally, positive inflows into fixed income despite the increase in [bond] yields. But you highlighted that this is tend[ing] to be short duration, so investors less at risk of rising yields and able to pick up some income in the meantime.

Daniel, thank you very much for joining me.

DD: Thank you, Daniel. Always a pleasure.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in ETFs, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at Viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better-informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

Consistency Through Cycles: Private Market Secondaries

Apollo Academy

October 13, 2026

LinkedIn

Email

Email

LinkedIn

Twitter

Close

Private market secondaries have evolved from a niche liquidity tool into an essential component of the private markets ecosystem. With 2025 volume reaching record highs, secondaries trading still represents only ~2% of overall private market size—pointing to a market with significant room to grow.1 Secondary strategies acquire seasoned portfolios, often at a discount, and can offer a distinct combination of attributes, potentially delivering competitive returns in normal markets, smaller losses in downturns, and full participation in recoveries. In our view, this turnkey access to a diversified portfolio makes the asset class an increasingly important complement and potential core portfolio allocation. As the market continues to grow and evolve, however, we believe manager selection and platform capabilities will become increasingly important to navigating a broader and more complex opportunity set.

Attractive Excess Return per Unit of Risk versus other Private Market Strategies

When comparing historical returns across alternatives over a 15-year period, secondaries earned a 12.6% median net IRR with a 16.4-point spread between bottom- and top-decile outcomes, which is a much narrower band of outcomes compared to other strategies.

Secondaries: Competitive historical returns…

…with the narrowest range of outcomes

Note: Represents top minus bottom decile net IRR across equity private market strategies with 2005 to 2020 vintages. Source: PitchBook Global Fund Performance Report as of Q4 2025 (Vintages 2005-2020). Latest data available. Data is a comparison of private secondary investments and private capital investments sourced from PitchBook’s database. PitchBook data is typically compiled from funds that elect to self-report to Pitchbook and where publicly available. Thus, this data may not be representative of all funds and may be biased toward those funds that generally have higher performance. This performance data reflects the fees, carried interest, and other expenses of the funds included in the data set.

The median return for secondaries outperformed real assets, venture capital and real estate, and delivered nearly the same median return as private equity (12.6% versus 13.5%), but with a range of outcomes that was approximately 39% narrower. At the bottom decile, secondaries still generated a positive 4.8% net IRR, compared with 1.4% for private equity, demonstrating the strong nature of the asset class for the period.

The contrast is even more pronounced relative to higher-risk strategies such as venture capital, which had a 35.6-point spread and a bottom-decile return of negative 3.5%.

Secondaries can offer attractive entry points during periods of market dislocation

When comparing PitchBook’s full population of active secondaries funds versus all other private capital strategies that the database tracks (private debt, real estate, real assets, venture capital, private equity and fund of funds), secondaries have outperformed many private capital strategies through every major shock of the past two decades. For example, in the Global Financial Crisis secondaries fell about half as much, roughly negative 10% against negative 20% for the full private capital universe, and stayed positive through the inflation shock, earning about 7% in 2022 against roughly 1.5% for private capital. They also captured the upside, leading the rebound with 44% in 2021 against 34% for private capital broadly. By buying seasoned portfolios at discounts when other investors need liquidity, secondary strategies can turn market stress into attractive entry points.

This strength of secondaries is broad-based. The past two decades saw four market shocks with four different causes: a credit crisis, a sovereign debt crisis, a pandemic, and an inflation spike. Secondaries have demonstrated relative outperformance in each instance.

Secondaries’ Long Track Record Across Market Cycles

Source: PitchBook; based on calendar-year returns through year end 2025. The Secondaries dataset covers PitchBook’s full population of active secondaries funds and includes both newer and more mature funds; the Private Capital data set is private capital investments sourced from PitchBook’s database.

Beyond Returns: Secondaries may offer additional portfolio construction benefits

Because secondaries invest in funds that are already well into their lifecycle, capital can be deployed more quickly, distributions begin sooner, and the J-curve effect is significantly reduced. Exposure can be diversified across managers, vintages, sectors, and hundreds of underlying companies, potentially reducing concentration risk. At the same time, investors acquire portfolios with established assets rather than committing to blind pools, which may provide greater transparency into the underlying investments.

Market shocks can have less impact on assets that are closer to exit than entry. As a result, valuations and cash flows may be less sensitive than those of newly raised primary funds deployed at market peaks. During periods of dislocation, the opportunity set often expands as liquidity needs drive attractive secondary transactions. Investors with flexible capital can acquire LP interests at discounts or provide liquidity through GP-led continuation vehicles, turning periods of market stress into potential opportunities to deploy capital on favorable terms.

Taken together, these characteristics are what make secondaries a differentiated strategy, and one that we believe will continue to perform well through cycles and generate attractive risk-adjusted returns.

Manager selection is increasingly important

Investors considering secondary allocations in today’s market have important dynamics to consider. Through 2020, the secondary market opportunity set was largely LP-led, i.e., institutional investors selling fund stakes to rebalance portfolios or raise liquidity. Since 2021, however, GP-led deals, particularly single-asset continuation vehicles, have become a meaningful share of supply. That shift expands the opportunity set and, we believe, has the potential to lift median returns. But it also introduces more dispersion as GP-led transactions tend to be more concentrated investments with greater return potential.

The structural advantages that have made the asset class strong across cycles remain firmly intact. What’s changed is that the asset class has become more dynamic, as the secondary market reached $226 billion of annual volume in 2025, a record high and a 41% year-over-year increase.1

This dynamic and expanding landscape requires a manager and investment platform with the sourcing relationships, analytical breadth and depth, unique portfolio perspectives and industry and company-level insights, and structuring capability to navigate a more complex market.

As part of Apollo’s broader investment platform, S3 can also draw on perspectives and insights across strategies, industries and individual companies to inform underwriting and identify opportunities across the secondary market.

For investors, that’s ultimately good news. A larger, more sophisticated opportunity set in the hands of the right manager can mean more ways to put capital to work at attractive terms, in any market environment.

1 Source: Evercore 2025 Secondary Market Highlights (January 2026).

articles.title: First Meeting with a Financial Advisor | Wells Fargo Advisors
articles.text:
Day One With Your Financial Advisor

Preparing for your first meeting

Your first meeting with your Financial Advisor marks the beginning of an important professional relationship. Just as you rely on your doctor with your health and your mechanic with your car, you’ll be entrusting your Financial Advisor with something of great value too — your financial goals.

call out

Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client.

end call out

Our Financial Advisors work with many types of investors and value their diversity. Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client — so he or she can understand the best way to help you with your investment needs and life goals.

The right fit

Meeting with a Financial Advisor for the first time, you should expect a friendly, casual conversation — you’re just getting to know each other. There’s no obligation, no pressure, no judgment — and no cost for your first meeting. You should be candid about your level of investing experience, overall financial situation, and financial goals. You should also feel comfortable asking as many questions as you’d like.
It’s important you choose a Financial Advisor who listens to your concerns, understands your financial needs, and values your input. The relationship between you and your Financial Advisor is a critical one — through the years, you should have many sensitive, private conversations. The relationship may even expand to include friends and future generations of your family.

Getting ready

Before the meeting, your Financial Advisor should send you a checklist of items to bring. Your privacy is a top priority, and your Financial Advisor is committed to maintaining strict confidentiality.
A good Financial Advisor will want the right fit for you as much you seek the right fit in him or her. Before your first consultation, you’ll want to reflect on and be prepared to discuss:

Your values about money and your vision for your future
What life events are happening or could potentially happen
Short- and long-term life and financial goals
Investment questions
Your current financial situation
Preferred account management style

Remember, the more you share about your financial picture, investment goals, and risk tolerance, the better your Financial Advisor will be able to recommend strategies and create an investment plan. You’ll find the initial meeting with your Financial Advisor will set the stage for many conversations to come.

Next steps

Think about how you prefer to work with your advisor and what types of investments you’re interested in.
Gather the necessary documentation for your initial meeting and prepare answers to questions your advisor may ask.

articles.text: Market update - October 8th, 20263 min readDataFlows cooled, long yields hit a two-decade high, and Bitcoin ground higherDigital asset fund flows have lost momentum over the week, a marked slowdown after US$11.1B of inflows since mid-July. Much of that earlier demand appears to have reflected investors buying at depressed valuations, though we also believe concerns around US fiscal sustainability have become an increasingly important part of the allocation case.The Treasury is intervening, and it is not workingTreasury yields have continued to rise despite the government’s expanded long-end buyback programme, with 10-year yields moving above 5.3% and 30-year yields reaching 5.7%, their highest levels in more than two decades.¹ The Treasury has not stopped intervening, but the response has not intensified as yields have climbed. Long-end liquidity-support buybacks were doubled in August to at least US$4B per operation and remain in place through early November.² The limited effect on yields reinforces the sense that investors are focused on the underlying fiscal position rather than on short-term market support. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also softened his rhetoric, acknowledging that Treasury cannot simply control the bond market and pointing instead to higher oil prices as an important driver of the rise in yields.The Fed is being pulled in two directionsMonetary policy signals have meanwhile remained unusually mixed. Some Fed officials continue to emphasise elevated inflation, while others have highlighted growing downside risks from the labour market. September payrolls were considerably weaker than expected and pushed the implied probability of an October hike down to 23%, from 71% three weeks ago. Despite that move, markets still expect inflation rather than employment to determine the next major policy decision.That helps explain why the weaker employment picture has not produced a more decisive rally in Bitcoin. Economic activity remains comparatively resilient: PMIs this week have continued to point to expansion, while consumer spending and other activity indicators have held up better than the labour data might suggest.3 At the same time, energy prices remain elevated, partly because of the Iran conflict, leaving the Fed with an uncomfortable combination of softer employment and persistent inflation pressure.In our view, the absence of flow momentum reflects uncertainty rather than deteriorating fundamentals. Investors are trying to reconcile three conflicting signals: weaker employment, stubborn inflation and an increasingly uncomfortable fiscal position.Why the bond market may matter more than the FedOf those three, the bond market may ultimately prove the most important. September was the worst month for US government bonds in four years, with the 10-year yield rising by more than 50 basis points. Higher yields would normally be a headwind for Bitcoin through tighter financial conditions. But if those yields increasingly reflect concerns about the sustainability of US public finances rather than stronger growth, the interpretation changes. Bitcoin begins to look less like a conventional risk asset and more like an alternative to government-issued money.The market has not resolved that question yet. The labour market is weakening, growth is holding up and inflation remains the Fed’s primary concern. That combination has been enough to keep Bitcoin moving gradually higher. What would turn a grind into a breakout is flows following the fiscal argument rather than the rate argument, and that is the number to watch over the coming weeks.Sources:1. 16 October 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Staying defensive and diversified
We turned defensive towards equities two weeks ago. Since then, the Nasdaq-100 index has recorded its biggest weekly decline in three months as September’s hotter-than-expected US inflation report briefly lifted bond yields, tightening financial conditions
We have extended our defensive stance this week, closing our opportunistic bullish Communication Services idea and initiating a bullish idea on Healthcare, where earnings visibility and defensive characteristics appear more attractive.
In fixed income, we see opportunities in the US 10-year government bond. We await clearer AI profit margin and spending guidance, broader earnings growth or lower bond and equity market volatility before turning positive on equities. Until then, diversification and disciplined entry levels remain important.

What are the takeaways from US bank earnings? Are you still positive on Japan banks?

How does the September US inflation report impact your USD and bond views?

Can Big Tech earnings guidance sustain confidence in the AI investment cycle?

Charts of the week: No capitulation

A hotter-than-expected US inflation report triggered a pullback in risk assets, but there are few signs of capitulation so far

US core and supercore inflation; US inflation breadth*

Our ‘Fear and Greed’ indicator

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *share of US consumer inflation components rising more than 3%
Editorial

Staying defensive and diversified

Strategy summary: Two weeks ago, we turned defensive towards equities, locking in semiconductor equity gains amid elevated bond volatility, narrowing market breadth and political uncertainty before the US mid-term elections. The near-term outlook reflected a less favourable risk-reward balance. Since we turned defensive, the Nasdaq 100 index has recorded its biggest weekly decline in three months as September’s hotter-than-expected US inflation report briefly lifted bond yields.
We have extended our defensive stance this week, downgrading US Communication Services equities to Neutral and upgrading US Healthcare to Overweight. We also closed our opportunistic bullish Communication Services idea and initiated a bullish idea on Healthcare, where earnings visibility and defensive characteristics appear more attractive. In fixed income, we see opportunities in US 10-year government bonds. We await equity market capitulation, clearer AI profit margins and spending guidance, broader earnings growth or lower bond volatility before turning positive on equities. Until then, diversification and disciplined entry levels remain important.
Hot US inflation triggers equity pullback; not hot enough for an October Fed hike: Risk assets pulled back after September’s hotter-than-expected inflation data (headline 3.7% y/y; core 2.6% y/y). Higher gasoline and diesel prices were the main drivers, but passthrough appeared in airline fares, used cars and transportation services, showing pressures were not confined to energy. Almost half of inflation components are still rising above 3%, a measure recently cited by Fed Chair Warsh. Producer inflation also beat estimates. The reports revive the possibility of an October Fed rate hike, but we expect a divided Fed to weigh it against September’s soft jobs report and narrowly hold this month. A December hike appears more likely if inflation remains firm. Although Fed Chair Warsh did not comment on policy at an IMF speech this week, New York Fed chief Williams said he saw no need to hike in 2027. Our base case remains two further hikes by June 2027.
Limited equity pullback so far. Equities fell sharply after the US inflation report, but the pullback is limited. The Nasdaq 100

is 4.5% below its record high, while the S&P 500 remains close to all-time highs despite the latest decline. The S&P 500 volatility index (VIX) has risen from below 15 to 18.2, still well under the 25–30 range typically associated with capitulation and forced selling. Meanwhile, US government bond volatility (MOVE) remains elevated after surging since September. Our stock-bond quant model turned more negative (-2) this week, signalling elevated equity volatility in the near term.
When to turn more constructive on stocks? We would turn more constructive when capitulation signals align: the Nasdaq 100 approaches a 10% drawdown, the VIX rises to 25–30 and our ‘Fear and Greed’ index enters “extreme fear”. Greater confidence would also require easing concerns about AI spending and technology firms’ exposure to neocloud revenue, lower bond volatility and our stock-bond model turning positive again. Until these conditions emerge, volatility may remain elevated, favouring a defensive equity stance. Political risk should ease after the US mid-term elections. We continue to seek selective opportunities following excessive corrections.
US financials remain a preferred sector after Q3 earnings: US large banks’ earnings were mixed, but underlying trends remain encouraging. Healthy loan and deposit growth supports net interest income, while resilient consumer spending, wealth management activity and a solid M&A and refinancing pipeline strengthen the outlook. Credit risks appear manageable. We remain constructive and favour stronger, diversified franchises.
US government bonds offer value as yields spike: The reversal in US government bond yields after their initial inflation-driven spike suggests limited further upside. The 10-year yield briefly reached 5.32% before slumping as falling equities prompted short-covering. We expect a near-term 5.00–5.25% range and view moves above 5.25% as attractive entry points for our opportunistic 10-year government bond idea. Structural pressures, including term premium and increasing supply to fund fiscal deficits and AI investments, prevent us from turning outright bullish on longer maturities. We, therefore, continue to prefer 3–7-year maturities in broader bond allocations.
— Rajat Bhattacharya and Sundeep Gantori

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as negative for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Strong China exports, ramped up fiscal supports(-)factors: Higher-than-expected US inflation and weak US sentiment; hawkish central banks

US Michigan consumer sentiment index fell to 46.3 as high prices and borrowing costs continue to weigh on households

US Michigan consumer sentiment, 1-year and 5-10-year inflation expectations

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

US headline producer price inflation rose to 6.3% y/y, beating estimates and marking its second-highest level since November 2022

US headline and core producer price inflation

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

China consumer price inflation missed consensus estimates, while producer prices rose at the fastest pace since June 2022 due to fuel costs
China consumer and producer price inflation

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions

How does the September 2026 US Consumer Price Index (CPI) report alter your view on the USD and bond yields?

Our view: The hotter-than-expected CPI print raises the odds of an October Fed hike, though we still expect a hold followed by a rate hike in December. In the near term, we maintain our view that the US 10-year government bond yield will range between 5.00% and 5.25%, while the USD will remain supported as markets reassess the likelihood of further Fed hikes. Additional gains would depend partly on markets pricing a faster or more prolonged tightening cycle, while clearer signs of an approaching policy rate peak could see the USD ease back.
Rationale: September US consumer inflation came in above consensus across the board – headline CPI rose 3.7% y/y (vs. 3.6% estimate), and core CPI rose 2.6% y/y (vs. 2.5% estimate) – marking the fastest headline acceleration in five months. This shifts the balance of risks modestly hawkish. Unsurprisingly, the market-implied probability of an October Fed hike rose over 50% overnight but closed the day at 32.7% – 9ppt higher than Tuesday’s close.
We believe a split Fed will weigh this inflation report against the soft September jobs report and narrowly vote to keep rates on hold this month. Our base case remains for two more Fed hikes by June 2027. A December rate hike now looks more like a done deal, especially as persistently higher oil prices keep headline and core inflation elevated for at least the next few months. Any re-escalation of the Middle East conflict after the US mid-term elections would exert pressure on the Fed, although we believe Republicans would show greater restraint in US foreign action if they suffer steep Senate losses, which looks increasingly likely.
The intra-day price action in US government bonds was instructive. The US 10-year yield briefly spiked to 5.32% on the print before closing materially lower, as pre-existing bearish positioning was unwound and Fed speakers (Barkin, Goolsbee) stopped well short of signalling an imminent move. This dynamic reinforces our view that the technical selling pressure driving yields towards the upper end of our range is fading. Structural drivers – term premium, fiscal supply concerns and ‘higher for longer’ Fed repricing – remain intact and keep us from turning outright bullish on duration. However, our opportunistic bullish idea in US 10-year government bonds initiated at September-end remains, as we continue to view spikes in US 10-year yields over 5.25% as a good risk-reward entry. From a longer-term portfolio standpoint, we continue to favour the 3-7-year tenor.
On FX, elevated US government bond yields should sustain the USD’s interest rate appeal. However, expected hikes alone will not drive further appreciation. Stronger data or firmer Fed guidance would provide fresh support, while evidence that tightening is nearing completion would temper the USD’s strength.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Ray Heung, Senior Investment Strategist

The US Dollar Index (DXY) is likely to stay rangebound between 102 and 103, supported by elevated US government bond yields
The DXY and technicals

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

The US 10-year government bond yield spiked initially after the US CPI print, but closed the day lower. We expect the US 10-year yield to stay rangebound within 5.00-5.25% in the near term
US 10-year government bond yield

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What are your key takeaways from US bank earnings?

Our view: Q3 2026 earnings results from major US banks have been mixed, but underlying trends remain encouraging. Healthy loan and deposit growth, resilient consumer spending and wealth management activity continue to support the sector. Credit risks remain manageable. We remain constructive on the US financial sector, favouring stronger, diversified franchises.
Rationale: Healthy loan and deposit growth continue to support net interest income (NII), hinting that the US economy remains resilient. Capital markets revenue grew year-on-year (y/y), but moderated sequentially after a very strong Q2 2026, although performance varied across banks. Management commentary points to a healthy deal pipeline, supported by M&A activity and debt refinancing demand, although execution will depend on market conditions.
Provisioning and net charge-off trends were mixed across banks, with no clear signs of broad deterioration in credit quality. Firmer US inflation raises the risk of further monetary tightening. While higher rates can support asset yields, they can also increase funding costs, pressure borrowers and weigh on securities’ valuations. We will continue to monitor lending demand, credit costs, NII trends, capital markets momentum and capital returns.
— Robin Xie, Senior Investment Strategist

US banks’ revenues remain resilient despite moderation from a record-high Q2 2026

Aggregate quarterly revenue (USD bn) of six major US banks

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Can Big Tech’s earnings guidance sustain confidence in the AI investment cycle?

Our view: We expect Big Tech’s AI spending to remain elevated, supporting our constructive AI capex outlook. However, we await guidance on the pace of capex growth and the sustainability of profit margins.
Rationale: Semiconductor leaders’ latest company guidance points to supply constraints extending through 2028, supporting continued capacity expansion for compute. However, while AI capex is still likely to rise, y/y growth is expected to moderate from c.100% in Q3 2026 to c.20% in Q3 2027. This normalisation in growth could raise concerns about the AI investment cycle’s durability.
The Nasdaq-100 Index has rallied alongside accelerating AI capex. Slower capex growth is likely to moderate semiconductor revenue growth, while hyperscalers continue to incur depreciation costs on past investments. The slower growth is already partially reflected in the Nasdaq-100’s valuation de-rating this year. While we remain constructive on the AI investment theme, we prefer to stay prudent in the near term and await Big Tech’s guidance for greater visibility into spending plans in H2 2027 and beyond.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

AI capital expenditure (capex) growth is expected to moderate to around 20% in Q3 2027
AI capex growth (y/y) vs. the Nasdaq-100 Index

Source: FactSet, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Would France face a credit rating downgrade by rating agencies this month? What might be the market implications?

Our view: A rating downgrade is unlikely unless France’s 2027 budget passes the National Assembly very soon with material changes to the proposal. We see French government bond yields remaining elevated relative to German Bund yields.
Rationale: The French National Assembly began debating France’s 2027 draft budget on 13 October 2026, with the first vote scheduled for 20 October. Near-term budget approval appears unlikely, as opposition parties have tabled motions to reject the proposal. The French Parliament has up to 70 days from the budget’s submission to complete the legislative process, although its final adoption and the resolution of political challenges could extend into early 2027.
Last October, two of the three major rating agencies downgraded France by one notch to the high-single-A category with stable outlooks. The remaining agency rated France in the low-AA category with a negative outlook. As negative outlooks are typically resolved within 12-18 months, agencies have time to await fiscal clarity before acting. We believe downgrade risks are largely priced in after the recent rise in yields, but volatility is likely to persist amid fiscal uncertainty and the approaching presidential election. Banks and domestically-focused issuers would face the greatest near-term pressure. However, we would view wider spreads as an opportunity to add exposure, particularly to French banks’ subordinated debt, given their stronger balance sheets and the fact that France contributes less than 50% of major French banks’ overall revenue.
— Ray Heung, Senior Investment Strategist

France’s government bond yields remain elevated amid fiscal and political turmoil
France and Germany’s 10Y government bond yields and the yield spread

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Are you still positive on Japanese banks?

Our view: We are positive on Japanese banks despite the recent market correction, as the structural drivers of improving profitability and shareholder returns remain intact. While political risk and shifting BoJ rate hike odds could sustain near-term volatility, we see the recent pullback as an opportunity to build selective exposure to Japanese bank stocks.
Rationale: Japan’s gradual monetary policy normalisation should support banks’ NII as floating-rate loans reprice and maturing assets are reinvested at higher yields. Healthy corporate lending demand, improving capital efficiency and continued share buybacks provide further support. While uncertainty over the pace of BoJ tightening could weigh on sentiment, we see gradual interest rate normalisation as supportive of medium-term bank profitability.
Key risks include rising deposit costs, mark-to-market losses on bond portfolios and a disorderly increase in Japanese government bond yields. We continue to favour well-capitalised banks with strong domestic deposit franchises and improving returns on equity.
— Robin Xie, Senior Investment Strategist

Japanese banks’ longer-term outperformance puts recent volatility in perspective
TOPIX Banks vs. TOPIX performance (rebased to 100)

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Could NZD/USD rebound from its one-year trough? If so, how far could it recover?

Our view: New Zealand’s improving domestic conditions, persistent inflation and technical support provide a basis for NZD/USD’s initial recovery towards the 0.57 level, although elevated US bond yields could slow its progress.
Rationale: In Q3, New Zealand’s seasonally-adjusted business confidence reading rose to a net 40% of firms expecting the economy to improve, up from net 14% in Q2. Hiring intentions improved, and filled jobs rose 0.2% m/m in August. These developments suggest domestic conditions remain supportive for the NZD.
New Zealand’s above-target inflation keeps further RBNZ tightening in focus. The 22 October consumer inflation data release and the 28 October RBNZ policy meeting are key catalysts: persistent price pressures and improving demand are expected to prompt firmer policy guidance and strengthen the NZD’s interest-rate appeal.
NZD/USD’s position near the lower boundary of its downtrend channel suggests scope for a technical rebound. We see 0.57 as the first recovery hurdle; a sustained break above this level would strengthen the case for further gains. Firmer US consumer inflation remains a headwind, making a gradual recovery more plausible than a sharp reversal.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

NZD/USD is likely to rebound towards near-term resistance at 0.57
NZD/USD and technical indicators

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Can the proposed Russia-Ukraine ‘energy ceasefire’ contain oil prices as Middle East risks rise?

Our view: We expect escalating Middle East tensions to keep oil prices elevated. We maintain our three- and 12-month West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil price forecasts at USD 100/bbl and USD 80/bbl, respectively, and continue to favour US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) as a portfolio hedge against persistent inflation risks.
Rationale: The proposed Russia-Ukraine ‘energy ceasefire’ still looks some way off. In our view, even if an agreement is reached, it would do little to ease the supply risks building in the Middle East. Gulf oil exports have recovered to above 80% of pre-conflict levels in recent weeks, helping moderate the pace of price increases. However, the recovery remains vulnerable to disruptions, particularly following the latest Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. Diesel and jet fuel remain under the most pressure, with Gulf exports of these fuels in September at only around 60% of pre-conflict levels. A sustained disruption to major Saudi production or export infrastructure remains the principal upside risk to oil prices.

— Anthony Naab, Investment Strategist

articles.title: Three Tests For French Spreads
articles.text:
Three Tests For French Spreads

Cedric Gemehl

Gavekal Research | 8 Oct 2026

After touching 150bp last Friday, October 2, the 10-year OAT-bund spread retraced to 127bp on Tuesday, before widening again to 139bp Thursday. Rather than beginning a meaningful tightening, the spread appears to be undergoing a repricing which is likely to see it settle somewhere between 125bp and 300bp (see How Wide Can French Spreads Get?). However, this is a remarkably broad range. So, what forces could push spreads towards either the floor or ceiling of this band over the coming months?Wednesday’s price action was a reminder that global bond markets will play a role. The French spread widened as much as 14bp during the day’s session as the global bond sell-off resumed, pushing US treasury yields higher. Equally, any rally in global bonds (see Reasons To Start Buying Bonds) could ease the widening pressure on French spreads. Whatever happens globally, however, idiosyncratic French risk is unlikely to disappear.
