articles.title: Daily: Semis stumble. Time to reboot expectations?
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Market Playbook | Asia beyond the AI trade (6 mins)Video: The AI Show | Is the AI trade under strain? (4 mins)Thought of the dayPressure has ratcheted up on global chip stocks in recent days, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down around 8% over the last five sessions and South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi falling over 12% since the start of the month.Investors have been grappling with concerns over the durability of AI spending, competitive risks from China's rising memory maker, higher-for-longer rates, and the debate surrounding OpenAI's reported revenue trajectory. Sentiment was further affected after Broadcom's CEO warned earlier this week that financing the AI infrastructure buildout could eventually become a greater constraint than component shortages, highlighting the demanding expectations embedded in AI-linked stocks.But while volatility could persist as markets brace for third-quarter results and investors scrutinize the sustainability of AI-related investment, we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural opportunity. ASML earlier on Wednesday reported stronger-than-expected earnings and raised the low end of its 2026 revenue forecast for a third consecutive quarter.Without taking a view on any individual companies, we see the chip-centered sell-off as more of a reset in expectations than a deterioration in the underlying AI investment cycle:AI monetization trends remain strong. The market reaction was amplified by media reports suggesting OpenAI's revenue growth was falling short of expectations. Subsequent clarification indicated much of the discrepancy reflected differing accounting treatments rather than a meaningful change in demand. Looking beyond a single company, we continue to view cloud growth as one of the clearest real-time indicators of AI monetization. Expectations for further acceleration in hyperscaler cloud growth suggest AI investment is increasingly translating into commercial revenues rather than remaining solely a capital-spending story. Recent launches of agentic AI products also point to continued momentum in AI adoption and monetization.Earnings expectations remain constructive. Positive EPS guidance among S&P 500 companies is tracking at a five-year high, while AI-related spending and cloud demand continue to support profit growth across the technology ecosystem. We expect another strong reporting season, with S&P 500 earnings growth of around 28%, supported by AI infrastructure spending, resilient consumer demand, and an improving cyclical backdrop. Semiconductors remain a key contributor to earnings growth, and the upcoming reporting season is likely to be a more important driver of sentiment than recent headlines around competition or financing constraints. Though earnings growth is moderating from exceptionally strong levels, we think the direction of markets will depend more on the outlook for profits and earnings revisions than on the pace of deceleration itself.Valuations, rates look manageable. The current backdrop differs meaningfully from the technology correction of 2022. Our base case remains for only modest tightening by the Federal Reserve, well below the scale of tightening experienced during that period. Technology earnings growth remains robust, while semiconductor valuations are still below long-term historical averages. We also believe that rising rates should have a more limited impact on corporate earnings than in prior cycles, given generally long debt maturities and continued economic resilience. We reflect this outlook in our AI thematic positioning, favoring diversified exposure across AI infrastructure beneficiaries, platform companies, and select defensive technology businesses.So, while increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements, and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story. We suggest investors focus on where AI spending is translating into sustainable earnings growth and broader enterprise and consumer adoption.With valuations now more attractive and growth trends remaining resilient, investors may consider adding exposure to the "Magnificent 6." Within the AI supply chain, we continue to favor semi-cap and robotics equipment companies, followed by foundry/OSAT and compute beneficiaries. Memory remains lower in our pecking order despite optically attractive valuations, reflecting medium-term supply concerns and the risk of additional capacity coming to market over time. More broadly, we favor diversified and active exposure across the AI value chain, balancing semiconductor exposure with platform companies and defensive technology segments that can benefit from growing software, cloud, and productivity adoption.

How our approach to sustainability helps investors navigate a changing world

By
BNP PARIBAS ASSET MANAGEMENT 12.10.2026

By BNP Paribas Asset Management

The world in which our clients invest is being reshaped by powerful structural forces: environmental pressures, demographic shifts, geopolitical fragmentation and rapid innovation.

The transition to a low carbon world is driving transformation across markets, countries and companies. This is creating new risks, but also potential opportunities, for investors.

These factors shape economies, industries, companies, consumers and communities. They influence capital allocation, asset resilience, operating models and long-term returns. Understanding these dynamics is therefore essential to fulfilling our fiduciary duty and supporting clients in a changing world.

As such, it is crucial that investors can implement forward looking strategies that aim to mitigate non-financial risks and capture emerging opportunities.

At BNP Paribas Asset Management, environmental, social and governance considerations are firmly embedded in our investment processes and grounded in the conviction that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture the full spectrum of risks and opportunities in today’s global economy.

This conviction is translated into a practical framework for action in our Global Sustainability Strategy – catering for all investment objectives.

What this means for investors

For institutional investors, BNP Paribas Asset Management offers more than just “green” products; we offer a sophisticated investment engine designed for a changing world. By blending thematic foresight, proprietary ESG research and data, and active stewardship, we ensure that sustainability is a key driver of portfolio resilience and long-term financial performance.

Furthermore, our coordinated stewardship, including public policy advocacy, aims to help foster a stable and sustainable economic environment, to protect the long-term value of diversified portfolios.

Forward-looking perspective

We undertake thematic research to identify long-term structural changes and risks as well as potential investment opportunities before they are fully priced by markets.

Sustainability is inherently linked to global megatrends – it acts as a driver of and a necessary response to the transformations occurring across technology, geopolitics, and demographics. Sustainability intersects with these trends to reshape how economies and societies function.

We focus on four global megatrends, which we believe help explain how the world may develop and where risks and opportunities may emerge:

Geopolitics: How sovereignty and international cooperation shape market access – here sustainability is increasingly a core element of national security and international diplomacy

Environment: Assessing the impact of resource constraints and pollution on asset resilience as sustainability is the fundamental response to environmental degradation

Demographics: Evaluating how ageing, inequality and migration shape labour demand and supply – population characteristics and changes in terms of structure and distribution directly impact the scale and nature of sustainability efforts

Innovation: Identifying the business models unlocked by technological disruption – technology acts as the primary enabler for sustainability, while simultaneously sustainability goals drive technological research and development

Cutting across these four megatrends are three major sustainability themes which will guide our research going forward:

Transition: Financing and enabling the shift to a low-carbon, nature-positive, resilient and inclusive economy

Sustainable AI: Assessing how artificial intelligence supports sustainable development while managing its environmental and social impacts

One Health: Understanding how human, animal and environmental health underpin long-term economic and investment outcomes

ESG research and due diligence

Our ESG integration is not a separate ‘overlay’ but is embedded directly into the investment decision-making process. Robust data, research excellence and innovative analytics serve as critical foundations of ESG integration.

What differentiates BNPP AM is our combination of quantitative rigour and qualitative insight:

Data architecture: We use a multifaceted data set, combining forward-looking and backward-looking metrics, alternative data, and proprietary models to move beyond simplistic ESG scores

Investment accountability: Portfolio managers and analysts are directly accountable for ESG integration and must be able to clearly articulate how material ESG factors influence their investment decisions

Asset class specificity: We recognise that ESG materiality differs between asset classes, tailoring our methodologies to the specific context of each investment

Stewardship

As a global investor, we view stewardship as a core fiduciary duty that is an essential part of managing risks and aiming to deliver sustainable long-term financial returns for clients.

We employ a coordinated approach combining active voting, targeted engagement with issuers, and public policy advocacy to promote strong ESG standards and drive sustainable economic development and change.

Exclusions

We expect companies to meet their fundamental obligations in terms of human and labour rights. We expect them to protect the environment and ensure anti-corruption safeguards are in place, wherever they operate. Accordingly, we assess companies against internationally recognised norms and standards1 and apply policies tailored to sensitive sectors.

By combining exclusions and engagement, our investment policy supports consistent risk management and encourages issuers to improve practices in areas with material environmental, social and governance risks.

Sustainability-focused products and solutions

Investors face a rapidly evolving regulatory environment as well as a changing market backdrop, so we support our clients with a range of options that aim to translate different sustainability ambitions into robust strategies.

We have over 20 years of experience providing bespoke solutions ranging from customised exclusions to portfolios with highly specific sustainable objectives.

Our comprehensive approach allows us to embed sustainability from the initial research phase through to final client reporting. Our goal is to deliver an end-to-end investment experience to meet our clients’ financial and sustainability-related objectives.

Institutional investors have diverse mandates. BNPP AM provides a scalable range of approaches to meet these varied needs, spanning risk mitigation to measurable impact.

Minimum exclusion standards: Baseline safeguards rooted in our Responsible Business Conduct policy for clients seeking standard responsible investment

ESG commitment strategies: Strategies with binding ESG exclusions, minimum thresholds, sustainability indicators, or specific targets

Decarbonisation and transition strategies: Specialised solutions including Paris-Aligned Benchmarks and net-zero alignment to finance the low-carbon transition

Sustainable thematic strategies: Targeted exposure to specific transition themes (e.g., water, energy transition)

Impact strategies: Designed to deliver measurable positive environmental or social outcomes alongside financial returns. They are guided by three core principles of intentionality, additionality and impact measurement and reporting

Walking the talk

We aim to maintain high standards in corporate practices and disclosures at both portfolio and corporate levels, underpinned by a strong sustainability culture across our organisation. We embed sustainability into our operations, with a strong focus on educating, engaging and empowering our employees while contributing positively to society.

BNP Paribas Asset Management has entered a new phase of transformation and growth, building on deep investment expertise, extensive capabilities and a conviction that sustainability is central to long-term value creation.

This evolution strengthens our position as a leading European asset manager and reinforces our ability to support clients across public and private markets, regions and investment needs.

Sustainability is fundamental to this ambition. It is embedded in our AMplify 2030 strategy where our objective is to deliver sustainable, resilient outcomes for clients, while contributing positively to the real economy.

articles.title: Southeast Asia’s stablecoin race: dollar vs local coins
articles.text: Inside the race to win Southeast Asia's stablecoin transformation15 min readAcross Southeast Asia, stablecoins are rapidly becoming financial infrastructure. The question is which currencies will power it: US dollar tokens that already dominate the market, or a growing crop of local-currency alternatives.On payday in Jakarta, 28-year-old Erika Yuliani Lukmawati doesn't wait for an international transfer to clear. A trained accountant, she receives payment for a web3 side gig through Bitget Wallet, settled in USDT on the BNB Chain, "since it's the most liquid and lowest-fee option," she says. Her most recent outgoing payment from the self-custodial wallet was for lunch: the merchant received Indonesian rupiah instantly, with a fee close to zero. Before switching in 2025, Erika told The Node she relied on Wise and PayPal for international transfers. Settlement took around three days, she says, "plus the fees were high and had a bad rate conversion FX"... worse if a payment landed on a weekend. Now the money lands in seconds. She splits it on arrival: about half is converted to Indonesian rupiah through a local exchange, a portion is kept for spending, and the rest is moved to a wallet she treats as dollar savings.Erika's integration of stablecoins into her daily financial life is part of a much larger shift: Southeast Asia's crypto industry is rapidly turning into a payments industry. The region of 700 million people is where the world will first see what a stablecoin economy actually looks like.Nations like Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, and Indonesia make a natural proving ground: fragmented currencies, large underbanked populations, and some of the world's largest remittance corridors.But the same shift that liberates Erika from high transfer fees and long waits is also giving the US dollar a stronger foothold in local economies. With the USDC and USDT dollar tokens dominating the market and local-currency versions, such as the Philippine peso's PHPC and Singapore dollar's XSGD, struggling to gain traction, governments are wary of an erosion of monetary sovereignty. At the same time, regulators are having to play catch-up with a system that citizens have already adopted.Grassroots growth Global stablecoin payment volume roughly doubled in 2025, to an estimated $390 billion, according to McKinsey. Asia as a whole accounts for 60% of that total, far ahead of North America and Europe. The ASEAN region, led by Singapore, is powering a significant part of that growth. More significant is the type of use that’s becoming predominant in Southeast Asia – real grassroots crypto adoption by people like Erika rather than financial trading. Chainalysis ranked Vietnam #4, Indonesia #7 and the Philippines #9 in the world for grassroots adoption in its 2025 Geography of Crypto Index.In the Philippines, stablecoins are becoming financial plumbing — flowing through everyday apps like GCash, moving over $50 million a day on Coins.ph, and delivering overseas wages in minutes.Wei Zhou, the CEO of Coins.ph and former CFO of Binance, said the big two dollar tokens are developing distinct user bases. “USDT is the go-to for retail users, Web3 gamers, and sending money friend-to-friend because it’s everywhere and cheap to move on networks,” he said. USDC, meanwhile, is “winning over companies and institutions” because its regulatory and transparency credentials make compliance teams more comfortable moving larger sums.Across the region, stablecoins are increasingly moving from exchanges to the point of sale for millions of consumers.Naqib Noor, a 38-year-old father of two children, used USDC held on a crypto-linked credit card to help buy an SUV from a Singapore dealership in March 2025. The transaction was little different from an ordinary card purchase: he took out the card and swiped it to cover a down payment of more than $40,000 on the car.For Noor, a crypto industry professional, the motivation was less about speed or cost than simply spending the assets he already owned. “I have more crypto than fiat,” he said. “I needed the fiat to pay bills and debts that I have, so I try not to touch my fiat.”“Way back it was so hard to even use crypto for anything outside of Web3,” he said. Would he buy another car this way? “Yes, 100%.”In the same month as Noor’s car purchase, the Philippines' dominant e-wallet GCash integrated Circle's USDC into its GCrypto feature, allowing users to swap pesos for a dollar stablecoin directly within the app most Filipinos already use for daily payments. Late in 2025, Southeast Asia's largest “super-app” Grab signed an MOU with Singapore digital payments firm StraitsX to explore Web3 wallets and a stablecoin settlement layer. Consumers can now use stablecoins to make everyday payments at thousands of GrabPay merchants, following a tie-up with crypto exchange OKX.Much of Southeast Asia runs on remittances – a vast opportunity for crypto rails. The Philippines alone pulled in a record $35.6 billion from overseas workers in 2025, about 8–9% of GDP. Vietnam and Indonesia take in over $16 billion each per year.A tie-up announced in November 2025 between Coins.ph and the UK’s BCRemit allows Filipinos working in the Europe, the US, and Canada to send stablecoin payments to their family members’ Coins.ph wallet. The funds arrive in minutes rather than days and at a cost saving of around 80%, according to the firms.From traders to treasury teamsStablecoins are increasingly being used by ordinary businesses for payments and treasury operations, rather than predominantly by crypto traders moving money around during market activity.One sign this shift is structural, not cyclical, is who's asking the questions now. Renna Ba, director of partnerships at stablecoin infrastructure provider Morph, has watched inbound interest change. "Two years ago, stablecoin interest came from traders and remittance platforms," she said. "Now we're getting inbound leads from treasury teams, payment processors, and businesses that had no experience with crypto before."Inquiries have matured too. They now focus on "settlement finality, audit trails, and uptime," Ba said. Settlement volume climbs through quiet price periods, she added, "because it's tied to trade flows and payment schedules, not market sentiment."SB Seker, head of Asia-Pacific at Binance, sees regulation rather than demand as the constraint. “The demand side of the economy is there, but the supply side is lacking, because the regulatory framework for these activities is not that mature in a lot of markets,” he told The Node.The dollar’s headstartAsk almost anyone building stablecoin infrastructure in the region and you get the same answer: USDT and USDC got there first, and their lead has proved hard to dislodge.Paul Kim, founder and chairman of New Frontier Partners Group, has watched several Asian countries struggle to build alternatives. The core problem, he said, isn't technical. Liquidity begets liquidity. "Policymakers may want to issue a ringgit or won-backed stablecoin and see it used globally, but the real challenge is getting global market participants to accept it as a settlement currency. Someone still has to buy it."According to Tiger Research’s 2026 Asia Stablecoin Market Overview,1 USDT and USDC together account for roughly 99% of the stablecoin market in the region. Ben Charoenwong, associate professor of finance at INSEAD, argues the dollar's advantage is structural, not merely first-mover. "A stablecoin is a commodity: every USDC is identical to every other USDC, so competition comes down to where it is accepted at par and how deep the book is. That is a pure network-effect market."Underneath the market-share fight sits a harder policy question. What happens to a country's monetary sovereignty if the dollar quietly becomes the settlement currency of choice for its own domestic economy?"It's a real concern, not a hypothetical one,” says Ba. The numbers don't support panic yet: global stablecoin volume was around $35 trillion in 2025, against roughly $2 quadrillion in total payments.2 That’s less than 2% of the volume of payments globally.Ba stresses that not all dollarisation is equal: "A business settling a cross-border invoice in USD stablecoin isn't dollarizing its economy any more than it was when it settled that invoice in USD wire transfers before stablecoins existed. The risk is concentrated in domestic, retail-facing use."Where local currency coins can winIn the Philippines, this plays out daily. Workers abroad send USDT or USDC to recipients who convert to pesos through Coins.ph, Zhou told The Node, while companies use dollar stablecoins to pay overseas suppliers and remote workersBut dollar stablecoins do not necessarily remain in domestic circulation. Zhou said people mainly use them as a bridge for transfers or as a store of value rather than to pay for groceries or bills. Taxes, rent and utilities remain denominated in pesos.That leaves a potential role for peso-backed stablecoins, provided they connect to domestic payment rails such as QRPh, develop sufficient liquidity and are integrated into high-volume services such as remittances and gaming. Zhou expects USDT and USDC to remain dominant for cross-border transfers, while peso-backed tokens could handle more domestic payments, with apps converting between the two.“I don’t think it’s a competitive frame,” Angela Ang, APAC managing director at BitGo, told The Node. “Local-currency stablecoins are solving a different problem: settlement finality and FX bridging for domestic commerce, not global liquidity.”XSGD illustrates the distinction. Through StraitsX's GrabPay integration in Singapore, overseas visitors pay from their existing wallets while merchants receive Singapore dollars — the stablecoin working behind the scenes as FX and settlement.Charoenwong is less convinced. He points to a natural experiment: StraitsX issues both XSGD and a dollar-pegged token, XUSD, from the same regulated entity."Same issuer, same regulator, same chains, same distribution. Yet the dollar-denominated token has attracted greater demand. Hold everything constant except the denomination and the dollar wins anyway. That is a demand problem, not a policy problem." Singapore's own banking efficiency undercuts the case further, he argued: "DBS could just accept USDC and convert you to fiat SGD right away, without the need for XSGD."Ba is more precise about which domestic use cases pull local-currency demand: payroll, merchant settlement, and pilots "where a foreign-currency instrument creates regulatory friction such as capital controls or monetary sovereignty." There's a cost argument too: "Adopting local-currency stablecoins not only addresses settlement speed, it also prevents FX leaks,” she said.For Ba, infrastructure readiness, not appetite, is the real constraint on stablecoin adoption more broadly. Regulatory clarity is the big one. "Compliance and legal teams won't sign off on ambiguity,” she said. Banking integration is another, since converting to usable fiat still runs through relatively few partners, and finance teams still lack a clear answer on how to book stablecoin holdingsMost overlooked, Ba said, is counterparty readiness: "If suppliers can't receive it and customers won't pay with it, there's no pull to adopt even where the licensing is clear."Singapore: The institutional anchorSingapore is building the institutional plumbing the rest of the region increasingly plugs into.StraitsX, licensed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) as a Major Payment Institution, issues XSGD. It’s the first and only Singapore dollar-pegged stablecoin the MAS has acknowledged as substantively compliant with its Single-Currency Stablecoin framework, alongside XUSD. Both have processed more than $18 billion in combined onchain volume.Ba calls Singapore's framework the most consequential regulatory development in the region, because it has replaced ambiguity with a testable checklist: reserve backing, redemption rights, disclosure standards. That clarity lets issuers like Paxos and Circle join the framework on top of their existing licenses.Institutional rails are the other half of the play: Partior, the cross-border settlement network backed by Temasek, DBS, J.P. Morgan and Standard Chartered, shows that banks are building their own tokenised settlement rails rather than relying on public stablecoins.Thailand and Indonesia: Regulating an existing realityThailand and Indonesia show a more common pattern: regulators racing to formalise a dollar-stablecoin economy that businesses and users had already built for themselves.Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission officially approved USDT and USDC for use in digital asset transactions in March 2025, allowing licensed exchanges to use them as base trading pairs – a recognition of existing usage rather than an attempt to seed a new one. That has come with tightening scrutiny: the Bank of Thailand and the SEC have opened a joint investigation into large USDT transactions that may be structured to circumvent disclosure and remittance rules, and from Q4 2026, customers depositing more than five million baht (roughly $140,000–$150,000) in cash will need to document the source of funds. The central bank is separately finalising its own baht-backed stablecoin for interbank settlement.Indonesia seems to be taking a more structural approach: its financial services authority, the OJK, assumed oversight of crypto markets from the commodities regulator in 2025, treating digital assets as financial instruments rather than commodities. Usage there is mostly driven by hedging against rupiah depreciation and by fragmentation across roughly 17,000 islands, which creates banking barriers that stablecoins bypass.Indonesia still classifies stablecoins as an investment instrument rather than a legal payment method. When Erika receives her income, she immediately swaps around half of the USDT into rupiah for everyday expenses, triggering a 0.21% tax on the crypto sale. She keeps the remainder in USDT for spending and saving.Asked if she'd go back to bank transfers, however, she doesn't hesitate: "No, I'd still choose stablecoins. They're easy for transactions, especially cross-border ones. Plus, you only need a wallet address with no other data required."What decides the winnerRather than a single model emerging as a winner, market players see the USD vs. local-currency stablecoin balance being determined over time by use cases and habits. "I don't think this ends with one model displacing the other,” said Ba. “There's a good chance it ends with a split based on whether the transaction crosses a border. USD-backed stablecoins will remain dominant for cross-border and trade use cases, because that's already how trade is priced and settled in the region." Technology may no longer be the deciding factor. The bigger test is whether local-currency issuers can build enough liquidity and trust to secure their domestic markets before dollar stablecoins become the region's default settlement layer. By then, the contest may already have been decided by habit.For Erika, that shift is already part of everyday life. Easier payments have even changed her behaviour. “I’ve become more of a spender,” she said, laughing. “But on the bright side, it actually motivates me more to work, since I’m earning income in dollars and stablecoins.”By Tanzeel AkhtarSources1 Tiger Research. 2026. "2026 Asia Stablecoin Market Overview." Tiger Research.2 McKinsey & Company. 2025. "Global Payments Report." McKinsey & Company.Published onOct 16th, 2026WriterCoinShares

articles.title: European sovereignty: Energy security presents strategic investment advantage  - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
Europe is redesigning its energy architecture – transforming energy security from a supply chain issue into a cornerstone of geopolitical sovereignty and economic security

The transition is guided by structured roadmaps – the EU’s 2019 European Green Deal, and more recent 2026 initiatives focused on AI integration in the energy sector and the comprehensive Electrification Action Plan

The EU’s commitment to clean energy is creating vast amounts of potential long-term investment opportunities in sectors such as renewable energy, grid modernisation, and the electric vehicle supply chain

For decades, energy security was chiefly viewed through the lens of supply chain stability. But in Europe, it has evolved into a cornerstone of economic stability and geopolitical sovereignty.

Driven by a necessity to decouple from volatile external dependencies and by its shift towards a more sustainable future, the European Union is not merely replacing one fuel source with another; it is redesigning its energy architecture. For investors, we believe this direction of travel represents a hugely significant long-term investment opportunity.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was undoubtedly a watershed moment, as it accelerated a structural pivot that was already underway. The EU demonstrated remarkable agility in reducing its reliance on Russian oil imports, which plummeted from approximately 26% in 2021, to around 2% today.1

But this was just the first step to energy resilience and sovereignty. Recent years have robustly highlighted that energy security is no longer a niche policy concern; it is now central to industrial competitiveness, national security, and inflation mitigation. Europe is treating energy resilience as a sovereign priority.

Solid policy backing

For investors, Europe has a keen advantage. Thanks to its solid, long-term commitments, today it is an international hive of innovation and investment opportunity.

Its drive to achieve energy independence is underpinned by a robust regulatory and strategic ecosystem. For years it has been at the epicentre of global sustainability – it was in France over a decade ago where the Paris Agreement was adopted by 196 parties at the 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference COP21.

The 2019 European Green Deal serves as the foundational blueprint to make Europe the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. The deal is not a vague ambition – it is a structured roadmap backed by significant capital. The bloc is a huge investor in clean technology, green infrastructure and renewable energy, including wind and solar power.2

This includes mobilising €1 trillion of sustainable investments between 2020 and 2030, while a record €7 billion of investment is being earmarked for sustainable and smart transport infrastructure.3

The EU spends 10 times more money investing in clean energy than it does in fossil fuels – all of which means it represents a truly vast hub of potential for investors.4

Gearing up

Then, in July 2026, the EU unveiled itsElectrification Action Plan, the goal of which is to make Europe the first electro-powered continent by doubling the electrification rate of final energy consumption from 23% to 46% by 2040. This move alone is projected to reduce annual fossil fuel import costs by approximately €260 billion.5

Two recent initiatives highlight the precision of Europe’s energy strategy: The Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector (June 2026) aims to integrating artificial intelligence and digital tools into the energy grid.

Both schemes are creating potential investment opportunities across four vital areas, namely industry, transport, buildings, and grid flexibility, creating a more predictable, high-growth environment.

We also see potential opportunities for investors across several high-growth sectors including renewable energy; infrastructure and grid modernisation;andthe transition to electric vehicles and the critical battery supply chain.

Notably, the EU is increasingly prioritising the allocation of these investments to European companies, fostering a localised industrial renaissance spurred by policies like the EU’s Clean Industrial Deal, which aims to turn decarbonisation into a driver of growth for European industries.6

Resilience amid volatility

Europe’s commitment to sustainability and strategic autonomy remains steadfast and progress is accelerating – and the economic logic is undeniable. Fossil fuel imports are projected to drop dramatically while the importation of energy technology will increase, meaning a drastic reduction in geopolitical vulnerability.

By treating energy resilience as a sovereign priority, Europe is positioning itself to lead the global transition. While energy policy remains somewhat fragmented on a national level, the EU is leveraging a centralised, directive-driven approach to ensure that the transition to clean energy is not just an environmental necessity, but a competitive advantage.

For investors, the value proposition is clear: Europe’s systemic shift toward sovereignty means it offers a unique combination of targeted policy support, a massive addressable market, and an abundance of innovative investment potential from renewables to grid modernisation – and much more in between.

[4] How the energy crisis sped up Europe’s green transition

[5] Electrification – European Commission

[6] Clean Industrial Deal – European Commission

articles.title: The OCC Report Says Operation Choke Point 2.0 Was Real
articles.text:
Insights / Research / OCC Debanking Report Shows ‘Choke Point 2.0’ Was No Fever Dream

Written by:

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Topics

Regulation

research • October 16, 2026

OCC Debanking Report Shows ‘Choke Point 2.0’ Was No Fever Dream

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.WHAT HAPPENEDThe U.S. regulator for national banks pulled back the curtain on Operation Choke Point 2.0 this week, releasing its final report on debanking at the nation’s nine largest national banks. Following an August 2025 executive order from President Trump, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) combed through nearly 100,000 complaints, hundreds of individual account decisions, and roughly 420,000 pages of internal documents from 2020 through September 2025. The OCC’s stark findings have Nic Carter, the crypto VC who has been on the forefront of OCP muckraking, doing a victory lap. Banks relied on “reputational risk” policies with no clear or measurable standards, and those policies were used to cut off customers over their political, religious, and social views, the OCC’s review confirmed. Examples range from a JPMorgan-owned payments processor closing a merchant’s account for selling MAGA gear, to a Capital One business line turning away partisan groups on both sides of the aisle. Industry-wide (unofficial) restrictions on firearms, coal, Arctic drilling, private prisons, tobacco, and digital assets hit small and midsized firms hardest, while lucrative clients often got exceptions. The OCC also warns that some banks are simply rebranding reputation risk as “franchise” or “brand” risk, and notes that no bank has publicly acknowledged its past debanking decisions. For crypto, it’s vindication, but does this mean we are protected going forward?OUR TAKEThe regulatory landscape around banks has evolved drastically since I entered the workforce. I went through college at the beginning of the Great Financial Crisis, then worked on Deutsche Bank’s structured credit desk, focusing on CLOs and CDOs. After the crisis, the banks were absorbed into the regulatory apparatus of the U.S. government. The Dodd-Frank Act and enhanced capital requirements for global systemically important banks (GSIBs) became an effective way for the government to regulate the broader financial system. This face turn of banks from foes to friends of the regulators can be seen most clearly in the turnaround of the commentary from the Elizabeth Warren camp. To that crowd, banks used to be the enemies of Main Street; now they are central to making sure regulations are enforced and the will of the government enacted.Toward the end of my career at Deutsche Bank, after Jan. 6, there was a stressful week or two on the trading desk. Desk heads and business managers were pulled in to decide whether to keep banking Donald Trump. The question being contemplated was reputational risk; would the profits from having Trump as a client be more than offset by the losses from upset clients taking business elsewhere? It was the first high-profile debanking driven by reputational risk, and we later saw the same thing happen to the artist Ye (formerly Kanye West), for his…colorful commentary. Banks also worked the other side of the reputational ledger, polishing their image through ESG (environmental, social, and governance) investing, “socially responsible investing,” and other flavors of “stakeholder capitalism.” Having read plenty of ESG prospectuses during my time on the desk, I can tell you most simply didn't invest in certain categories (sin stocks, firearms, etc.). They also didn’t invest in anything actually productive on the E, S, or G front. The ESG fad eventually faded. The pruning of “toxic” clients from the Rolodex did not. Publicly, debanking was used sparingly. There were few explicit cases, the Canadian truckers during COVID being the notable one. The real activity was happening behind closed doors in Washington, under what critics referred to as Operation Choke Point 2.0. The regulators took the lever that the banks had been using: the right to refuse business. Legally, banks don’t have to give anyone an account, they have the right to refuse or cease doing business with law-abiding people and businesses, and reputational risk was a convenient rationale to do so. With post-2008 regulation in place, the government had far more control over the banks than before. It could use that lever to target legal industries an administration disfavored: firearms, oil and gas, and, most relevant here, crypto. Now the pendulum has swung back. The OCC report is welcome, and it proves that, hey, we in crypto were not crazy these past years. The crypto industry was being targeted by the government in an unfair manner. The facts support the good actors in the industry who were swept up in an opaque dragnet and what they have been striving toward. But the crypto industry, along with some of the affected banks, had the money to push back and the resources to investigate. OCP 2.0’s targets have power and weight in the economy. The everyday Americans who are unbanked for similar reasons have no such voice. Plenty of studies show minorities remain underbanked in the U.S. So I’d welcome a push for greater fairness in banking, not just for sin stocks and crypto, but for everyone who is underbanked. This all kind of comes together into one question: whose freedom is most paramount? Banks are businesses, and businesses typically aren’t compelled to serve people they don’t want to. “No shirt, no shoes, no service.” The executive branch and federal regulators are now challenging that assumption. If banks can’t refuse customers over perceived reputational risk, and given how much falls under the umbrella of “reputation,” do Americans have a right to banking services? And to be fair, high regulatory barriers to entry limit competition in banking, so it’s not as if spurned customers can just start their own bank. It’s a laudable ideal that access to finance should be fair regardless of one’s politics. Because it flows from constitutional protections for opinion and speech, it starts to sound almost like a right. But that’s a big claim when you don’t even have a right to drive; that’s a privilege. (Ask a “sovereign citizen” what “travel” means and you may get a different answer.) As a proponent of individual freedom, I am torn. I don’t like telling businesses they have to serve people they don’t want to, though The Civil Rights Act sets an appropriate precedent for addressing real harms. And I believe in your right to spend your money as you want. If Citizens United says money is speech, and banks can’t restrict your access based on your speech, does that mean you have a right to put your money in the banking system and use it? Crypto has pursued going bankless as an ethos for years. OCP 2.0 was a U.S. operation, but groups worldwide have been cut off from financial services for their opinions. Crypto is facts-based and doesn’t judge on merit, unlike the traditional trust-based system, which is a machine made of man, and man has biases. I work in crypto because I don’t believe that system is fair. I want to help build one so intrinsically fair that the option to transact freely always exists, no matter what the current administration says. Operation Choke Point 2.0 was real. Industries were systematically debanked amid government and regulatory pressure. There were no laws and no publications, just a back-door squashing of industries the administration of the day didn’t approve of. It can happen under any administration. We need a way to make sure nobody is targeted, no matter who’s in office. That could be a right guaranteed by law, or maybe, just maybe, a transition, driven by economic reality, to an open, blockchain-based financial system. From that point of view, this report is a useful accounting. Maybe we will get a right to financial access. If we don’t, I’m still in the right place to push it forward.

}Source: GettyCommentaryCarnegie PolitikaHow Will Trump and Putin’s Diesel Deal Impact Russia and Global Markets?Without a ceasefire with Ukraine on attacking each other’s energy infrastructure—to which the Kremlin is unlikely to agree—the diesel agreement between Putin and Trump is largely for show, rather than representing a genuine increase in the volumes of Russian diesel on the global market.Link CopiedBy Sergey VakulenkoPublished on Oct 13, 2026Under the new diesel deal between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, Russia will increase diesel exports to global markets and the United States in exchange for Washington suspending sanctions on Russian diesel through April 1, 2027. The deal has been greeted with dismay by Europe and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and skepticism among analysts and traders. It has also sent Russian oil company share prices soaring. But how much money does the Russian state stand to make from the deal? Will it help the global market, and will it mean lower prices at U.S. pumps?Russia on the Global Diesel MarketRussia has long been one of the biggest players on the world’s diesel market. In 2025, Russian exports accounted for about 3 percent of global diesel consumption, and almost 10 percent of international trade volumes, putting it in second place on the list of exporters, between the United States and Saudi Arabia.The war in Ukraine and ensuing Western sanctions against Russia have had little impact on Russian export volumes, which stood at around 40 million tons per year in both the pre-war 2021, and in 2025. What did change in that time was the main destinations: Türkiye, Brazil, and African countries took the place of the EU and the UK, while overland deliveries to Central Asia and Mongolia continued.As recently as April this year, Russia had about 3 million tons of diesel available for export per month. By September, that had fallen almost ten-fold to around 325,000 tons per month due to Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, seasonal fluctuations in consumption, and a deficit on the domestic market.To stabilize domestic prices, in July, the Russian government banned diesel exports outside of Central Asia and Mongolia. In theory, about 2 million tons of diesel could have been stockpiled under that ban by now, but that’s unlikely to have happened. Judging by data on tanker loading at Russian ports, seaborne exports of diesel did not in fact stop: 1.6–1.8 million tons were shipped by sea in the months since the ban was introduced, possibly using different customs codes to circumvent the ban. The authorities likely knew what was going on and chose not to intervene. After all, Russia’s diesel storage capacity is limited, and if it had become full, refining volumes would have had to be reduced, resulting in lower gasoline production. That’s the last thing the government wants at a time of shortages at the pumps. The export volumes agreed with Trump are unlikely to pose any particular difficulties for Russia. The deal is for 300,000 tons of diesel in October, 500,000 tons in November, and one million tons per month after that through April 2027—the period for which U.S. sanctions are suspended.The easiest solution for the Russian authorities would be to simply formalize the volumes still being exported in spite of the current ban. That would make it possible to export 500,000 tons even in October without siphoning any diesel from the domestic market.Diesel consumption in winter in Russia can be 25 percent lower than in September: there is a gradual decline from the peak in August and September to the lowest use in February. That frees up as much as a million tons of diesel for export every month.The Russian government, which has plenty of informal methods of convincing companies to keep enough diesel back for domestic consumers, announced a partial lifting of the export ban on October 10. That is unlikely to pose a threat to the domestic market. Similarly, there is no law that says Russian companies have to comply with the OPEC+ decision to limit production, yet Russian companies have been largely adhering to the quotas set by the Energy Ministry for nearly a decade.Russia doesn’t even need to redirect diesel away from the non-Western markets to which it has turned in recent years. Europe may be experiencing diesel shortages too, but it has no intention of buying it from Russia. And the United States itself does not need it, because it remains the world’s biggest exporter of diesel.Midterm ConsiderationsTrump’s interest in the deal stems not from diesel shortages in the United States, but from high prices for the fuel, which are a source of irritation for the majority of people who will be heading to the polls in three weeks’ time to vote in U.S. midterm elections.For U.S. oil refineries that turn crude oil into diesel, this is a boom time. Usually, diesel costs 20–30 percent more than crude, while right now, it is twice the price, with all the difference going straight to the refineries. The United States as a whole has seen a slight improvement in its trade balance (a gain of 1–2 percent), so Trump would appear to have nothing to worry about.But in reality, expensive diesel is bad for the rest of the U.S. economy: from freight and agricultural companies right up the chain of value creation and consumption. The losers from rising prices far outnumber the winners. U.S. refiners mostly make their profits not at the expense of foreigners, but from rising prices within the United States. In other words, this is not a case of value being created for the country, but of its redistribution.The United States produces more diesel than it consumes, but prices on the U.S. market are still rising to keep pace with global prices. With no U.S. diesel export ban or export duties in place, the only way of lowering prices at home is to influence prices on the global market by increasing supply.The most reliable and radical way to get new volumes of diesel onto the global market is to resolve the issue around the Strait of Hormuz. Increased supplies from Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates would quickly alleviate market instability. But Trump is currently unable to secure a swift victory over Iran, and signing a peace agreement on Iranian terms would mean an even greater loss of face and a drop in ratings. And so he has turned his attention back to another war: that between Russia and Ukraine.Will the agreement between Russia and the United States really mean a fall in prices? In theory, oil and petrochemicals are commodities with fixed demand. Even small shortages can send prices sky-high, and even minor adjustments, accordingly, can start to bring them down again.Yet 300,000 tons per month is too little to make a difference to a global market of 120 million tons per month, of which 30 million tons is traded internationally. And there is no way of obtaining any more diesel than that before the midterm elections on November 3.Prices could fall on expectations that the market will see an additional 5 million tons in the next six months. But the Russian volumes have already been factored in by market players, who all understand that Russia exports as much as it can, and that Trump has little impact on that. Russia would in any case release all of its surplus diesel because it has nowhere to store it. And there is no source of additional volumes, however much Putin might wish to oblige his U.S. counterpart.It might be another matter if there were expectations that Russian refining could return to 5.5 million barrels a day from its current 3.8–4 million barrels. But for that, Ukraine would have to stop the strikes against Russian refineries, and Kyiv is unlikely to do that, since the attacks are one of few levers it can apply to try to force Moscow to reduce the intensity of the conflict.Benefits for RussiaIn theory, the diesel deal is worth about $7 billion based on current prices and a volume of about 5 million tons of diesel sold over six months. That’s about half of what Russia made from exporting oil and petrochemicals in August 2026. But to say Russia will make $7 billion from the deal would be to count it twice: after all, that diesel would have been exported in any case, albeit on less profitable terms. The most Russia can gain is from reducing the discount it previously had to offer buyers because of sanctions.That said, there was no significant discount on Russian diesel even before—at least according to buyers’ customs statistics. Sales to Brazil are less profitable than sales to Europe before the war primarily because it costs more to transport the diesel. The suspension of U.S. sanctions won’t change anything in that respect, because EU sanctions on Russian diesel are still in force, which means transport costs will stay high.With U.S. sanctions suspended, Russia is not limited to its “shadow fleet” and can use other tankers too, which should decrease shipping costs somewhat. But it still won’t be able to use vessels belonging to EU shipowners, which will reduce the effect.In the best case, therefore, Russia stands to make $30–$40 per ton of product, or tens of millions of dollars per month: small fry for Russia. Furthermore, that cash will go not to the state budget, but to companies. The budget will only get its share in the form of tax paid on potentially increased profits. Nor can the Russian government allow oil companies to release more volumes of diesel for export to take advantage of the situation, as that would exacerbate the deficit on the domestic market and cost too much, both for the economy and for the government’s reputation.The Russian budget could itself actually benefit from a reduction in global diesel prices. The tax system in Russia is structured in such a way that state coffers gain nothing from increased prices for exported petrochemicals (in contrast with crude prices, which, when they rise, result in additional income to the budget via the mineral extraction tax). The more expensive fuel is on foreign markets, the more the budget has to pay oil companies to sell the fuel on the domestic market at regulated prices under the price-stabilization or damper mechanism. So if global diesel prices fall, so will payments issued under that mechanism.Ultimately, without a ceasefire with Ukraine on attacking each other’s energy infrastructure—to which the Kremlin is unlikely to agree—the diesel agreement between Putin and Trump is largely for show, rather than representing a genuine increase in the volumes of Russian diesel on the global market.About the AuthorSergey VakulenkoSenior Fellow, Carnegie Russia Eurasia CenterSergey Vakulenko is a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.Recent WorkCommentaryWhat Traffic Accident Numbers Reveal About Russia’s Gasoline CrisisSergey VakulenkoCommentaryBuilding Mini-Refineries Will Not Solve Russia’s Gasoline CrisisSergey VakulenkoClimate ChangeEnergyTradeForeign PolicyCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from Carnegie PolitikaCommentaryCarnegie PolitikaRussian Indoctrination in Occupied Ukrainian Schools Is a ShamDespite a new textbook, an influx of Russian teachers and managers, and an end to the teaching of Ukrainian, the Kremlin is unlikely to have “reprogrammed” locals.Konstantin SkorkinCommentaryCarnegie PolitikaInternational Demand for Russia’s Arctic Shipping Route Is Unlikely to LastCargo traffic through Russia’s Northern Sea Route has increased because of the disruption caused by the conflict in the Middle East, the Ukraine war, and U.S.-China tensions.Mikhail KorostikovCommentaryCarnegie PolitikaWhat Traffic Accident Numbers Reveal About Russia’s Gasoline CrisisAn analysis of traffic accident data suggests that Ukrainian drone attacks caused a material but not disastrous fall in Russian gasoline consumption over the summer. Sergey VakulenkoCommentaryCarnegie PolitikaBelarus Wants More From the West Than a ‘Massive Deal’ on PotashTrump has promised Belarus a massive potash deal. But Minsk is seeking something greater: restored Western transit and greater room for maneuver from Russia.Balázs JarábikCommentaryCarnegie PolitikaHave U.S.-Belarusian Negotiations Stalled?Minsk clearly expected the dialogue with Washington to yield more results, in particular the lifting of EU sanctions and permission to export potash.Artyom Shraibman

articles.title: Weekly Research Brief: Ledger’s $91M Theft, Papertrade's Launch, and the OCC’s Debanking Findings
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Weekly Research Brief: Ledgers Looted for $91m; Papertrade Pays You to Lose; Truth and Reconciliation for the Debanked

Research • October 16, 2026 • 18 mins
Weekly Research Brief: Ledgers Looted for $91m; Papertrade Pays You to Lose; Truth and Reconciliation for the Debanked
This week, Alex Thorn analyzes the $91m exploit of Ledger hardware wallets by third-party resellers, Thad Pinakiewicz breaks down the OCC’s report on debanking under the previous administration, and Will Owens shares takeaways on the Papertrade launch.

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Will Owens
Research Analyst

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Bitcoin

Cryptocurrency

Regulation

Weekly Research Brief

Welcome to Galaxy Research's Weekly Research Brief. Subscribe to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.This week, Alex Thorn analyzes the $91m exploit of Ledger hardware wallets by third-party resellers, Thad Pinakiewicz breaks down the OCC’s report on debanking under the previous administration, and Will Owens shares takeaways on the Papertrade launch.
Not Your Reseller, Not Your CoinsWHAT HAPPENEDLedger is investigating the theft of roughly $91 million from customers who bought its hardware wallets through CryptoBilis, a Southeast Asian reseller, after confirming that at least one of the devices sold contained a hardware implant that read the recovery phrase off the screen.On Friday, Oct. 9, Ledger said it was investigating reports of lost funds from users in Southeast Asia who purchased devices through CryptoBilis, which Ledger's own site listed as an authorized reseller for Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. Ledger asked the reseller to pause all sales and shipments and told anyone who bought from it in the past 90 days not to set up the device, or, if they already had, to move funds to a new device with a newly generated seed. The next day Ledger confirmed that "one of the impacted users' devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant," and on Tuesday it described how it works: a separate component inside the enclosure reads the screen during setup, captures the 24-word recovery phrase and sends it out over LTE through a provisioned eSIM. It leaves the Secure Element and Ledger's operating system untouched, which is why Ledger's Genuine Check passes on a tampered unit. Independent teardowns have found at least three generations of the implant, the latest a professionally fabricated flex circuit hidden under the display. Ledger says its own systems and direct sales channels were not compromised, that the volume is "limited," and that every confirmed case so far involves a device sold through CryptoBilis, which has suspended all hardware sales.Onchain, the theft looks less like a run of individual victims than a harvest. By our count, roughly $91 million left 474 victim addresses across bitcoin, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon and TRON: about $64.5 million in USDT and TRX from 146 TRON addresses, 213 BTC (about $17.6 million) from 279 bitcoin addresses, and $8.8 million of ETH and stablecoins from 49 Ethereum-type addresses. Trackers that also count BNB Chain, which we have not scoped, put it a little higher, at $93 million to $95 million; ours is a floor. The bitcoin sweeps began on Oct. 7, but 88% of the value, about $80 million, moved in a single hour starting at 05:00 UTC on Oct. 9, the morning of Ledger's first statement. Nearly all of the bitcoin victim addresses had never spent before. This was cold storage, most of it funded within the previous 90 days, though some addresses date to 2021, consistent with existing seeds being restored onto tampered devices.

As of Oct. 15, about $56.6 million is still parked at attacker-controlled addresses: roughly 208 BTC untouched at the bitcoin collectors, about 12,800 ETH (much of it bridged from TRON) and 7.5 million USDT in TRON relay accounts created the morning of the drain. About 5,400 ETH ($13.5 million) has gone through Tornado Cash, on the order of $2 million appears to have reached exchange deposit addresses, and Tether has frozen $10 million of USDT tied to the theft. At least one victim has resorted to writing to the thieves onchain, offering them a cut if they return the rest.

OUR TAKETwo weeks ago in this newsletter, Thad Pinakiewicz wrote that nobody attacks the private-key math anymore; they attack whatever tells the math what to do. The Ledger reseller theft is the physical-world version of the same lesson. The Secure Element did its job. The seed was simply read off the screen by a chip that was not supposed to be there. Three things about it are worth dwelling on.Cyber vulnerabilities in the age of AI. Last week Jianing Wu weighed the debate over whether AI will eventually break ECDSA. That is the wrong place to look for the near-term threat. Nothing in this quarter's losses required a mathematical breakthrough: a firmware build flaw at Coldcard, a verification-cache bug in Liquid, a compromised third-party security product at Bitget, and now a flex circuit and an eSIM. None of these incidents has been attributed to AI tooling, and we are not attributing them. But AI changes the economics of everything around the key. Frontier models now find real vulnerabilities in widely used code, and the window between a bug shipping and being exploited is collapsing: Hacken attributes 77% of third-quarter losses to vendor and developer tooling, disclosed-but-undeployed fixes, and infrastructure outside the audit scope. The same tools make the operation around an exploit cheap to run at scale: a plausible storefront, responsive "support," a backend that files away hundreds of recovery phrases and waits for the deposits to arrive. The implication for anyone building or holding in this industry is to assume that every dependency and every link in the supply chain is being probed continuously by adversaries who do not get tired, and to point the same automation at your own code, firmware and vendors before they do.The particular risk of digital bearer assets. This is what a bearer asset looks like when custody fails. The property that makes bitcoin impossible to confiscate makes it impossible to claw back. There is no issuer to call, no chargeback, no court order that moves a UTXO. Of the $91 million taken, the only portion now under anyone's control but the thief's is the $10 million Tether froze, which is itself a reminder that USDT is not a bearer asset at all but a liability with an admin key. The 208 BTC resting at three bitcoin addresses is visible to the entire world and reachable by no one. A bank theft of this size would come with a task force; here, 474 addresses, most of them belonging to retail buyers in Southeast Asia, are reduced to pleading in OP_RETURN. None of this is an argument against self-custody. It is an argument that self-custody is an operational discipline rather than a product you buy. The device is one link; the supply chain that delivered it, the screen you trusted, the backup and the plan for your heirs are the others. Buy direct from the manufacturer. Treat any device that arrives set up, or with a pre-printed seed, as compromised. For balances you cannot afford to lose, spread keys across vendors and locations so that a single tampered device or buggy random number generator is a scare rather than a loss, and for institutions, use custody controls that assume any one device or vendor can fail.A rough quarter for bitcoin's conservative infrastructure. Ledger closes out roughly ten weeks in which the "boring," bitcoin-native corner of the industry took hit after hit. On July 30, Coinkite disclosed that Coldcard firmware had been generating weak seeds since 2021; by our count more than 1,830 BTC (about $150 million at today's prices) has since been swept from more than 9,000 addresses. On Sept. 6, a bug in Liquid's Elements software let an attacker mint about 3,998 unbacked L-BTC and peg them out for real bitcoin, roughly $320 million at the time; the attackers, who styled themselves white hats, returned 3,400 BTC once Blockstream patched the bridge and kept about 600 BTC as a self-awarded fee. Bitget lost $387.5 million on Sept. 24 to a compromised third-party security product in an attack it attributes to North Korea, and NEAR Intents was hit for $3.8 million days after blocking the Bitget launderers. Third-quarter tallies from CertiK and Hacken land between $1.1 billion and $1.3 billion, and the Ledger theft arrived in the first week of the fourth quarter. What stands out is the profile of the targets. These were not unaudited DeFi contracts. Coldcard and Ledger are the two most trusted names in hardware self-custody, and Liquid is the most conservative sidechain in bitcoin, operated by a federation of long-standing bitcoin companies. In every case the cryptography held; the failure was in implementation, supply chain or operations. The response is the silver lining: within hours there were onchain tallies, Tether froze funds, NEAR Intents blocked flows, and the Liquid attackers negotiated onchain and returned 85%, a long way from the Mt. Gox era. But the lesson of the quarter is uncomfortable for anyone who assumed the bitcoin-native stack was the safe part.Bitcoin's math had a great quarter. Everything wrapped around it did not. – Alex Thorn
Papertrade Pays You to LoseWHAT HAPPENEDPapertrade opened trading on HyperEVM on Oct. 10, an ominous anniversary for the crypto industry, but the protocol is off to a promising start ... for now. It is a fully onchain application that allows up to 1,000x leverage on BTC and ETH perpetuals with no funding rates and no slippage. Trades are effectively swaps against a single protocol-owned USDC pool, the “Martingaler LP,” which started at $0 and is funded only by trader losses. Prices are the Hyperliquid BBO (best bid and offer) midpoint read onchain via precompiles (something HyperEVM uniquely enables). Losing trades mint PAPER, which is currently non-transferable and can be staked. PAPER stakers receive a share of realized PnL and fees while the LP fills toward a ~$5m soft cap, and essentially all surplus above it.The ability to take 1,000x leveraged positions is attractive for crypto degens, and it’s also enticing that you get “rewarded” for losing in the form of PAPER tokens. Many traders have been purposely getting liquidated to farm PAPER in the hopes that these tokens will make back their losses. This has been a hyped-up launch for a while, particularly because of the background of the founders, Jez (@izebel_eth) and Blurr. Watch this interview for a more in-depth explanation of the protocol and its backstory.As of Oct. 15, the venue has processed ~$1.11t in total volume and total trader PnL is -$54.1m. Total PAPER staking rewards stood at $45.6m and total PAPER supply at 8.07b tokens. To see live metrics, check out this dashboard.OUR TAKE One interesting development was the emergence of a “manipulator” on the day of Papertrade’s launch. This address (0x2025137a136bea7446deba681cbfc7cf1970840e) was moving the underlying Hyperliquid ETH reference price while holding synthetic exposure on Papertrade. The trader was taking advantage of a weakness in the design that was explicitly acknowledged in the risks section of the project’s docs. Essentially, the strategy goes as follows: take large amounts of synthetic exposure on Papertrade, nudge the HL mid by a few basis points, close Papertrade position, flip opposite direction, and move HL mid the other way, repeat. The team responded by tightening open-interest caps both onchain and at the relayer level. The protocol’s revenue is absurd. DefiLlama data shows cumulative revenue at $43m after five days, or roughly $8 million to $9 million per day. This has put Papertrade behind only the major stablecoin issuers and ahead of Hyperliquid and Pump.fun. But “revenue” here just means trader losses, and the losers are the shareholders. It’s mandatory that every staker is a prior loser because it’s not possible to acquire PAPER in any other way. That makes valuing PAPER unusually tricky. Many traders have lofty targets for the token, but it’s hard to know this early what will happen with a protocol. The math many people are posting on X will hold only if volume does, and much of the volume is farming that makes sense only while PAPER is worth more than the loss it takes to mint it. Once PAPER becomes transferable, the market price will determine how much farming happens, and that, in turn, will determine long-term revenue. Over 99% of supply is staked today because there’s nowhere else for it to go. – Will Owens
OCC Debanking Report Shows ‘Choke Point 2.0’ Was No Fever DreamWHAT HAPPENEDThe U.S. regulator for national banks pulled back the curtain on Operation Choke Point 2.0 this week, releasing its final report on debanking at the nation’s nine largest national banks. Following an August 2025 executive order from President Trump, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) combed through nearly 100,000 complaints, hundreds of individual account decisions, and roughly 420,000 pages of internal documents from 2020 through September 2025. The OCC’s stark findings have Nic Carter, the crypto VC who has been on the forefront of OCP muckraking, doing a victory lap. Banks relied on “reputational risk” policies with no clear or measurable standards, and those policies were used to cut off customers over their political, religious, and social views, the OCC’s review confirmed. Examples range from a JPMorgan-owned payments processor closing a merchant’s account for selling MAGA gear, to a Capital One business line turning away partisan groups on both sides of the aisle. Industry-wide (unofficial) restrictions on firearms, coal, Arctic drilling, private prisons, tobacco, and digital assets hit small and midsized firms hardest, while lucrative clients often got exceptions. The OCC also warns that some banks are simply rebranding reputation risk as “franchise” or “brand” risk, and notes that no bank has publicly acknowledged its past debanking decisions. For crypto, it’s vindication, but does this mean we are protected going forward?OUR TAKEThe regulatory landscape around banks has evolved drastically since I entered the workforce. I went through college at the beginning of the Great Financial Crisis, then worked on Deutsche Bank’s structured credit desk, focusing on CLOs and CDOs. After the crisis, the banks were absorbed into the regulatory apparatus of the U.S. government. The Dodd-Frank Act and enhanced capital requirements for global systemically important banks (GSIBs) became an effective way for the government to regulate the broader financial system. This face turn of banks from foes to friends of the regulators can be seen most clearly in the turnaround of the commentary from the Elizabeth Warren camp. To that crowd, banks used to be the enemies of Main Street; now they are central to making sure regulations are enforced and the will of the government enacted.Toward the end of my career at Deutsche Bank, after Jan. 6, there was a stressful week or two on the trading desk. Desk heads and business managers were pulled in to decide whether to keep banking Donald Trump. The question being contemplated was reputational risk; would the profits from having Trump as a client be more than offset by the losses from upset clients taking business elsewhere? It was the first high-profile debanking driven by reputational risk, and we later saw the same thing happen to the artist Ye (formerly Kanye West), for his…colorful commentary.Banks also worked the other side of the reputational ledger, polishing their image through ESG (environmental, social, and governance) investing, “socially responsible investing,” and other flavors of “stakeholder capitalism.” Having read plenty of ESG prospectuses during my time on the desk, I can tell you most simply didn't invest in certain categories (sin stocks, firearms, etc.). They also didn’t invest in anything actually productive on the E, S, or G front. The ESG fad eventually faded. The pruning of “toxic” clients from the Rolodex did not. Publicly, debanking was used sparingly. There were few explicit cases, the Canadian truckers during COVID being the notable one. The real activity was happening behind closed doors in Washington, under what critics referred to as Operation Choke Point 2.0. The regulators took the lever that the banks had been using: the right to refuse business. Legally, banks don’t have to give anyone an account, they have the right to refuse or cease doing business with law-abiding people and businesses, and reputational risk was a convenient rationale to do so. With post-2008 regulation in place, the government had far more control over the banks than before. It could use that lever to target legal industries an administration disfavored: firearms, oil and gas, and, most relevant here, crypto. Now the pendulum has swung back. The OCC report is welcome, and it proves that, hey, we in crypto were not crazy these past years. The crypto industry was being targeted by the government in an unfair manner. The facts support the good actors in the industry who were swept up in an opaque dragnet and what they have been striving toward. But the crypto industry, along with some of the affected banks, had the money to push back and the resources to investigate. OCP 2.0’s targets have power and weight in the economy. The everyday Americans who are unbanked for similar reasons have no such voice. Plenty of studies show minorities remain underbanked in the U.S. So I’d welcome a push for greater fairness in banking, not just for sin stocks and crypto, but for everyone who is underbanked. This all kind of comes together into one question: whose freedom is most paramount? Banks are businesses, and businesses typically aren’t compelled to serve people they don’t want to. “No shirt, no shoes, no service.” The executive branch and federal regulators are now challenging that assumption. If banks can’t refuse customers over perceived reputational risk, and given how much falls under the umbrella of “reputation,” do Americans have a right to banking services? And to be fair, high regulatory barriers to entry limit competition in banking, so it’s not as if spurned customers can just start their own bank. It’s a laudable ideal that access to finance should be fair regardless of one’s politics. Because it flows from constitutional protections for opinion and speech, it starts to sound almost like a right. But that’s a big claim when you don’t even have a right to drive; that’s a privilege. (Ask a “sovereign citizen” what “travel” means and you may get a different answer.) As a proponent of individual freedom, I am torn. I don’t like telling businesses they have to serve people they don’t want to, though The Civil Rights Act sets an appropriate precedent for addressing real harms. And I believe in your right to spend your money as you want. If Citizens United says money is speech, and banks can’t restrict your access based on your speech, does that mean you have a right to put your money in the banking system and use it? Crypto has pursued going bankless as an ethos for years. OCP 2.0 was a U.S. operation, but groups worldwide have been cut off from financial services for their opinions. Crypto is facts-based and doesn’t judge on merit, unlike the traditional trust-based system, which is a machine made of man, and man has biases. I work in crypto because I don’t believe that system is fair. I want to help build one so intrinsically fair that the option to transact freely always exists, no matter what the current administration says. Operation Choke Point 2.0 was real. Industries were systematically debanked amid government and regulatory pressure. There were no laws and no publications, just a back-door squashing of industries the administration of the day didn’t approve of. It can happen under any administration. We need a way to make sure nobody is targeted, no matter who’s in office. That could be a right guaranteed by law, or maybe, just maybe, a transition, driven by economic reality, to an open, blockchain-based financial system. From that point of view, this report is a useful accounting. Maybe we will get a right to financial access. If we don’t, I’m still in the right place to push it forward. – Thad Pinakiewicz
