articles.title: Conditional Markets Are Beginning to Blossom
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Conditional Markets Are Beginning to Blossom

Research • October 15, 2026 • 30 mins
Conditional Markets Are Beginning to Blossom
Decision markets are scaling, impact markets are heading to mainnet, and new infrastructure is pushing event-driven finance beyond prediction markets.

Zack Pokorny
Research Associate

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Markets & Macro

Prediction Markets

IntroductionGalaxy Research has covered prediction markets and their progeny, decision and impact markets, extensively over the last 18 months. We’ve looked at everything from decision markets’ applicability to decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) governance, to their potential as a cold-start mechanism for early-stage crypto projects, to the use of prediction and impact markets as hedging instruments, to Hyperliquid's HIP-4 outcome markets. A throughline in our coverage was the idea that prediction markets served as a sort of “version zero” for event-driven markets and hedging instruments and that experimentation with the broader concept, via decision and impact markets, was blossoming in the background. At the time much of the space was simply an idea that lived in X posts and whitepapers, with some exceptions including MetaDAO. This has begun to change with a number of projects in beta and a new generation of experiments beginning to unfold. The following covers where the sector currently stands, who is building in it, and the intellectual conversations and experiments the movement it created is heading toward.
Why Conditional Markets? Previously, we framed impact and decision markets as two distinct concepts. Today it is best to treat them as subsets of a broader category, which we will call “conditional markets.” The two functionally hold the same market mechanic (i.e. conditional trades are placed in markets and only settle when a specific outcome occurs). The primary difference is that decision markets also settle an explicitly binding outcome (e.g. if price in the conditional market exceeds 5% from spot, then a management team adds a new protocol feature). Given the shared mechanic, and looming expansion in event-driven market types and hedging instruments, it makes most sense to bucket them together. Definitions aside, conditional markets have distinct characteristics that differentiate them from prediction markets as event-driven markets and hedging tools. We covered this point in greater detail here and here, but a few key differentiators include: Transcending the binary, “all or nothing” nature of prediction markets. Allowing participants to trade real assets and their prices as opposed to synthetic probability-based ones. Emitting future events’ impacts on asset values as an informational byproduct as opposed to the probability of whether an event will occur. These qualities, among others covered in the linked reports, set forth different possibilities that prediction markets fundamentally cannot offer from hedging, payout profile, and market signal perspectives.
What Is Happening with Conditional Markets? Both decision and impact markets have progressed meaningfully since our last coverage. The sections below cover the state of each, the projects building at the market and infrastructure layers, and the experiments taking shape around them.
Decision Markets The decision market design space expanded with the September launch of Umia, an ownership token-style launchpad for Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)-compatible chains. Previously, decision markets were mostly confined to Solana through MetaDAO, which trailblazed the concept and was the first implementation at scale. Up to this point, decision markets have been binary: either the decision being traded passed or failed. Proposal drafters solicit feedback from the community, craft the proposal, and launch the market. This approach allowed decisions to be traded through markets, but the social element attached to the drafting process and the fixing of all proposal variables (e.g. increase monthly burn from $50,000 to $65,000 or convert 50% of the DAO treasury to a yield-bearing stablecoin) introduce friction. Traders must base their decision on a proposal's fixed parameters, even if they agree with it directionally but not precisely. (A trader might agree monthly spend should be increased but only to $60,000 or a that the DAO should put its treasury to work but no more than 30% of funds). This pushes the most optimal outcome to be socially filtered, possibly through repeated proposals, or never get priced and traded in the first place. The graphic below highlights how these markets look from a high level.

With the launch of Umia, we now have multi-outcome decision markets where traders can make decisions on a proposal’s parameters (e.g. should we increase spend from $50,000 to $55,000 or $60,000 or some higher amount?). In this case, traders can directionally agree with the proposal, then express their view on its individual details. As a result, traders are pricing the parameters of a proposal, and the overall scope of the proposal is kept more general. By allowing traders to price individual parameters rather than a fixed proposal, this design can reduce the social element that binary pass/fail decision markets depend on, in order to converge on the “most optimal” outcome pre-launch. Rather than relying on drafters to socially filter the “right” version of a proposal before it becomes a market, multi-outcome markets let that filtering happen through price discovery. The practical result is that decisions can be priced more accurately and more efficiently. The market surfaces the specific parameter specification the community supports, rather than forcing judgement on whichever parameter happened to make it into the proposal and price whether the market agrees with it. Rather than relying on drafters to socially filter the “right” version of a proposal before it becomes a market, multi-outcome markets let that filtering happen through price discovery. The graphic below highlights how these markets look from a high level. They are nearly identical in nature to binary outcome decision markets but have multiple markets that can be traded.

One challenge with multi-outcome markets is that liquidity can become fragmented, as the number of tradable markets scales linearly with the number of possible outcomes a proposal carries. Rather than requiring traders to split capital across each market, Umia’s design allows a single deposit (either in stablecoins or DAO tokens) to be converted into a corresponding position across every outcome simultaneously (i.e. a single 5 USDC deposit can be used to trade each of the increase spend $5k, $10k, $15k, and no-op markets). This works because the markets are conditional on one another and only trades in the winning market ultimately settle. So, a trader’s capital can be present everywhere at once without ever being at risk of loss in more than one place. In effect, a given deposit covers the complete outcome space, letting the trader position across every possible proposal parameter without pre-committing to which one they believe will pass. This is what keeps multi-outcome markets liquid. Because one deposit is tradable across every market, adding more outcomes doesn’t divide capital, so depth doesn’t thin out as the number of markets scales. Assets in Market-Governed Treasuries There is now $50.5 million in total value managed by decision markets across 22 DAOs. This figure includes all stablecoins and tokens held by the treasuries (e.g. DAO tokens held on balance sheet, liquidity provider positions, and all other tokens held by the DAOs) of DAOs exclusively using decision markets to govern themselves. The MetaDAO universe commands the majority of assets in market-governed treasuries, occupying 21 of the 22 DAOs using decision markets and 78% of total assets in market-governed treasuries. While $50 million may sound small, MetaDAO’s market-governed DAO launchpad held its first raise just 11 months ago.

Only looking at the stablecoin portion of these DAOs’ balance sheets, there is $35.8 million in value managed by decision markets. This is an important figure to track because it represents the liquidatable value of these organizations in the event investors elect to claw back their funds. As is the case with cumulative assets in market-governed treasuries, the MetaDAO universe controls the majority of the stablecoin value governed by decision markets at 82%.

The Importance of Competition Umia's launch introduces a facet of competition the decision market sector has not previously seen. This is important for the growth and proliferation of decision markets for two reasons: it helps scale assets in market-governed treasuries, and it expands the universe of chains decision market-based organizations can launch on. Scaling assets in market-governed treasuries is arguably the sector’s most important key performance indicator (KPI), because the value of assets governed by decision markets determines how much is economically at stake in any given proposal, and that stake size is what can pull volume into the market. A proposal sitting on top of a small treasury or token market cap only has a small dollar impact if it passes, so traders have little incentive, or absolute inability, to commit meaningful capital to price it. As assets under market scales, the same category of decision carries a bigger value impact, which allows the market to support larger positions and draws in more capital and more sophisticated traders competing to price the outcome correctly. With multiple projects now able to launch decision market DAOs rather than relying on a single incumbent, the sector should also see more organizations running proposals through this mechanism at any given time, adding to aggregate volume even before any individual market grows larger. Competition also expands the possible universe of chains these organizations can launch on. Previously, decision markets were effectively confined to Solana, because MetaDAO was the only project that had launched tokens most suitable for decision markets, a function of the "validity of objective function" problem we have outlined in the past. With Umia's launch, projects can now choose to launch decision market-based DAOs with valid tokens on either Solana or the EVM, which together account for roughly 92% of TVL by chain type, meaningfully widening the addressable market for this design.

Impact Markets Impact markets have made real progress since our earlier coverage of the sector, with a few projects moving through the beta testing phase heading toward mainnet and new projects entering the arena at the market and infrastructure layers. Teams are taking notably different design approaches, and building at different layers of the stack, from standalone markets to the underlying infrastructure meant to support them. Soon, we should see tradable products launched on mainnet applications. Markets need to be short duration and high velocity, closer to the rapid-fire cadence of prediction markets, enough to compensate for trader attention spans. It is becoming clear that competition in this segment is set to expand over the next year. Understanding what is needed for individual projects to succeed as competition picks up clearly indicates what makes these markets useful in the first place, and it starts with traders. The information these markets produce is genuinely valuable, but it's a byproduct of a healthy market, not the product itself. What's being sold to traders is exposure, and exchanges have to be built around giving users a real reason to take, hold, and hedge risk, because that's what generates the volume on which the information depends. This means the approach to who wins needs to be trader-focused: liquidity has to be high enough for these markets to be cited with the same authority mainstream media now gives Polymarket and Kalshi odds, exposure needs to be potent, and leverage needs to be competitive with perps. Conditional markets also don't exist in isolation. Their relationship to underlying perpetual and prediction markets is central to their overall health, so hedging and arbitrage between them need to be practical and economical. Finally, markets need to be short duration and high velocity, closer to the rapid-fire cadence of prediction markets, enough to compensate for trader attention spans. Market Layer The following details several projects building impact markets. Lightcone Lightcone was the first team to publicly lay out the impact market product as it is known today, announcing the project in October 2025, with other teams following shortly after. Lightcone also coined the term “impact market,” effectively naming the category. The project is in beta testing and targeting a public launch before the end of the year. Proof Proof is taking a vertically integrated approach, building a full-stack exchange on its own infrastructure. The team has experience building and operating derivatives exchanges, with a strong trader focus and design decisions centered on supporting liquidity and attractive exposure to traders. The chart below highlights Proof’s vertically integrated design across its conditional market, perps, and prediction markets (it calls them “binaries”).

Proof was founded this year and has launched a testnet of its appchain alongside a v0 exchange, running a trading contest that onboarded roughly 500 traders to test the market design. The team is targeting a gated mainnet launch in the next one to two months (roughly November 2026). Capital efficiency and the relationship between primitives are central to Proof's design. Its margin framework supports leverage and netting across both perpetual and conditional markets. This serves three functions: It gives traders more efficient exposure on individual positions; It lets makers efficiently hedge conditional exposure against the underlying perp; It allows for capital-efficient direct arbitrage between conditionals, perps, and prediction markets (this is important for pricing/market health and is a potential accelerant because the markets can connect flow from two previously disconnected market types). Proof is also building its own perpetual exchange rather than layering conditionals on top of third-party infrastructure. This is necessary to allow margin netting between conditionals and the underlying. Because conditionals sit on top of this underlying exchange, its execution quality directly affects how much liquidity and pricing quality can be supported at the conditionals layer. Proof’s broader view is that a well-executed exchange can capture arbitrage flow from prediction markets and perpetuals against the same underlying liquidity. This matters because shared liquidity can improve market depth, tighten pricing, and make the resulting exposure more attractive to traders. Proof also believes this integrated design can address some of the liquidity constraints that have historically limited event markets, potentially enabling deeper prediction-market exposure on non-sports/election market categories. Proof’s rationale for vertically integrating these primitives is that markets do not exist in isolation. To make conditionals a compelling product, the surrounding components, underlying perpetual liquidity, margining, execution, settlement, and arbitrage pathways, need to work together as a unified system. If Market If Market uses a different design than Proof’s. Rather than creating an onchain solution, it offers exposure as a synthetic, cash-settled position. Users deposit stablecoins and positions settle in cash to the underlying asset’s spot price at market resolution. Nothing is tokenized or custodied through the entire flow. The team’s reasoning for this approach is twofold and runs along the lines of product demand and user experience (UX). There’s possibly less natural interest in holding tokenized versions of markets’ underlying assets, and a pure cash-settled design can create a simpler UX for a product meant to price event impact rather than custody assets. Each market on the platform is organized around a shared event (e.g. “will the Fed cut in the next FOMC?”). Individual markets underneath represent different framings of that event (say, the price of Brent crude oil or gold or Microsoft shares if the event happens and if it doesn’t). Each market splits between YES and NO universes, and each universe carries its own full set of per-asset orderbooks, alongside one shared prediction market book used across each of that market’s assets. The prediction market serves two purposes. One, obviously, is pricing the odds of the event itself. The other is absorbing crystalized profit and loss (P&L) when traders close an impact market position before resolution, converting it to prediction market tokens they can sell immediately or hold till resolution. At resolution, positions in the losing universe return their committed margin in full.

Leverage on the platform went live in September. Positions use isolated margin per position, with position caps tiered by notional. Leverage is available up to 10x on select markets. Unlike perpetual-style designs, If Market has no funding rate. Instead, arbitrage keeps conditional prices anchored to spot, and that risk is managed through the position caps rather than by steering price toward the oracle. Liquidation marks use time-averaged book prices rather than single trades. Resolve prices come from outlier-filtered external sources and, where a market’s rules specify one, a short time-weighted window, which makes settlement harder to manipulate around anticipated resolution moments. The product is still in beta, but the platform’s first trading competition ended Sept. 30 with more than 2,000 traders and over 6 million trades. Infrastructure Layer Aside from exchange and market development, impact markets have also begun seeing some movement at the infrastructure layer. Branchpoint Branchpoint is building Branchmap, a semantic namespace layer for “multiverse finance” (a term originally coined by Dave White, a research partner at VC firm Paradigm) in which impact markets are one supported application among several. Rather than building an exchange first, Branchmap is meant to function as shared infrastructure that gives events, predicates, and outcomes stable, machine-readable identities onchain. This allows prediction markets, DEXes, lending protocols, and any other onchain application to reference the same underlying event data and compose around it. For example, a single registered event, such as whether the Fed hikes rates at a given FOMC meeting, can be referenced simultaneously by a prediction market pricing the probability of a hike, a DEX listing BTC conditioned on that outcome, and a lending protocol accepting that conditioned BTC as collateral, all without each protocol needing to separately define or reconcile what the event is or how it resolves. 'Will the Fed hike at the next FOMC meeting?' can be referenced simultaneously by a prediction market pricing its probability, a DEX listing BTC conditioned on that outcome, and a lending protocol accepting that conditioned BTC as collateral, all without each protocol needing to separately define the event or its resolution. The graphic below highlights how this namespace is structured. It offers an event context (e.g. a Fed rate decision) that contains a predicate (e.g. did the target rate increase?), which in turn produces named outcome entries for each possible result. The combination of outcomes selected across one or more predicates defines a “verse,” or the financial world in which conditional assets live, even though the verse itself is not a stored namespace entry.

The core idea is that prediction markets already function as a kind of numeraire for a given outcome: a binary contract that pays out $1 if an event resolves a certain way is economically equivalent to holding $1 in the universe where that outcome occurred. Branchmap builds upon this idea by letting any asset be split into versions conditioned on each possible outcome of an event, then recombine it once the event resolves. The graphic below shows this mechanic: a root asset splits into verse-conditioned copies for each outcome of a predicate, and once that predicate resolves, the surviving branch recombines back into the plain unconditioned asset.

This splitting mechanism creates a direct link between the probability a prediction market assigns to an outcome and the price of an asset conditional on that outcome, the same decomposition that impact markets are built to price. Branchpoint frames this linkage explicitly as one of its applications: the price of an asset’s claim in a given verse (its “branch price”) factors into a state price, supplied by the prediction market, and an in-verse value, the asset’s market-implied value inside that verse. The state price is the price of the prediction market’s token for that outcome, which approximates the market-implied probability when discounting is negligible. In practice, the conditional-asset market reveals the branch price, and dividing it by the state price recovers the in-verse value. The log of the ratio between an asset’s in-verse value across the “yes” and “no” branches of an event is, in Branchpoint’s framework, a measurable “impact” statistic (illustrated below). Because the namespace gives both sets of prices the same event, outcome, and settlement identities, impact markets can in principle be built on top of it rather than requiring bespoke infrastructure for each one.

Suppose the predicate is whether temperatures in Florida fall below 28°F for more than three straight hours in December, and the prediction market prices a freeze at 10%. If a claim on frozen concentrated orange juice (FCOJ) that pays only in the “yes” verse trades at $0.40 per pound, and the equivalent “no” verse claim trades at $1.80, dividing each branch price by its state price gives the in-verse values: $4.00 in the “yes” verse and $2.00 in the “no” verse. The market therefore expects OJ to be worth twice as much if a freeze occurs, and the impact is the natural log of that ratio: ln($4 / $2) ≈ 0.69. The two branch prices also sum to OJ’s unconditioned price of $2.20.

Branchpoint’s pilot deployment is expected to be a single-chain EVM namespace, initially controlled by the team, with a longer-term roadmap toward a decentralized, cross-chain namespace that other venues and protocols can claim and govern independently. As with other infrastructure-layer plays, Branchpoint's usefulness to the impact market segment specifically will depend on venues and market operators adopting Branchmap as the shared substrate for their events and conditional assets, rather than each building isolated event definitions and resolution logic of its own.
In the Background The world is becoming more complex, and the downstream impacts of individual events, whether they be political, regulatory, technological, or environmental, are becoming more consequential for asset prices and company balance sheets. Some of the risks investors and businesses may want to more actively hedge today were more benign or absent in the past, or instruments to hedge certain risks or achieve certain payout profiles did not exist. The natural conclusion is that market participants and companies should have the ability to hedge against any event, not just the narrow set of risks traditional financial instruments were originally built around, and to achieve payout profiles tailored to their needs. Conditional markets are one expression of this idea, but they’re likely just one step along a broader path toward more flexible, event-based financial tooling. The world is becoming more complex, and the downstream impacts of individual events, be they political, regulatory, technological, or environmental, are becoming more consequential for asset prices and balance sheets.The primary hedging instrument onchain today, perpetual futures, also has some limitations that can push demand toward alternatives. Perps hold a linear payout profile (i.e. exposure scales directly with underlying price, independent of the level), which doesn’t fit every use case. Some risks are better expressed with a non-linear or event-contingent payout rather than constant 1:1 exposure. Perps also come with liquidation risk (see “10/10”), which not all traders are willing to take. There are a few projects working on and greater thought going into the above ideas.
Options Protocols Since Jan. 1, Derive's options business has grown meaningfully. Monthly options notional volume dipped from $1.47b in January to a low of $629m in February, then climbed steadily through the summer before accelerating sharply to $3.82b in September, roughly 2.6x January's level, with the trailing 30 days (Sept. 13–Oct. 12) running about 195% above the January pace. Options open interest followed a more uneven path, starting the year at $590m, sliding to a trough of $359m in late June, then rebuilding to a peak of $2.49b on Sept. 21 before settling at $1.66b by Oct. 12. That is up about 181% since Jan. 1, more than 4.6x off the June low, and roughly 34% below the September peak.

Onchain options have historically been kneecapped relative to their offchain counterparts due to funding requirements that made them structurally more expensive, particularly for sellers, who had to post 100% of margin upfront onchain rather than the smaller, dynamically margin-called positions available offchain. Nonetheless, the recent trajectory is a meaningful signal that onchain traders appear to be actively seeking alternative hedging vehicles beyond perps, which bodes well for adoption of the more exotic conditional and event-driven instruments covered elsewhere in this report.
Castle Tech Castle Technologies is a New York-based startup founded this year. Its value proposition is to turn event risk that traditional insurance and derivatives markets don't price (e.g. tariffs, geopolitical disruption, or a specific piece of legislation) into structured, tradable hedges. Castle's recent deal with a goat herding company in California is a useful illustration of what a hedge looks like when the risk is too narrow and idiosyncratic for any insurer to price, and there's no existing market to plug into.

Conditional markets are literally goated. A lapsed wage exemption for California goat herders threatened to roughly triple or quadruple labor costs, to as much as $240,000 a year, at Western Grazers, an operator running roughly 4,000 goats for wildfire-fuel clearing. No insurance company writes a policy against a specific legislative outcome, and there was no options market, no perp, and no prediction market on this question before Castle got involved; it isn't the kind of event that generates natural two-sided retail interest on its own. Castle's job was to build the pipeline for that exposure from the ground up by translating an ongoing legislative situation into a precise, self-certifiable settlement condition, then finding a counterparty willing to price and hold a risk no traditional underwriter would touch. Western Grazers entered into a swap agreement with Castle, structured so the company would receive a payout of roughly $500,000 if California's legislature failed to address the wage issue before an Oct. 1 deadline, and no payout if lawmakers fixed it. Castle laid off that risk through a back-to-back swap with quant trading firm Susquehanna, which priced and warehoused the exposure, with the trade ultimately routed through a Kalshi prediction market for liquidity and settlement. A legislative change affecting California goat herders isn't the kind of event that generates natural two-sided retail interest on its own.The result was a custom-underwritten policy executed through prediction-market exchange rails with one print, one counterparty, and one settlement condition drafted specifically for this trade rather than pulled off a shelf. Castle manufactured, end to end, a hedge that had no prior instrument, no prior market, and no insurer willing to offer it, and prediction market infrastructure was able to facilitate it all. This transaction signals demand for “hedge everything products.” Businesses increasingly face risks (regulatory, legislative, hyper-local) that sit outside what conventional insurance and derivatives markets are built to cover and are willing to pay a real premium for someone to structure a bespoke answer on demand.
Statebook Statebook is more theoretical than a live product, but it offers a useful reframing of how event-based hedging instruments could be organized. Introduced in a working paper titled “Markets for All States of the World,” the idea is to design financial markets around a payoff profile (i.e. the exposure a given trader wants) first, then work backward to figure out which existing contracts, or combinations of contracts, can deliver the payoff, as opposed to starting from whatever instruments happen to already be listed and forcing traders to make do with them. The math underpinning this idea echoes the state-price theory walked through in the Branchmap section earlier, but the two arrive at their state definitions from different places. Branchmap's state prices come from Arrow-Debreu-style partitions where a predicate (e.g. "did the Fed hike?") resolves via an oracle, and the resulting outcome directly defines a verse. No option chain is required for a verse to exist. Statebook's state prices come from a narrower but more specific model, Breeden-Litzenberger. Differentiating a European call option's price with respect to its strike recovers the market's implied price of the underlying finishing above (or within) any given level or range, turning an option curve into a ladder of boundary and interval claims. Branchmap uses its state definitions to give conditional assets a shared semantic identity, so onchain protocols can reference and compose around the same event. A statebook, by contrast, operationalizes its state definitions as an execution layer by treating ordinary options, boundary or threshold claims (e.g. "pays $1 if the index finishes above 100"), and interval claims (e.g. "pays $1 if the index finishes between 100 and 110") as different views into the same option-implied state-price data, so that a claim with no order book of its own, like a narrow interval bet, can still be filled by assembling it out of two more liquid boundary claims or a matched pair of options, with the statebook responsible for finding the cheapest available route and disclosing it as a firm, executable price. This is, in effect, the same ambition driving conditional markets more broadly by building infrastructure that can hedge any precisely definable event or price outcome, not just the handful of payoffs that happen to have deep, purpose-built markets today. Statebook arrives at that goal through execution and routing rather than through the onchain semantic-namespace approach Branchmap takes, and it’s grounded overwhelmingly in TradFi and U.S. regulatory market structure rather than DeFi. Onchain venues such as Hyperliquid and Polymarket appear only as comparators rather than as the paper's primary subject. Still, the throughline is the same. Conditional markets, impact markets, and statebooks are all variations on the idea that markets should be organized around the states of the world traders want exposure to, rather than around whatever contracts happen to already exist. Notably, the statebook paper also points out that perpetual futures, the dominant onchain hedging instrument today, don't fit into this framework at all, because they have no fixed maturity and therefore no terminal payoff to define a state around, implying that perps and statebook-style claims are likely to serve different, complementary hedging needs rather than compete for the same one.
Conclusion The design space for conditional markets is beginning to expand, as projects approach mainnet on the impact market front and multiple teams build on the concept of decision markets. What started as prediction markets serving as a “version zero” for event-driven finance has, over the last 18 months, created a Cambrian explosion of experimentation. Decision markets add binding governance outcomes to the mechanic. Impact markets isolate the effect of an event on an asset's price rather than the probability of the event itself. Now infrastructure and downstream concepts like Branchmap and statebook are pushing the underlying idea, that markets should be organized around the states of the world traders actually want exposure to, into new territory entirely. With Umia introducing competition to decision markets for the first time and multiple teams now building impact markets at both the market and infrastructure layers, competition across this stack should meaningfully pick up over the next year. What started as prediction markets serving as a “version zero” for event-driven finance has, over the last 18 months, created a Cambrian explosion of experimentation. That said, this is all still early. The education curve for traders and builders is steep, and every impact market project covered here is either in beta or, in the case of statebook, still a working paper rather than a live product. Liquidity for these new instrument types will need to be built up largely from scratch, demand for some of them may prove more niche than proponents expect, and the sector as a whole is still converging on what the best underlying designs actually look like, whether Proof's vertically integrated stack or If Market's cash-settled, non-tokenized approach. Decision markets, on the other hand, are further along, with DAOs actively using MetaDAO and Umia designs, and proliferation of decision-market-governed organizations is underway. The next year should offer a much clearer signal on how the open questions facing impact markets get resolved, and on how much further decision market adoption can scale from here.

articles.title: The Curse Of Good Intentions
articles.text:
The Curse Of Good Intentions

Udith Sikand

Gavekal Research | 13 Oct 2026

The Reserve Bank of India’s increasingly heavy-handed efforts to defend the rupee risk doing more harm than good. By imposing administrative curbs on currency hedging, the central bank may deter the very foreign capital inflows needed to ease depreciation pressures. It is the sort of policy predicament that the economist Lant Pritchett had in mind when he dubbed India a “flailing state” where limited state capacity often frustrates even well-intentioned policies.The Indian rupee has been sliding since mid-2025, with its decline accelerating after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March sent oil prices soaring. Pressured by higher fuel prices, foreign capital outflows and rising global interest rates, the rupee has been one of Asia’s weakest currencies this year, falling -5.5% against the US dollar. To stem the sell-off, the RBI launched a special scheme in early June to attract US dollars from wealthy expatriate Indians, generating inflows of US$130bn over the summer. Against an expected current account deficit of around US$80bn in 2026 and equity portfolio outflows of around US$30bn, it seemed the worst was over for the currency (see India’s Hawkish Turn).

articles.title: More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales
articles.text:
More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales

Given at Association of Financial Mutuals Annual Conference 2026

Published on
05 October 2026

Speech
Opening remarks
Thank you for inviting me to speak today.
Having been in my role for a few months, I have been reflecting on the insights it has given me into how firms operate. One thing that has stood out about mutuals is not just that they are owned by their members, but how that ownership shapes the decisions they make. We can see this in the important role they play in serving parts of the market that may otherwise be underserved.
Against this background, you can understand why the Mutuals Landscape Report sets out our ambition to support the sector’s sustainable long-term growth. What that means will differ from one mutual to another. Many mutuals will continue to operate sustainably. Some will grow organically, while others may pursue acquisitions.
For some mutuals, the strategic challenge is different. They have told us that their current business models may not be sustainable over the longer term. The reasons for this include high levels of competition, keeping pace with technological change, and responding to rapidly-changing economic pressures. Some of these firms are responding by adapting their strategies and exploring new opportunities. Others are considering whether a solvent exit, including through transferring some or all of their business to another firm, may provide the best outcome for their members.
Where the firm being acquired is a friendly society, the transaction will take place through the Part VIII transfer process under the Friendly Societies Act 1992, with the PRA being ultimately responsible for deciding whether a transfer should proceed. While that process is grounded in legislation, we heard feedback that firms would benefit from having a clearer understanding of both the process itself and the factors that inform our decisions. In the Mutuals Landscape Report, we committed to providing more clarity, and CP12/26 (the CP) fulfils that promise. It sets out proposals intended to make our approach clearer and gives firms a more structured sequence of steps to follow. And alongside that, we are also improving the way we manage these transactions internally.
With these initiatives, we aim to promote a dynamic market and support sustainable growth of the mutuals sector.
But the PRA is not the only one working to make this process more efficient. We have also observedfootnote [1] practical approaches developed by firms to improve how these transactions are managed. Today, I want to provide an overview of the Part VIII process. As I do so, I will weave practical insights on how we have seen firms successfully navigate that process, so that others can benefit from the experience of previous transactions.
Reflections from a recent mover
Before turning to those insights, let me take a step back and explain why the process matters.
A Part VIII transfer can offer significant strategic benefits, such as realising economies of scale, improving service standards, and becoming more resilient. All of these improve outcomes for members. But it also requires firms to commit considerable time and resources, with the costs ultimately borne by members. At the PRA, we are very conscious that if a transfer cannot be confirmed, those costs may still have been incurred without the expected benefits being realised. That’s why we work with firms to try to help them build the evidence needed to demonstrate that the legislative requirements have been met.
Meeting those requirements is not just about ticking a legal box. Members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, to protect their interests.
So, how should firms approach the Part VIII process?
While no analogy can fully capture the significance of a Part VIII transfer, particularly for mutuals with long histories and strong member communities, it may be helpful in illustrating the process itself, especially for those who are less familiar with Part VIII transfers. The decisions surrounding a transfer are often complex and significant. But when it comes to the process, it has some parallels with moving house. Driving the moving van into your new driveway may feel like the culmination of the journey, but a successful move depends on everything that happened beforehand. You need to understand why you are moving, weigh up the options, complete the necessary checks, and prepare carefully for what follows.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer.
As the slide shows, we have split that journey into five parts. Let me take each in turn.

Chart 1: Part VIII Transfer Process

Part A: Planning and preparation
Let me start with planning and preparation.
Every house move begins with a reason for moving. When my wife and I bought our home, we spent as much time discussing why we wanted to move as we spent choosing the house. Did we need more space? Or a shorter commute? Once we were clear about our objectives, many of the decisions that followed became easier.
A1: Intention to transfer, A4: Details of transfer plans
When similar questions are considered in the context of a Part VIII transfer, firms may have many avenues to explore. To help firms navigate these factors, the CP highlights the matters the PRA is likely to focus on early in the process, including members' interests.
Of course, firms will generally pursue a transfer because they believe it will deliver better outcomes for members. However, those benefits may not be shared equally between all members, and they may emerge at different times. It is possible that in some circumstances, particular groups of members could be worse off. The key question then is whether the transfer is in the interests of the members of each friendly society participating in the transfer.
Part of answering that question comes from how the benefits are expected to arise. Where a proposal relies on cost savings, operational changes, or integration programmes, those assumptions help explain how the combined business is expected to operate after the transfer. They can provide an important indication of whether there is a credible strategy and a realistic plan to deliver the expected benefits to members.
We have also found it helpful to consider the proposal from another perspective: in what circumstances might some members be worse off? Firms often undertake careful analysis of that question to understand whether potentially adverse impacts have been appropriately considered.
We can work with you as you develop your thinking in this area, which will help with later stages of the transfer. For example, some benefits may depend on integrating the two firms and could take several years to emerge. Whilst there are different ways to ensure that members will be protected in the meantime, the PRA can work with firms to establish what evidence could help show that the legal test has been met. These discussions could inform the transfer documentation, actuarial analysis, and communications with members.
A2: Preparations, updating rules, and applying for permission
Moving on to the preparations step, we have seen firms take a careful and considered approach to the practical aspects of the process. That includes considering whether the acquirer has the necessary regulatory permissions. This matters because permissions do not transfer with the business.
As an extra check, some firms have used the FCA’s register to compare the transferring society’s permission with the acquirer’s permission. This has allowed the acquirer to confirm whether it has identified and addressed any gaps in its permission.
This has also helped firms explain why a permission will no longer be required to cover specific regulated activities and, in doing so, show that the relevant statutory test has been met. These checks may appear relatively small. But when carried out early, they help the wider process run more efficiently.
A3: Considerations of overseas members and regulators
Turning to overseas members, this relates to one of the statutory tests, where the PRA must assess whether there is a substantial risk that the acquirer will be unable legally to carry on the business being transferred. This is usually relatively straightforward for members in the UK, but firms have found it more challenging for members based overseas.
Much of that work begins with a simple question: where are your members based? Maintaining up-to-date member records has helped firms with this work. There are other useful ways of checking those records. Some firms may find it helpful to consider payments to and from non-UK bank accounts to identify any other overseas members.
With that information in hand, firms can consider their overseas members in the context of the legal test and develop a reasoned explanation of why the legal test is met. There is a range of different forms of evidence to consider, from local legal advice to the relevant EIOPA recommendationfootnote [2]. The CP highlights engagement with overseas regulators, which firms may find to be a practical and cost-effective way of exploring the position.
While these steps should help, we recognise that firms continue to face challenges in this area. Indeed, we engaged with the Law Commission on the issue ahead of its recently published proposals. At our recent roundtablefootnote [3], firms also suggested ways in which the PRA could help firms with the overseas member part of the process. We are considering if we can further clarify what information we might need from firms in order for the PRA to assess the legal test under the existing legislation. We will, of course, consider this feedback alongside any responses we receive to the CP.
A5: PRA’s approach to special resolution: consent for Part VIII transfers
Let me turn to the final part of planning and preparation: what many firms call the dispensation process. This is where the acquiring society can seek the PRA's consent for the transfer to be approved by its board, rather than through a special resolution voted on by its members.
Giving the acquirer’s members the opportunity to vote is an important safeguard, so it is not a requirement the PRA will dispense with lightly. But we also recognise that holding a vote comes at a cost, which is ultimately borne by members.
In the past, firms have told us that this is one of the less predictable parts of the process, so we have added more clarity on our approach in the CP. It provides some reference points for how the PRA is likely to consider whether to consent to a dispensation. One of these is that firms will also need to show that the transfer is in the interests of the acquirer’s members and that there are no factors likely to lead a material number of them to vote against it. Firms are likely to benefit from discussing this with their transfer partner and considering this point together.
For example, that collaboration may bring to light a history of tension between the societies that could influence how members would vote if they were given the opportunity. Factors like this don’t necessarily mean that consent couldn’t be granted. But open discussions on such matters can help the PRA understand the position more quickly and reduce the need for further questions.
Part B: Recording and analysing the transfer
Let me move on to recording and analysing the transfer.
Once my family had decided which house to buy, our attention turned to the practicalities. The paperwork began, surveys were commissioned and the important decisions had to be documented.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer. Once firms have developed their proposal, the focus shifts to documenting the terms of the transfer and analysing its effects.
B1: Instrument of Transfer
Once firms are clear about the purpose and structure of the transaction, that understanding must be captured in the Instrument of Transfer. Producing the Instrument is a statutory requirement, but it can also provide important protections for the members of both firms.
The Instrument can cover a wide range of matters, from service standards to membership rights. We have seen firms benefit from bringing together legal, risk, and actuarial specialists to develop it. It has also helped firms consider not only what is needed to give effect to the transfer, but what additional protections could be provided to members, both now and over the long-term.
Those protections will depend on the circumstances of each transfer. We have seen firms consider important safeguards for the management of transferred funds, appropriate governance arrangements, and commitments about the future treatment of policyholders.
Where with-profits policies are involved, firms have found it helpful to specify the fund to which those policies will be allocated and how expenses will be apportioned. They have also considered what support may be available from other funds, particularly where this could affect the receiving fund’s investment strategy. Setting out these details in the draft Instrument can then provide a clear basis for the actuarial analysis supporting the transfer.
B2: Internal actuarial reports, B3: Independent actuary report and supplementary report(s)
The actuarial analysis is an important part of the process. Internal actuarial reports help boards and regulators understand how a proposed transfer is expected to affect members. Clear and balanced reports can also provide a strong foundation for communications with members, particularly where outcomes are uncertain or depend on judgement. The more useful reports explain the assumptions, evidence, and reasoning behind the conclusions they reach.
In our experience, the more complete internal actuarial reports consider how members are expected to be affected before the transfer, immediately after the transfer, as well as after any integration of the two businesses. This helps all of us – including members – understand both the destination and the journey to get there.
The firms’ own analysis is important. However, in some cases, the process also requires an independent perspective. Much as an independent surveyor provides an objective assessment when someone is purchasing a property, the Independent Actuary provides independent scrutiny of the firms’ analysis. The CP provides greater clarity on when we are likely to require a report from an Independent Actuary. We hope this will help firms better understand the likely costs of a transfer.
Where an Independent Actuary provides a report, the legislation requires it to address the likely effects of the transfer on members who are long-term policyholders. We have found that reports are most useful when they explain both the positive and adverse effects, how those effects may differ between groups of policyholders, and the basis for any conclusions about materiality. Of course, this balanced analysis helps members understand the proposal. But it also supports the PRA’s assessment of whether the transfer is in members’ interests, alongside the FCA’s consideration of fairness.
As an aside, we have found that it is often a good idea for firms to also consider any FCA requirements that apply to the transaction (for example, if the FCA's reattribution rules for with-profits business apply).
There is also an important relationship between the internal actuarial reports and the Independent Actuary’s report. If an internal report contains material information that is not reflected in the summary of the Independent Actuary’s report included in communications sent to members, firms will need to consider whether members have received all the information they need to understand the proposal and make an informed decision. This is one of the statutory tests the PRA must assess. In previous transfers, we have worked with firms to understand how they have met it.
Even where an Independent Actuary is not appointed, another form of independent review may still be valuable. We have seen firms benefit from independent peer review of their internal actuarial analysis and key judgements. This can strengthen the overall assessment and give members greater confidence in the analysis, particularly where they are considering whether to make representations about the proposed transfer.
Part C: Member engagement and member vote(s)
Having considered the key documents supporting a transfer, the next stage is to translate them into communications that members can understand and engage with.
When my family moved house, it wasn’t enough for me to know the plan. Everyone needed to understand what was happening, why it was happening and what it means for them (or, in our case, who was getting the biggest bedroom). Member engagement is similar. The technical analysis may be robust, but it only serves its purpose if members can understand what the transfer means for them.
C1: Member engagement: general approach, C2: Member engagement: Schedule 15 statement, C3: Resolutions
Member communications play an important role in informing how members vote. So, as you would expect, the FCA considers them through the lens of the Consumer Duty, with a focus on ensuring that they are clear and easy to understand. What makes the Part VIII transfer process slightly different is that the PRA also has a statutory role in reviewing one of the key communications sent to members: the Schedule 15 statement.
The CP provides more details on what the PRA considers as part of that review. I want to reflect on some practical approaches that we have seen work well in previous transfers.
The more developed Schedule 15 statements are those that clearly explain what the transfer means for members. They present the key considerations fairly and help members reach their own view. One approach that could work well is testing communications before they are finalised. We have read documents that include all the relevant technical details, but it is not always clear whether these messages are framed in the best way for members to fully understand them. To ensure that the proposed messages can be understood, it may be helpful to run the proposed communications past a colleague who has not been involved in the transfer or seek feedback from a small group of members.
We have also seen the value of careful and balanced drafting. The stronger summaries of the Independent Actuary’s conclusions tend to be those that faithfully reflect the full report while focusing on the matters most relevant to members’ decisions.
Of course, even the clearest communication is only effective if it reaches the people for whom it is intended. The legislation requires the Schedule 15 statement to be sent to all eligible voting members. Where firms have faced challenges contacting members, we have seen a range of practical approaches, including tracing exercises, updating records, using alternative contact methods, and contacting members directly to confirm their details. Firms have also used press notices and other engagement channels to raise awareness of the transfer and the voting process. In some cases, firms have supplemented this with dedicated webpages containing information about the transfer.
Although I have focused on the Schedule 15 statement, we have seen firms engage with their members in different ways. This includes with letters, frequently asked questions, presentations, webinars, and online material. The aim is to help members understand the proposed transfer and give them a genuine opportunity to engage with the proposal before casting their vote. Where members are effectively engaged, it helps firms address issues and reduce the likelihood of unexpected representations arising later in the transfer process.
Part D: Formal application, public notices, and representations
When buying a house, arguably the most important stage is the period leading up to the exchange of contracts. During that stage, surveyors, solicitors, mortgage brokers, and banks can all raise questions, identify risks or challenge assumptions underlying the proposed purchase.
D1: Formal notice of the application
The formal notice of the application plays an important role in the period leading up to the transaction, bringing it to the attention of interested parties and ensuring that those affected have an opportunity to engage with the process.
Firms will submit the formal notice after the member vote. So, whilst the progression of these tasks remains subject to member approval, there is preparatory work we can do ahead of that. In previous transfers, firms have provided draft notices for our review.
The PRA will also direct firms to publish the notice in the London, Edinburgh, or Belfast Gazettes as well as other newspapers where appropriate. However, firms can suggest which Gazette(s) and newspapers they feel would be the most appropriate.
D2: Approach to representations, D3: Representations Hearing
Once the formal notice has been published, the representations period begins. It gives members and other stakeholders an opportunity to raise concerns about the transfer.
But the representations process is about more than formal representations submitted directly to the PRA. Firms also consider whether concerns, complaints, or queries received through their own channels raise issues that are similar in nature to a formal representation. These interactions can provide valuable insight into the matters that are most important to members.
Part E: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s) and related processes
The final stage of buying a house is exchanging contracts and moving into the property. By that point, much of the hard work has already been done. The legal issues have been addressed and the financing agreed. What remains is to finalise the purchase arrangements. The same principle applies to the final stage of a Part VIII transfer.
E1: Preparations for the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s), E2: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
The Preclusion Grounds Analysis sits at the heart of this stage. It explains why none of the statutory grounds that would prevent the PRA from confirming the transfer have been met. The stronger submissions tend to be balanced and leverage the evidence already generated throughout the transfer process and present it in a thorough and structured way.
Let me give you an example. When looking at the solvency ground, some firms carefully consider whether the acquiring society will maintain an adequate margin of solvency after the transfer. They bring together the evidence supporting that conclusion, such as post-transfer financial projections, actuarial analysis, audited financial information, and any material changes since the latest valuation date.
We have seen a similar approach taken when considering whether the members’ vote was representative. Firms’ analysis usually explains why the requirements of the legislation and the relevant society rules have been met. The more developed analyses also consider factors such as how voting turnout compares with previous member votes and whether the outcome would have changed under different assumptions. For example, where some members could not be traced despite reasonable efforts being made to contact them, firms could consider whether the outcome of the member vote would have been different if those members had voted against the transfer.
Perhaps the area where we have seen the greatest variation is the assessment of whether the proposed transfer is in the interests of the members of both societies. The more developed analyses bring together actuarial, risk, and legal evidence to consider factors such as benefit security, benefit expectations, service standards, and membership rights. They also identify situations in which some members may be disadvantaged and explain how those risks have been assessed and mitigated.
In considering firms’ post-transfer target operating models, we have taken a proportionate approach, with discussions often centred on three related questions.

How will the enlarged business operate immediately after the transfer?
What is the target operating model?
How does the firm intend to move from one to the other?

E3: The PRA’s decision, E4: Processes after the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
After the PRA has reached its decision, it is not the end of the journey. There are a few procedural steps left including issuing the decision notice and registering the Instrument of Transfer.
Firms will also continue implementing aspects of their target operating model after the transfer has completed. Boards should continue to satisfy themselves that members are seeing the expected benefits from the transfer.
Closing remarks
I appreciate that this statutory process may feel a long and complex journey. But members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, so it’s right that we approach the statutory requirements with care.
At the same time, we recognise that members ultimately benefit from an efficient process. CP12/26 sets out our proposals to make our approach clearer, more transparent, and easier to navigate. Your engagement has already informed those proposals, and I would encourage you to respond to the consultation so that we can continue refining our approach together.
I don’t want to close without recognising the important work being undertaken by the Law Commission to modernise the legislative framework for friendly societies. We have engaged with the Law Commission as it has developed its final report and draft bill Opens in a new window. Should any legislative changes be made, the PRA stands ready to update its approach and guidance as necessary.
I hope that what I’ve shared today will highlight that a successful transfer is not simply about completing a transaction or changing an address. It’s about finding the right long-term home for a friendly society’s members.
I am grateful to Hannah-Kousar Rashid for preparing these remarks. I am also grateful to Abi Batchelor, Alex Tapp, Giles Woodruff, Nozipho Gazi, Robert Kipling, Robyn Dwyer, Sanjeev Chandran, and Wayne Snow for their support and comments.

The observations shared in this speech are based on a range of firms and transfers at different times. They are illustrative of the general approach taken. Some details may have been changed or combined from different transfers to ensure confidentiality. As such, the information included should not be considered attributable to any one firm or transfer.

articles.title: Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code
articles.text:
Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code

The Bank of England chairs the Money Markets Committee, which has endorsed the voluntary UK Money Markets Code setting out best practice for participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets.

In this section

Fair and Effective Markets
Foreign currency reserves
Market intelligence
Bank of England Market Operations Guide
Settlement and collateral management
SONIA interest rate benchmark
Transition from LIBOR to risk-free rates

On this pageMoney Markets CommitteeUK Money Markets Code CommitteeSecurities Lending CommitteeMoney Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo CommitteeUK Money Markets Code

Money Markets Committee
The Money Markets Committee (MMC) is a senior-level forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to discuss issues concerning the UK unsecured deposits and funding market, the securities lending market and the repo market.
The MMC is chaired by the Bank of England.
The committee meets quarterly and also has two permanent sub-committees: the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee and the Securities Lending Committee.
Objectives of the Money Markets Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK money, repo and securities lending markets.
Where appropriate, to propose responses to any issues identified.
To aid understanding and enhance monitoring of the functioning of the UK money markets.
To endorse and facilitate continuing market-wide adoption of the UK Money Markets Code, a voluntary code of good practice for the money and securities financing markets.
To identify and address any high-level issues concerning contingency planning in the UK money markets and payment systems, having regard to international developments.

Increasing diversity in our committees
The UK Money Markets Code includes an expectation that market participants will promote the development of a diverse and inclusive within their money market teams. This includes working to create a diverse pipeline of potential future Committee members.
We also aim for diversity within the Money Markets Committee and its Sub-committees, in order that they can best represent the people of the United Kingdom. Diverse membership means that these Committees benefit from diversity of thought, which bring different viewpoints and help to ensure well-informed decision-making.
We work with members from the Money Markets Committee to diversify its membership. As part of this, we provide opportunities for members to bring observers to Committee meetings, in order that these observers can gain a better understanding of the Committee, and to help identify potential future diverse candidates.
You can find out more about ‘Meeting Varied People’ – our initiative to increase the diversity of the market contacts that we engage with – on the Market intelligence page.

UK Money Markets Code Committee
The project to update and revise the former codes for non-foreign exchange market products in the UK market led by a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee is a permanent sub-committee of the MMC, and is co-chaired by, and made up of, senior market participants. The sub-committee meets regularly to ensure that the code remains relevant and up to date as markets evolve.

Terms of reference for the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee

UK Money Markets Code Committee minutes

Letter to Signatories of Statement of Commitment to UK Money Markets Code (PDF 0.1MB) Opens in a new window

Securities Lending Committee
The Securities Lending Committee (SLC) is a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The SLC is chaired by a market participant. It is a forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to meet to discuss issues concerning the UK securities lending market, including all collateral activities.
Objectives of the Securities Lending Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK securities lending market.
To discuss legal, regulatory, trading, settlement, infrastructure, tax, disclosure and other related developments in this market.
Where appropriate, it will propose responses to these issues.
To aid the understanding and enhance the monitoring of the functioning of this market.

Working Group on Settlement Efficiency
The Bank of England Securities Lending Committee has established a Working Group to examine the issue of settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. It provides a senior-level forum for market participants to meet to identify root causes for settlement issues in the UK securities lending market and suggest best practices.
The Working Group will examine drivers and impact of fails and determine potential solutions to settlement failure in the UK securities lending market. Part of this work will be to advocate best practice in the securities lending market.
Membership of the group will reflect a diverse group of market participants with relevant expertise, perspective and knowledge. It is chaired by Tim McLeod (Blackrock, Inc.). The Bank of England will participate as Ex-Officio members and provide administrative support.
Please note that views and outputs of the Working Group do not constitute guidance or legal advice from, and are not necessarily endorsed by, the Bank of England (including the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)).

Money Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo Committee
The Money Markets Committee was formed in March 2017 to replace previous markets committees, the Money Markets Liaison Committee (MMLC) and Securities Lending and Repo Committee (SLRC).
Please see the National Archives for historic MMLC and SLRC minutes.
The National Archives Opens in a new window
UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code is a voluntary code written by market participants. It incorporates revised relevant sections of the Non-Investment Products (NIPs) Code, and also a revision and update of the Gilt Repo Code and Securities Borrowing and Lending Code.
The UK Money Markets Code was published on 26 April 2017.

The UK Money Markets Code
The UK Money Markets Code: explanatory notes

Voluntary codes of best practice can help to establish the basis on which financial markets function, ensuring trust between participants. This in turn creates an environment so that a fair, effective and transparent market can flourish and in which, by adhering to such codes, high standards of behaviour can be assured.
The code sets out such standards and the best practice expected from participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets in the UK. It supersedes previous guidance for participants in these markets provided by the NIPs Code, the Gilt Repo Code and the Securities Borrowing and Lending Code. By bringing these together it will more clearly establish the framework for transacting in UK money markets. The code is endorsed by the Money Markets Committee and will be updated regularly.
The Money Markets Committee has also established a Public Register of Institutions who have signed a Statement of Commitment or a Statement of Support to the Code. The purpose of the Register is to further restore trust in financial markets by making it easier to see which institutions have taken the important step of committing to the principles set out in the Code.

The UK Money Markets Code Committee and the Association of Corporate Treasurers have produced this guide to promote and encourage wider adherence to the Code among the Corporate sector.

Take Two: Fed signals further rate increase; US stocks hit record high

By
BNP PARIBAS ASSET MANAGEMENT 12.10.2026

What do you need to know?Around the worldFigure in focus: $6 trillionChart of the weekWords of wisdom: Pre-COP31What’s coming up?

LinkedIn

What do you need to know?

US interest rates are likely to increase again before the end of 2026, the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s latest meeting showed. All members of the rate-setting committee voted in favour of a 25 basis-point rate hike to 3.75%-4.0% in September, and “most” felt that another hike “would likely be appropriate by year end”. They agreed that inflation risks were “skewed to the upside” – more likely to rise than to fall – though the unemployment rate is expected to remain stable, and economic activity was expanding at a solid pace.

Around the world

Wall Street profits hit $45.9 billion in the first half of this year, up 51% from the same period last year, according to a report from the New York State Comptroller, the state’s financial watchdog. If the pace continues, corporate profits could exceed $90 billion in 2026, it said. The blue-chip S&P 500 index closed above 7,800 for the first time last week while the tech-heavy Nasdaq also hit a fresh record high. Meanwhile government bond yields in the Eurozone, UK and US rose early in the week, fuelled by worries over fiscal deficits and inflation, before retreating as oil prices fell.

Figure in focus: $6 trillion

An estimated $6 trillion in artificial intelligence-driven revenue will be needed every year to justify the expected spending on AI infrastructure, according to a new report from consultancy Bain & Company. Annual AI infrastructure spending could reach $1.5 trillion by 2031, it said, and if capital expenditure represents around 25% of industry revenue, “sustaining this level of investment would require an AI market approaching $6 trillion annually.” Productivity gains from existing business and consumer applications are not enough to warrant this scale, Bain said, and new markets must emerge to close the gap.

Chart of the week

The yield on US 10-year Treasuries now exceeds the expected earnings yield of the S&P 500, suggesting that equities are expensive relative to fixed income. This implies that investors are accepting lower compensation for taking equity risk, likely in anticipation of stronger medium-to-long-term earnings growth. While this reflects robust investor confidence, further increases in bond yields would necessitate either upward earnings revisions or an equity market correction. Conversely, should earnings keep pace with rising yields, the upward trend in equity markets may persist.

Words of wisdom: Pre-COP31

A gathering of ministers and high-level government representatives took place last week to lay the political groundwork for the United Nations climate change conference COP31 in November. The goal of the Pre-COP was to explore solutions for accelerating global climate action, improving access to climate finance and ensuring a fair energy transition. The event, which took place in Fiji and Tuvalu, also highlighted climate policy and solutions for the Pacific island states which are vulnerable to climate change.

What’s coming up?

The Reserve Bank of Australia publishes minutes of its latest monetary policy meeting on Tuesday – it hiked rates by 25bp in September. On Wednesday, China and the US each report their latest inflation data followed by the Eurozone on Friday. The International Monetary Fund and World Bank ‘s annual meetings take place in Bangkok from Monday through to Sunday.

articles.title: Daily: Semis stumble. Time to reboot expectations?
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Market Playbook | Asia beyond the AI trade (6 mins)Video: The AI Show | Is the AI trade under strain? (4 mins)Thought of the dayPressure has ratcheted up on global chip stocks in recent days, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down around 8% over the last five sessions and South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi falling over 12% since the start of the month.Investors have been grappling with concerns over the durability of AI spending, competitive risks from China's rising memory maker, higher-for-longer rates, and the debate surrounding OpenAI's reported revenue trajectory. Sentiment was further affected after Broadcom's CEO warned earlier this week that financing the AI infrastructure buildout could eventually become a greater constraint than component shortages, highlighting the demanding expectations embedded in AI-linked stocks.But while volatility could persist as markets brace for third-quarter results and investors scrutinize the sustainability of AI-related investment, we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural opportunity. ASML earlier on Wednesday reported stronger-than-expected earnings and raised the low end of its 2026 revenue forecast for a third consecutive quarter.Without taking a view on any individual companies, we see the chip-centered sell-off as more of a reset in expectations than a deterioration in the underlying AI investment cycle:AI monetization trends remain strong. The market reaction was amplified by media reports suggesting OpenAI's revenue growth was falling short of expectations. Subsequent clarification indicated much of the discrepancy reflected differing accounting treatments rather than a meaningful change in demand. Looking beyond a single company, we continue to view cloud growth as one of the clearest real-time indicators of AI monetization. Expectations for further acceleration in hyperscaler cloud growth suggest AI investment is increasingly translating into commercial revenues rather than remaining solely a capital-spending story. Recent launches of agentic AI products also point to continued momentum in AI adoption and monetization.Earnings expectations remain constructive. Positive EPS guidance among S&P 500 companies is tracking at a five-year high, while AI-related spending and cloud demand continue to support profit growth across the technology ecosystem. We expect another strong reporting season, with S&P 500 earnings growth of around 28%, supported by AI infrastructure spending, resilient consumer demand, and an improving cyclical backdrop. Semiconductors remain a key contributor to earnings growth, and the upcoming reporting season is likely to be a more important driver of sentiment than recent headlines around competition or financing constraints. Though earnings growth is moderating from exceptionally strong levels, we think the direction of markets will depend more on the outlook for profits and earnings revisions than on the pace of deceleration itself.Valuations, rates look manageable. The current backdrop differs meaningfully from the technology correction of 2022. Our base case remains for only modest tightening by the Federal Reserve, well below the scale of tightening experienced during that period. Technology earnings growth remains robust, while semiconductor valuations are still below long-term historical averages. We also believe that rising rates should have a more limited impact on corporate earnings than in prior cycles, given generally long debt maturities and continued economic resilience. We reflect this outlook in our AI thematic positioning, favoring diversified exposure across AI infrastructure beneficiaries, platform companies, and select defensive technology businesses.So, while increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements, and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story. We suggest investors focus on where AI spending is translating into sustainable earnings growth and broader enterprise and consumer adoption.With valuations now more attractive and growth trends remaining resilient, investors may consider adding exposure to the "Magnificent 6." Within the AI supply chain, we continue to favor semi-cap and robotics equipment companies, followed by foundry/OSAT and compute beneficiaries. Memory remains lower in our pecking order despite optically attractive valuations, reflecting medium-term supply concerns and the risk of additional capacity coming to market over time. More broadly, we favor diversified and active exposure across the AI value chain, balancing semiconductor exposure with platform companies and defensive technology segments that can benefit from growing software, cloud, and productivity adoption.
