articles.title: View from the markets: Is high-yield credit flashing a warning sign? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

High-yield credit markets are often seen as ‘the canary in the coal mine’ when it comes to economic activity. Highly levered companies often feel the pain of a slowing economy sooner than others, and worries about profitability are then seen in the spreads of corporate high-yield bonds over Treasuries.

Over the last month, US high-yield option-adjusted spreads have jumped suddenly and significantly, from 267 basis points on 8 September to a peak of 318 basis points on 1 October. This level is not far from the peak reached at the end of March, when high oil prices raised fears of an energy-shock-induced slowdown in the US and Europe (see Exhibit 1).

The pattern of higher oil prices leading to wider spreads initially repeated itself following the jump in oil prices that began in July. But then the correlation broke down: oil prices continued to rise to near their peak April levels, but high-yield spreads fell back. Subsequently, oil prices fell but spreads rose.

One reason spreads may have retreated in August is because of the lessons learned from the oil spike in April, when economic slowdown worries proved unfounded. In fact, economic data has come in better than expected.

The most recent surge in spreads has been driven primarily by the jump in fixed-income volatility, as measured by the MOVE index. Strong US economic data has raised concerns about an overheating economy and the prospect for further policy rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve. In France, the upcoming elections and the country’s precarious fiscal situation have spilled over to government bond yields globally.

Another contributor to wider spreads has been the supply/demand imbalance. Heavy issuance by hyperscalers has driven up investment-grade yields as their highly-rated offerings put pressure on government bond yields. Within high yield, September was the fifth busiest month ever for gross and net issuance. At the same time, the jump in interest-rate volatility put off debt buyers: two weeks in the month saw net outflows.

A large part of the index spread widening has been concentrated in a few names in the lower-ranked parts of the index (CCC), with spreads for higher-rated names being dragged along. Our portfolio managers see the rise in yields across the ratings spectrum as creating opportunities among BBB rated names. If interest-rate volatility declines, the current yield on the high-yield index looks attractive.

Economic fundamentals

The idea that the increase in high-yield spreads is an indicator of economic stress is hard to square with the data coming from the US. Recent non-farm payrolls figures did show a deceleration in job creation and negative revisions for prior months, but this release was the exception. Moreover, the data may not be as weak as it first appears.

One challenge in interpreting each month’s payrolls release has been the frequent revisions and occasionally odd seasonal adjustment factors, which have added to the volatility in the monthly data.

For example, September’s low headline private payrolls growth figure of just 46,000 jobs was due to a large decline in the Administrative & Support Services segment. This could indeed be a sign of a slowing economy as one of the first things companies often do to reduce costs is to lay off temporary workers. The drop, however, is the largest in a year and does not align with other anecdotal evidence of a solid labour market. The adult unemployment rate was steady at 3.8%.

An alternative way to get a sense of the underlying trend in employment, avoiding the complications introduced by seasonal adjustment factors, is to look at the year-on-year change in the non-seasonally adjusted data. By this measure, employment growth actually improved slightly in September to 0.5% (see Exhibit 2).

The positive impact of artificial intelligence investment can perhaps be seen in the improving growth rates for goods industries (mining, construction and manufacturing), and the destructive impact in the negative growth rates for the information industries and financial activities. The youth unemployment rate, another area where one might anticipate AI reducing demand for entry level workers, jumped from 7.1% to 8.0%.

Outlook

Economic growth momentum in the US is supporting corporate profits and fundamentals have improved. Our fixed-income team is overweight US high yield, but investors must still remain vigilant as higher official rates may put pressure on some sectors.

articles.title: US oil production starts to respond to higher prices | Wood Mackenzie
articles.text:
Get Ed Crooks' Energy Pulse in your inbox every week

Opinion
US oil production starts to respond to higher prices
Uncertainty and logistics mean the response is not immediate. But it is coming

13 October 2026
10 minute read

Email
Share by email

Ed Crooks
Vice Chair Americas and host of Energy Gang podcast

Ed Crooks
Vice Chair Americas and host of Energy Gang podcast
Ed examines the forces shaping the energy industry globally.

View Ed Crooks's full profile

“No plan survives first contact with the enemy.” That military maxim, adapted from the writings of the Prussian general Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, could be usefully applied to a lot of the thinking around US energy security.
When the US tight oil industry emerged in the 2010s, setting the country on course to become the world’s largest producer, there was a lot of speculation about how calculations around American energy security had changed forever.
The US no longer needed to care about what happened in the Middle East, said some. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve had become obsolete, said others.
The unfolding crisis created by the war with Iran has shattered those illusions. The integration of the US into world markets for crude and refined products means that disruption to supplies from the Middle East still has a direct impact on American consumers.
The average retail price of regular gasoline in the US is about US$4.36 a gallon this week, up 41% from a year ago, according to the American Automobile Association. Diesel is about US$6.28 a gallon, up 71%.
The importance of global supplies for US consumers was underlined on Friday, when President Donald Trump announced a commitment from Russia to sell diesel on world markets in return for sanctions relief. Russia’s ban on diesel exports, imposed in July, will be partially lifted.
President Trump said he expected Russia to sell 800,000 tons (about 6 million barrels) of diesel to world markets in October and November, representing about 120,000 barrels per day and another 1 million tons (about 7.5 million barrels) “immediately thereafter.” Over the weekend, President Trump told President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to end the attacks on Russian refineries that have disrupted global diesel supplies. “He’s not going to affect our farmers, and he’s not going to affect our ranchers, and he’s not going to affect the rest of the world. So he better damn well stop,” he said.
Meanwhile,the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), along with reserves held by other countries, has been playing a vital role in the crisis. About 132 million barrels of crude have been released from the SPR since March, at an average rate of about 630,000 b/. The administration announced that the total planned release – conducted as an exchange, to be repaid with interest – would be 172 million barrels. A further 4 million barrel release was announced over the weekend to relieve the disruption created by Hurricane Isaias.
Set against these numbers, the contribution to increased global supplies coming from the US upstream oil industry has so far been negligible.
In February, just before the war began, the US Lower 48 states were producing about 11.29 million barrels a day of crude and condensate. This month, they will produce about 11.35 million b/d, Wood Mackenzie estimates, an increase of only about 60,000 b/d.
In the short term, American consumers have seen little visible benefit from the nation’s position as the world’s largest oil producer.
In the longer term, being a net oil exporter should mean that the US as a whole benefits from higher prices. But the impacts will be distributed unevenly across the country, with oil producers gaining and consumers losing.
A surge in US production that helps ease tightness in world oil markets and brings down prices would be one clear way for American consumers to benefit. But so far they are still waiting for that benefit to arrive.
The Wood Mackenzie view
When thinking about how the US oil industry will respond to the crisis in the Middle East, there are two opposite fallacies that people can fall into. The first is the naïve view that US production will respond quickly to rebalance markets. The US tight oil industry is sometimes described as the new “swing producer”, playing the same role of market management that has for decades been played by OPEC.
That kind of analysis often misses the fact that US production is determined by hundreds of separate decisions by separate companies, not set by the government as it is in OPEC member states. Unlike some OPEC members, the US has no reserve of spare production capacity that can be brought on stream quickly. Its companies will act to increase output only if they believe that will maximise shareholder value.
On the other hand, expecting the US tight oil industry not to respond to higher prices would also be a mistake. Wood Mackenzie’s rule of thumb is that production typically takes about nine to 12 months to respond after prices have moved. That means we are starting to see around now the first increases resulting from the surge in crude prices that followed the start of the war at the end of February.
There are several factors behind that lag, says Nathan Nemeth, Wood Mackenzie’s director of Lower 48 Upstream research. Once companies take the decision to ramp up activity, it takes time to mobilise rigs and pressure pumping fleets, drill and frac wells, and bring them into production.
A volatile environment, where the oil price outlook is highly uncertain, is a deterrent to increased activity. Companies are reluctant to commit to increased spending if they see a risk that by the time their additional wells are on stream, prices will have fallen back again.
“The volatility in the oil price makes companies cautious,” Nemeth says. “One tweet can drop crude by US$20 a barrel.”
An oil futures market in steep backwardation, with prompt prices well above levels for six months or a year out, which has been the case for much of this year, makes it difficult to hedge against that risk.
As one commenter to the latest Dallas Federal Reserve bank survey put it: “Pricing volatility is near an all-time high given the backdrop of Iran. Swings of $5, $10 and $20 up or down are common. It is very challenging to select a planning price or budgeting price.”
The oil Majors and larger independents, that have built their appeal to shareholders on disciplined capital management and reliable dividends, are particularly reluctant to commit to increased spending that may seem unjustified if prices fall.
However, there are some companies that have already started to ramp up activity. There were 462 rigs drilling for oil in the US last week, according to Baker Hughes, up from 418 a year ago. Typically the companies that are drilling more will be smaller and privately-held operators that are taking the opportunity to scale up, Wood Mackenzie’s Nemeth says.
That increased activity has led him to raise his forecasts for US Lower 48 oil production. Before the war, back in February, Wood Mackenzie was forecasting that production would be close to 11 million b/d in December of this year. Now we are projecting that it will be about 11.4 million b/d.
As companies enter the autumn budgeting season, setting plans for 2027, the fact that there is no clear resolution to the Middle East conflict in sight may incline more boards to commit to increased activity.
By December 2027, Wood Mackenzie projects that US Lower 48 production will be about 11.8 million b/d, a full 1 million b/d higher than we were forecasting before the war began.
Before the war, Wood Mackenzie was projecting that world oil markets would be well supplied this year, as the OPEC+ group unwound its production cuts. Brent crude could have dropped into the US$50-US$60 range. If the war ends and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returns to its pre-war normal, those conditions could reassert themselves, once global inventories have been rebuilt.
There are other factors complicating the outlook, including the United Arab Emirates’ decision to leave OPEC, and the revival of Venezuela’s oil industry now international investment is returning.
But even allowing for that uncertainty, it seems likely that next year US Lower 48 oil production will be higher, exerting downward pressure on global prices. The US tight oil industry may not be an immediate swing producer, but given time it can play something like that role.
In brief
Devon Energy has announced a deal to rationalise its portfolio following the US$58 billion merger with Coterra Energy, which was completed in May. It is exiting the Eagle Ford play, selling its assets there to Crescent Energy for US$4.2 billion. Wood Mackenzie analysts described the assets as “firmly in the non-core category” for Devon, and said the sale price was broadly in line with our valuation. For Crescent, which was already the second-largest producer in the Eagle Ford, the deal offers increased scale and the opportunity for synergies valued at US$140million a year.
Other views

Quote of the week
“The disruption in the energy world… gives us plenty of opportunities if you’re able to capture them… I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world. There are more opportunities, but you need to have the assets.”
Patrick Pouyanné, chief executive of TotalEnergies, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London that the company gained from being vertically integrated. Refineries in Europe, which had been thought of as liabilities, had become “goldmines” this year, he added.
Chart of the week
This comes from our recent Strategic Planning Outlook for European power. It shows historic and forecast power generation in the EU, plus the UK and Norway, from 2005 out to 2060. One of the key messages: renewable power in Europe is expected to be on a rising trend for many years to come, despite current headwinds.

articles.title: China's Deposit Insurance Fund is strikingly underfunded
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

China's Deposit Insurance Fund is strikingly underfunded

Tianlei Huang (PIIE)

Date
October 13, 2026 10:40 AM

Photo Credit: CFOTO/Sipa USA via Reuters

Author's note: I thank Zhuowen Li for excellent research assistance; Bert Van Roosebeke and colleagues at the International Association of Deposit Insurers for providing feedback on an earlier version of the figure in this blog post; and Joseph Gagnon, Patrick Honohan, Nick Lardy, Arvind Subramanian, Nicolas Véron, and David Wilcox for helpful comments. All errors remain my own.

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
China's Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF), a key pillar of the country's financial safety net, has a remarkably small financial buffer relative to the deposits it protects. At the end of 2025, its reported balance was only RMB130 billion ($18.5 billion), equivalent to an estimated 0.1 percent of insured deposits—far below the fund's 1.5 percent target reported by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the funding levels of other major economies.
A low reserve ratio does not necessarily mean that insured depositors will suffer losses: Funds recovered from failed banks' assets and additional financing, including government support, can help meet payout obligations. But the low ratio leaves insufficient prefunded industry resources to absorb losses. The central concern is who ultimately pays. If government support is not subsequently recovered from the banking industry, bank failure costs shift onto the government balance sheet. China should rebuild the DIF toward its reported target. This would require higher bank contributions now, reducing the need to raise them during a future crisis.
Generous coverage backed by a small fund
Established in 2015, China's deposit insurance system has helped resolve distressed regional banks, including Baoshang Bank in 2019, and supported mergers of several troubled smaller lenders in recent years. While the system has helped reinforce public confidence in the banking system, extensive use of the fund—including to support payments to creditors beyond those covered by deposit insurance—has depleted its resources.[1] Bank resolution also remains heavily reliant on public funding and does not force creditors to absorb significant losses.
The system covers nearly 3,000 banks and protects up to RMB500,000 per depositor per bank. According to the People's Bank of China, this limit fully protects more than 99 percent of depositors. At about five times China's GDP per capita, the coverage limit also makes the Chinese deposit insurance among the most generous in the world. By comparison, the International Association of Deposit Insurers reported a median coverage limit of 2.5 times GDP per capita among Group of 20 (G20) economies in 2022.
Yet this relatively generous coverage is backed by limited prefunded resources. Chinese authorities do not publish figures for deposits insured within the payout limit, making the DIF's reserve ratio—the DIF balance as a share of insured deposits—difficult to calculate directly. Using the IMF's reported target fund balance and target reserve ratio to calculate insured deposits, such deposits accounted for approximately 37 percent of China's total bank deposits at end-2023.[2] Applying this calculated share to the People's Bank of China's reported total deposits at the end of 2025 yields approximately RMB124 trillion of insured deposits and a reserve ratio of about 0.1 percent.
By comparison, the figure below shows that the US Deposit Insurance Fund had a reserve ratio of 1.42 percent at the end of 2025, above its statutory minimum of 1.35 percent, while the European Union generally requires national deposit guarantee schemes to maintain a ratio of at least 0.8 percent, a requirement most members have met.[3] Japan maintained a reserve ratio of 0.43 percent at end-March 2026. Brazil and India have much higher reserve ratios than many advanced economies.

Who ultimately pays?
A low reserve ratio alone does not determine whether insured depositors will be protected. The deposit insurance system can recover funds from failed banks' assets and potentially draw on additional financing. Chinese financial regulators established a Financial Stability Guarantee Fund in 2022 that may provide funding support when needed, though little public information is available about its size or functions. The central and local governments could also use other public resources to fill any shortfall. Indeed, expectations of government support may help explain why the DIF's tiny size appears to have done little to undermine depositor confidence.
The greater concern is who ultimately would bear any future losses. A small DIF increases the likelihood that the system would have to raise additional financing during periods of financial stress, either through additional bank contributions or government support. Raising bank contributions during a crisis could increase the strain on banks precisely when they are already under pressure. Government support can bridge a funding gap, but unless its costs can be subsequently recovered from the banking industry through higher assessments, it essentially socializes losses by shifting them onto the public balance sheet, which can encourage banks to take greater risks. Depositors may receive the same protection either way, but the allocation of costs and resulting riskiness of the banking system differs.
China should rebuild the Deposit Insurance Fund
China should reform the system in several ways. Most urgently, regulators should start requiring higher bank contributions now—especially from riskier banks—to boost the DIF's balance toward its reported target while financial conditions remain relatively stable. Replenishing the DIF should be accompanied by stricter limits on its use. Shareholders and uninsured creditors should bear losses in accordance with the legal hierarchy, while protection beyond the statutory coverage limit should be avoided. Any government support should come with a clear mechanism for subsequently recovering its costs from the industry. Officials also should clarify the role of China's Financial Stability Guarantee Fund and its relationship with the deposit insurance system.
Notes
1. For example, when Baoshang Bank failed in 2019, not only were all household deposits protected, other claims of up to RMB50 million also received full protection, far above the statutory limit of RMB500,000. Meanwhile, larger claims received partial protection. In 2020, the Deposit Insurance Fund spent RMB93 billion, roughly three quarters of its reserves, on resolving Baoshang's failure alone. The People's Bank of China provided additional funding support.
2. The IMF's 2025 Financial Sector Assessment Program report (paragraph 76 and footnote 38) reports a target balance for China's Deposit Insurance Fund of approximately US$224 billion (RMB1.6 trillion) and a target reserve ratio of 1.5 percent as of end-2023. Dividing the target balance by the target reserve ratio implies insured deposits of approximately RMB107 trillion. Relative to total deposits of approximately RMB290 trillion reported by the People's Bank of China at end-2023, this implies an insured share of about 37 percent. The end-2025 estimate carries forward this calculated share and applies it to the People's Bank of China's reported total deposits of RMB336 trillion, yielding estimated insured deposits of approximately RMB124 trillion. Dividing the reported end-2025 DIF balance of RMB130 billion by this estimated amount gives a reserve ratio of approximately 0.1 percent.
3. The EU Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive includes a derogation clause that allows member states with highly concentrated banking sectors to adopt a lower target level of 0.5 percent. France, for example, makes use of this clause and currently meets the lower target.

articles.text:

Long-term yields at high levels

EDM

Long-term yields at high levels

5 minutes

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

Summary

Bond yields are increasingly attractive, but volatility is likely to stay high, calling for a flexible approach to bond investing.

Long-term bond yields remain near multi-year highs across major countries, alongside increased volatility. The move reflects a combination of forces: persistent inflation in several major economies, monetary policy uncertainty, concerns about government finances, and geopolitical tensions affecting energy prices.For investors, the key implication is the need for a more flexible approach in fixed income and stronger diversification.

Government bond yields across major developed economies have risen to levels not seen in years. The move has been accompanied by increased volatility, as markets have become more sensitive to macroeconomic data and policy expectations. US 10-year yields reached their highest level since 2002 before easing, as oil prices fell and following a well-received bond auction. Meanwhile, UK 10-year yields climbed to their highest level since the Global Financial Crisis, while German and Japanese yields have also risen sharply over the past few weeks. The move reflects several overlapping forces. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have kept oil prices elevated and added to inflationary pressure, while stronger US activity data and heavy corporate issuance linked to the AI build-out have pushed long-term yields higher. European bonds have also come under pressure from concerns over energy prices, inflation and a degree of fiscal and political uncertainty.

This week at a glance

Rising government bond yields dominated the week, with multi-decade highs reached in the US and UK before a recovery, following strong auction demand in the US. Equity markets came under pressure before recovering on renewed AI optimism and falling oil prices. Annual outlook 2026: Investing in tomorrow

In our PERSPECTIVES 2026 publication, we look to the year ahead across our ten key investment themes, identifying opportunities and risks on the horizon.

Get in touch

Click here to activate this content.

Investing in tomorrow – Opportunities and risks

The global economy is in constant flux. Trade flows are shifting, regions are gaining or losing influence, and new technologies are also reshaping the economic map. 2025 has been challenging in some respects, but many local equity indices did deliver very good performance. Given the positive macro environment, we expect 2026 to be another constructive year, albeit with continuing market volatility. Although we anticipate a reduction in some uncertainties, it will definitely not be a time for complacency – especially as global trade relations are far from settled. The continued rise of artificial intelligence (AI) may open up new growth opportunities, which should encourage companies to increase their investment activity, potentially giving fresh impetus to both private and public consumption.

The US administration’s tariffs agenda appears to have now been largely implemented. While the disorientation that followed the declaration of “Liberation Day” in early April still lingers globally and domestically, most US trading partners have managed to significantly reduce initial steep tariff hikes through renegotiation. Overall, markets seem to have priced in the effects of the new environment, with overall tariffs still considerably higher than in January 2025 when the current administration began its tenure.

US growth is likely to be supported by the continuation and introduction of extensive tax relief measures, as well as increased spending on security and defence under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The three interest rate cuts expected from the Federal Reserve by the end of 2026 and planned deregulation in the banking sector should also further improve the investment and consumption environment. What makes these government stimuli remarkable is that they come at a time when the US economy is not in recession but is already growing robustly. The US also appears to be close to full employment. Despite the long-term risks such an environment may pose – including inflationary pressures and rising public debt – we expect fiscal and monetary measures to deliver noticeable economic support in 2026.

We also anticipate that policy will deliver a cyclical impulse in Europe, for example due to Germany’s EUR500bn special fund. Planned investments, particularly in infrastructure and climate neutrality, could trigger a short-term upswing. To achieve sustainably higher growth, however, improving domestic economic flexibility remains crucial to foster entrepreneurial initiatives and create an investment climate that enhances productivity. In my view, urgent action is still needed here.

We maintain a broadly constructive outlook for equity markets in 2026. This will be partly due to strong demand for new AI-based applications, which should continue to drive substantial corporate investment flows. Beneficiaries will not only include US “Big Tech” but also a wide range of sectors – construction (thanks to new data centres), utilities (via higher electricity demand) and industrial and basic materials along the supply chain. Our earnings growth forecasts for companies across all major regions are therefore firmly in double-digit territory.

As outlined in our annual outlook themes, investors should also consider potential risks in equity markets. In the area of highly energy-intensive AI applications, for instance, a global power shortage could dampen investor expectations for progress. Not every stock will be a winner in 2026, and short-term corrections at index level remain possible.

Investors should therefore continue to act with discipline. This means focusing on fundamentals rather than chasing perceived trends, while utilising the broad spectrum of investment opportunities. Diversification remains key. Alongside equities, corporate bonds may be attractive – depending on your risk appetite, both investment-grade and high-yield segments. Gold and some non-traditional investments, such as in private equity or infrastructure, also merit consideration. We explore these in detail in the “Alternative Investments” section of this annual outlook.

Overall, we expect a dynamic year for capital markets in 2026 with numerous compelling opportunities. The central question will be whether constructive forecasts can hold up amid a backdrop of economic and geopolitical challenges. Further disruptions to global trade flows or a renewed escalation of tariff tensions could, for example, temporarily pressure corporate earnings and increase market volatility.

In a complex and uncertain environment, investors would therefore be well advised to actively manage risks. This will enable them to respond to market developments in line with their personal investment strategy. Staying invested with a defined strategic asset allocation will be key, as attempts to perfectly time market entry and exit points can often result in missing the best-performing days and weeks.

I hope you find our annual outlook insightful and full of stimulating ideas for your portfolio. We are always available to review and discuss these ideas and look forward to hearing from you.

Christian Nolting

articles.title: Canada's carbon pricing at a crossroads | RBCCM
articles.text:
Last week, in partnership with ClearBlue Markets, we had the privilege of hosting an exclusive, off-the-record roundtable during the Energy Disruptors Summit in Calgary, Alberta. We brought together 15 senior voices from across Oil and Gas, Power and Utilities, and Industry for a candid conversation on the state of industrial carbon pricing in Canada. Key themes emerged amidst this period of generational change for carbon and economic policy in Canada, along with a notion that there is an opportunity for a win-win for both climate and economic growth if we manage to get this right.

Here are our top takeaways:
1. Policy certainty is the single most important input but remains elusive
If there was one theme that united participants across every sector, it was this: without long-term, credible policy certainty, nothing else in the carbon market ecosystem can function as intended. Investors cannot allocate capital, project developers cannot secure financing, and banks cannot provide liquidity. One participant made a particularly striking observation, that even if a program like the Clean Fuel Regulations technically ran through to 2050, but did so on a year-to-year basis without a firm federal commitment, the market would still be uninvestable, even if the program outperformed all expectations. This highlights how the signal for the market matters just as much as the substance of the market itself.
A necessary part of this is the federal government being unequivocal about the purpose of industrial carbon pricing. In the absence of any other meaningful climate policy instrument in Canada, carbon pricing is effectively the only mechanism capable of driving emissions reductions. Saying that clearly and consistently would go a long way.
2. Financial infrastructure is a must
Quebec’s linkage to the Western Climate Initiative was broadly described as a success story from a market perspective. The WCI’s mature financial ecosystem, deep liquidity, sophisticated hedging instruments, robust price discovery, and an options market that helps smooth volatility, is what separates a functional carbon market from one that stays in its infancy. The contrast is stark, participants noted that you can relatively easily offload $1 billion of risk for up to five years in the WCI but cannot execute a $1 million, two-year hedge in Ontario. No other Canadian carbon market currently has this infrastructure and that gap will continue to hamper any ambition to scale. The good news is that financial sophistication follows certainty so if you can build the policy foundation, then the market infrastructure will come.
3. The price debate is less about the headline number and more about the collar
There was healthy debate on the carbon price trajectory, with some arguing the near-term priority should be establishing the floor price as described in the Canada-Alberta MOU, and others noting that several provincial programs, BC’s in particular, remain closely indexed to the headline number. What the group broadly agreed on is that the WCI’s price collar model, a defined floor and ceiling with price containments / market stability reserves, is the right design for managing volatility, supporting investment certainty, and enabling long-term project financing. The collar gives both supply and demand participants what they actually need, a range they can plan around.
4. Focus on the carrot or the stick?
Several participants raised whether Canada is at risk of over-indexing on carbon market mechanisms at the expense of direct investment incentives, such as investment tax credits, production tax credits or providing additional value for lower carbon commodities (ex. lower carbon oil or steel). The concern is not that carbon pricing is wrong, but that it is working in a vacuum. Without complementary incentives for low-carbon products, the carbon price creates a compliance cost without fully creating an investment case. The most durable frameworks are likely to be those that combine both.
5. The CFR is becoming a successful Pan-Canadian carbon market, but challenges to growth remain
Participants broadly viewed the Clean Fuel Regulations as a credible national carbon market in its early stages — but its primary spot market structure and short track record make it difficult to finance against. The ask from industry is straightforward: make it a binding, long-term commitment and more importantly, reframe it. A carbon program tied explicitly to industrial policy, i.e. jobs, economic growth, and attracting foreign direct investment, has political durability in a way that a standalone climate instrument simply does not. The lesson from other jurisdictions is that the markets that have scaled are the ones that solved for both.
6. ITMOs offer a dual-sided opportunity for Canada
The federal government’s exploration of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) generated optimism in the room. On the supply side, Canadian companies — particularly in engineered carbon removals — are well-positioned to generate and sell high-quality credits to foreign governments. On the demand side, allowing heavy emitters to purchase ITMOs to offset emissions growth tied to economic expansion could meaningfully benefit the broader economy while preserving compliance integrity. It is one of the more compelling near-term levers available to policymakers.
7. A Pan-Canadian carbon market — or something bolder — is the long-term answer
The fragmentation of Canada’s carbon market landscape was a recurring source of frustration. A Pan-Canadian market would directly resolve the liquidity gaps and financial complexity that currently limit scalability, and participants broadly agreed the logic is compelling. But the most provocative idea of the session came from one participant who went further: why not explore Canada joining the EU Emissions Trading System as part of its associate membership in the EU? The group acknowledged that this would, in theory, resolve most of the existing market challenges in one move — delivering the depth, liquidity, and financial infrastructure that no Canadian market currently has. However, it was recognised as likely impractical given the makeup of Canada’s economy versus the EU’s, among other challenges. Regardless, any form of a Pan-Canadian market will require bold vision, political will and compromise from all the provinces and territories, but the opportunity to make this work is too large to ignore.
RBC’s capabilities
To help navigate the rapidly evolving carbon markets, RBC Capital Markets offers extensive expertise and full capabilities in emissions trading across both compliance and voluntary carbon markets. The Environmental Markets Solutions Group partners with RBC Capital Markets’ Environmental Commodities desk, established in 2008, to offer bespoke solutions to clients looking to operationalize their net-zero targets through carbon and renewable energy solutions.
In April 2023, RBC announced a strategic investment and partnership with ClearBlue Markets, an award-winning carbon markets advisory firm. ClearBlue Markets provides carbon markets services to hundreds of clients worldwide, helping them optimize their strategies for compliance requirements and voluntary net zero ambitions through its deep advisory expertise and AI enabled technology.

articles.title: Private equity beyond the target: how buyouts reshape supply chains
articles.text: 08 OCTOBER 2026 · RESEARCH BULLETIN NO. 147Private equity beyond the target: how buyouts reshape supply chainsby Olivier De Jonghe and Cédric Huylebroek[1] This article was written by Olivier De Jonghe (Directorate General Research, European Central Bank and National Bank of Belgium) and Cédric Huylebroek (Deutsche Bundesbank and KU Leuven). The authors gratefully acknowledge the comments of Diana Bonfim and Alexander Popov. The views expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank or the Eurosystem. The importance of private equity (PE) for euro area firms is increasing, with annual growth rates in PE funds’ assets under management exceeding 10%. PE buyouts affect more than just the firms being acquired. Using data for Belgium that encompass virtually all the firms in the country, this article shows that the sales volumes of suppliers grow faster when there is a higher proportion of business with customers backed by PE. But this advantage is lost during downturns, as such investors press for cost savings. Buyouts can also crowd out competitors that depend on the same suppliers, with implications for competition policy. And finally, high leverage implies greater interest rate sensitivity, so PE buyouts can intensify the transmission of monetary policy to target firms and beyond.Private equity travels through production networksPE buyouts are often judged by what happens inside the acquired company: does it grow or become more productive, does its management improve? Past research has documented the effects on jobs and productivity of firms being bought out by private equity (Davis et al., 2014). In line with their results, we find that after a PE buyout the financial leverage of target firms significantly increases and they grow faster than their peers (or “matched controls”). Moreover, also consistent with previous studies, we find that target firms outperform their peers even more strongly during economic downturns, when PE investors’ managerial expertise may be particularly valuable (Bernstein et al., 2019). However, firms do not operate in isolation. They buy inputs from suppliers, sell to customers and compete with other firms that may rely on the same production networks. A change in ownership can therefore affect businesses well beyond the company that is being acquired.In Huylebroek and De Jonghe (2026), we examine these effects using data from Belgium. The dataset links firm-to-firm sales, company accounts and PE transactions for 2002-21. It covers virtually all firms, including small private companies, which are the targets of most PE buyouts but are often absent from commercial supply-chain data. We compare the economic trajectories, both before and after a buyout, of two types of firms: suppliers linked to customers backed by PE and similar suppliers connected to customers not backed by PE.Figure 1How to examine the effect of buyouts on suppliers of target firms?Notes: This figure illustrates our empirical strategy for estimating how PE buyouts affect target firms’ suppliers. Suppose one of Supplier A’s customers is acquired by a PE firm in year t. Our difference-in-differences design compares Supplier A’s economic trajectory before and after the acquisition with that of a comparable Supplier B without a PE-backed customer.Growing customers boost suppliersAfter a PE buyout, suppliers of the acquired firm perform better than comparable suppliers not linked to a PE-backed customer. Across the full post-buyout period their sales are around 8% higher and employment around 4% higher (Chart 1). Chart 1Sales and employment growth of suppliers of the acquired firmDynamic difference-in-differences estimates for the effect of PE buyouts on suppliers of target firmsSource: Huylebroek and De Jonghe (2026).Notes: This chart presents the dynamic difference-in-differences estimates of the effect of PE buyouts on the suppliers of target firms. The y-axis corresponds to the coefficient estimates (dots). The vertical bars represent confidence intervals at the 95% level. The x-axis corresponds to years relative to the year in which the target firm was acquired. The outcome variables are, in the left-hand panel, the natural logarithm of sales and, in the right-hand panel, the natural logarithm of employees.The evidence points to an explanation: PE-backed firms pursue new growth opportunities and increase their purchases of inputs. The suppliers already embedded in their production process receive more orders and respond by expanding. The gains are strongest when either the target has more room to grow, the supplier provides a relatively large share of the target’s inputs, or the relationship between them is more established.Customer-level comparisons confirm that the increase in supplier sales is driven mainly by purchases from PE-backed customers. Demand matters more than knowledge transferA buyout can benefit suppliers through knowledge transfer, trade credit and/or certification as result of the change of ownership. We establish that suppliers do not increase research and development or highly-skilled employment and changes in trade credit are not significant. Some suppliers gain customers within the PE investor’s network, but this reputational “certification effect” is small compared with the direct increase in demand.Downturns reverse the balanceThe pattern changes sharply when the economy weakens.During downturns, suppliers of PE-backed firms no longer outperform their peers. Their markups fall by approximately 8%, suggesting that they concede part of the value created in the buyer-supplier relationship through lower prices or less favourable terms.Our paper attributes this reversal to more intensive PE involvement in cost-cutting. This is consistent with evidence that PE investors can be especially active when portfolio companies face financial fragility (Bernstein et al., 2019). Buyouts are typically leveraged, so preserving cash and meeting debt obligations become particularly important when sales and profits come under pressure. Investors can seek savings by renegotiating contracts, threatening to switch suppliers or actively redesigning the supply chain.The pressure is concentrated on suppliers with weaker bargaining positions. It is greater for suppliers of standardised inputs, which are easier to replace, and for suppliers operating in highly competitive industries where customers have more alternatives. The pressure is also greater when the PE investor is larger and more experienced, as measured by past deal activity.Consistent with this interpretation, PE-backed firms are more likely to terminate supplier relationships during downturns as they reduce their input costs.Shared suppliers can transmit the shock to rivalsThe market structure consequences of PE buyouts extend beyond direct suppliers. A PE-backed firm that expands may absorb more of a supplier’s available capacity. Its competitors, especially those relying on the same upstream firms, may then find it harder to maintain their relationships if suppliers prioritise their faster growing PE-backed customers over others, as illustrated in Figure 2.Figure 2Crowding-out competitorsIllustration of potential crowding-out effects of PE-backed firms on other firms through shared suppliersWe find that suppliers affected by a PE buyout are more likely to terminate relationships with rivals of their PE-backed customers. This finding connects to research showing how shared suppliers and bargaining relationships can shape downstream competition (Giannetti et al., 2021). The pattern is strongest when supplier capacity is constrained and when their rivals are already performing poorly, which is consistent with suppliers prioritising fast-growing customers.The effect is economically meaningful. An increase of one standard deviation in a competitor’s exposure to common suppliers is associated with a 1% decline in employment, a 2% decline in core earnings (EBITDA) and a 1% decline in markups. More broadly, the result illustrates how firm-level shocks can propagate through production networks (Acemoglu et al., 2012), even when the acquired firm and its rivals do not have a direct ownership link.Implications for policyOverall, our findings underscore the central role of supply chains in understanding how PE investors create and redistribute value. On average, PE ownership benefits upstream suppliers, but PE-owned firms exert greater pressure on suppliers during periods of economic distress. These results suggest that policymakers, such as central banks and competition authorities, as well as practitioners should consider the full implications of changing ownership patterns. These encompass not only the direct effects of PE investments but also the broader spillover effects on supply chains and the implications for market competition. In some countries, listed firms are required to publicly disclose their primary suppliers. Regulators could utilise this information to assess the degree of upstream overlap between PE targets and their competitors before approving a transaction.Our finding that PE buyouts benefit suppliers through increased input demand – an effect we do not observe for firms funded by bank debt – can inform the debate on the role of bank versus non-bank financing in stimulating economic growth.Finally and more broadly, our findings suggest that the growing role of PE may ramp up the transmission of monetary policy through production networks. PE activity and financing conditions are particularly sensitive to the interest rate environment (Ivashina, 2022). Therefore tighter monetary policy could affect suppliers more by inducing highly leveraged PE-backed firms to shift away from expanding, which benefits them, towards stronger cost cutting, supplier bargaining, and supply-chain reconfiguration. ReferencesAcemoglu, D., Carvalho, V.M., Ozdaglar, A. and Tahbaz-Salehi, A. (2012), “The network origins of aggregate fluctuations”, Econometrica, Vol. 80, No 5, pp. 1977-2016.Bernstein, S., Lerner, J. and Mezzanotti, F. (2019), “Private equity and financial fragility during the crisis”, The Review of Financial Studies, Vol. 32, No 4, pp. 1309-1373.Davis, S.J., Haltiwanger, J., Handley, K., Jarmin, R., Lerner, J. and Miranda, J. (2014), “Private Equity, Jobs, and Productivity”, American Economic Review, Vol. 104, No 12, pp. 3956-3990.Giannetti, M., Serrano-Velarde, N. and Tarantino, E. (2021), “Cheap Trade Credit and Competition in Downstream Markets”, Journal of Political Economy, Vol. 129, No 6, pp. 1744-1796.Huylebroek, C. and De Jonghe, O. (2026), “The supply chain spillovers of private equity buyouts”, Working Paper Series, No 3234, European Central Bank, Frankfurt am Main.Ivashina, V. (2022), “The Private Equity Industry in the New Interest Rate Environment”, VoxEU. This article was written by Olivier De Jonghe (Directorate General Research, European Central Bank and National Bank of Belgium) and Cédric Huylebroek (Deutsche Bundesbank and KU Leuven). The authors gratefully acknowledge the comments of Diana Bonfim and Alexander Popov. The views expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank or the Eurosystem.

articles.title: Searching for signposts − speech by Alan Taylor
articles.text:
Searching for signposts − speech by Alan Taylor

Given at the 2026 Dow Lecture, National Institute of Economic and Social Research

Published on
29 September 2026

In this speech, Alan Taylor discusses a key macroeconomic challenge facing the Bank of England: the risk that higher energy prices generate persistent inflationary pressures through expectations and so-called “second-round” effects. He examines the balance of risks, how the Bank monitors these effects, and how the current restrictive monetary policy guards against inflation persistence.

Speech
It is very much an honour and a pleasure to be here with you today at NIESR, and my thanks to David Aikman for inviting me to give the 2026 Dow Lecture.
I am conscious that I follow in the footsteps of a number of my esteemed current and former colleagues at the Bank of England, including Swati Dhingra, James Talbot and Silvana Tenreyro. The Dow Lecture has provided an important forum for thinking seriously about the major macroeconomic challenges facing the United Kingdom, and I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to that tradition.
Today I want to focus on one such challenge facing monetary policy right now: the ongoing and still unpredictable energy shock.
I should emphasise that this is only one of the challenges currently facing policymakers. The world economy is again being shaped by geopolitical uncertainty, by shifts in global trade and production, and by changes in financial conditions. But time is scarce, so I will not spend this lecture trying to predict geopolitical events or venturing too far down those other avenues.
Instead, as we look down the macroeconomic road ahead, I want to ask a narrower but, in my view, more tractable question: how do inflationary energy shocks pass through the economy; how far and wide do their effects subsequently persist; what role do expectations play in that propagation process; and what does all of this mean for monetary policy?
Unfortunately, that road ahead is not clearly illuminated, even at the best of times. The signposts policymakers would like to rely on are often sparse, partial and difficult to interpret. That is especially true after a large inflation shock, when the accumulated evidence can point in different and sometimes contradictory directions and the distinction between temporary pressure and longer-term persistence is hard to draw in real time.
So where should we look?
The answer, I will argue, is not to search for a single decisive indicator that will reveal the route ahead. Rather, the better approach is to look across a set of imperfect signposts: the initial energy-price impulse; the response of inflation expectations, especially among households and firms; the extent to which those expectations feed into wages and prices; and the wider state of demand, slack and policy credibility that will shape that transmission. Together, this array of signposts can help us judge whether an energy shock is likely to fade, or whether it risks becoming embedded in more persistent inflation.
A useful starting point is to recap the distinction the Bank has often drawn between so-called direct, indirect and second-round effects in the transmission of energy price shocks.
The direct effects are the mechanical impact of higher energy prices on headline CPI. For example, increases in petrol prices, household gas and electricity bills feed directly into measured inflation as faced by consumers in items they directly buy.
The indirect effects occur when higher energy prices raise the costs of producing and distributing other goods and services, leading firms to pass some of those costs through to consumers. This is particularly likely in energy-intensive sectors or where margins are under pressure. These effects can be powerful, but they are still relatively easy to conceptualise. They tend to work through the economy over a fairly short horizon, and input-output tables give us a benchmark for judging the relative magnitude of the pass-through.
The more difficult issue concerns the second-round effects. This phrase is often used rather broadly, even loosely. I think it best to use it narrowly and precisely to describe the behavioural, general-equilibrium dynamics that can follow an initially temporary rise in inflation and make the inflation process more persistent.
These dynamics should not surprise us. Most of the prices and wages in our economy are largely determined by private decisions without policy intervention. If inflation rises sharply, workers may seek higher nominal wages to recover lost real income. Where labour demand is strong, firms may have to accept those costs to recruit and retain workers. Firms may also raise prices not only because their own input costs have risen, but because they expect competitors, suppliers and customers to behave differently in a higher-inflation environment.
The key policy question is not whether these dynamics exist, but how large and persistent they are likely to be, for a given shock, and how monetary policy should respond.
Our flexible inflation-targeting mandate is central to that judgement. Like most central banks, we have not been assigned a price-level target; our task is not to reverse the increase in prices caused by an energy shock, but to return the rate of inflation to target.
And the flexibility embedded in the mandate instructs us to do so over a period that avoids undesirable volatility in output. Together with the lags in monetary transmission, this means that policy can ‘look through’ short-lived relative-price shocks, which is the relevant case for most external commodity price shocks in the most normal times.
But monetary policy cannot look through the emergence of more persistent inflationary pressure. Here, its influence lies not in reversing the original price-level increase, but in preventing that shock from propagating into an ongoing inflation process.
The question is therefore how much policy should lean against that risk, given uncertainty about its magnitude and the trade-off between stabilising inflation and real economic activity.footnote [1] This is the nature of the policy problem created by second-round effects that we now face.
And inflation expectations are central to that problem. If households and firms expect a rise in inflation to be short-lived, they are less likely to respond in ways that sustain it. If instead they expect inflation to remain high, workers may seek greater compensation for future price increases and firms may raise prices to protect their margins. Those responses, all else equal, can then make the original shock more persistent, making matters worse.
This is why inflation expectations matter for second-round effects. Let me now make it concrete with an example.
The experience of 2022 is instructive. If we look first at the evolution of headline CPI and energy CPI, the basic pattern is clear (Chart 1). Headline inflation initially moved with energy inflation but remained persistently high even as energy inflation dropped sharply. That divergence is important. It suggests that the initial shock was doing more than mechanically raising the energy component of CPI. Rather, broader forces were contributing to a more persistent inflation process that unfolded gradually in waves (Taylor, 2025; Ramsden, 2024).

So, what drove those general-equilibrium dynamics? They reflected the interaction of the original shock with wage and price-setting behaviour, inflation expectations, slack in the economy, and the stance of monetary policy. No single factor explains the persistence of inflation. Rather, the key point is one of state dependence: the effects of an energy shock depend not only on the size of the shock itself, but also on the economic environment into which it arrives.
In other words, the economy responded as an interconnected system in which households, firms and financial markets, in the UK and globally, formed views about what that particular shock meant in that particular context, and acted on those views.
That experience points to the first major signpost: inflation expectations. What do economic actors think is coming?
During the 2022 energy shock, expectations among financial markets, firms, and households rose markedly. Chart 3 compares CPI inflation expectations among households and firms, and a market-implied measure of inflation compensation over the coming year.footnote [2]
We see that the inflation expectations evolved differently across agents. Market implied expectations normalised relatively quickly as energy prices fell and policy tightened. By contrast, firm and household expectations, declined more slowly and remained elevated for longer. The heterogeneity in dynamics across measures shown in Chart 3 is therefore important not simply because expectations rose, but because it illustrates that expectations can move at different speeds and remain elevated even after the original shock begins to unwind.

For instance, a machine-learning model produced by Buckmann et al., (2025), summarised in Chart 4, attributes a notable share of the persistence in inflation, reflected in a relatively slow-moving trend component, to what we might call the inflation-expectations channel.

The sceptic would call that a black-box explanation, and I would not want to overstate the precision of any single model-based decomposition. But together the divergence between energy and headline inflation, the Bank’s forecast decomposition, the behaviour of expectations and the statistical evidence suggest that the 2022 shock propagated well beyond its direct and indirect effects.
But a model decomposition does not reveal the mechanism. Expectations rising is not the same as expectations becoming inflationary in practice, in a causal sense. To affect realised inflation, they must change wage bargains, spending or price-setting, and the ability of households and firms to act on them will depend on labour-market conditions, demand, competition and margins.
This is why the second major signpost we come to is transmission: whether expectations actually feed into realised behaviour.
For monetary policy today, that distinction is central. The UK is again facing an energy shock, but in a different environment from 2022: the labour market is looser, excess demand has given way to excess supply, and monetary and financial conditions are restrictive. Those conditions may not fully eliminate the risk of second-round effects, but they should serve to limit their magnitude.
In the remainder of this speech, I assess the evidence across the two stages of the expectations channel. Stage 1 asks how inflation expectations did, and likely will, respond to the ongoing energy shock. Stage 2 asks whether those expectations are likely to be transmitted through into wages, prices and other economic decisions, making inflation more persistent. I then sum up by considering the implications, in my view, for policy strategy, given the evidence and uncertainties.
Stage 1: Drivers of inflation expectations and dynamics
Inflation expectations are relatively easy to obtain, but much harder to interpret. They matter for policy not simply because people report a number in a survey, but because those numbers may shape the decisions households and firms go on to make. So let me begin with the first part of the mechanism: how expectations are formed.
Over the past decade, we have learned much more about how different groups form inflation expectations. A key message from that work is that financial markets, professional forecasters, firms and households are not simply interchangeable sources of the same signal (Coibion Opens in a new window & Gorodnichenko, 2025 Opens in a new window; Weber et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2024 Opens in a new window; Reis, 2023) Opens in a new window. They pay attention to different information, update at different speeds, display different biases, and bring different experiences to bear when thinking about inflation.
Financial markets are, in some sense, the easiest case to understand. They are strongly incentivized to process information as quickly and as accurately as possible. They react to data releases, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, changes in the expected path of policy, and form expectations that are, by construction, highly forward-looking and information-sensitive.
In levels, households and firms look rather different to financial markets. Both form expectations that are highly dispersed in the cross-section, and importantly they tend to biased upwards with a skew (Chart 5). This upwards bias translates into means that typically sit above realised inflation, at least in the pre-2022 period, and since 2024. For households, this caveat applies not only to expected future inflation but also to perceptions of inflation today. Those perceptions also tend to be biased upwards, meaning that expectations are formed from a subjective starting point rather than directly from the same benchmark as official statistics (D’Acunto & Weber, 2026 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., May 2024 NBER Opens in a new window).

Of course, these surveys are not perfect instruments; responses are noisy, question wording matters, and the average can conceal a great deal of disagreement (Assenza et al., 2026 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2024 Opens in a new window). But that is precisely why the distribution of beliefs, not just the mean, might be informative.
For policymakers, however, the key signal may lie less in the level of expected inflation than in how expectations respond to shocks over time. On this dimension, we can see that firms appear closer to households than to financial markets, while still occupying an intermediate position.
Neither households nor firms, in general, continuously process every piece of macroeconomic news in the same way as financial market participants. One of the key lessons from recent research is that they often use relatively accessible information when forming and updating expectations. That is not irrational. Attention is scarce and information is costly to acquire and process. And, for most households and firms, the returns to doing so are much smaller than for financial markets, particularly in a world with low and stable inflation.
Indeed, low attention to inflation is not a failure of credibility; but a reflection of it. One of the achievements of the inflation-targeting era was that inflation became sufficiently stable that most people did not need to think about it very much.
Whether the recent inflationary episode disrupted that low-attention equilibrium is an empirical question to which I will return. To interpret that evidence, however, we first need to understand how households and firms form expectations when inflation does attract their attention.
Households appear to pay particular attention to price changes in salient items of the consumption basket, rather than headline CPI per se. Food, energy and fuel prices are clear examples: they are visible, often purchased or closely noticed, and feature prominently in people’s sense of the cost of living (Anesti, Esady, Naylor, 2025; D’Acunto et al., 2021 Opens in a new window; Coibion & Gorodnichenko, 2015 Opens in a new window).
This indicates that the effect of inflation on expectations may depend on where that inflation shows up. An increase in the price of something households buy frequently may shift expectations more than an equivalent increase in a less visible component of the index (D’Acunto et al., 2021 Opens in a new window). A risk is that expectations may respond asymmetrically to changes in inflation in these components: rising quickly when visible prices increase but falling slowly when those prices stabilise (Anesti, Esady, Naylor, 2025). In that case, a temporary shock can leave a longer imprint on beliefs than its direct arithmetic contribution to inflation would suggest.
Firms, too, appear to respond to realised inflation, but with a greater focus on Headline CPI. Recent high-frequency evidence from the UK Decision Makers’ Panel (DMP) finds that firms’ inflation perceptions and expectations respond around official CPI releases (Chart 6). Those responses appear related to the reported change in CPI inflation, with little evidence of an additional response to the surprise relative to expectations, such as professional forecasts.

Putting these pieces together, we see a common theme. While financial markets are more forward-looking, both households and firms form expectations partly by looking backwards — to realised inflation, to perceived current inflation, to observed price changes (with a bias toward salient ones), and to the economic environment they have just experienced. That distinction captures an important contrast between “Wall Street” and “Main Street”.
That backward-looking behaviour is not necessarily mistaken: where inflation itself has a (possibly time-varying) inertial component, recent inflation contains information about its likely path.
In the UK data, this backward-looking component shows up clearly (Chart 7). A one percentage point increase in perceived inflation is associated with a rise in expected inflation one year ahead of around 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points. Put differently, expectations appear to be partly conditioned by what households and firms believe inflation to be today, with the implication that biases in the latter can be passing through into the former.

However, expectations are not only backward-looking. Experimental evidence shows that both households and firms do update their inflation expectations when they are provided with clear forward-looking information, including information from central banks (Coibion Opens in a new window, Opens in a new windowGorodnichenko Opens in a new window & Weber 2022 Opens in a new window; Coibion, Gorodnichenko & Kumar 2018 Opens in a new window).
That matters for monetary policy communication. It tells us that economic agents are not unreachable. But it also tells us that communication must compete with expectations that may already have taken shape from subjective experience, media coverage and observed prices. The question is not whether central bank information can matter. It can. The question is how much it matters relative to the information people have already gathered from what they see around them.
A simple way to frame this is as a competition between signals from the recent past and signals about the likely path ahead. The UK evidence is consistent with financial market expectations being more strongly associated with forward-looking information, and households and firms responding to elements of both channels (Chart 8).

Among households, those with more accurate perceptions of current inflation appear more responsive to both backward- and forward-looking information, while those in the tails respond less to macroeconomic signals. The distribution may therefore contain information obscured by the average.
For policy, the distinction between attentiveness to backward- and forward-looking signals matters: the backward-looking component may warrant particular attention. If a temporary increase in inflation leads households and firms to revise up their expectations persistently (Stage 1), and those expectations then feed through into wage and price-setting (Stage 2), the original shock can become more persistent and the force of transmission could mean that perceptions self-validate.
So did the inflationary episode of 2022 disrupt that low-attention equilibrium and take us some way down that path? There are reasons to think that it did, and that expectations may now be more sensitive to inflation shocks than before 2022. Whether that makes them more useful as a guide for policy is less clear.
That 2022 inflationary surge was large, visible and prolonged. It not only affected prices across the economy; it also generated intense media coverage and made inflation a normal topic of conversation again. We see this behavioural shift through online data; with Google searches and media references to inflation rising sharply in 2022 (Charts 9a and 9b).

We should be careful not to overstate precision here. Some of the post-2022 evidence is based on short samples, and it is difficult to separate cleanly the effects of inflation itself, media attention, energy prices and broader uncertainty. But the broad direction of travel is clear enough to matter for policy: today’s shocks may now have larger effects on expectations than similar shocks would have had before 2022.
I would not call this de-anchoring. But I would call it a change in the environment in which expectations are formed. A central bank that could previously assume a high degree of inattention among households and firms may no longer be able to do so.
That observation cuts both ways. Greater attention means that clear and credible central bank communication may have more traction. But it may also allow adverse price news to travel more quickly into beliefs. Louder noise is not necessarily offset by louder signals, especially if attention to recent inflation crowds out the forward-looking information policymakers seek to convey.
The conclusion I draw is deliberately cautious. Household and firm expectations may now respond more strongly to inflation shocks than before 2022. We should not treat every rise in those expectations as evidence of a wage-price spiral, but neither should we dismiss them simply because they are noisy or imperfectly measured.
But expectations are only the first stage of the mechanism. Whether they ultimately matter for inflation depends on whether they feed through into behaviour. I turn to that second stage next.
Stage 2: The importance of inflation expectations in generating persistent inflation
Survey expectations are not behaviour. They are an input into behaviour. For monetary policy, the crucial question is whether they feed into wage bargaining, price setting, consumption and investment and, ultimately, inflation itself.
That is Stage 2, and it is harder to establish empirically.
In theory, the mechanisms are straightforward. On the nominal side, households expecting higher inflation may seek higher nominal wages to protect real incomes; and firms may raise prices. In the extreme, as Lorenzoni and Werning (2023) Opens in a new window formalise, when workers’ real-wage aspirations and firms’ desired margins are jointly inconsistent with the real income available, attempts to protect those positions through wage and price setting can generate persistent inflation.
On the real side, expectations may also affect household spending decisions, with two competing effects: higher expected prices can bring consumption forward, while concern about future real incomes can push households in the opposite direction (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, 2005) Opens in a new window. For firms, the effect on employment and investment depends not only on price expectations but also on what they expect to happen to demand.
Identification is difficult because inflation influences expectations, as we saw in Stage 1, while expectations may also influence inflation, and both respond to wider economic conditions. As a result, the evidence base is thinner than the importance of the question might suggest.
I would organise the evidence in two buckets: microeconomic studies that ask whether changing expectations changes behaviour; and aggregate evidence on whether expectations help explain or predict inflation dynamics. Considered as signposts, neither bucket is perfect. But together they help us assess which expectations matter most, and why.
Micro evidence
The micro evidence is strongest for firms’ price setting. Experimental and survey studies find that higher inflation expectations lead to higher intended price increases. Estimated pass-through is not one-for-one, but economically meaningful at around 20 to 30 per cent in (Abberger Opens in a new window et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Coibion, Gorodnichenko, Ropele, 2019 Opens in a new window), and larger in some UK survey evidence (Ghassibe et al., 2025; Yotzov et al., 2025 Opens in a new window). Expectations are therefore not merely epiphenomenal: in at least some settings, they enter directly into decisions that matter for inflation.
The wage evidence is positive but weaker, and much of it predates the recent inflation surge (Guerreiro et al., 2024 Opens in a new window; Jain et al.,2024 Opens in a new window; Savignac et al., 2024 Opens in a new window; Hajdini et al., 2023 Opens in a new window). Crucially, the ability to translate an increase in inflation expectations into wage outcomes is likely to depend on labour-market conditions, institutional arrangements and bargaining power.
Evidence on real decisions is more mixed. Higher expected inflation can bring some households purchases forward (D’Acunto et al., 2022a Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2022b Opens in a new window),footnote [3] but it can also make them more cautious if they associate inflation with weaker real income or greater uncertainty (Coibion Opens in a new window, et al., 2023 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2023 Opens in a new window; Coibion et al., 2022 Opens in a new window),footnote [4] as growing evidence suggest they do (Zhang Opens in a new window, 2026 Opens in a new window, Debortoli & Iovino, 2025 Opens in a new window). Similarly, firms’ employment and investment decisions similarly depend on whether higher inflation is interpreted as stronger demand or as a cost shock squeezing margins (Coibion Opens in a new window et al., 2019 Opens in a new window; Coibion et al., 2018 Opens in a new window). That ambiguity is not a nuisance in the data; it is part of the economics.
Aggregate evidence
The aggregate evidence begins with a deliberately simple question: do expectations predict inflation? Using UK data, we can look at the relationship between headline inflation and the one-year-ahead expectations reported one year earlier by different groups. We focus short-horizon expectations, which evidence suggests matter more for transmission to aggregate dynamics (Reis, 2026 Opens in a new window; Coibion & Gorodnichenko, 2025 Opens in a new window; Werning, 2022 Opens in a new window).
Chart 12 summarises the results. Financial-market expectations have the strongest correlation with future headline inflation and explain the largest share of the variation. Firms come next, followed by households. Among households, those with more accurate perceptions of current inflation have relatively greater predictive power, as one might expect.

Policymakers need to distinguish between those roles.

Whether expectations influence inflation is also likely to depend on the state of the economy. Households have more scope to translate inflation expectations into wage outcomes when labour markets are tight. Firms have more scope to translate them into prices when demand is strong, and pricing power is greater. A given movement in expectations may therefore have considerably more traction in some economic conditions than in others.
One suggestive test of that state-dependence is to compare the periods before and after 2022 (Chart 15). The later period combined high inflation and elevated attention with a tight labour market and pressure on firms’ margins. During that period, the predictive power of household and firm expectations appeared to have increased.
