articles.title: View from the markets: A critical earnings season approaches - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

As the third quarter earnings season kicks off, investors are nervous given the recent sharp rise in bond yields, which have so far had only a modest impact on equities. While the MOVE index, which measures expected bond market volatility, has returned to levels last seen with the start of the Iran war, the VIX index of equity volatility is not far from the lows for the year.

The dominance of technology hardware in driving earnings growth and equity price appreciation means that any disappointing announcements from these companies will likely be keenly felt. Expectations are high, with the sector globally forecast to see a doubling of earnings compared to the same quarter a year ago. For emerging markets, it is twice that.

These growth rates are substantially higher than those for other sectors, leading some to see the concentration of earnings growth this quarter as a sign of the market’s fragility. It is true that tech earnings will likely dominate the season. They account for nearly two-thirds of the increase in profits for equities globally, followed by energy stocks at 20% (see Exhibit 1).

The dominance of tech earnings, however, is not inherently bad if the other sectors are themselves generating sufficiently positive growth in profits, even if the absolute increase in profits is far less than for technology. For this quarter, however, that is only partly the case.

The median earnings growth for the remaining sectors (that is, excluding tech and energy) is 7%, which is not particularly high. The materials sector is the one expected to see the strongest growth, but most of the forecasts for the other sectors are comparatively low (see Exhibit 2). If this pattern were to continue into the quarters ahead, one would indeed expect the market to be vulnerable as technology would be practically the sole source of profit expansion.

For 2027, however, the pattern is forecast to be different. Earnings growth for the energy sector turns negative, while it moderates for the tech sector. The growth rate for the remaining sectors rises to 12%, spread more evenly across the sectors. That should be sufficient to support ongoing market appreciation.

Third quarter forecasts

The importance of the tech and energy sectors for earnings is reflected in the third quarter forecasts for country and regional indices. Growth rates for indices with a large share of tech or energy stocks are high, while excluding these sectors results in lower figures. For example, we noted that emerging market tech stocks earnings are expected to increase more than four-fold, but for the remaining sectors the forecast is just 11%. In Europe, the 29% gain expected for the index this quarter is reliant on the energy sector; if we exclude it, the growth rate drops to 17% (which is still good; see exhibit 3).

EM tech volatility

Despite the renewed increase in oil prices over the last week, and the higher-than-expected US CPI (consumer price index) inflation data, Treasury yields have dropped by more than 20 basis points from their recent peak. This has prompted a modest rebound in non-tech equities globally. The tech hardware sector, however, has seen another wave of selling, concentrated in South Korea, as it was last July.

We have always expected above-average volatility in the tech sector because of the newness and significance of the artificial intelligence phenomenon. Price gains have been so large, and earnings expectations so high, that any marginal change in sentiment has a commensurately bigger impact.

We remain positive on the medium-term outlook and see volatility along a rising trend. Nonetheless, the impact of AI investment should continue to broaden to other sectors, notably in the US, allowing for the wider breadth of earnings, as shown in Exhibit 2.

Government Bonds’ Safe-Haven Property and Inflationary Pressures
Canlin Li and Emre Yoldas1
1. Introduction

Earlier this year, escalation of the conflict in the Middle East resulted in sharp declines in major stock indexes as energy prices rose and the global economic outlook deteriorated, but prices of long-term government bonds in major advanced economies also declined (Figure 1). This prompted some commentators to question the premise that government bonds in these major advanced economies will rally in times of increased risk aversion and serve as a safe haven for investors (see for example, Kim, 2026). In this note we argue that the type of economic shock and inflationary dynamics matter greatly in determining whether bonds provide portfolio insurance and how investors assess their riskiness.

Figure 1. Stock and Bond Returns in March 2026

Note: Bond returns are approximated using 10-year on-the-run government bond yields and duration of 7 years. Stock returns are based on the S&P 500, Euro Stoxx, and FTSE 100 indexes for the United States, the euro area, and the United Kingdom, respectively. Euro-area bond yields are German 10-year government bond yields. Key identifies in order from left to right.

Source: Bloomberg.

Accessible version

Conventional wisdom suggests that central banks should look through temporary adverse supply shocks, such as the recent oil price spikes caused by the Middle East conflict. However, these shocks may prove persistent and have second-round effects leading to higher inflation expectations by households and firms. Such considerations are crucial when adverse supply shocks hit the economy in an environment of above-target inflation as persistent deviations from inflation targets may eventually lead inflation expectations to settle at a higher level. Against such a backdrop, bond markets could price in a significantly higher policy path in response to these adverse supply shocks as a tighter policy stance can ensure inflationary effects do not broaden and inflation expectations remain stable. This undermines the traditional safe-haven dynamics. In contrast, when inflation runs close to target and policymakers are not concerned about stability of inflation expectations, bonds can rally even in response to an adverse supply shock as policymakers can lower interest rates to cushion the hit to economic growth.

Motivated by these ideas, we use historical data on stock-bond correlations and inflation forecasts in three major advanced economies to show that the hedging property of bonds crucially depends on stability of inflation expectations and inflationary pressures. We also provide evidence from reactions of stock returns and bond yields to economic news that supports this hypothesis.

2. Stock-Bond Correlations and Inflation Regimes

Before examining the historical patterns, it is useful to understand conceptually how inflation dynamics can affect stock-bond correlations.2 In this note, we focus on the correlation between stock returns and bond yield changes. Therefore, positive correlation means falling stock prices coincide with falling yields (i.e. rising bond prices), as bonds provide portfolio insurance to investors. Negative correlation means falling stock prices coincide with rising yields (i.e. falling bond prices), amplifying portfolio losses on risky assets such as stocks.

Bonds' hedging property depends critically on the inflation environment and the kinds of shocks hitting the economy. When inflation is near target and expectations are well anchored, central banks can ease in response to adverse demand or supply shocks without threatening price stability, so bond prices rise when stock prices fall. However, if inflationary pressures are rising and output is close to potential, central banks may face a tradeoff between supporting growth and maintaining price stability. Adverse supply shocks, particularly those arriving amid above-target inflation, may pose similar challenges as central banks may need to keep policy tight to ensure stability of long-term inflation expectations (Covitz and Engstrom, 2026). In these cases, stock and bond prices can fall together.

2.1 Stock-Bond Correlations Across Three Historical Periods
Figure 2 shows how our measures of stock-bond correlations have evolved in the U.S., the euro area, and the U.K. using a 1-year rolling window. The figure reveals some broad patterns: the correlations were deep into negative territory in the early 1990s, were positive for most of the two decades from 2000 to the Covid pandemic, and then switched to negative in recent years. Table 1 provides a summary of the correlations for each period, isolating the noise from short-term fluctuations in the rolling sample. The patterns are broadly consistent with three distinct inflation regimes, which we will analyze next.

2.2 Inflation Regimes
We examine the historical evolution of forward-looking inflation measures over the periods discussed above with respect to inflation forecasts from the Consensus Economics survey.3 Figures 3 and 4 plot 1-year and 6-to-10-year ahead inflation forecasts, respectively, over time with the 2 percent inflation goals marked by dashed lines. Pre-2000 (Establishing policy credibility): In the early 1990s, inflation expectations were elevated but moved lower and stabilized in the subsequent years as central banks established credibility. The evolution of stock bond correlations in 1990s was consistent with this change in inflation dynamics. Early in the decade, bonds amplified stock downturns in a portfolio, but later in the decade became a hedging asset. The anchoring of inflation expectations gave central banks flexibility to ease in response to adverse demand and supply shocks and support the economy, which made bonds a safe haven for investors in times of falling stock prices.

2000-2021 (Low inflation era): Correlations rose to strongly positive levels, and bonds became an excellent hedging asset during the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and subsequent years, in part because of quantitative easing (QE). Long-term inflation expectations remained anchored, giving central banks flexibility to ease aggressively in response to market stress and economic weakness. This policy flexibility ensured that bonds rallied when stocks fell, producing the strong positive correlation observed during this period.

Post-2021 (Inflation makes a comeback): In recent years correlations returned to negative territory across all three economies, indicating severe deterioration in bonds' hedging property (Amundi Investment Institute, 2025). The key change was not a fundamental shift in the stability of longer-term inflation expectations, but rather a change in the mix of economic shocks requiring a different monetary policy response. First, the pandemic-induced inflationary pressures proved more persistent and required significantly higher real rates to bring inflation down and ensure stability of longer-term inflation expectations. This created a market environment where it was common for stock and bond prices to fall simultaneously. More recently, adverse supply shocks pushing prices higher in an economy already experiencing above-target inflation led to expectations of tighter policy even during periods of market stress. Bonds' safe-haven dynamics of the low-inflation era broke down.

The historical relationship between stock-bond correlations and the inflation backdrop strongly suggests a systematic relationship between inflationary dynamics and the hedging property of bonds. We next turn to an event study analysis to offer further evidence for this hypothesis.

2.3 Asset Responses to Inflation News
Prior work has established that U.S. macroeconomic news has substantial effects on global financial markets (Boehm and Kroner, 2026), making it natural to study responses across multiple countries simultaneously. Hence, we estimate regressions of each country's daily stock returns and bond yield changes on all three countries' daily inflation surprise indices from Bloomberg (we also include the growth surprise indices as control variables).4

As a result, stock prices did not react significantly to inflation news. The modest bond yield increases likely reflected the change in inflation compensation component in response to incoming inflation data.

Post 2021, the picture changes dramatically. Higher-than-expected U.S. inflation news now raises U.S. 10-year yields about three times as much as before and also significantly lifts euro-area and U.K. yields, which did not respond to U.S. inflation news in the 2000–2019 sample. The Fed's global influence was present in both periods, so this change in spillovers likely reflects how much more U.S. inflation news moved investor expectations for Fed policy as U.S. inflation has remained above target since 2021. Stock returns also fall significantly on own-country inflation surprises in the post 2021 period, reflecting increased inflationary pressures. When inflationary pressures are strong, each inflation data release may carry heightened significance because investors reassess central banks' future policy paths and surrounding risks. Moreover, expectations for significantly tighter monetary policy in reaction to adverse inflation news suggest potential growth headwinds, which is bad news for stock investors.

Together, these patterns demonstrate that bond hedging property is not a fixed characteristic but depends critically on the macroeconomic environment and the types of economic shocks. The amplification of bond yield sensitivity to inflation news is the central mechanism breaking bonds' traditional safe-haven dynamics.

3. Discussion and Conclusion

Our analysis shows that government bonds' hedging property depends critically on the inflation environment and the types of economic shocks hitting the economy. When inflationary pressures are limited and inflation expectations are well-anchored, bonds provide reliable hedging because central banks can ease in response to both adverse demand and supply shocks that weigh on stocks. This was the typical experience during the GFC and its aftermath, which solidified bonds' safe-haven role. However, when inflationary pressures build up, such as following the Covid pandemic, the required monetary policy response changes; central banks must balance supporting real activity against their price stability objectives, which breaks the traditional flight-to-quality dynamics. In addition, adverse supply shocks may lead investors to expect tighter monetary policy as central banks seek to keep inflation expectations stable. The result is again a deterioration in bonds' hedging property. Our analysis of historical evolution of stock-bond correlations in relation to inflation regimes and different responses of asset prices to inflation news over time support these conjectures. The post 2021 deterioration in bonds' hedging property largely reflects this shift in the economic environment, not necessarily a fundamental change in bond characteristics. If inflationary pressures abate and the frequency of adverse supply shocks declines, bonds' hedging property is likely to improve.

articles.text:
Published on
Voices

Jobs are the test of change

Lisandro Martin

October 11, 2026

This page in:

English

Français

Español

العربية

中文

English

Français

Español

العربية

中文

Photo © Dominic Chavez/World Bank

The most important test of World Bank Group reform happens outside the World Bank Group. It happens when a business can expand, a worker can earn more, and a young person can see a future worth preparing for.
That test is getting harder. Aid budgets are shrinking. Debt is squeezing public investment. Conflict and climate shocks are eroding livelihoods. Skepticism about international cooperation adds another demand: show that change inside our institutions makes a difference outside them.
The FY26 Scorecard offers evidence that we are strengthening the conditions for jobs. It also reveals the logic connecting our reforms. A sharper focus on outcomes tells us what to pursue. Global knowledge helps identify what stands in the way. Private capital and better risk sharing expand what is possible. Working as one World Bank Group brings those capabilities together.
The three pillars of our jobs strategy give that effort a practical direction: build the foundations, open the way, and back the opportunity. The three pillars of our jobs strategy give that effort a practical direction: build the foundations, open the way, and back the opportunity.
Build the foundations
Jobs begin long before a vacancy is advertised. They begin with learning, good health, reliable electricity and a route to market. Across the Scorecard reporting portfolio, 326.6 million students received better education, 615 million people accessed quality health services, and 258.4 million people gained electricity access.
Delivery is expanding. All 15 indicators with comparable data on achieved results show gains since FY24. Access to financial services rose 159 percent, broadband use 114 percent, and electricity access 51 percent. Ambition is expanding too, as the expected results show. Better measurement is part of that story – we are tracking more and tracking it more precisely.

Uzbekistan shows what that foundation looks like in practice. Private solar investment needed credible auctions, workable contracts and confidence that electricity buyers would pay. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) brought transaction advice and financing; the World Bank provided payment guarantees. The Samarkand and Jizzakh plants added 440 megawatts of capacity and generated more than 930 gigawatt-hours by the time the project closed.
The partnership also strengthened Uzbekistan’s ability to procure private renewable power independently. That is the larger ambition: deliver the result, and build the system that can repeat it.
Open the way
A business can have workers, customers and a good product — and still be unable to grow. Unpredictable rules, weak credit information or a government that pays late can close the path to expansion. The second pillar of our jobs strategy targets exactly those barriers: the regulatory, financial and institutional obstacles that prevent businesses from acting on the opportunities in front of them.
Global knowledge becomes useful when it reaches the decisions that shape a business’s day. In Morocco, the Country Growth and Jobs Report and Country Private Sector Diagnostic are informing a connected agenda on regulation, finance, skills and digital transformation. World Bank and IFC support connects improvements in financial infrastructure and financing rules to practical changes in how lenders serve firms.
Consider getting paid. In Marrakech-Safi, IFC advisory support helped cut public-contract payment times from 39 to 22 days and clear $14.4 million in arrears. For a firm, those 17 days mean less money tied up while wages and suppliers still need paying. Better public systems can change private possibilities.
Knowledge also travels. Experience with crop receipts in Ukraine is being adapted in the Western Balkans and South Caucasus; Albania has adopted a Crop and Warehouse Receipts law. Crop receipts allow farmers to use their harvests as collateral to secure financing — and the approach is proving transferable.  The value of a global institution grows when countries can build on one another’s experience.
Back the opportunity
Stronger foundations and better rules create opportunities. Capital allows firms to act on them. The Scorecard records $328.7 billion in expected private capital mobilized — up 67 percent since FY24 — and $242.5 billion in expected private capital enabled, up 50 percent since FY25 when it was first reported.
These are two complementary routes to investment. Mobilization brings private capital alongside our operations. Enabling changes the conditions that attract investment in the first place. IFC accounts for about 63 percent of expected mobilization; IBRD and IDA account for about 71 percent of expected capital enabled. The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) helps investors manage political and regulatory risk, extending the Group’s reach into markets where private capital would otherwise not go. One World Bank Group means making these strengths work together.

Ecuador shows what reaching smaller business can do. World Bank support helped Corporación Financiera Nacional channel finance through other financial institutions, strengthening a system for reaching smaller firms. By the end of 2025, 22 institutions had provided more than 26,000 sub-loans. An evaluation using 2019–2023 data estimated an 8.9 percent employment gain among the formal firms studied, rising to about 27 percent among firms without previous bank credit.
The lesson goes beyond lending more. Build institutions that can reach more firms—and learn which firms benefit most.
Risk sharing extends that possibility. Annual private capital mobilization reached $112 billion in FY26, and the Group issued more than $25 billion in guarantees, supported by a platform providing a single point of access. A guarantee matters when it changes an investor’s decision and makes productive investment possible. These figures are annual flows, distinct from the Scorecard’s portfolio amounts.
That purpose matters especially in difficult settings. The Scorecard reports electricity access for 54.8 million people in fragile and conflict-affected economies, alongside services and livelihoods support for 19.5 million displaced people and host-community members.

In the Horn of Africa, DRIVE — a resilience program combining drought insurance, savings and payments with stronger livestock markets — reached approximately 475,000 policyholders with $12.5 million in payouts in FY26. Protecting livestock protects productive assets. Building insurance and market systems helps livelihoods survive the next shock.
Make the next decision better
There is much more to do. Low-income economies account for only about 6 percent of expected private capital mobilization. And even where capital does flow, it does not always reach those who need it most — Ecuador’s evaluation found that lenders still favored firms with established credit relationships, even though gains were larger among first-time borrowers. Those findings should influence the next product, the next incentive, and the next allocation of risk.
Nor should we attribute every result to recent reform. These achievements reflect country leadership and years of partnership. They show approaches worth expanding, and systems worth strengthening. The test ahead is whether we can make them work more widely.
Upcoming reporting on the More and Better-paid Jobs indicator will sharpen how we measure progress. It translates gains in labor income — from additional employment and better-paid work — into an equivalent number of jobs. First reporting is planned for the IDA21 Mid-Term Review. It will help connect what our operations support to what people earn.
Our global listening tour is helping improve the Scorecard itself. Through its Mid-Term Review, we are working toward more credible evidence, a better account of country realities and knowledge contributions, and results that are easier to use. Transparency makes progress visible — and scrutiny helps us decide what to change.
That is the Outcome Reflex: “What will this decision do to the outcome?” It belongs wherever we design a project, advise a government, or share a risk. The Scorecard should help us move from storing results to steering decisions.
Build the foundations. Open the way. Back the opportunity. And judge our reform by the lives those decisions change.

Jobs & Development

Lisandro Martin

Director of the Outcomes Department in the Senior Managing Director's Office at the World Bank Group

articles.title: How active ETFs can help reduce a portfolio’s tax liability
articles.text:
By

Christopher Murphy, CIMA®,
Thomas Guarini,
Brian Navin, CFA

Share the Article

Print the Article

Download the PDF

How active ETFs can help reduce a portfolio’s tax liability

Active ETFs may help advisors manage taxes, costs, and portfolio transitions.

October 2026, Personal Finance

Key Insights

Exchange-traded funds generally have a more favorable structure for tax efficiency than some other investments, such as mutual funds.
Transitioning from a traditional mutual fund to an ETF may turn an initial tax liability into long-term savings.
Tax loss harvesting opportunities should be evaluated throughout the year, not just at year-end.

With year-end approaching, advisors may be reviewing portfolios for potential capital gain distributions and opportunities to apply tax-smart strategies in eligible accounts. Decisions made now—such as harvesting losses or realizing gains ahead of distributions—can meaningfully influence a client’s after-tax outcomes.

One way to enhance long-term tax efficiency is by reallocating assets into exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds. Actively managed ETFs, in particular, allow investors to pair those structural tax advantages with professional oversight, flexibility, and the potential for added return. With established managers like T. Rowe Price offering active ETFs, investors can combine the benefits of convenience, cost-effectiveness, and capital gains efficiency in a single vehicle—making them a timely tool for this year’s tax planning season.

Why consider using an active ETF as we approach year-end?

1. ETFs have been more tax-efficient

In terms of capital gains tax, ETFs have historically been a more tax-efficient vehicle than some other investment structures, such as mutual funds. The main reason ETFs have been more tax-efficient is due to the ETF’s unique create/redeem mechanism and the ability for ETFs to facilitate outflows in-kind. Even though ETFs may still generate a capital gain distribution, shareholder activity of buying and selling shares typically doesn’t create taxable events for ETFs, unlike in mutual funds.

Keep in mind, there are many factors that will impact the tax efficiency of an ETF and should always be taken into consideration (e.g., trading activity, issuer procedures, time in market). For investors who want the structural tax advantages of ETFs along with the benefits of active management—such as research-driven security selection, flexibility to adapt to markets, and risk management—active ETFs have the potential to add value to an investor’s portfolio.

Over the past five years, fewer ETFs than mutual funds paid capital gains

From December 31, 2021, to December 31, 2025.

Figure 1 illustrates the percentage of U.S. large-cap active and passive U.S.-listed mutual funds and ETFs that made capital gain distributions in each of the past five calendar years. It’s a myth to say that an ETF will never generate a capital gain, but structurally speaking, ETFs have done so at a much lower rate than mutual funds—even actively managed strategies. Some of T. Rowe Price’s active equity ETFs, for example, have distributed little (or in some cases, even zero) year-end capital gains over the past three years.

2. ETFs could turn a short-term tax hurdle into a long-term advantage

While transitioning a client from a mutual fund vehicle to an ETF may trigger an initial capital gains tax liability, the ongoing impact from staying invested in a mutual fund could pose a significant tax drag on total return over the long term.

As shown in Figure 2, the one-time tax cost of transitioning from a mutual fund to an ETF may be recovered over time through the ETF’s greater tax efficiency. Based on this hypothetical example, a mutual fund that has a cost basis equal to 50% of its current market value and carries a 20% average turnover rate could recoup the initial tax liability in approximately 2.6 years, after which the ETF structure may provide meaningful long-term tax savings. Beyond potential tax savings, clients may also benefit from many of the other well-known advantages of ETFs, including lower fees, enhanced transparency, and intraday trading flexibility.

ETFs could potentially generate significant tax savings over time

The concept is similar to a Roth conversion: Investors accept a tax cost today in exchange for potential tax benefits in the future. While transitioning from a mutual fund to an ETF may present upfront tax costs, the ETF’s greater tax efficiency may help offset that cost in the short term and has the potential to provide significant performance benefits over the long term.

3. Lower fees for an active approach

Just as active ETFs can add value through performance, they can also help reduce the overall cost of investing. When considering a move from mutual funds to ETFs, actively managed ETFs may also offer investors a way to reduce overall portfolio expenses in the process. Reduced expenses can help with the overall long-term outcome. ETF operational costs are often streamlined relative to active mutual funds with fewer shareholder services, client statement reporting, and other expenses. Well-established firms may have additional pricing advantages. By leveraging the global scope and scale of our firmwide resources, T. Rowe Price active ETFs are competitively priced relative to their peer groups. For example, illustrated in Figure 3 are some examples where T. Rowe Price active ETFs offer competitive fees relative to category averages.

Tax-loss harvesting opportunities should be evaluated throughout the year

Beyond structural efficiency and lower expenses, advisors can apply active ETFs in tactical ways as well. One of the most important tools—especially in periods of heightened market volatility—is tax loss harvesting. This should be an ongoing, disciplined part of an advisor’s portfolio management process.

The technology sector provides a compelling example. Its relatively high volatility and broad return dispersion created meaningful tax-loss harvesting opportunities earlier this year as a first-quarter sell-off gave way to a strong rebound. Investor concerns around elevated valuations, artificial intelligence (AI) spending, inflation, interest rates, and geopolitical risks pressured prices, allowing advisors to harvest losses and potentially reposition clients into active strategies designed to better manage uncertainty and evolving market conditions.

An active technology ETF like the T. Rowe Price Technology ETF (TTEQ) not only offers the flexibility to adapt to changing market conditions but has also delivered strong results—outperforming many passive peers since the March lows (Figure 4).

articles.title: 2026 North America Crypto Adoption: $3.02T, Agentic Rails
articles.text:
Summary
North America’s $3 trillion crypto economy remained the most influential in the world, with advancements in agentic commerce, exports of dollar stablecoins, and tokenization shaping global activity.
The U.S. crypto economy shrank 2.2% in the 2026 period (in line with bear market expectations) while the Canadian crypto economy bucked the trend, growing 2.3%.
Agentic commerce, or AI agents using crypto to pay autonomously, grew rapidly over the 12-month period, with U.S. providing a nexus for growth.
Canada is the G7’s most robust peer-to-peer crypto economy, potentially driven by its large immigrant population. Cross-border stablecoin remittances to India, China, and the Philippines reached $2.36 billion this period, up 141% year-over-year.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Reserve your copy
North America was the most influential region for crypto markets globally in the 12 months ending July 1, 2026 (our 2026 reporting period). With the United States’ deep investor base providing the capital, lawmakers updating regulations, stablecoins providing a currency, and businesses bringing crypto ever-closer to traditional finance, what happens in North America’s crypto industry gets exported to the world. Indeed, the U.S. and Canada topped our “big-money index,” an unweighted measurement of the sheer crypto-economic power of the countries we cover. In the 2026 period, their respective crypto economies totaled $3.02 trillion, a modest 1.9% drop from the period before.The regional contraction stems from a slowdown in the U.S. The United States’ $2.78 trillion crypto economy fell by 2.2% period-over-period, an unsurprising outcome in the context of a brutal bear market. Still, the world’s single-biggest crypto economy largely retained in 2026 the near-doubling it posted for the 2025 period. Institutional forces such as the rise of crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs), accelerating tokenization and the proliferation of stablecoins helped it retain those gains.“A lot of what we’re seeing vs. 2025 comes down to maturation of the industry,” said Hoolie Tejwani, Head of Coinbase Ventures. “The building blocks set in 2025 are turning into products with real users, liquidity, and markets in 2026.”In this chapter we’ll look at a trio of U.S.-developed crypto products attracting major activity in-country and around the world: AI commerce, stablecoins, and tokenized assets. All three are manifestations of the U.S. influence on the global crypto market.We’ll also examine the Canadian market, which, while far smaller than its southern neighbor, resisted the downtrend: Canada’s crypto economy rose 2.3% in the 2026 period. Focusing on a subset of that $250 billion economy, we will explain how Canada’s immigrant populations affect its surprisingly strong peer-to-peer economy.The US is leading the AI on-chain economyThe United States’ lead in the global AI development race is influencing all corners of the economy, including crypto. We researched x402, one of the most popular digital payments rails that lets AI agents spend money, to better understand how this economy is taking shape.Autonomous software has begun to pay for things on-chain, and the United States has emerged as its dominant builder. Crypto’s cornerstone American companies, including Circle, the issuer of USDC (a leading currency for agents), and Coinbase, builder of the x402 system itself, are supporting their rise. We spoke to both companies for this report to get a sense of the technology. Agentic commerce is also drawing interest from the U.S.’ most important financial institutions. BlackRock’s Head of Digital Assets Research Will Su told us the firm is watching agentic commerce closely “with AI agents potentially creating meaningful demand for frequent, low-value payments around the clock.”By the end of the 2026 period over 138 million x402 transactions had occurred on Base, the most popular blockchain for agentic commerce.On-chain payments allow for economic activity infeasible on traditional payment rails, such as micro-payments. Transactions worth less than a dollar (and especially less than a penny) don’t make fiscal sense for a credit card network to process. But stablecoins that themselves cost less than a cent to settle make it economically viable for agents to spend tiny amounts of money. This possibility opens up a whole new market of pay-as-you-go goods and services, such as a data pull through an API call.Circle describes a clean division of labor emerging: “card rails for consumer-prompted agent payments, stablecoin rails for machine-to-machine settlements that are too small for card economics.”Indeed, the vast majority of x402 activity registered as a micropayment in the 16 months ending in September 2026 (we extended our review period given how new this technology is). Over 87% of payments fall between a hundredth of a cent and a dime, with the most common size between one and ten cents.While agentic commerce is still in its “experimentation phase” (as multiple experts we spoke to put it), we’re noting signs of maturation. The earliest days of x402 were marked by one-off users trying something out (like making a crypto trade) but then leaving as soon as they ran out of funds. That dynamic seems to be shifting.AI payments are becoming stickierEach successive group of wallets has arrived more committed than the last. Grouping wallets by the quarter they were first funded, the share that got a second funding within 30 days of the first rose from 70.6% for wallets first funded in Q3 2025 to 89.3% for those first funded in Q2 2026, the most recent group whose 30-day window has fully closed. Topping up a depleted wallet is the on-chain equivalent of renewing a subscription after the first invoice lands. We counted only wallets that sent on two or more separate days, to exclude the one-and-done experimenters and focus on the wallets actually using agentic payments in an enduring way. These numbers show that users are increasingly finding enough utility in x402 to keep funding their wallets after their balances are depleted.Users of x402 are also becoming more purposeful. We can discern this by looking at the decreasing gap in time between a wallet’s seed funding and its first x402 spend. In late 2025 (when the protocol was still new) wallets were, at the median, 73 days old when they initiated an x402 payment; by Q3 2026 that gap had dropped to 18 minutes. This temporal compression shows that these newer wallets are being purpose built to engage in agentic commerce and to spend on x402.Since launch, the share of wallets spending on x402 within their first hour of being funded has climbed. In Q3 2025, just 4% of wallets made their first payment within an hour of funding. By Q3 2026, that figure had jumped to 67%, meaning roughly two in three new wallets are now spending almost immediately after being topped up. That is another strong signal of purposeful adoption. People are not funding wallets to park value or test the protocol; they are funding them because a specific job is already queued up and the money needs to move.What AI agents are buying with x402“AI agents are becoming economic actors where every agent is effectively a new ‘user’ of the blockchain,” said Tejwani of Coinbase Ventures. “We’re especially excited about projects building on the x402 protocol, which Coinbase incubated, and what it means for the future of open-sourced standards and internet-native payments.”All the data on agentic payments had us asking: what are AI models actually buying on-chain? In the early days of x402 the answer was predominately fads; memecoins such as PING attracted huge numbers of new wallets only to fade. But the maturation of x402 has also produced more enduring forms of agentic commerce, especially in the information sector. The robots are buying AI-generated knowledge on-chain.We’ve tracked millions of transactions flowing from AI wallets into information-focused services like code review, financial intelligence, and data and search API. This tracks with what we know about agents in general: they’re hungry for machine-readable data. It’s an area where on-chain micro-payments can be especially useful, as we discussed earlier.AI agents are also paying through payment rails, for gaming, token issuance and gambling services, and for agent frameworks and agentic tooling. Notably, the AI agents are also paying for AI agents. One of the largest categories for x402 transactions is model inference.The U.S. dominates in AI-to-AI commerceAmerican-funded AI agents are transacting more with x402 services than agents funded from any other country. The U.S. holds a 30% share of the agent-to-services transactions that we can geolocate (using the same methodology we apply to other on-chain activity).American wallets account for 88.1% of all geolocated AI model inference transactions on the protocol, 41.8% of payments to agent frameworks and tool catalogs, and 23.2% of payments to data and search APIs — the three categories that supply the inputs to building agentic software.To compare, Chinese-attributed wallets were most prominent in the security space. Nine out of ten transactions we tracked going into “Security and code analysis” originated from Chinese-linked wallets. Almost all of this activity flowed into AgentLISA, a service that audits Solidity smart contracts using a language model. They were also prominent customers of market and financial intelligence, with 46.7% share, and payment and settlement rails, with 35% share. But Chinese-funded AI agents took just 0.1% of model inference. Chinese operators are scarce only in paying for inference.One possible explanation is AI nationalism. The Chinese market is perhaps more readily accepting of Chinese-developed models, led by DeepSeek and Qwen, than the American market is. This AI nationalism intersects with economic reality. China’s open-weight models are free to use; US-developed, metered models, led by ChatGPT and Claude, are not.The implication is that the visible market for machine-bought intelligence will be largest in jurisdictions where buying it remains the cheapest option, and American demand sits at the center of that market today. The experimental phase appears to be ending faster than many observers assume. Recapitalization cadences and funding-to-spend intervals, describe a provisioned system with a recurring budget line, not a demonstration.The monitoring surface is unlike anything in conventional payments. Individual transactions are too fast, too small, and too frequent to serve as the compliance checkpoint. But the model offers different controls: the funding event identifies the sender, the budget authorization is a reviewable human decision, the receiving service is a known counterparty, and the mechanical regularity of agent spending makes behavioral anomalies easier to detect than in human-driven payment flows. The compliance logic shifts from screening each payment to screening the setup, the destination, and the pattern.Accountability must trace to whoever deployed and funded the agent, not the agent itself. The reviewable checkpoints are the funding event, the counterparty, and the behavioral pattern. Those three can operate at machine speed. Per-transaction review cannot. Frameworks that do not account for this will either block agentic commerce entirely or miss it completely.The US is importing digital gold and exporting digital dollarsCongressional passage of the GENIUS act in mid-2025 formalized what crypto economies around the world already know: the U.S. is the leading exporter of digital dollars. Stablecoins have turned US debt into a currency-of-choice for peer-to-peer economies as well as businesses working across borders. In the 2026 period we continued to see stablecoins enter new use cases most especially abroad, benefitting the U.S. companies, and the U.S. government, with billions of dollars in economic activity.While the U.S. has been exporting stablecoins, it has also been importing bitcoin. Since the January 2024 launch of the spot bitcoin ETFs, the U.S. share of global bitcoin activity has consistently risen through every reporting period. Meanwhile, stablecoins make up a smaller share of American crypto activity than of activity elsewhere, and the gap has widened each period Indeed, the chart below shows this trend. It pools three measures (bitcoin’s share of service inflows, of exchange trading and of net cross-border receipts) into a single index, so the distance between the lines, not their height, is the finding. The divergence shows the growing US dominance in Bitcoin and the rest of the world becoming increasingly dependent on USD stablecoins.A dollar stablecoin is a way to hold dollars without an American bank account, and Americans already have one. The rest of the world is pivoting to a digital dollar because it meets a need that American users don’t share. Meanwhile, Americans are leaning harder on bitcoin as an infinitely scarce store of value. “Investor interest in bitcoin as a monetary alternative remains strong, particularly as government debt and spending reach new highs globally,” says Will Su, Managing Director and Head of Digital Assets Research at BlackRock.Counting all cross-border bitcoin flows into and out of the US, the country became a net importer in 2026 for the first time since 2022. Transfers under $10,000 ran net outbound every period measured. But larger denomination transfers flip to net inflows, with the bracket above $10 million alone accounting for 53,200 coins arriving. Retail sends bitcoin out; institutions bring it in. A federal Strategic Bitcoin Reserve has added implicit sovereign demand to the private bid, even without an explicit buying program.99.1% of stablecoin order book volume traded is pegged to the dollar, and tokens leave American issuers without touching a correspondent bank or appearing in any payments statistics. They also come back as demand. Every token is a claim on reserves held largely in short-dated US government debt. Circle reported $73.3 billion of USDC in circulation at quarter end, up 19% year on year, against $14.8 trillion of on-chain volume for the quarter alone. “More institutions now use stablecoins as the routing layer between fiat, local stablecoins, and global dollar liquidity,” Circle told us. “The mechanism that moves a position between assets, jurisdictions, or venues, not the position itself.”Both trends benefit the U.S. market. The imported bitcoin is accumulated; the exported stablecoins help proliferate the dollar, bolstering U.S. economic strength.These two legs differ in durability. Bitcoin accumulation is an institutional allocation decision that moves with the market’s changing proclivities. As Blackrock’s Su explained, “the first half of 2026 saw ETP outflows as AI attracted capital away from digital assets. Inflows resumed in the third quarter as the AI investment theme moderated.” Comparatively, stablecoin proliferation is broad and incremental; users who adopt digital dollars are unlikely to turn away.Order book data underscores the challenge any competing stablecoin has in unseating the dollar. Despite the implementation of EU laws such as MiCA that created a more favorable landscape for euro-backed stablecoin issuers, those assets account for just 0.45% of orderbook volume. Still, more competitors are gathering; Singapore and Hong Kong have both introduced stablecoin licensing frameworks designed to support locally denominated offerings. All face the same gap: regulatory readiness has outpaced market adoption. User demand is not yet there.The US impact on tokenizationThe United States continued to dominate the fast-growing tokenization sector in the 2026 period. For one, U.S. debt (Treasury bonds) were the single-largest real-world asset (RWA) in the period with $15.42 billion on-chain: 42.8% of all tokenized RWA value. The tokenization market overall finished Q2 2026 with $36.07 billion, posting 135% growth period-over-period.“We are seeing asset managers launch tokenized funds, public companies explore putting their equity on-chain, financial institutions build stablecoin infrastructure and tokenized assets become usable within lending, collateral and trading markets,” said Tom Murphy, head of communications for Securitize.As tokenized assets broadly become more useful on-chain, the types of assets being tokenized have expanded. Corporate credit grew 3,156% and private equity 1,340%, but those gains moved categories from tens of millions to a couple of billion. Treasury debt’s 125% growth is a move from $6.86 billion to $15.42 billion, more than the next three categories combined in dollar terms. The market is diversifying around US government debt rather than away from it.US holders are 11.7% of the global tokenized RWA holder base and account for 11.4% of its value, a near match. Tokenized Treasuries break that symmetry decisively. By value, Italy accounts for 29.9% of geolocated tokenized Treasury holdings, Portugal 18.8%, and Singapore 18.2%, against 10.5% for the United States in fourth place. By share of holders the ranking rearranges almost entirely: Japan leads with 16.4% of holders but just 0.4% of the value. The distance between the two measures is the finding. A small base of large foreign holders is driving the tokenized Treasury market, while a broader retail base is accumulating smaller positions.The policy reading is the one Morva Rohani of the Canadian Web3 Council draws for stablecoins later in this chapter, and it transfers directly: a holder outside the United States who buys a tokenized Treasury product is creating demand for US government debt rather than for their own government’s. Tokenization lowers the minimum position size and removes the need for a US brokerage relationship, which turns a wholesale instrument into one a retail holder in Lisbon or Singapore can buy directly.Lending patterns reinforce the point that tokenized Treasuries are being bought and held rather than put to work as collateral. Wallets lending private credit grew 1,618% over the period, and private credit now accounts for 77% of all value lent against tokenized RWAs. Commodities lending grew 875%. Treasuries went the other way, contracting 23%, the only category to do so. The divergence is consistent with what tokenization does for each asset. Private credit is illiquid in its untokenized form, so a tokenized position that can be posted as collateral is worth more to its holder than the underlying loan. Treasuries are already the most liquid collateral in conventional finance; a holder who wants cash against them has established ways to get it.Securitize also frames what adoption will come to mean: “Over time, investors may care less about whether they are ‘using crypto’ and more about whether their financial assets can take advantage of the speed, programmability and global interoperability that blockchain infrastructure can provide.”“The end state is not a separate crypto financial system sitting alongside traditional finance,” Securitize told us. “It is increasingly one financial system using better technology.” That convergence extends beyond the public-chain data captured here. A parallel institutional tokenization layer continues to build on permissioned infrastructure like Canton, where regulated participants settle tokenized securities and cash in environments designed around existing custody and compliance frameworks. That activity does not show up in on-chain holder counts, but it suggests the full tokenization story is larger than any single dataset captures.Canada is a global leader in peer-to-peerCanada, the second largest country in our “big money index” and 10th in our grassroots adoption index overall, saw its crypto economy grow 2.3% between July 2025 and June 2026 (the 2026 period) to reach $247.7 billion overall.Inside this modest growth story are residents using crypto for their everyday lives. And they’re doing so at rates far higher than we normally see in highly developed economies. In fact, among G7 nations Canada had the most robust overall peer-to-peer crypto economy in our 2026 rankings; it placed seventh globally in both domestic and cross border flows.Stablecoins, a highly popular asset for peer-to-peer commerce globally, feed the largest share of Canada’s crypto appetite. By June 2026 stablecoins took 44% of Canadian dollar-based order book volume, up from 30% a year earlier. USDC is the dominant stablecoin within this bucket; very little trading activity flowed to Canadian dollar-backed stablecoins.This purchasing dynamic creates a somewhat undesirable setup for Canada: the country’s most in-demand cryptocurrency is essentially a stablecoin denominated in USD, so a foreign asset. As we mentioned above with regard to purchasing tokenized U.S. Treasuries, buying U.S. dollar stablecoins creates demand for U.S. government debt at the expense of potential demand for Canadian government debt, according to Morva Rohani, Executive Director of the Canadian Web3 Council.“This is a trend that Canadian policy-makers are following closely,” she said.Canada’s proximity to the US sharpens the point, but the dynamic applies globally. Any value flowing into U.S. treasury-backed stablecoins, instead of local debt-backed alternatives, weakens demand for local sovereign debt. The global strength of the U.S. dollar makes this more likely, but no less problematic, and Canadians are not the only ones looking to reduce the dollar dominance of stablecoin volumes.Canada recently adopted a stablecoin act that will clear the way for issuers to launch Canadian Dollar stablecoins. Some of those prospective issuers are specifically targeting the domestic and international payments as use cases, according to Rohani. But their CAD stablecoins are thus far minuscule in market cap and overall adoption compared to their USD counterparts.Canada’s cross-border crypto economyCanada’s embrace of stablecoins plays into another important crypto story that we track: its cross-border flows. Canada is first in the world in cross-border flows in our unweighted “big money” index, the complement to the grassroots index, where Canada ranks seventh.One important factor in Canada’s surprising cross-border strength is likely its thriving immigrant population. “About 23% of Canada’s population is foreign-born, the highest share in the G7,” said Rohani. She credits Canada’s large immigrant population as one of the key drivers of remittances; we will discuss another area of strength for immigrants (peer-to-peer economy) later in the report.“Remittance corridors to India, the Philippines, Nigeria, Pakistan, and China are heavily used,” Rohani said.Canada’s remittance strength tracks a specific financial profile: residents who need to move money across borders regularly and face high costs doing so through traditional channels. Many in this group maintain financial obligations in their country of origin, whether supporting family, servicing debt, or managing assets. Conventional remittance fees make those obligations expensive. Stablecoin remittances make them cheaper.We looked at three of those countries with the fastest cross-border growth — India, China, and the Philippines — which together account for 19.4% of Canada’s outbound cross-border stablecoin value, up from 10.9% a year earlier.Remittance-sized stablecoin and bitcoin transfers from Canada to India, the Philippines and China totaled $2.36 billion this period (up 141% YoY). This activity spread across 3.56 million transactions with an average of 75,100 unique senders per month throughout the period. Their average transfer size was $663.These corridors are huge before crypto enters the picture. Global remittances hit about $905 billion in 2024, and Canada’s top destinations lead the recipient table: India ranks first worldwide at roughly $129 billion, China draws about $48 billion, and the Philippines about $40 billion. Canadians sent an estimated $8.3 billion abroad in 2023, much of it to those same three countries. Against that total, the $2.36 billion we measured on crypto rails is a small but fast-growing slice.Cost explains why that slice keeps growing. The World Bank pegs the average cost of sending money from Canada near 6.7%, with banks above 7%. A stablecoin transfer settles for a cent or less, whatever the amount, and those savings add up across the many payments a regular sender makes each year.The population behind Canada’s domestic volumeGlobally, peer-to-peer crypto payments often make the most sense for immigrants; they may have limited access to traditional financial tools like bank accounts, and therefore a need for a viable alternative. These populations may find crypto especially useful in conducting their daily business.Ebbs and flows within that population track with patterns we saw in Canada’s P2P activity. For example, we looked at data on study permit holders from China, India, and the Philippines, (three of Canada’s most popular remittance corridors) since mid-2021. As this group swelled, so too did Canada’s domestic peer-to-peer crypto economy. Then, as policy changes began to cut the number of permits issued, and reduce the number of permits held, activity shrank.The correlation shows up in the data. Canada’s domestic P2P crypto volume has tracked closely with the size of its population holding temporary visas, rising and falling in parallel since mid-2021. The relationship is associational, not causal, but the direction is consistent in both expansion and contraction. The likeliest explanation is straightforward: people with active cross-border financial lives are more likely to adopt a cheaper settlement option when one exists.While these trends are only associational, domestic peer-to-peer crypto volumes tracking the trend in temporary visas both up and down is highly suggestive. Anecdotal evidence also suggests that Canadians are using crypto as part of their daily lives. We’ve heard stories of landlords accepting rent payments in bitcoin, of residents paying their bills in crypto, and even of small businesses accepting payments for their goods.The infrastructure layer is American; the user base is globalNorth America’s story this period is less about who holds crypto and more about who builds the rails that others use. American institutions, issuers, and developers now sit at the center of three overlapping on-chain markets: the Treasuries being tokenized, the dollars being held in stablecoin form, and the AI services being bought agentically. In each case, the users driving demand are increasingly outside the United States, while the infrastructure monetizing that demand is inside it. Canada is one such user, with growth running outward through dollar-denominated rails that neither its banks nor its regulators control.That concentration is not going uncontested. The EU’s MiCA framework now requires euro-denominated reserves for stablecoins marketed in Europe. Singapore’s stablecoin regulatory framework, finalized in 2023, is designed to make locally issued tokens viable. Brazil’s Drex pilot is testing a central-bank-backed digital real on programmable rails. Each is an explicit attempt to build domestic alternatives to dollar-denominated infrastructure. Whether those efforts gain traction or simply confirm the dollar default will depend on adoption, not legislation alone.The regulatory decisions ahead, from the Canadian Stablecoin Act to pending US guidance on tokenization and agentic payments, will set the terms for how large that gap between builders and users becomes in the period to come.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Reserve your copy
FAQsHow large is North America’s crypto economy in 2026?North America received $3.02 trillion in on-chain value during the 2026 reporting period, down slightly from $3.08 trillion the year before. The United States remains the region’s dominant market and ranks near the top of Chainalysis’s global adoption index.What is x402 and why does it matter?x402 is an on-chain payment protocol published by Coinbase in May 2025 that lets AI agents and other autonomous software pay for things without human involvement at the moment of purchase. It enables a class of micro-transactions, typically between a hundredth of a cent and a dime, that traditional card networks cannot process profitably.Which country leads AI-to-AI payments on-chain?The United States, by a wide margin. American wallets account for 88% of all AI model inference payments on x402 and dominate the categories most closely tied to building agentic software.Do Americans use stablecoins less than the rest of the world?Relative to their overall crypto activity, yes. Stablecoins take a smaller share of US crypto activity than of activity elsewhere, and that gap widened in the 2026 period. Americans already have dollars through their banking system. Users in other markets are turning to dollar stablecoins to meet a need their local banks don’t address.How large is the tokenized real-world asset (RWA) market in North America?The global tokenized RWA market reached $36.07 billion in 2026, up 135% year-over-year. Tokenized US Treasury debt is the single largest category at $15.42 billion, with most of the value held by retail investors outside the United States.Why does Canada have such a strong peer-to-peer crypto economy?Canada has the highest foreign-born population share in the G7, and much of its peer-to-peer activity is tied to cross-border remittances. Stablecoin transfers from Canada to India, China, and the Philippines alone reached $2.36 billion this period.What regulatory developments are shaping North American crypto in 2026?Canada’s Stablecoin Act received Royal Assent in March 2026, with implementing regulations now being drafted. In the US, pending guidance on tokenization and agentic payments will shape how institutional and AI-driven on-chain activity scales from here. INVESTMENT BANKING

Q3 2026 Shareholder activism: M&A demands rise as activity slows

Contributor: Jim Rossman

13 Oct 2026

Shareholder activism slowed slightly following a busy first half of 2026, but the global activist landscape continued to evolve. Barclays Corporate Finance Advisory’s Q3 2026 Review of Shareholder Activism report highlights record APAC activity, rising M&A demands and a shrinking pool of activists launching campaigns.

Key takeaways:

Global shareholder activism slowed in Q3 2026: 43 campaigns launched worldwide, returning activity to more typical seasonal levels after elevated H1 activity.
APAC recorded its highest share of shareholder activism campaigns: While the U.S. remained the dominant forum for activism, APAC accounted for a record 31% share of global campaign activity, with Japanese targets attracting the majority.
M&A was the leading focus of shareholder activists in Q3 2026: M&A-related demands represented 58% of all campaign objectives, rebounding from below-average levels earlier in the year.
Shareholder activism activity became increasingly concentrated by sector: A record 82% of campaigns targeted companies in five sectors, led by Industrials and Technology.

Shareholder activism slowed marginally in Q3, with 43 campaigns launched globally, bringing year-to-date activity to 179. While this represents a 7% decline compared with 2025, activity remains broadly in line with the four-year average.

Beneath the headline numbers, the activism landscape is shifting. APAC accounted for a record 31% of global campaigns, driven by heightened interest in AI and technology hardware manufacturing. Meanwhile the overall number of activists launching campaigns is down 14% year-over-year.
Activist priorities are evolving as well. Mergers and acquisitions accounted for 58% of Q3 campaign demands, with increasing calls for target companies to explore a sale. Sector concentration also increased. A record 82% of campaigns targeted companies across five sectors, led by Industrials and Technology.

Meanwhile, board seat wins remained below the four-year average following fewer US settlements and contested fights.
