articles.title: Euro Tax Flash from KPMG's EU Tax Centre: 16 October 2026
articles.text:
Go back to the Euro Tax Flash homepage.

CJEU decision on the application of the anti-abuse rule under Parent-Subsidiary Directive

At a glance: On October 15, 2026, the CJEU ruled in C‑203/25opens in a new tab that the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD) anti-abuse provision may apply even where the immediate parent company carries on genuine economic activities, is recognized as the beneficial owner of the dividends and is not a conduit company.Taxpayer impact: The judgment confirms that genuine economic activity and beneficial ownership at the level of the direct parent company are not, in and of themselves, sufficient to exclude a finding of abuse. Tax authorities may take into account transactions carried out in other jurisdictions, including events occurring after the dividend payment and advantages obtained by other participants in the structure, including the ultimate beneficial owner.

On October 15, 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU or the Court) rendered its decision in case C-203/25opens in a new tab, on the interpretation of the anti-abuse provision in the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (the PSD or the Directive).

Key findings of the CJEU

Broad scope of the PSD anti-abuse provision and assessment of the arrangement as a wholeThe Court confirmed that the PSD anti-abuse provision has a broad scope and is not limited to situations involving conduit companies. Importantly, the existence of genuine economic activity at the level of the direct parent company is not sufficient, by itself, to rule out abuse. Tax authorities must assess the arrangement as a whole and may consider all relevant facts and circumstances across the wider chain of transactions. In the case at hand, this included the transfer of shares, loan arrangements and assignments of receivables involving entities other than the immediate dividend recipient. The Court also noted that recognition of beneficial ownership under a tax treaty does not prevent the application of the PSD anti-abuse rule.Correspondence between dividend amounts and the timing of transfers may constitute indicators of a non-genuine arrangementBuilding on its previous "Danish cases" jurisprudence, the Court confirmed that tax authorities may take into account:the similarity between dividend amounts received by the parent company and amounts ultimately transferred through the wider structure;the onward transfer of funds within the group; andthe timing and frequency of such transfers.The Court clarified that abuse cannot be presumed solely because amounts correspond or because dividends are transferred onwards. Equally, the anti-abuse rule is not limited to situations where funds are transferred shortly after receipt. Repeated transfers over a longer period may also be relevant indicators when viewed in the context of the overall arrangement.Anti-abuse assessment may extend to transactions carried out outside the Member State of the distributing subsidiaryThe Court held that national tax authorities are entitled to take a holistic view of the arrangement when applying the anti-abuse provision. This includes considering:transactions carried out in other jurisdictions;events occurring after the dividend payment; andtax advantages obtained by parties elsewhere in the structure, including the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO).The Court rejected the argument that the relevant tax advantage must arise at the level of the distributing subsidiary.The relevance of the distributing subsidiary's knowledge in assessing the alleged abusive arrangementThe Court finally addressed whether the withholding tax exemption can be denied without proving that the distributing subsidiary itself knew, or could have known, about the abusive arrangement. The Court concluded that such knowledge is not required. Whilst abuse requires both objective and subjective elements, the subjective element need only be demonstrated in relation to at least one participant in the chain of transactions or the ultimate beneficial owner. Limiting the analysis to the knowledge of the distributing subsidiary would undermine the effectiveness of the PSD anti-abuse provision.

Background

The plaintiff is a Lithuanian entity wholly owned by a Cypriot parent company (HoldCo One). In 2016 and 2017, the parent company received dividends from the plaintiff and another Lithuanian entity. The plaintiff considered that the payments were exempt from dividend withholding tax under the local rules implementing the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD).In February 2017, the shares in HoldCo One were sold by a Belize company, the grandparent of the Lithuanian plaintiff, to a newly set-up Cypriot entity (HoldCo Two) while the purchase price remained payable by HoldCo Two (the loan). Despite this sale, the ultimate beneficial owner of the dividends (UBO), an individual not resident in Lithuania, who owned both the Belizean and Cypriot companies, remained unchanged. Following the sale, the Belize company assigned the loan to the UBO.In 2017 and 2018, HoldCo Two granted loans (the loan arrangements) and assigned receivables to the UBO. The combined amount of these loans and receivables was subsequently set off against the outstanding amount of the UBO’s receivable against HoldCo Two that was created in connection with the sale of the shares in HoldCo One. Over that period, HoldCo Two did not pay out any dividend to its shareholder (UBO).Following a tax audit, the Lithuanian tax inspectorate concluded that the dividends paid by the Lithuanian entity to HoldCo One should not have benefited from the PSD exemption and were instead subject to the standard 15 percent withholding tax. The Lithuanian tax authorities did not challenge the beneficial owner status of HoldCo One nor did they challenge the fact that HoldCo One actually carried on an economic activity. However, they argued that the transactions involving the dividends formed part of a non-genuine arrangement aimed at obtaining a tax advantage, thus triggering the application of the anti-abuse rule under the PSD as transposed into Lithuanian law1. In particular, the Lithuanian tax authorities concluded that economically, the dividends were ultimately paid to the UBO, through a chain of artificial transactions.Following an appeal raised by the taxpayer, the Lithuanian Tax Disputes Commission (Disputes Commission) acknowledged the CJEU’s rulings in joined cases C-116/16 and C-117/16opens in a new tab, commonly referred to as the “Danish cases”. Nonetheless, the Disputes Commission noted that the case at hand is different since the dividends were paid to an entity with genuine economic activity which, in the tax authorities’ view, participated in a chain of non-genuine transactions.On this basis, the Disputes Commission expressed doubts about the interpretation of the anti-abuse provision[1] of the PSD and referred to the CJEU the following questions:Is it compatible with the PSD anti-abuse provision for a national tax practice to deny a withholding tax exemption on dividends paid to a genuine parent company established in another EU Member State, on the ground that the dividend is a part of a chain of non-genuine transactions?Can a chain of dividend transfers be presumed to be artificial or abusive based solely on the similarity of amounts involved at different stages of the transactions?Is it compatible with the PSD anti-abuse provision for a national tax practice to deny tax benefits on a cross-border dividend payment based on a chain of non-genuine transactions that occurred entirely after the dividend payment and in another EU Member State?Can the tax advantage be attributed to the plaintiff if it was ultimately realized by another party – i.e., the ultimate beneficiary, through a chain of non-genuine transactions?Can the anti-abuse rule under the PSD apply if the dividends were passed over on a continuous basis – i.e., from one year to one month, instead of “very soon after their receipt” as mentioned in the Danish cases?What is the relevance of the plaintiff’s knowledge or intent to undertake non-genuine transactions when applying the anti-abuse rules under the PSD.On May 21, 2026, Advocate General Juliane Kokott of the CJEU recommendedopens in a new tab that the Court find that a withholding tax exemption under the Parent-Subsidiary Directive may be denied in exceptional cases (case C-203/25). In the AG’s view, this could apply even where the parent company receiving the dividends is the beneficial owner and carries out genuine economic activities, but it passes the dividends on to the UBO through an artificial arrangement.The AG stressed that to determine the purpose of an arrangement, all relevant circumstances must be taken into account, in particular the awareness of the person who decides to implement it, which is generally the controlling shareholder. According to the AG, an abusive overall plan exists, for example, where the PSD is used to generate income for the UBO that cannot be taxed in their hands. This could be the case where dividends are channeled through non-cooperative offshore jurisdictions, so that the UBO's state of residence receives no information about the final distribution.The AG also took the view that abuse of a Member State's national tax law does not, as a rule, constitute abuse within the meaning of the PSD. However, abuse under the PSD may exist where the subsidiary distributes profits to its parent company, which is the beneficial owner, for the purpose of evading taxes in the UBO's Member State.For more details, please refer to Euro Tax Flash Issue 580.

CJEU decision

Broad scope of the PSD anti-abuse provision and assessment of the arrangement as a wholeThe Court first focused on whether the anti-abuse provision in the PSD may apply where dividends are paid to a parent company that carries on genuine economic activities and is not a conduit company, but forms part of a broader chain of transactions containing one or more allegedly non-genuine elements. In addressing this question, the Court recalled that the PSD seeks to eliminate withholding taxes and double taxation on cross-border profit distributions within the EU. The Court then reiterated its settled case-law according to which EU law contains a general anti-abuse principle. The Court noted that the anti-abuse provision introduced by Directive 2015/1212 reflects that principle in the context of the PSD.The Court further recalled that two cumulative conditions must be met for benefits under the PSD to be denied:the arrangement or series of arrangements must be non-genuine, meaning that it is not put in place for valid commercial reasons reflecting economic reality; andone of the principal purposes of the arrangement must be to obtain a tax advantage that defeats the object or purpose of the Directive.The Court first focused on the condition related to the existence of a non-genuine arrangement. The Court emphasized that the anti-abuse provision must be interpreted by reference not only to its wording, but also to its context and objectives. In this regard, the Court reiterated its settled case law that, based on the wording, context and objectives of the provision, the PSD anti-abuse rule applies broadly to all types of non-genuine arrangements and is not limited to arrangements displaying specific characteristics. Accordingly, whether an arrangement is non-genuine must be determined through an objective assessment of all relevant facts and circumstances. Where a structure consists of several transactions or steps, the analysis cannot focus solely on a single element of the arrangement or on the circumstances existing at a particular point in time, but must consider the overall series of arrangements. The Court also confirmed that it is for the national tax authorities seeking to deny PSD benefits to establish the constituent elements of an abusive practice, although they cannot be required to produce evidence that would be impossible to obtain.Applying those principles, the Court rejected the argument that the PSD anti-abuse provision is limited to arrangements involving conduit companies. Referring to the Danish cases, the Court recalled that the interposition of a conduit entity is merely one example of a potentially abusive arrangement. Consequently, the fact that the immediate parent company carries on genuine economic activities and is not a conduit company does not, in and of itself, exclude the existence of an abusive practice.According to the Court, focusing solely on the economic activity of the immediate recipient of the dividends would be inconsistent with the requirement to assess the arrangement as a whole. Instead, all relevant facts and circumstances forming part of the broader chain of transactions must be taken into account. In the case at hand, those elements included the transfer of shares in HoldCo One and the loan arrangements and the assignment of receivables between HoldCo Two and the UBO.The Court also addressed the interaction between the PSD anti-abuse provision and the Lithuania-Cyprus double tax treaty. Referring to the OECD Commentary to the Model Tax Convention, the Court noted that beneficial ownership does not automatically entitle a taxpayer to double tax treaty benefits in abusive situations. More fundamentally, the Court reiterated that double tax treaties concluded between Member States cannot be relied upon to achieve a result contrary to EU law. Consequently, the recognition of beneficial ownership under a tax treaty does not, in and of itself, prevent the application of the PSD anti-abuse provision.The Court therefore concluded that the PSD anti-abuse provision does not, in principle, prevent a Member State from denying a withholding tax exemption where a dividend distribution forms part of a broader chain of transactions containing one or more non-genuine elements, even where the immediate parent company carries on genuine economic activities and is not a conduit company.Correspondence between dividend amounts and the timing of transfers may constitute indicators of a non-genuine arrangementThe Court also provided guidance on the interpretation of the anti-abuse provision in the PSD and, in particular, on whether the correspondence between dividend amounts transferred through a chain of transactions and the timing of those transfers may constitute relevant indicators when assessing the existence of an abusive practice.The Court recalled its findings in the Danish cases, where the onward payment of dividends, in whole or in substantial part and within a very short period following their receipt, was regarded as an indication of an arrangement aimed at benefiting unduly from the withholding tax exemption provided by the PSD. Building on that case-law, the Court held that, in assessing the existence of an abusive practice, national tax authorities may also take into account the correspondence between the amount of dividends received by the parent company and the amounts ultimately received, through the chain of transactions, by the person controlling the entities involved. The Court nevertheless emphasized that neither of these elements can, in isolation, give rise to a general presumption of abuse.The Court further clarified that, whilst a rapid onward transfer of dividends may constitute a relevant indicator, a short interval between the receipt and subsequent transfer of dividends is not required for the purposes of the anti-abuse provision. According to the Court, transfers carried out on a recurring basis over a longer period may also be relevant in assessing whether a chain of transactions contains one or more non-genuine elements.The Court therefore concluded that both the similarity of the amounts transferred through a chain of transactions and the fact that such transfers take place continuously over a certain period may constitute relevant indicators for the purposes of identifying a non-genuine arrangement, without prejudice to the need for the national tax authorities to verify, on the basis of all relevant facts and circumstances, whether the constituent elements of an abusive practice are present.Anti-abuse assessment may extend to transactions carried out outside the Member State of the distributing subsidiaryThe CJEU then examined whether the anti-abuse provision in the PSD, as interpreted in light of the principle of proportionality, precludes a Member State from levying withholding tax on dividends where the transactions deemed to be non-genuine were carried out outside that Member State and the resulting tax advantage was obtained by another person within the wider structure.The Court first noted that, when assessing whether an arrangement is abusive, national tax authorities must conduct a comprehensive examination of all relevant facts and circumstances, including transactions carried out outside the Member State seeking to deny the benefits of the Directive. The CJEU further recalled its previous case law – in particular case C-228/24 (Nordcurrent), based on which national tax authorities may also take into account events occurring after the arrangement was put in place when assessing whether it is genuine.Applying those principles, the Court held that the anti-abuse provision of the PSD does not require the tax advantage that runs counter the Directive’s objective or purpose to be demonstrated in relation to the distributing subsidiary. Instead, the advantage may be obtained by the ultimate individual controlling the group, resident in another Member State. The Court further noted that such undue advantages could not be addressed if the Member State granting the exemption were prevented from taking into account transactions carried out outside its territory using the dividends received under that exemption.The Court also rejected arguments based on the principle of proportionality. The CJEU took the view that allowing national tax authorities to assess the entire arrangement is both suitable and necessary to combat abusive structures that can only be identified through a holistic analysis of the relevant transactions. In addition, the Court reiterated its settled case-law, in particular the Danish cases, that taxpayers cannot rely on the fundamental freedoms guaranteed by the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to challenge measures that are intended to prevent abusive practices.The Court therefore concluded that the anti-abuse provision of the PSD, read in light of the principle of proportionally, does not preclude a national practice under which withholding tax is imposed on dividends where the deemed non-genuine transactions were carried out outside that Member State by non-resident individuals or legal entities, including the person who obtains the tax benefit through the dividend exemption, regardless of where in the transaction chain that benefit is obtained.The relevance of the distributing subsidiary’s knowledge in assessing the alleged abusive arrangementFinally, the CJEU examined whether a Member State may deny the withholding tax exemption under the PSD without proving that the distributing subsidiary itself knew, or could have known, that the dividend payment formed part of a chain of transactions or that some – or all of those transactions, lacked genuine commercial substance.The Court recalled its settled case-law, based on which merely classifying a subsidiary as a non-genuine arrangement is not sufficient to justify the denial of PSD benefits under the related anti-abuse provision. Instead, it must also be established that the arrangement was implemented with the principal objective, or one of the principal objectives, of obtaining a tax advantage that defeats the object or purpose of the Directive.The Court recalled that an abusive situation can be evidenced in the combined presence of:objective circumstances, in which the purpose of the EU Directives is circumvented, despite a formal observance of the conditions required for their application; andsubjective elements – the existence of a wholly artificial arrangement, as well as an intention to obtain a (tax) advantage.The Court further noted that dividend distributions may form part of a broader series of decisions taken within a corporate group. Against this background, the Court considered that limiting the assessment of the subjective element solely to the level of the distributing subsidiary – by verifying whether it knew or could have known about the existence of abuse, would undermine the effectiveness of the Directive’s anti-abuse provision. The Court therefore held that it is sufficient for the subjective element to be demonstrated in relation to at least one company participating in the chain of transactions, or the individual who ultimately benefits from the tax advantage.The Court concluded that the anti-abuse provision of the Parent-Subsidiary Directive does not preclude a national practice whereby withholding tax is imposed without establishing the distributing subsidiary’s knowledge of the abusive arrangement, as long as it is demonstrated that another group company involved in the arrangement, or the ultimate beneficial owner, knew or could have known of the existence of the chain of transactions aimed at obtaining the tax advantage.

ETC Comment:

The judgment is notable because it confirms and further develops the interpretation of the PSD anti-abuse provision established in case C-228/24. Whilst that earlier case concerned the exemption of dividends received from corporate income tax, the Court has now applied the same principles in the context of the withholding tax exemption for outbound dividends, clarifying that the broad interpretation of the Directive's anti-abuse rule also applies in the case of outbound payments.In line with the AG’s opinion, the Court clarifies that, whilst onward payments of dividends in comparable amounts and shortly after receipt, constitute an indication of abuse, such elements do not automatically establish abuse. The Court also clarifies that the distributing subsidiary’s knowledge of the existence of abusive arrangement is irrelevant, as long as it can be demonstrated that another group company or the UBO could have been aware of abuse.The judgment leaves unaddressed several important aspects of Advocate General Kokott's Opinion. In particular, the AG drew a distinction between abuse of the PSD and abuse of domestic tax rules in another Member State, suggesting that alleged abuse of domestic legislation in the state of the ultimate beneficiary should not, as a general rule, justify the denial of PSD benefits by the Member State of the distributing subsidiary. In this context, the AG placed considerable emphasis on the need for a direct link between the abusive element of the arrangement and the tax advantage granted under EU law. In the AG’s view, it is only where the arrangement is designed to obtain a tax advantage that runs counter to the purpose of the PSD itself that the source Member State may deny the Directive's benefits. While the Court confirmed that the anti-abuse assessment may extend to transactions carried out outside the Member State of the distributing subsidiary and to advantages obtained elsewhere within the structure, it did not expressly engage with the AG's distinction or provide further guidance on circumstances that could lead to a benefit contrary to the object and purpose of the Directive.The judgment is also noteworthy for its comments on the interaction between the PSD anti-abuse provision and double tax treaties. The CJEU noted that it is for the referring court to interpret national law and the relevant double tax convention, which that referring court considers must be interpreted in light of the commentary on the OECD Model Tax Convention. However, the CJEU took the opportunity to note that according to the commentary on the relevant article of the OECD Model Tax Convention (Article 10), which was published in 2014 after the conclusion of the relevant double tax treaty in 2013, the fact that the recipient of the dividends is the "beneficial owner" of the dividends does not mean that the treaty relief is automatically due, as regard must be had to whether the provision is being misused to obtain the advantage. Furthermore, the Court reiterated that tax treaties concluded between Member States cannot be relied upon to achieve a result contrary to EU law. This seems to suggest that qualifying for relief, at least if such relief provides for a benefit similar to the PSD’s benefit, under an applicable tax treaty does not preclude the application of the PSD anti-abuse provision.

articles.title: ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | PODCAST – 8:56 MIN
ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies

By
DANIEL DORNEL, DANIEL MORRIS 15.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

European UCITS ETFs (EU regulated exchange-traded funds) attracted a record €125 billion in the third quarter, taking year-to-date inflows to almost €350 billion. Global equities led the way, Europe rebounded and emerging markets recovered, while Chinese equity ETFs continued to see outflows.

As Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research, explains to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, fixed-income ETFs also attracted strong inflows, particularly into government bonds and ultra-short-duration products, despite rising yields. “Active ETFs also continued their rapid growth, which we believe highlights investors’ appetite for new strategies.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into the forces shaping ETF flows and investor positioning.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Daniel Dornel

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing the latest ETF (exchange-traded fund) fund flows. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research. Welcome, Daniel, and thanks for joining me.

Daniel Dornel: Thank you, Daniel. I’m very happy to be here.

DM: As always, Daniel, it’s been an eventful quarter. One of the key surprises has been the resilience of equity markets. When you’ve seen the big increase in yields for government bonds, typically a rise in interest rates goes with the decline in equity markets but, so far, they seem to have shrugged that off. In terms of ETF flows, what are the dynamics you’ve seen in the third quarter?

DD: It has been a remarkable period. Q3 was the strongest quarter ever, with inflows around €125 billion. What’s really impressive is that we are seeing a pattern of breaking records one quarter after another. If we look closer at the monthly breakdown, July and August were the two largest months ever recorded in the UC[ITS] ETF landscape, with July alone bringing in over €50 billion.

This momentum is carrying us into an historic year. Year to date, we have already seen almost €350 billion inflows into UC[ITS] ETF[s], which means we have already surpassed the total full-year figure from last year, €327 billion.

While the growth is broad, equity projects dominated the landscape this quarter, capturing almost €100 billion of those €125 billion of total inflows.

DM: It’s interesting that you say that because there’s been a long discussion about cash on the sidelines and whether or not investors are willing to put that cash to work. And it seems from the figures you cite for ETF flows, maybe they are. We also see the strong performance of equity markets being followed by flows into ETFs. Clearly that’s a strong support for the market. Are there any particular categories or products that stand out?

DD: Without doubt, global equities have been standing out. In Q3, they attracted just under €55 billion. This isn’t a sudden spike; it is a sustained trend we have been seeing from last year.

Just to give a few figures, the year-to-date figure for global equities is already €145 billion compared to just under €100 billion for last year. So global equities now represent about a third of all equity flows.

What is particularly interesting is the acceleration in all-country exposures – a blend between developed and emerging market equities. Historically, they have been behind developed-only global equities. But on this particular sub-category, we have seen a jump from €40 billion last year to €83 billion on a year-to-date basis. This suggests investors are looking for the more diversified product[s] they can find these days.

DM: I would imagine these inflows into global ETFs, including emerging markets, probably has something to do with the strong performance we’ve seen, particularly in Taiwan and [South] Korea, around semiconductors and tech hardware. I think investors are looking to try to tap into that dynamic. Speaking of dynamics, is there anything else that you see across equity markets?

DD: Let’s start with the US. After a very strong acceleration in Q2, the appetite for US equity remained, with €23 billion in flows in Q3, again mostly concentrated in core exposures.

Moving on to Europe, we saw an interesting rebound in Q3, with €9 billion inflows. This suggests a return in confidence from investors after a very difficult Q2 where we had around €5 billion [of] outflows. We also saw an acceleration in emerging markets, bringing in €6.8 billion, a recovery from a quiet second quarter on emerging markets.

However, it hasn’t been positive everywhere. China continues to be a challenge, and we saw another difficult quarter with €1.5 billion outflows from Chinese equity product.

Looking at sub-asset classes, sector and thematic ETF[s] brought in €15 billion, the lion’s share driven by IT and tech-related themes. But there were two interesting additional trends, with healthcare – we saw €1.5 billion inflows there – and Eurozone banks, with €1.3 billion inflows.

DM: That is encouraging that you’re starting to see inflows again into Europe. We’re seeing that all the investment that the region is putting towards strategic autonomy, defence and so on is starting to bear some fruit. It’s also interesting that, despite the inflows into emerging markets, you still see outflows from Chinese ETFs. And we appreciate that tech is a big driver for the interest in emerging markets.

I started out saying we’ve had [a] surprisingly strong performance for equity markets despite the big increase in [bond] yields. I’m curious if that increase in government bond yields has had an impact on flows for fixed-income ETFs?

DD: Fixed income had a very strong quarter as well, bringing in €27 billion. The primary engine was government bonds, with €10 billion inflows. It was a mix of all maturity exposures, especially on global and euro bonds, as well as short-term maturities, especially on US, but also on European exposures.

We also saw a significant interest in ultra-short instruments, which brought €8 billion. Roughly half of that was on overnight euro exposures and 25% in US Treasuries with a maturity from zero to one year on corporate investment grade.

We also see some flows there with €4 billion, a split between US all-maturity product and euro short term. The only area of weakness was a yield with a significant slowdown, only €500 million inflows over the quarter, primarily because of the September figures where we had very negative flows on euro high yield.

DM: The outflows for high yield are relevant, as I’ve heard from our portfolio managers. That was one of the key drivers behind the increase in yields and spreads that you saw for high yield, particularly in September. Last word on ETF flows for the quarter?

DD: I’d like to highlight the rise of active ETFs again. This is where things are moving quite rapidly. In Q3 alone we saw €11 billion of inflows. This brings us on a year-to-date basis to €34 billion, so roughly 10% of the flows and it’s already ahead of [the] 2025 figure, which was just under 30 billion.

So, the dynamic is very impressive, especially on enhanced strategies and equity income strategies. But it’s not just about the flows, it’s also about the product innovation. If you look at all the ETFs launched in Europe year-to-date, 40% were active ETF[s] – that’s already over 100 new funds this year.

DM: If I can summarise some of the key points, you said not only was the third quarter the strongest ever in terms of ETF flows, but recently almost every quarter is the strongest, so it really does seem there’s a lot of momentum behind ETFs.

You highlighted that flows are going more towards global equities, conceivably as investors are looking to tap into the tech dynamic in emerging markets. That said, you also saw a rebound of flows into Europe, so another renewed bout of optimism.

And finally, positive inflows into fixed income despite the increase in [bond] yields. But you highlighted that this is tend[ing] to be short duration, so investors less at risk of rising yields and able to pick up some income in the meantime.

Daniel, thank you very much for joining me.

DD: Thank you, Daniel. Always a pleasure.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in ETFs, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at Viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better-informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

Can it make energy operations more resilient?

Energy security and resilience have moved to the top of the agenda after repeated supply disruptions. As the industry gathers for ADIPEC 2026, AI is being pitched as a way to anticipate equipment failures, improve operations and respond faster to risk. But can it deliver measurable results in critical energy systems, or is the promise still running ahead of the proof?
Host Ed Crooks is joined by Saravan Penubarthi, Chief Technology Officer of AIQ, an energy-focused AI company. Saravan argues that AI creates value when it moves from pilots into day-to-day operations, with tools built around energy-sector problems and tested alongside customers.
He describes a model that spans prediction, recommendations and, in some cases, autonomous action. Examples include RoboWell, which adjusts well controls, and computer-vision systems used for safety, security and productivity. Saravan cites a 2 to 5 per cent production improvement for ADNOC, AI solutions deployed across its 148 rigs, and more than a billion camera-based predictions a day. He also outlines AIQ’s emissions-monitoring work and its expansion into international markets.
The central question is how much of that promise can be trusted at scale. Saravan distinguishes assisted AI, where people approve recommendations, from autonomous operations, which he says require extensive testing, fallback mechanisms and clear human oversight. He says AIQ is developing Genesis, an AI-native operating system for energy, for unveiling at ADIPEC.
For operators, the test is whether these systems can produce repeatable, measurable gains without compromising safety or accountability. As AI moves closer to controlling critical assets, evidence from real deployments will matter more than ambitious claims about what the technology might eventually do.
This episode of the Energy Gang is brought to you by ADIPEC, the world's largest energy event, taking place in Abu Dhabi from 2-5 November.
As demand rises and global energy markets evolve, ADIPEC 2026 brings together governments, industry, investors and technology leaders to accelerate investment, advance technology and build the partnerships needed to meet today's energy needs while building a more resilient system for tomorrow.

articles.title: Gavekal Technologies: New Energy
articles.text:
Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Most recent

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?

AJ Cortese
12 Oct 2026

China is the world’s biggest builder of nuclear power plants, but unlike in other energy sectors it has not become a significant exporter of reactors. While Chinese nuclear firms have figured out how to make reactors relatively cheaply, the complexity and safety needs of nuclear projects mean they will never be able to gobble up world markets through ultralow prices, as Chinese solar, EV and battery firms have done. But over the next decade it is likely China will become an important nuclear exporter.

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing

Great Tech In Search Of Profits

AJ Cortese, Laila Khawaja
5 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies held its inaugural China Tech Tour with 19 institutional-investor clients. Through a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives, we examined China’s semiconductor, AI, new energy, robotics and biotechnology industries. This week’s China Tech Brief explores some of the key findings. By far the biggest theme was the gap between technological capabilities and corporate returns. China has plenty of globally competitive tech companies, but few that generate really attractive earnings.

More research

GavekalTech On The Ground: 2026 China Tech Trip Takeaways

1 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies made its inaugural China Tech Trip with 19 institutional investor clients. The trip offered a close-up view of China’s tech ecosystem, including semiconductors, AI, new energy, robotics, and biotech, via a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives. This week’s Chips report summarizes our observations in the semiconductor and AI sectors.

Chinese EV Makers’ European Offensive

28 Sep 2026

Chinese EV makers have conquered their home market and are on track to export over 5mn vehicles this year, double the 2025 figure. Their next move will be to start moving production offshore, to get closer to key markets and evade tariffs. The biggest target is Europe, where half a dozen projects are under way and many more are planned.

Webinar: The State Of China Tech

25 Sep 2026

As presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare for their summit meeting in Washington, China’s fast-growing technology capabilities are a major topic. The big questions at the moment are how close Chinese artificial-intelligence labs are to matching the US frontier models, and whether the two sides can start negotiating rules on AI safety. But behind those lie even bigger questions: What is the balance of technological power between the US and China? And how far can the world's two big tech powers go in pulling apart the thick webs of interdependence that tie them together?

Breaking Up Is Hard To Do

21 Sep 2026

Both China and the US have devoted intense energy to slashing their technological reliance on each other. These efforts have had some impact, but the overall lesson is that decoupling is really difficult and even as old dependencies are cut, new ones pop up. This China Tech Brief examines the underlying causes.

The China New Energy Guidebook

16 Sep 2026

Over the past year Gavekal Technologies has explored most corners of China’s vast and unique energy system, with a particular focus on how electrification is transforming China’s economy and its position in the world. We have now distilled our insights into our first annual China New Energy Guidebook. This concise presentation outlines China’s strategies for its energy and electricity systems, assesses the progress of wind, solar and nuclear deployment, and analyzes the key electricity related sectors: batteries, electric vehicles, AI and the “electrotech stack.”

A China Tech Report Card

9 Sep 2026

Over the past year Gavekal Technologies has tracked China’s progress across a range of tech sectors. Today we take a step back and try to assess its overall capabilities. First, outside a handful of areas, China is still more of a fast follower than a global pace-setter. Second, China’s well-documented manufacturing dominance is mainly in products of medium or low complexity. Finally, China’s tech ecosystem still relies heavily on foreign-sourced components, equipment and intellectual property.

These shifts coincide with growing complexities in the peace process and the intertwining of the Yemen file with broader regional tensions, including maritime security in the Red Sea and the conflict between the United States and Iran.After years of relative calm, Yemen’s conflict is now entering a new phase, marked by renewed military hostilities between the Houthis and the Yemeni government; heightened tensions between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia; and escalating hostilities between the group and various tribes within the areas its controls. These developments have prompted debate over the power dynamics that have governed the conflict in recent years, and whether this escalation represents a temporary shift or the start of a new military and political trajectory. They also raise questions over what options are available to the parties to the conflict to navigate these shifting circumstances amidst a broader regional escalation.The Malcolm H. articles.title: China’s Growing Grip On Printed Circuit Boards
articles.text:
China’s Growing Grip On Printed Circuit Boards

Laila Khawaja

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 15 Oct 2026

China accounts for nearly 60% of the global production value of printed circuit boards, foundational components in numerous defense and civil applications. AI is driving the demand for advanced PCBs and tightening the supply of various critical upstream materials. Chinese PCB makers are investing unprecedented amounts to expand advanced capacity, while upstream suppliers allocate scarce supplies towards higher-value AI products, both of which squeeze conventional PCB manufacturers. These trends could accelerate industry consolidation and strengthen China’s leading players, at a time when foreign governments are seeking to reduce dependence on Chinese PCBs.

articles.title: European sovereignty: Energy security presents strategic investment advantage  - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Europe is redesigning its energy architecture – transforming energy security from a supply chain issue into a cornerstone of geopolitical sovereignty and economic security

The transition is guided by structured roadmaps – the EU’s 2019 European Green Deal, and more recent 2026 initiatives focused on AI integration in the energy sector and the comprehensive Electrification Action Plan

The EU’s commitment to clean energy is creating vast amounts of potential long-term investment opportunities in sectors such as renewable energy, grid modernisation, and the electric vehicle supply chain

For decades, energy security was chiefly viewed through the lens of supply chain stability. But in Europe, it has evolved into a cornerstone of economic stability and geopolitical sovereignty.

Driven by a necessity to decouple from volatile external dependencies and by its shift towards a more sustainable future, the European Union is not merely replacing one fuel source with another; it is redesigning its energy architecture. For investors, we believe this direction of travel represents a hugely significant long-term investment opportunity.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was undoubtedly a watershed moment, as it accelerated a structural pivot that was already underway. The EU demonstrated remarkable agility in reducing its reliance on Russian oil imports, which plummeted from approximately 26% in 2021, to around 2% today.1

But this was just the first step to energy resilience and sovereignty. Recent years have robustly highlighted that energy security is no longer a niche policy concern; it is now central to industrial competitiveness, national security, and inflation mitigation. Europe is treating energy resilience as a sovereign priority.

Solid policy backing

For investors, Europe has a keen advantage. Thanks to its solid, long-term commitments, today it is an international hive of innovation and investment opportunity.

Its drive to achieve energy independence is underpinned by a robust regulatory and strategic ecosystem. For years it has been at the epicentre of global sustainability – it was in France over a decade ago where the Paris Agreement was adopted by 196 parties at the 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference COP21.

The 2019 European Green Deal serves as the foundational blueprint to make Europe the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. The deal is not a vague ambition – it is a structured roadmap backed by significant capital. The bloc is a huge investor in clean technology, green infrastructure and renewable energy, including wind and solar power.2

This includes mobilising €1 trillion of sustainable investments between 2020 and 2030, while a record €7 billion of investment is being earmarked for sustainable and smart transport infrastructure.3

The EU spends 10 times more money investing in clean energy than it does in fossil fuels – all of which means it represents a truly vast hub of potential for investors.4

Gearing up

Then, in July 2026, the EU unveiled itsElectrification Action Plan, the goal of which is to make Europe the first electro-powered continent by doubling the electrification rate of final energy consumption from 23% to 46% by 2040. This move alone is projected to reduce annual fossil fuel import costs by approximately €260 billion.5

Two recent initiatives highlight the precision of Europe’s energy strategy: The Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector (June 2026) aims to integrating artificial intelligence and digital tools into the energy grid.

Both schemes are creating potential investment opportunities across four vital areas, namely industry, transport, buildings, and grid flexibility, creating a more predictable, high-growth environment.

We also see potential opportunities for investors across several high-growth sectors including renewable energy; infrastructure and grid modernisation;andthe transition to electric vehicles and the critical battery supply chain.

Notably, the EU is increasingly prioritising the allocation of these investments to European companies, fostering a localised industrial renaissance spurred by policies like the EU’s Clean Industrial Deal, which aims to turn decarbonisation into a driver of growth for European industries.6

Resilience amid volatility

Europe’s commitment to sustainability and strategic autonomy remains steadfast and progress is accelerating – and the economic logic is undeniable. Fossil fuel imports are projected to drop dramatically while the importation of energy technology will increase, meaning a drastic reduction in geopolitical vulnerability.

By treating energy resilience as a sovereign priority, Europe is positioning itself to lead the global transition. While energy policy remains somewhat fragmented on a national level, the EU is leveraging a centralised, directive-driven approach to ensure that the transition to clean energy is not just an environmental necessity, but a competitive advantage.

For investors, the value proposition is clear: Europe’s systemic shift toward sovereignty means it offers a unique combination of targeted policy support, a massive addressable market, and an abundance of innovative investment potential from renewables to grid modernisation – and much more in between.

The AI Investment Boom Goes Beyond America

0:00

Key takeaways

The AI boom is bigger for U.S. demand than for U.S. GDP. Much of the equipment behind the AI buildout is imported, reducing the direct contribution to domestic production even as investment and rising equity wealth support the broader economy.
America invests, while a global supply chain produces. U.S. AI spending is transmitting a substantial growth impulse abroad, particularly to Asian economies deeply embedded in semiconductor and technology manufacturing.
The key risk is deceleration, not necessarily a bust. With AI now a key support to global investment, trade, industrial production, and financial conditions, even still-high capex could become less supportive of global growth if its pace of expansion slows.

In light of accelerating global fragmentation and geopolitical conflict, many governments and businesses are investing in resilience. That imperative has coincided with the emergence of AI, a technology that can expand the frontier of what is possible. As a result, technology security is becoming a pillar of national economic security strategy.
As we discuss in our latest Cyclical Outlook, “Growth Holds, Risks Widen,” the result has been an unprecedented wave of investment commitments to expand AI-related infrastructure. At the time of this writing, announced capital spending by large U.S. technology companies points to more than $1 trillion of investment in 2026, according to company filings, with roughly $1.5 trillion in additional outlays forecast thereafter.
But AI was never simply a U.S. investment story. The infrastructure buildout is supporting U.S. demand, production across the global technology supply chain, and increasingly investment in other economies. That has made AI an important source of support for both the U.S. and global expansions.
By the same token, it is also becoming an important cyclical risk. Crucially, AI investment does not have to collapse for its contribution to growth to fade. Because economic growth depends on the change in spending rather than its level, even still-high investment can provide a diminishing impulse if its growth rate slows.
Below, we highlight three observations about how the AI investment cycle is already reshaping the global economy.

AI is supporting the U.S. economy through more than just investment

First, AI investment is lifting U.S. domestic demand, but its high import content substantially reduces the direct impact on real U.S. GDP growth. Nevertheless, AI is also lifting the U.S. economy in other ways. Expectations for higher productivity have propelled the U.S. stock market and appear to have shifted consumer habits toward more spending – and this “wealth effect” is contributing to stronger demand.
Some background on how U.S. economic output is measured is useful here. GDP records where production occurs, not simply where investment spending occurs. A server or graphics card purchased by a U.S. data center raises U.S. investment regardless of where it was produced. But if that equipment is imported, the transaction also raises imports, which are subtracted in the expenditure calculation of GDP. In other words, the investment data capture the acquisition of productive capital, while the import adjustment ensures that foreign production is not counted as U.S. output.
The National Income and Product Accounts (NIPAs), published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), do not identify AI investment as a stand-alone category. Instead, AI investment spans several components of nonresidential fixed investment, including information-processing equipment, software, R&D, data center structures, and power infrastructure. By combining the main AI-related investment categories with corresponding trade and inventory flows, we can estimate the net domestic growth impulse.
From these calculations, we estimate that AI-related investment has directly contributed only about 0.4 percentage point to annualized quarterly real U.S. GDP growth on average since the beginning of 2025, out of roughly 2% overall GDP growth over that period (see Figure 1) – a relatively minor amount.

Figure 1: AI’s contribution to real U.S. growth has fluctuated and is modestly net positive

Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis National Income and Product Accounts data and PIMCO calculations through 30 June 2026

But that substantially understates the scale of the investment boom itself. We estimate AI-related investment has contributed roughly 1.2 percentage points to the 2.7% average annualized growth in U.S. domestic demand over the same period (see Figure 2). In other words, the boost to U.S. spending has been much larger than the boost to U.S. production because a significant share of that spending has been on imported goods.

Figure 2: AI has driven meaningful contributions to U.S. domestic demand

Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis National Income and Product Accounts data and PIMCO calculations through 30 June 2026

Direct investment is not the only channel through which the AI boom is supporting the U.S. economy. AI-related optimism also appears to be supporting growth through financial conditions. Expectations for higher future productivity and earnings have contributed to strong U.S. equity valuations, boosting household wealth and supporting consumption.
Using the Federal Reserve’s framework for estimating the growth impulse from financial conditions (see our 30 September 2026 Macro Signposts), we estimate that the equity wealth channel has provided roughly an additional 0.5–0.7 percentage point of support for growth – roughly 1x to 1.5x the growth impulse of the investment itself.
Taken together, these estimates suggest that AI-related forces have provided meaningful support to U.S. growth, even though the direct domestic investment effect is considerably smaller than the headline capex figures might imply.

America invests, Asia produces

Second, what leaks out of U.S. GDP through imports does not disappear from global GDP. The processors, servers, and networking equipment imported to construct U.S. data centers represent production and income somewhere else.
Robust U.S. demand (see Figure 3) has consequently provided a powerful impulse to economies embedded in the AI hardware supply chain. Our updated trade data show particularly large AI-related export exposures equivalent to roughly 30% of GDP for Taiwan and more than 15% for South Korea (see Figure 4), illustrating how large the technology cycle has become relative to the underlying economies. Mexico has also become an important part of the North American supply chain.
These measures capture gross export exposure relative to GDP, rather than the domestic value-added contribution of AI-related exports. Nevertheless, they illustrate the scale of the global supply chain exposure to the investment boom.

Figure 3: U.S. and other developed markets are importing AI-related components

Source: UN Comtrade Database and PIMCO calculations as of 30 June 2026

Figure 4: AI-related exports have become a meaningful share of key producers’ overall GDP

Source: UN Comtrade Database and PIMCO calculations as of 30 June 2026

In other words, high import content limits the direct U.S. growth contribution from AI investment, but the U.S. simultaneously exports part of the investment impulse to the rest of the world. The U.S. capex boom is therefore increasingly supporting a much broader manufacturing and trade cycle, particularly across the Asian technology supply chain.

The investment cycle is broadening beyond the U.S.

Third and finally, the U.S. is no longer the only important source of AI infrastructure demand. China was also an early mover, and other parts of Asia and the Middle East are increasingly investing in computing capacity, data centers, and the supporting infrastructure needed to power them.Footnote1 As more economies seek to build domestic computing capacity, AI infrastructure investment is increasingly interacting with broader national priorities around technology security, energy availability, and supply chain resilience.
The result is that the global AI capex cycle has become an important driver of global industrial production and trade. Even against relatively muted aggregate global industrial production growth, production of computers, electronics, and related equipment has been exceptionally strong. In other words, it is producing a distinct global industrial cycle that is helping global production, while also increasing the number of economies that could be affected by an eventual slowdown.

Figure 5: Global industrial production of computers and electronics is on a multi-year upswing

Source: Various national statistical agencies, Haver Analytics, and PIMCO calculations as of August 2026. PIMCO Global IP (industrial production) data aggregates industrial production across sectors and countries using TIVA (trade in value added) weights.

Implications: A global growth engine, and a source of risk

AI was never simply a U.S. investment story. In the U.S., the direct contribution from investment is actually much smaller than the headline spending numbers suggest because so much of the equipment is imported. But the overall growth effect is larger once the equity wealth channel is included, and what subtracts from U.S. growth is added to global growth.
AI is therefore delivering several impulses at once: investment demand in the U.S. and other economies, manufacturing and exports across the global technology supply chain, and a financial conditions impulse through equity markets. Together, these forces have become an important source of support for the global expansion.
But that support also creates a new source of cyclical concentration. For the growth outlook, what matters is not simply the level of AI investment, but how long investment can continue to accelerate. The infrastructure buildout does not need to collapse for the growth impulse to diminish. It merely needs to slow. And when it does, it would have global implications – especially if the productivity gains aren’t being realized fast enough to be an offset.
Bottom line: The same forces that have made the global expansion more resilient have therefore also created a new source of cyclical concentration. AI is supporting U.S. demand, Asian production, and global investment simultaneously. That makes the boom a powerful global growth engine, but also one of the more important downside risks to the outlook if momentum fades.

1 François de Soyres, Alex Haag, Mike Liu, and Eva Van Leemput. “The Global Trade Effects of the AI Infrastructure Boom.” U.S. Federal Reserve FEDS Notes (13 February 2026). Return to content↩

articles.title: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
articles.text:
Energy and Oil ministers of countries participating in the Declaration of Cooperation (DoC) held a meeting on the sidelines of the 17th IEF ministerial meeting and the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh

Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation (DoC) met on the sidelines of the 17th IEF ministerial meeting and the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh on 12 October 2026.The Ministers reviewed market conditions and agreed to continue consultation with all OPEC plus countries, through already established mechanisms including the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC) and the OPEC and Non-OPEC Ministerial Meetings (ONOMM) and reaffirmed their commitment to the decisions made on 7 June 2026 (41st ONOMM) to achieve and sustain a stable oil market.In this context, the Ministers affirmed the critical importance of safeguarding the international maritime routes to ensure the uninterrupted flow of energy. They also noted that the current interruption of energy flows has elevated the cost of shipping and insurance which have reached unprecedented levels of more than one third of the commodity value, impeding the timely and efficient movement of crude oil and products, and placing additional inflationary pressures on the global economy. The Ministers further stressed that these exceptionally elevated costs are ultimately transmitted across the oil value chain increasing and prolonging the cost burden on producing and consuming countries and impacting global economic growth. The Ministers will continue monitoring the situation, and will engage with governments, industry stakeholders, and international organizations such as the IEF, IEA, and others to improve global shipping conditions.

Ahead of the UK Autumn Budget, the consensus view is that higher borrowing costs and a weaker fiscal backdrop have left the Chancellor of the Exchequer with little room to manoeuvre. But what if markets are focusing on the wrong part of the story?
In this episode of the Barclays Brief, host Patrick Coffey sits down with Jack Meaning, Chief UK Economist at Barclays, to examine why expectations of a sharp squeeze of the Chancellor’s fiscal headroom may be overstated. While higher gilt yields have dominated the debate, stronger nominal earnings and tax receipts could leave the Chancellor in a more resilient position than many investors assume, at least for now.
The conversation explores the outlook for inflation, interest rates and the UK Budget, alongside signs of stronger business investment, the potential productivity benefits of AI and why the UK may be emerging as a relative source of stability in Europe.
For investors, businesses and households alike, the key question is whether the prevailing narrative on the UK has become too negative and what that could mean for growth, markets and policy in the months ahead.
This episode was recorded on Wednesday 7 October at 10:30am British Summer Time.

Listeners can hear more on this topic:​​​

Brexit, Burnham and Britain's next decade

French bonds: OAT of control

Do debt managers or markets set the price of long bonds?

Clients can read more on Barclays Live:​

Headwinds on the horizon

The direct fiscal effects of quantitative easing and tightening

UK Rates Strategy: Chancellor Healey meets the bond market: ‘let sleeping dogs lie’

This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice or a recommendation. Views expressed are those of the speakers and may not reflect those of the firm. Any forward-looking statements are based on current assumptions and subject to risks and uncertainties.

The IFS Green Budget 2026

Important content disclosures

Transcript

Patrick (00:00)
It's Patrick Coffee and this is the Barclays Brief podcast.
So, the UK budget is fast approaching and conversations with friends, colleagues and clients keep drifting back to what Chancellor John Healey might announce on the 28th of October. But is it all doom and gloom? At the recent Labor Party conference, the Prime Minister struck a pretty optimistic tone, talking about the prospect of a better future and the need for the country to hope again.
So today I want to explore the UK economic backdrop ahead of the budget, what options are actually open to the Chancellor, and is the outlook better than many people think? To discuss all of that, I'm delighted to be joined here in London by Jack, meaning our chief UK economist, a regular on the Barclays Brief podcast and the coauthor of the latest green budget with the Institute for Fiscal Studies, and report.
This very likely to be sitting on the Chancellor's desk as we speak.
Okay, so, Jack, you've just completed one of the most comprehensive reports on the UK economy ahead of the budget. What stood out as the most interesting thing you uncovered in that process?
Jack (01:00)
Well, Patrick, I think the thing that surprised me most was when we brought together, you know, our macro expertise and how we assess the backdrop with the fiscal expertise of the IFS.
Actually, the combination of those two things, which, you know, we're really privileged to be able to have really gave me a challenge to the market narrative that the Chancellor is going to find himself really squeezed on headroom at this budget. And the reason for that was because I think the market has been focused on the increase in interest rates and yields, which absolutely will take away from the Chancellor's capacity to to spend and tighten up the fiscal picture.
But when you kind of marry that with actually what's going on with inflation and nominal tax bases, which is where we could draw on the IFS, you find that actually those two things marry out pretty neutrally. And so the Chancellor may ultimately have headroom. That is broadly where he was back in the spring. And therefore that means that this narrative that he'll have to do quite a lot of fiscal tightening just to keep the show on the road is maybe misplaced. And actually, it could be that he doesn't have to make big changes at this budget just to keep the right side of his fiscal rules.
Patrick (02:14)
Okay. So I can speak on behalf of a lot of people in the country. That's a bit of a relief hearing you say that, Jack, I want to talk about inflation. I want to talk about rates a little bit about growth, and then turn to the options available for Chancellor John Healey thinking about inflation.
My concern is that there are going to be second round effects from the energy price spikes. What's your view on that?
Jack (02:30)
Yeah I mean look, there's unavoidable that we are going to have a near-term inflation peak. The forecast that we and the OBR had had back in the spring, that we would be broadly coming down towards 2%, that is out the window.
It looks like inflation is traveling towards 4%. We think we will probably stop just shy of 4% when we come to January. In the next off gen price cap pushes up prices even further. But ultimately this is happening against the backdrop where there is slack in the labor market. So the unemployment rate has been rising. We're seeing vacancies in the economy drop in, so there's not much price pressure coming through in terms of wage negotiations.
But also firms are telling us they don't see the demand in the economy is strong enough to be able to pass on their input cost increases to more broad prices.
There is really not much evidence yet that this narrow energy shock is passing out into broader prices in the economy. And so we think that the risk of second round effects, it's there.
There will probably be some. But we think the risk of them being anything other than limited is small at the moment.
Patrick (03:42)
Well, that's interesting if you think about how markets are pricing, a pretty aggressive response from the Bank of England to this increase in energy costs and inflation. Do you think there is a scenario where the bank doesn't need to raise rates as much as investors currently expect?
Jack (03:58)
Yeah, the market is expecting four quarter point hikes over the next 12 months. I think if our view of the economy is right and actually the labour market is soft, that growth is going to slow over the next few quarters because of the shock coming from the Middle East, depressing demand. If that's the case, then ultimately inflation won't stay sticky and the bank will maybe only have to increase interest rates once, twice.
Maybe if there's a more protracted conflict going into the start of next year, and therefore that market expectation could be misplaced.
Patrick (04:34)
Okay, so there's another reason for you to be a little bit different to market expectations.
I have to say, when I was reading your note last night, I highlighted the bit where you said the expected neutral interest rate, which for listeners is the bank rate that neither slows nor stimulates the economy, is between 3 to 3.5%.
And as someone remortgaging in a nine months time, that really matters to me.
So let's turn to the budget then. So you started by saying that actually the market narrative might be wrong going into the budget. Clearly the narrative going in is higher yields mean less fiscal headroom. But actually you're talking about higher inflation boosting nominal GDP and tax receipts, which offset some of that pressure.
Talk to me about the dynamic between higher gilt yields and higher inflation.
Jack (05:18)
Yeah. So I mean look let's have some rules of thumb to just give us context. So for every one percentage point that you see bank rate and gilt yields going up, you're probably talking about somewhere like 14 billion pounds off of the kind of the current budget rule.
So that's a squeeze for the Chancellor. But for every one percentage point that you see nominal earnings going up, because people are pulled into higher income tax bands and because there's just a bigger nominal tax base, you're probably talking around about 8 billion pounds back for the Chancellor. So you can broadly say given the guilt yields we've seen come through and given what we expect to see come through in nominal earnings, those two things might broadly balance out.
So the bit that I'm interested in is why is the market missing that I think markets are always prone to focusing on the things that are in front of them in terms of the market. And I think this combination of the kind of the cash story is kind of slightly past people by or at least the extent of it has maybe passed people by, but it also isn't a panacea.
So when you think about that, higher inflation increases nominal earnings. So it brings in that extra money. It's also eroding the budgets of government departments that are set in cash terms. And that's going to create a problem for the Chancellor further down the road.
Patrick (06:40)
We'll hear more about that next year with the spending review.
Jack (06:44)
Right, exactly. He'll have to make a decision, and the chance will have to decide whether to let those budgets stay fixed in cash terms as they've been.
Which means that in real terms, government spending is taking a bit of a hit, or whether he'll have to supplement them to try and offset some of this inflationary shot.
Patrick (06:57)
So is what you're saying here, then, that the really tough decisions around spending will be taken next year? But if you're the Chancellor sitting in 11 Downing Street at the moment with your red briefcase next to your desk, there is a way where the Chancellor doesn't do much that's that dramatic and delivers a largely, to quote George Osborne from a while ago, a steady as she goes budget.
Do you think, if that's the case that businesses and markets will react positively?
Jack (07:22)
Yeah, I think so. I think the Chancellor delivering something that seems sensible continuity will be beneficial.
Now that's true in markets. I think markets will be looking at the UK as one of the less volatile kind of debt markets. I think it's true if you kind of go beyond debt markets into FX as well, but also it's true in the real economy. So we've surveyed recently a whole range of UK businesses and corporates, and eight out of ten of those told us that if the Chancellor can deliver something that is instilling confidence in the outlook, then they would increase their investment.
And that's on top of plans to already increase investment over the coming year. This would just amplify and provide the confidence and certainty that businesses need. So yeah, steady as she goes. I think Patrick is the watchword.
Patrick (08:19)
What about capital gains tax? That's something that lots of people are talking about. Do you expect to rise there?
Jack (08:30)
The difficulty with capital gains that the Chancellor faces is depending exactly how it's calibrated and designed, it probably won't raise very much money.
And if it does, it will change incentives around the economy and potentially be distortions in a way that the Chancellor may not want over the longer term. So there are cases that can be made for equalizing the taxation that you do via wealth and profit versus those that you have on labor. That's an open discussion. But fundamentally, if what you're thinking about is trying to raise revenue in the future, capital gains seems like a pretty difficult one to to pull the lever on.
And it will also be a hard one for businesses to digest that the looking for that steady as she goes.
Patrick (09:10)
Okay. So we've got all these near-term challenges with inflation concerns, interest rate concerns. I guess one of the most encouraging parts of the report was around business investment. And I scribbled a couple of numbers down. So between 2015 to 2025, UK business investment grew on average around 0.6% quarter on quarter.
But for the first half of 2026, it averaged roughly 2.4%. That's a big step up when you look under the surface. A lot of that came from ICT related investment. So am I extrapolating too much that actually below the surface we're seeing a bit of an AI boom that's being missed in the UK?
Jack (09:45)
No, I think there are nascent signs of that coming through actually in the UK.
So as you say, a large part of the growth that we saw in the first half of the year was coming from not just AI, but AI adjacent being. So there's part of it, which is data centers as part of it, which is people investing in the decision to kind of skill up within their workforce and those type of things that are beneficial for long term productivity and long term growth.
I guess question now is how much does that continue and how much does it spread over more widely into the economy? So we ran a scenario in a report where we showed that if this is just a narrow, AI focused investment boom, maybe akin to some of what you've seen in the US that will have a near term growth impact, it will boost demand, but it doesn't lead to a prolonged and sustainable impact on growth unless it spreads over into total factor productivity and starts percolating through the economy more widely.
And so really, that's what we need to see, is it's not just the investment boom, it's the associated increase in productivity more widely.
Patrick (10:40)
But if that spillover effect of percolating, as you call it, does happen, that could be the UK's kind of best route out of this low growth, high, high tax environment, right.
Jack (11:00)
Absolutely. Productivity growth is the secret sauce that really drives, you know, improve standards of living. It helps boost tax revenues, boost growth per person.
Patrick (11:08)
Okay. So let's just wrap this up by thinking about the UK in the broader European context. There's investors. Look at Europe right now. They see challenges everywhere right.
So concerns around France's fiscal position Germany struggling with some pretty tough budget choices. Political uncertainty in parts of southern Europe. You know we've got the Spanish snap election coming up. And against that backdrop, the UK is starting to look relatively stable, isn't it?
Jack (11:34)
Yeah I mean, look, we've had our moments. Let's be clear over the last few years, 2022 is not that long ago and lives long in the memory of the market, I think. But I'm an economist. Let's look at the data and the numbers. The UK's deficit is broadly in the middle of the pack.
We're not an outlier in terms of how much we're borrowing. Our debt to GDP is broadly again in the middle of the pack. We're not an outlier. We now have a Chancellor who is continuing to be committed to a consolidation to improve that fiscal outlook. That may be difficult to do, but everything we hear is that that is staying on track.
And it's a Chancellor with a large majority behind him and a fixed kind of term of the parliament, unless they choose to call an early election. But let's assume they run the next three years without one. That is a base for stability.
So, if the Chancellor can deliver that again at this budget, then, as you say, against the backdrop of a French economy that is looking very volatile, other European peers looking volatile, a US political situation running into the midterms, actually, the UK could be that island of stability that many in the market are looking for.
Patrick (12:43)
Island of stability. Well Jack, if they do call in an early election, we'll have you back up here very quickly to talk about it. But otherwise, thanks a lot for joining. Absolute pleasure. So I have to admit, when I invited Jack up here to talk about the budget, I was pretty nervous. But I think I'm finishing this conversation walking out of the room a bit more optimistic.
Clearly, there are reasons to be cautious on the UK in the next 3 to 4 quarters, and the Chancellor needs to maintain fiscal credibility while supporting growth. But there is some room for manoeuvre and some scope for optimism. Investments holding up productivity may finally be improving and compared with some of its European peers, the UK's position actually looks relatively stable.
So let's see what happens at the UK budget on the 28th of October. Thanks a lot for listening to the Barclays brief. We'll be back again next week and do hit subscribe if you enjoyed this conversation.

Jack Meaning

Chief UK Economist, Barclays Research

Jack Meaning is Barclays’ UK Chief Economist, responsible for devising and delivering the bank’s view on the macro outlook for the UK economy. He joined Barclays in 2023 from the Bank of England, where he spent three years as the Economic Advisor to the BoE’s Chief Economist. He also led the team that designed and evaluated the Bank’s monetary policy tools. In 2022, Jack coauthored the now international, best-selling pop-econ book Can’t We Just Print More Money? Jack has published a number of academic papers and earned his PhD in Economics from the University of Kent, where he was awarded the prestigious ESRC scholarship. He is also a fellow of the Royal Society of Arts.

Patrick Coffey

Global Head of the Product Management Team, Barclays Research

Patrick Coffey is Global Head of the Product Management Team in Research. Previously, he was Deputy Head of European Equity Research and prior to this, he was an equity research analyst for a decade. Before joining Barclays in 2013, Patrick covered the sector for four years at another firm and has also held roles at Manchester United and in strategy consulting.
