articles.title: A snapshot of America’s schools: Trends and global comparisons | Brookings
articles.text:
Research

A snapshot of America’s schools: Trends and global comparisons

Jon Valant,

Jon Valant

Director
- Brown Center on Education Policy,

Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies,

Herman and George R. Brown Chair in Education Studies

Nicolas Zerbino, and

Nicolas Zerbino

Research Associate
- Governance Studies, Brown Center on Education Policy

Emma Mills

Emma Mills

Former Research Intern
- Brown Center on Education Policy, The Brookings Institution

October 16, 2026

NAEP scores for 4th and 8th graders show large gains in math and reading in the early 2000s, followed by a plateau and gradual decline starting around 2013, a steep drop during the pandemic, and only a slight rebound since.
International tests show that U.S. 15-year-olds compare favorably with peer countries in reading and science but poorly in math.
The U.S. is making little progress in closing test score gaps between student subgroups, and the gap between high-scoring (90th percentile) and low-scoring (10th percentile) students is now larger in the U.S. than in most, if not all, peer countries.
In international comparisons, U.S. students are negative outliers in self-reported well-being and time spent on screens.

Source: Shutterstock

32 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Back to top

Introduction

America is not pleased with its schools.
A Gallup poll conducted in August 2026 found that only 8% of adults are “completely satisfied” and 24% are “somewhat satisfied” with the quality of K-12 education in the U.S. today. That combined total of 32% is the lowest level of satisfaction that Gallup has measured in nearly three decades of annual polling on this question. It represents a precipitous drop since the onset of COVID-19—a drop now evident among both Democrats and Republicans. Recent poll results from Pew and PDK are similarly bleak.
Discontent with the nation’s schools is evident in (and, likely, fueled by) prolonged culture-war conflicts over issues related to race, gender, and sexuality. It’s also evident in the language used by a wide variety of leaders to describe the nation’s schools. President Trump has decried America’s education system as “dead last” in performance despite being “the most expensive” system in the world. (We’ll scrutinize those claims shortly.) Education reformers and researchers have referred to this era as a “learning recession” or “education depression.” It’s hard to find prominent voices in education—from the political left, center, or right—saying that all is well.
To get out of the slump we’re in, we need to understand the nature of that slump. That is, we need to be sure that our critiques of the nation’s education system are tethered to what the best available data and evidence say about where we stand.
That is the focus of this report. It provides a 30,000-foot view of America’s schools, largely through a series of charts. We examine trends in student outcomes—overall and by subgroup—and place those outcomes in the context of other countries’ performance. We also examine indicators of students’ well-being and how U.S. students are spending their time.
The result is a troubling—but nuanced—portrait of how America’s students are doing. For example, in some areas we are performing well relative to peer countries, even if we still have room to improve. In other areas, we are performing poorly by any reasonable measure.
Our key takeaways are the following:

NAEP scores show years of academic progress in the early 2000s giving way to steep declines. Math and reading scores for 4th and 8th graders rose substantially during the late 1990s and early 2000s before plateauing around 2013. They began to slide shortly afterward, plummeted during the pandemic, and have since recovered only modestly, if at all. While COVID-19 clearly hurt student performance, scores began declining well before the pandemic.
America’s 15-year-olds compare favorably with peer countries in reading and science but poorly in math. On PISA 2025, the U.S. ranked 6th in reading and 7th in science when compared with 23 OECD countries. We have steadily improved our standing in those comparisons over the last two decades, though that is largely attributable to steep declines across OECD-23 countries in recent years. In math, the U.S. continues to perform poorly relative to peer countries, placing 16th of 24 on PISA 2025.
Achievement gaps have remained stubbornly large, and the gap between our high and low scorers now far exceeds that of most peer countries. Test score gaps by race, ethnicity, and economic disadvantage remain large and are not narrowing at a pace sufficient to close them in the foreseeable future. Meanwhile, scores for the lowest-performing students (10th percentile) have dropped sharply over the last decade, while scores for the highest performers (90th percentile) have held fairly steady. America’s 90-10 gaps have widened far more rapidly than those in peer countries—and now stand out in international comparisons.
U.S. students are negative outliers on self-reported well-being and time spent on screens. America’s 15-year-olds rank near the bottom of OECD countries on PISA’s measure of well-being, as they have for some time. They stand out in how often they report feeling like outsiders, out of place, and lonely at school. This is consistent with other measures that indicate very high rates of youth depression and student disengagement in the US. American students are also outliers in the amount of time they report spending on social media and playing video games relative to 15-year-olds in peer countries.

The data in this report do not point conclusively to any single cause of our schools’ challenges, nor to any silver-bullet solution. They do, however, offer a clearer view of where we stand and the work that lies ahead.

Back to top

Math and reading trends from The Nation’s Report Card

Declines on the NAEP that predate the pandemic
We begin by examining trends in academic performance, for which the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) is a natural starting point. Known as “the nation’s report card,” NAEP periodically tests and surveys representative samples of U.S. students. Its results shape public narratives about how America’s schools are performing and which states are over- or underachieving. Recent releases, for example, have prompted consternation about national trends and intrigue about relatively strong performances in states such as Mississippi, Louisiana, and Massachusetts.
These first results will be familiar to many readers: math and reading trends for grades 4 and 8. NAEP’s scales are not easy to interpret, but as a benchmark, 8th graders have historically outscored 4th graders by about 40 points. Because the grades are four years apart, that gap implies about 10 points of learning in a typical year. The Educational Opportunity Project at Stanford measured this more precisely and estimates that a year of learning equates to 10.4 NAEP points in math 11.2 NAEP points in reading.
Figure 1 plots average scores from 1996 to 2024.

Figure 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Across grades and subjects, the pattern is broadly similar. Average scores rose—in some cases sharply—in the late 1990s and early 2000s. They started to plateau around 2013, began to slide shortly thereafter, plummeted during the pandemic, and have since recovered only modestly, if at all.
NAEP is not designed for drawing conclusions about the causes of test score changes over time, as tempting as that may be. Still, a few events from this period are worth noting.
The first is the No Child Left Behind (NCLB) Act of 2002, along with related school accountability policies that many states adopted in the preceding years. NCLB is the kind of policy one might expect to raise 4th and 8th grade NAEP scores. It pushed states to set content standards for grades 3 through 8 (and 10) and to hold schools accountable for students’ mastery of that material. It also created incentives to move students over state-defined “proficiency” thresholds, which may have steered resources toward low-scoring students. This does not mean NCLB was good for America’s schools on balance. That question remains fiercely debated. However, the best available evidence indicates that it likely raised test scores, especially near the bottom of the test score distribution.
The second is the Great Recession, which ran from late 2007 to mid-2009. Child poverty increased over this period. At the same time, school spending declined by about 7%, which may (or may not) have contributed to declining test scores and widening achievement gaps. The recession also serves to underscore the point that schools do not exist in a vacuum but are subject to broader societal forces.
The third is the COVID-19 pandemic. Most schools quickly moved to online learning in response to the pandemic, and many stayed there for an extended period. This shift, along with other harms brought on by COVID-19, undermined student learning and mental health, especially among marginalized students.
Of course, the last two decades brought many other changes, too. This includes the rise of cellphones and social media, which we return to later. In a recent paper, James Wyckoff of the University of Virginia argues that the field still lacks a clear account of why NAEP scores have fallen. He cautions against overemphasizing the role of COVID-19, noting that the downward trend from 2013 to 2019 would have predicted roughly half of the declines since 2020.1
Achievement gaps that remain stubbornly wide
Average NAEP scores tell only part of the story. Stubbornly large gaps between historically advantaged and marginalized groups, and growing gaps between our highest and lowest scorers, are also important characteristics of this period.
Figure 2 shows NAEP scores from 1996 to 2024, disaggregated by socioeconomic status. Here, too, we show 4th and 8th grade scores in math and reading.

Figure 2

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Gaps between economically advantaged and disadvantaged students remained large and mostly steady over this period. However, caveats apply. First, NAEP’s measure of economic disadvantage has changed over time.2 Second, NAEP offers only one view of the complicated picture of income-based achievement gaps (albeit a useful one). Researchers using different income and test score measures have sometimes reached very different conclusions about these gaps.
Next, we look at NAEP scores disaggregated by race and ethnicity. These scores appear in Figure 3.

Figure 3

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Here, too, we see large, persistent gaps. Students who identify as Asian/Pacific Islander, white, or multiracial have consistently and substantially outscored those who identify as Hispanic, Black, or American Indian/Alaska Native.
Figure 4 draws on Figures 2 and 3 to show how gaps between various student subgroups, measured in standard deviations, have changed over time. As a very rough rule of thumb, an average year of learning between 4th and 8th grade equates to about one-third of a standard deviation.

Figure 4

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The story is consistent across these comparisons. At the current slow pace of progress, these gaps will persist for many years to come.
A growing “90-10” gap between high and low scorers
Next, we turn to a comparison that has featured prominently in recent NAEP discussions: the widening gap between high scorers (students at the 90th percentile) and low scorers (students at the 10th percentile). Unlike the gaps just discussed, this one does not compare defined groups of students based on their background characteristics. It compares students at the top and bottom of the score distribution itself. The concern is that today’s struggling students are falling further and further behind.
Figure 5 shows trends in this 90-10 gap over the last two decades.

Figure 5

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Of particular concern is the sharp drop in 10th percentile scores over the last decade (with scores in the 90th percentile mostly stable). Today’s lowest-scoring students perform substantially worse than their counterparts a decade ago.
Below, we present data from international assessments showing that ballooning 90-10 test score gaps are largely an American phenomenon. Many OECD countries have seen test score declines in recent years, and some have seen a widening gap between their high and low scorers. Few, if any, have seen their 90-10 performance diverge as rapidly as they have in the U.S.

Back to top

International comparisons of academic performance

Strong performance in reading and science, weak in math
Placing America’s performance in an international context helps to illuminate where our trends and challenges may be uniquely American and where they may reflect wider challenges.
Currently, there are two major international assessments of student performance: the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) and the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS). PISA is more useful for our purposes because it is administered by the OECD, whose members are mostly economically prosperous countries and thus a reasonable comparison group for the United States. PISA also has 23 countries that have consistently participated in the assessment for the last decade and a half (PISA labels this group as the OECD-23).3
TIMSS, however, offers a useful starting point because of its similarities to NAEP. It tests students in grades 4 and 8 and, unlike PISA, is designed to measure mastery of material taught in schools.
Figure 6 shows U.S. average math scores for grades 4 and 8. The faded lines in the background show corresponding results for the small number of OECD-23 countries that participated in TIMSS throughout the years displayed. (We will have a more useful set of comparison countries momentarily, once we get to the PISA results.)

Figure 6

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Trends in TIMSS scores for the U.S. roughly mirror those for NAEP math results (Figure 1). That is, we see steady gains in the early 2000s followed by plateauing scores and then declines that accelerated with the pandemic.
For richer international comparisons, we turn to PISA. Like NAEP, PISA tests a sample of students every few years and is designed to compare students’ knowledge, skills, and perspectives across time and place. Unlike NAEP, it tests 15-year-olds and focuses less on mastery of specific content than on assessing “key knowledge and skills essential for full participation in social and economic life.” Tom Loveless contrasts the tests’ philosophy and scope. TIMSS, he notes, measures how well students have learned the school curriculum, whereas PISA measures whether they can apply what they know—whether learned in or out of school—to real-world problems.
The next figures compare U.S. students with the OECD countries that have consistently participated in PISA over the past two decades. Notably, U.S. students fare very differently across the three subjects tested: math, reading, and science.
Figure 7 shows math trends. The orange line is the U.S. average, and the solid blue line is the average for OECD countries that took part in every PISA math assessment from 2003 to 2025. Each faded blue line shows an individual country.

Figure 7

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The United States is—and long has been—a low scorer in math. In 2003, we ranked 19th of the 24 countries in this cohort. By 2025, our rank had risen to 16th, though our average score slid. This reflects declining math scores across the OECD countries.
We should note that these PISA trends diverge somewhat from the trends we saw in NAEP math (Figure 1). America’s NAEP scores rapidly climbed in the early 2000s before peaking around 2013. Given that the 8th graders tested by NAEP are only a year or two younger than the 15-year-olds tested by PISA, it is not immediately clear why the NAEP gains are not evident in PISA. One possibility is that this reflects quirks in what PISA assesses (relative to NAEP), as discussed by Loveless.
America’s 15-year-olds stack up much more favorably in reading. Figure 8 shows results for the U.S. and the other 23 OECD countries that took part in every PISA reading assessment from 2000 to 2025.4

Figure 8

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

In reading, the U.S. climbed from 13th of 24 in 2000 to 6th in 2025. This came despite relatively flat scores and then a post-COVID-19 decline. As in math, the climb reflects other countries’ declines more than U.S. gains. Across the OECD, reading scores began falling before the pandemic and dropped sharply afterward, as both the dark blue average line and the downward arc of the faded lines show.
In science, America’s average score has risen over the past two decades, and our corresponding rank has jumped from 19th of 24 in 2006 to 7th in 2025 (see Figure 9).

Figure 9

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Stepping back, these PISA results indicate real differences across subjects in how U.S. 15-year-olds’ scores stack up against their peers in OECD countries. American students continue to lag in math but hold their own in reading and science, albeit partly because of the comparison countries’ recent performance slides.
Next, we turn to a clearer area of concern: the growing gaps between our high- and low-scoring students.
Larger “90-10” gaps between high and low scorers than peer countries
Our discussion of the NAEP trends noted a recent widening of the gap between high-performing students (90th percentile) and low-performing students (10th percentile). The TIMSS and PISA results show that the U.S. is an outlier in this regard.
Let’s start with a look at the most recent PISA reading results. This is a subject where, on average, the U.S. is performing well relative to peer countries. Figure 10 presents each country’s range of scores from the 10th percentile to the 90th percentile. By default, the chart is sorted by countries’ 10th-percentile scores, which places the U.S. very near the OECD average. However, the U.S. has the largest difference between its 10th and 90th percentiles relative to these OECD countries. In fact, our 90th-percentile performers score higher than every country except New Zealand.

Figure 10

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

We see similarly wide 90-10 bars for the U.S. when we look at PISA math, PISA science, and TIMSS 4th grade math, and TIMSS 8th grade math. (Click the links to open the charts for those various tests.)
What is even more striking is how quickly America’s 90-10 gaps have widened relative to other OECD countries. Figures 11 (math), 12 (reading), and 13 (science) show countries’ PISA 90-10 gaps from the early 2000s to 2025.

Figure 11

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 12

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Figure 13

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

America’s 90-10 gaps have widened far more rapidly than those in other OECD countries, especially in reading and science. The gaps are all U-shaped, and they all started to climb in the early-to-mid-2010s.
PISA, like NAEP, is not designed to identify the causes of the patterns it reveals. We should note, though, that the timing of the U.S. uptick roughly corresponds with possible U.S.-specific factors (e.g., the end of the NCLB era) and with possible global factors (e.g., the rise of social media). Other OECD countries’ 90-10 gaps have grown over the last 10 to 15 years but far more slowly than America’s gaps.

Back to top

Student engagement and well-being

We just saw one area where the United States is a negative outlier in international comparisons (90-10 test score gaps). Unfortunately, student well-being is another.
Disconcerting evidence on students’ sense of belonging and mental health
Alongside its assessments, PISA surveys 15-year-olds on a wide range of topics, including their perceptions of school, experiences outside school, and time use. These are self-reported measures, but they are measured consistently across time (year) and place (country).
We begin with PISA’s composite measure of well-being. This measure is based on students’ responses to six questions, which we detail below. Since PISA has asked these questions for several years, we can track trends and compare countries. We do this in Figure 14.

Figure 14

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

In 2025, America’s 15-year-olds scored near the bottom of participating OECD countries on this well-being measure. Unfortunately, the U.S. has ranked near the bottom on this measure for some time.
Figure 15 shows 2025 PISA results for the six questions that feed into this composite measure of well-being. If student well-being were high, responses would approach 0%for the top three items and 100%for the bottom three items.

Figure 15

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

U.S. students compare the least favorably on the top three items. Our 15-year-olds are outliers in how they report feeling like an outsider at school, awkward and out of place at school, and lonely at school.
These results echo troubling findings in a recent report from the State of the Nation Project. That report compares the United States with other countries around the world on measures ranging from greenhouse gas emissions to press freedom. It shows that youth depression is among the categories in which the U.S. fares the worst relative to other countries. (The U.S. compares more favorably in academic performance and educational attainment.) The report’s authors note that youth depression began rising around 2007, especially among girls. That timing coincides with expanded cellphone use, though the authors caution that causal evidence remains limited.
Signs of disengagement and far more screen time than peer countries
Recently, education experts have raised concerns about declines in student engagement. Some of the concern centers on attendance, which dropped sharply during the pandemic. But there’s also a broader worry that students aren’t meaningfully engaged even when they are in school. For example, in “The Disengaged Teen,” Rebecca Winthrop and Jenny Anderson examine how adolescents navigate their middle and high school years. They find that far too few students are driven by curiosity and genuinely invested in their learning (what Winthrop and Anderson call “explorer mode”).
Here, we look at data from a variety of sources to get a clearer picture of student engagement. We begin with attendance.
Nat Malkus of the American Enterprise Institute has tracked chronic absenteeism (the share of students missing at least 10%of the school year) from before the pandemic to the present. As Figure 16 shows, rates spiked after the pandemic and have fallen only slowly since, suggesting they may settle well above their pre-pandemic baseline.

Figure 16

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Next, we look to PISA for indicators of student engagement. The PISA data offer a mixed picture of how America’s 15-year-olds compare with their OECD peers.
As Figure 17 shows, about one-third of U.S. 15-year-olds admit to having skipped at least one day of school in the last two weeks. This exceeds most peer countries. On an item that asks whether they had skipped a class (not the full day), the U.S. is near the middle of the pack.

Figure 17

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

America’s teens stand out much more in the time they report spending on screens and social media. They are outliers in the share of students that report spending at least five hours per day playing video games, browsing social media, and communicating and sharing content on social media (Figure 18).5

Figure 18

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Excessive screen time and social media use are widely speculated to be harmful to children. Researchers have noted that declines in student learning and mental health coincided with upticks in time spent on devices and social media. Wyckoff, while noting that the causal evidence on these questions is still developing, describes a “strong intuition and correlational evidence of the negative effects of smart-phones and social media on the learning development of students.”
Technology use could affect students in both direct and indirect ways. For example, students could consume content on social media that has direct, negative effects on their body image. Less directly, time spent on devices could displace positive activities such as sleep, physical activity, and socializing with peers.
One activity that American children are spending much less time on than they once did is reading for pleasure. The NAEP student questionnaire has, for decades, asked students how often they read for fun on their own time. The percentage of 9- and 13-year-olds who report reading every day has plummeted since about 2012. These trends appear in Figure 19.

Figure 19

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

To be clear, PISA and other assessments ask hundreds of questions between them, and we cannot cover the responses to all those questions in one report. On many of these measures, the U.S. does not stand out. Still, the data raise real concerns about American students’ well-being, both in absolute terms and relative to their peers abroad. The U.S. is an outlier in its rates of youth depression, share of students who report little sense of belonging, and time spent on video games and social media.

Back to top

Discussion

Taking stock of what we’re getting and what we’re spending
This report opened by noting that President Trump has described American education as “dead last” in the world. The evidence above shows that the claim is accurate in some respects and inaccurate in many others.
Academically, American students’ performance declined sharply after the onset of the pandemic, following a long period of stagnation and slow decline. But those declines were not unique to the United States, and U.S. students compare favorably with their peers in some subjects, especially reading and science. (We perform much worse in math.)
Where the U.S. is an outlier is in the widening gap between its highest- and lowest-scoring students, as defined by 90th- and 10th-percentile scorers, respectively. Far too many U.S. students are falling well behind their higher-achieving peers, and this pattern looks substantially worse in the U.S. than in its peer countries. Addressing this must be a priority for leaders in education and public policy.
This is not the only area of immediate concern. The U.S. is also an outlier in youth well-being and mental health—a problem that predates the pandemic, has grown more serious since, and requires a concerted response of its own. In fact, in international comparisons, the United States looks considerably worse on measures of mental health than measures of academic performance.
We also can evaluate the other side of the president’s claim, which is that the U.S. has the world’s most expensive education system. This, too, is an exaggeration. As Figure 20 shows, U.S. education spending is comparable to that of many peer countries, both as a share of GDP and per pupil.

Figure 20

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

What is true, however, is that we could and should be getting a whole lot more for our investment.
A changing landscape for K-12 education
The challenges outlined in this report are complex. They are the product of many different factors, some that have roots in education policy and practice and others that do not. They would be hard to solve at any time. Current changes in the educational landscape make this work even more difficult.
One such change is the arrival of AI in our schools. AI brings vast risks along with vast opportunities. Maximizing its benefits while minimizing its harms, and ensuring that those benefits reach all students rather than just the most advantaged, may be the defining challenge for the next generation of education reform.
The second is rapid change in how many states govern and fund their education systems. As public sentiment toward America’s schools soured, many states have turned to universal school choice programs that redirect funds from public to private schools. Combined with enrollment declines, this trend leaves many systems facing potentially severe budget cuts and instability.
The problems facing America’s schools are serious, but we have solved serious problems before. After a period defined by culture-war conflicts, we need a renewed and sustained focus on what matters most: ensuring that every student has the opportunity to learn and flourish.

articles.title: The top cities in the Asia Pacific in 2026
articles.text:
Blog

16 Oct 2026

The top cities in the Asia Pacific in 2026

Scott McEwan
Lead Economist, Cities & Regions

With Asia Pacific (APAC) hosting some of the world’s largest and most advanced city economies, as well as some of its fastest growing, the region’s challenge to the dominance of Europe and North America in the global economy continues to intensify. This economic strength of APAC’s major cities, augmented by impressive standings across Human Capital and Quality of Life metrics, is demonstrated by their high and rising rankings in our latest Global Cities Index for 2026.

APAC’s most advanced cities hold their ground at the highest ranks of the Global Cities Index

Asia Pacific’s (APAC) major cities are continuing to drive the pace of global economic growth and are increasingly shifting the world’s economic centre of gravity eastward. Over the next 25 years, we forecast real GDP growth across 396 cities in Asia Pacific to average 2.7% per year, faster than the city averages of any other region outside of Africa. By 2050, APAC’s cities will account for 40% of the GDP produced by the world’s 1,000 largest cities, up from 35% today and just 23% in 2001.

With the region hosting some of the world’s biggest, most advanced, and most established city economies, as well as some of its most dynamic and fastest growing, Asia Pacific hosts a breadth of opportunity and is increasingly challenging the dominance of Europe and North America. The economic strength of APAC’s major cities, augmented by their impressive standings across Human Capital and Quality of Life metrics, is demonstrated by their high and rising ranks in our 2026 Global Cities Index.

The pinnacle of Asia Pacific’s economic strength today is exemplified by the region’s most mature and advanced cities, which maintain their standings in the top reaches of our index. Principal among them is Tokyo, the world’s second-largest city economy and second-most populous, placing ninth globally in the overall index. While the Japanese capital generally experiences slower economic growth than elsewhere in the world, and is no doubt exposed to the challenges of the Far East’s ageing populations, its sheer size and economic might combined with its reputation as a premier location for corporate headquarters, world-class universities, and astounding cultural assets mean it remains a vibrant city of enormous international importance.

Demonstrating their remarkable record across all categories of the Global Cities Index, from Economics and the Environment to Quality of Life and Governance, five of Australia’s state capitals also feature in the top 50 of our index. Sydney leads the pack in 13th place, just ahead of Melbourne in 16th, and Brisbane and Perth in 36th and 44th, respectively. Meanwhile, the national capital Canberra in 45th place can also boast taking the top spot among the 1,000 Global Cities for the Quality of Life metric, with its residents enjoying some of the highest and relatively equally distributed incomes, lowest crime rates, and longest life spans globally.

Rounding out Asia Pacific’s highest-ranking cities are Singapore (29th), Seoul (38th), and Taipei (48th), with the latter a new addition to the top 50 this year. These cities arguably characterise the heart of Asia Pacific’s dominant semiconductor industry, with the AI-related surge in demand for advanced chips supercharging their economies recently. While these cities also represent some of Advanced Asia’s most acutely ageing populations, the size of their economies, their strengths across other Human Capital and Quality of Life metrics, and their position at the centre of a world-changing technology means they rightly stand among the world’s most important cities.

Emerging APAC’s rapidly growing cities are poised to climb higher

While Advanced Asia’s mature megacities maintain their places at the very top of our global rankings, Emerging cities in the region are poised to join them. A common theme among the most exciting prospects in Emerging Asia is the fast pace of their demographic and economic growth, characterised by a virtuous cycle of sectoral compositions moving up the value chain to higher-productivity, higher-wage activities, which attract, retain, and train high-calibre workers. In our 2026 report, we have highlighted five “Cities to Watch”, including Kuala Lumpur, Shenzhen, Bengaluru, Ho Chi Minh City, and Tashkent, as some of the leading representatives of Emerging Asia’s multitudinous growth opportunities and some of its top candidates for future top spots in our index.

The highest-ranked of these today is Kuala Lumpur, knocking on the door of the top 50 in 65th place. For decades, Southeast Asia’s urban economic landscape has been dominated by Singapore, however, Kuala Lumpur is gaining attention as a fast-growing, dynamic city with global relevance, leveraging its deep pool of human capital, relatively lower operating costs, and expanding finance and technology sectors to challenge for a top spot. Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s foremost finance, business, and trade hub, at 205th, represents similar qualities to the Malaysian capital, serving as a cost-effective centre for international activity and a gateway into South Asian markets. We notably expect the city to rank among the 50 fastest-growing cities over the next five years.

Shenzhen, our pick for mainland China, and arguably the crowning jewel of the country’s economic ascent over the past 50 years, is the country’s highest-ranked city in our index and the first to reach a top 100 spot at 93rd. The city’s rising stature among the world’s most important cities is driven by its economic strength and leading role in creating and commercialising new technologies, from robotics to green innovations. Shenzhen’s strong position is reinforced by its human capital with workers from across China, long drawn to the economic opportunities created within the city, driving its fast population growth. Already the 14th-biggest metropolis in the world, we expect Shenzhen to become the 11th-largest by 2050.

No other country, however, comes close to India for the sheer breadth of urban growth. By 2050, we project Delhi to be the most populous city in the world and expect six of the top 10 fastest-growing cities by real GDP over the next 25 years to be in India. Indeed, Indian cities combine exceptional GDP growth, deep university and corporate networks, and rapidly expanding labour markets to deliver strong economic momentum, even as weaker Quality of Life and Environment scores continue to hold its cities back from the upper echelons. The country’s strengths are exemplified by the southern tech metropolis Bengaluru (311th), which is expected to be among the 10 fastest-growing cities in the world for forecast GDP growth.

The final Asia Pacific City to Watch is the Uzbek capital of Tashkent. The city ranks 343rd in the index and epitomises the ongoing ambitious programme of economic liberalisation and WTO accession in the country. As a hub of Central Asia, Tashkent is rocketing up our rankings: with rapidly expanding construction, finance, and business service sectors, Tashkent ranks in the top 10 for long-term GDP growth and rightly deserves a spotlight, despite being in an often-overlooked region.

Overall, Asia Pacific’s major cities showcase a breadth and depth of opportunity, from the world’s most advanced and established markets to those rising in profile and economic strength. Our Global Cities Index helps business decision makers understand the enormous range of potential investment prospects available as the balance of global economic activity tilts to the east.

articles.title: CIO Perspective: Asking Better Questions | BlackRock
articles.text:
Fixed Income

Oct 15, 2026

Rick Rieder

"Judge a man by his questions rather than his answers." - Voltaire
Voltaire probably didn't have the 10-year Treasury in mind, but the principle translates. The Federal Reserve (Fed) raised rates this month, bringing the policy rate to 3.75%-4.00%, and every commentator within earshot has an eight-word explanation for what it means. Markets in September 2026 are drowning in answers: the energy shock, fiscal deficits, higher-for-longer Fed policy, Treasury supply, the next consumer price index (CPI) print, and the next jobs report. What almost nobody is doing is asking the questions that actually determine investment returns from here. We think the best investors don't have more answers; they ask better questions. The structural questions facing us today are unusually clear and important and, for those willing to act on them, potentially well-compensated.
U.S. economic growth: Strong headline, fractured underneath
Is the economy strong? Yes. Is it uniformly strong? Not even close. Corporate profits are growing at a rate consistent with 7% nominal GDP growth, a level that points to strong expansion.1 But peel back one layer and the picture changes dramatically. Growth is increasingly concentrated in rate-insensitive services and nonresidential investment, particularly AI-related capital expenditure. Computers and peripheral equipment represent roughly 1% of GDP but have generated approximately 27% of recent growth.2 That is not broad-based growth; it is a capex boom channeled through an extraordinarily narrow pipe.
Meanwhile, sectors most sensitive to financing costs, housing chief among them, remain in something resembling a recession. The income needed to qualify for a median-priced home has reached $125,000, nearly double the median household income, while the average age of a first-time homebuyer has climbed to 40.3 For the first time on record, households in the fourth income quintile may not be able to afford today's median-priced home.
Chair Warsh said this week that policy is "not restrictive" given the headline strength of the economy, and the aggregate data supports that view. But the composition says something far more useful for investing: monetary policy is biting hard in some places while barely touching others.

Source: Bloomberg, Bureau of Economic Analysis, as of June 30, 2026

Inflation and Fed policy: The wrong question is “how high?” the right one is “how responsive?”
This month's 25-basis point rate increase was widely anticipated, while the updated Summary of Economic Projections leaned hawkish. The 2026 median dot now implies two hikes (4.125%), with 2027 and 2028 medians each raised by 50 basis points, suggesting policy remains on hold next year before a cut in 2028. The Fed also revised 2026 core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation a tenth higher to 3.4%, though we suspect officials did not incorporate expected negative methodology revisions due later this month, that could lower the reported number. Chair Warsh was clear in his press conference: progress on underlying inflation has been "inadequate," and he views the economy as strong enough that policy is not yet restrictive.
We agree that the economy has appeared remarkably resilient at the aggregate level, and that modest further rate increases may not put overall growth at risk. But the more important question for portfolios is not the level of inflation; it is its sensitivity to rates. The drivers of today's inflation are increasingly acyclical: energy, insurance, healthcare, education, and products tied to chips and asset prices. The San Francisco Fed's acyclical versus cyclical framework illustrates the divergence. Cyclical components have normalized toward long-term averages, while the acyclical portion continues to push headline inflation higher.
Acyclical components are driving more of today's inflation

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, as of Aug. 31, 2026.

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, as of Aug. 31, 2026.

The Fed is committed to returning inflation to its 2% target, and inaction is clearly not its preferred route. Yet higher rates bite hardest in the housing and consumer borrowing channels that are already under stress, with the 90-day credit card delinquency rate at 12.9%.4 Higher rates do relatively little to slow the AI-fueled investment cycle or global energy dynamics driving the acyclical components. It is the equivalent of turning down the thermostat in one room and wondering why the other room isn't getting cooler. For investors, understanding inflation composition matters far more than tracking the headline number. We don't think this rate increase necessitates a long series of further increases, particularly with employment growth having weakened materially from the pace of recent years.
AI productivity and the labor market: Profits without paychecks
The labor market shows why the right question matters. Is employment strong? At 4.1% unemployment, sure. But the hires rate is at its lowest since 2010, and private-sector wage growth has cooled to 3.1%. Strip out healthcare, and average monthly payroll growth over the past year is just 6,000 jobs.5 Economy-wide profit per employee is growing faster than at any point in the last 25 years (outside the rebounds following the global financial crisis and COVID), while many industries are growing output without hiring at all.
Productivity was rising well before AI, which is now accelerating the trend. The right questions for investing are: how durable is this corporate profit cycle, how much will AI amplify it further, and what happens to economy-wide consumption when the winners and losers diverge this sharply? These are not questions the market can answer with a single payroll print or a Fed dot plot. They are structural, and the portfolio implications extend well beyond the next meeting.
Profit per employee is growing at a historically strong pace

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, as of Aug. 31, 2026.

Retail investing and market structure: The fantasy football problem
Sports betting is now a $17 billion revenue industry in the U.S., up 23% in 2025, and that same impulse is increasingly visible in financial markets.6 Zero-day-to-expiry options continue to take a larger share of total U.S. options volume. Leveraged ETF launches have surged, with almost 200 new ones this year carrying an average AUM of just $3.9 million.7 The dynamic resembles fantasy football: the game outside the arena can become bigger than the game itself. The obsession with what happens in the next minute, hour, or day can undermine the discipline of compounding capital over years. The structural questions, not the daily answers, are what generate returns.
Fixed income yields: The math has rarely been this powerful
For all the debate about current rate levels, the more useful question for investors is: What return can be generated from this starting point? The answer is compelling. What makes today’s opportunity unusual is that investors do not need to reach very far for that income. It’s now possible to build a diversified fixed income portfolio yielding more than 7%, with less than three years of duration and an average credit rating of A-.8 That combination of income, quality and limited interest-rate sensitivity is historically unusual, particularly as inflation continues to moderate.
US 10Y Treasury Average 1Y Forward Returns since 1995 by Starting Yield

Source: Bloomberg, as of Sept. 11, 2026.

In fixed income, the math is unusually transparent: return equals carry plus price change. Carry today provides a substantial cushion against price volatility. This does not mean rates cannot move higher in the near term; they can. It means pulling the bowstring back further only increases the forward return embedded in the entry point. Real yields are at historically attractive levels, pension funding ratios are high enough to create durable demand for long-duration assets at these levels, and the volatility required to build a portfolio with a 7% return target is the lowest it has been since before the financial crisis (2.6% annualized for a hypothetical A-rated portfolio today, versus 11.1% in 2021).9

Moreover, the ability to source yields above 6% across a range of sectors, not just high yield or emerging markets, changes the calculus. Bespoke, well-structured financing assets, including data center asset-backed securities (ABS), whole-business securitizations, and private placements, offer more yield and considerably stronger structural protection than traditional credit. When yield meaningfully exceeds volatility, optimizing portfolios for the prevailing regime can be particularly powerful. Today's environment offers just that opportunity.

Source: Bloomberg, as of Sept. 11, 2026.

Equities: Earnings growth matters, but so does the entry level
For equities, the starting multiple tells us little about future returns. The R-squared between forward price-to-earnings (P/E) and one-year returns is just 0.07. Strong earnings can continue to support equity returns. The AI ecosystem still has the fundamentals to do so. Data center infrastructure and semiconductor companies show expected earnings growth above 25%, while multiples have de-rated 10 to 13 turns from their year-to-date peaks. A meaningful share of that future growth is already under contract.10 The entry point today, after the recent pullback, looks more attractive than it has in months.
But the range of outcomes has clearly widened. From today's starting point, equities could plausibly return anywhere from -5% to +20% over the next year depending on whether earnings deliver and multiples hold or compress. With fixed income able to fund a larger share of portfolio return targets, equity risk can be spent more selectively. The trailing two months tell the story: the S&P 500 returned 1%, while stocks characterized by high free cash flow returned 16%, those with stable sales growth returned 9%, and those with low capex-to-sales returned 8%.11 Cash flow durability and capital efficiency are the filters. This is not the market to own beta for the sake of it.

Source: Citi, as Sept. 4, 2026.

U.S. government debt and fiscal risk: The elephant in the room
Before leaving the discussion on portfolio allocations, it is worth confronting a risk that underlies all markets, one that the rate increase makes more urgent. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) baseline projects debt-to-GDP reaching approximately 120% by 2036, assuming 3.9% nominal growth and a 3.7% average cost of debt. Higher funding costs make that trajectory considerably worse: a sustained 1% increase in the cost of debt adds 8 percentage points to the terminal debt burden; a 2% increase adds 16 percentage points and implies roughly $7.5 trillion in additional net interest expense through 2036.12
Nearly half of marketable Treasury debt matures within two years, and 89% of issuance is concentrated at the front end. Higher rates feed directly into the government's interest bill.13 Refinancing that short-term debt at rates just 1 percentage point lower would generate $144 billion in annual savings, enough to fund the combined FY 2027 discretionary budgets of the Departments of Health and Human Services, Agriculture, Treasury, Labor, and Commerce.14 The arithmetic of this fiscal trajectory makes managing fixed income volatility and optimizing portfolio construction not just sensible, but urgent.
Bottom line: From explaining markets to building better portfolios
The framework is simple and powerful: the edge does not come from having more answers. It comes from asking the five structural questions that actually matter.

What return do we need over the next three to five years, and how much of that can today's starting yield deliver without reaching for additional risk?
With real yields at historically attractive levels, how much interest-rate risk do we actually need to own when carry alone can do so much of the work?
In credit, where is the yield coming from, and where do leverage, refinancing, and rollover risk make the incremental spread not worth taking?
In equities, which earnings growth is durable, cash-generative, and not already fully reflected in the entry price?
As yields reset higher, how quickly should we add duration, and where on the curve do supply and the carry cushion justify that risk while fiscal pressures remain unresolved?

The direction of travel is clear even if the pacing is hard. When a diversified fixed income portfolio can yield more than 7%, carry less than three years of duration and maintain an average A- credit rating, the portfolio math changes materially. If inflation continues trending toward a 2% range, that income becomes even more meaningful in real terms. Equities still matter for long-term growth, but investors no longer need them to carry as much of the return burden. Built deliberately, that combination can create a portfolio that does not depend on the next payroll print, the next CPI surprise, or the next geopolitical headline..

Sources: Bloomberg, BlackRock, as of Sept. 12, 2026.

Markets will keep generating noise, headlines, and reasons to wait. But the math of starting yields, the breadth of investable debt, and the narrowing path to strong equity returns all point in the same direction: investors should focus on the right structural questions, rather than chasing the next data print. In today's markets, the edge comes from asking better questions.

articles.text:
The Sterling Bond Portfolio

The Bank of England’s cash ratio deposits and free capital and reserves are invested through the Sterling Bond Portfolio.

In this section

Bank of England Market Operations Guide
Bank of England Market Operations Guide: Our objectives
Bank of England Market Operations Guide: Our tools
Information for applicants
Information for participants
Results and usage data
Settlement and collateral management
Documentation
Consultations and other information

On this pageOverviewHow the Sterling Bond Portfolio is investedAnnouncing Sterling Bond Portfolio Purchases

Overview
The Sterling Bond Portfolio is an investment portfolio. Income earned on Sterling Bond Portfolio investments is used to grow the Bank of England’s capital base.
There are two main components of the Sterling Bond portfolio, the Free Capital and Reserves and the legacy Cash Ratio Deposit holdings.
The Free Capital and Reserves consists of the Bank’s own capital. Income earned on investments in the Free Capital and Reserves is used to grow the Bank of England’s capital base.
Under the legacy Cash Ratio Deposit scheme, deposit-taking financial institutions (i.e. banks and building societies) placed non-interest bearing deposits at the Bank of England. The scheme has now ended, but income from the residual portfolio is used to offset some of the payments due from financial institutions under the Bank of England Levy. The CRD gilt portfolio will reduce in line with its maturity profile, with over half of the gilts in the portfolio maturing by 2029, and the remainder steadily running off over the following 10–15 years. The Bank does not intend to sell the gilts from the CRD portfolio. While the Bank maintains the discretion to change this approach in the future, any change in approach would as far as possible be communicated well in advance, and ultimately designed to minimise any resulting impact on market functioning and/or conditions.
For more information please see the Bank of England Levy.

How the Sterling Bond Portfolio is invested
The Bank of England invests the Sterling Bond Portfolio in high quality sterling assets. Only the Free Capital and Reserves part of the portfolio is currently actively invested. This part of the portfolio is invested in gilts, with the potential to invest in highly rated supranational bonds.

We do not purchase ultra-short bonds (bonds with a maturity of less than three years). We do not currently purchase gilts with a residual maturity of over 22 years, and this is kept under review annually. The actual maturity profile of purchases may vary in order to adhere to the Bank’s internal risk limits.

The transactions we carry out to invest the Bank’s Free Capital and Reserves are separate from the purchases of sterling bonds that we make for monetary policy purposes through the Asset Purchase Facility.

Announcing Sterling Bond Portfolio Purchases
We provide transparency regarding Sterling Bond Portfolio purchases and holdings. Within the first few weeks of the quarter, we provide information about the stock of assets and the most recent purchases. For gilts, we provide information about the stock, and purchases made in the most recent quarter, both broken down by maturity bucket. We publish the total amount accounted for by supranational bonds. These announcements will be made on the Bank’s wires pages.
The latest figures are provided below. The below includes all holdings within the Sterling Bond Portfolio – the Free Capital and Reserves holdings, as well as the legacy Cash Ratio Deposit holdings.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesEnergyWill Oil Prices Decline as Middle East Supply Recovers?Oct 16, 2026ShareOil prices are expected to moderate over the next year as supply from the Middle East gradually recovers, according to Goldman Sachs Research. However, high prices may last longer than anticipated given the risk of renewed escalation in the conflict involving the United States, Israel, and Iran.
A barrel of benchmark Brent crude oil is expected to trade at $90 in December 2026, a slight increase from a recent forecast of $85, according to Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research. Struyven predicts the Brent price will average $80 a barrel in 2027.
“We maintain our base case that continued adaptation of Middle East supply will eventually reduce crude oil prices, while potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” Struyven and his team write in a report.
The supply of oil from the Middle East declined after the outbreak of the conflict, but exporters have adapted faster than expected. Our researchers estimate that Persian Gulf oil exports have rebounded and have been around their 2025 average since late September. That calculation includes an estimated four million barrels per day (mb/d) of “dark” exports—shipments on tankers that keep their transponders turned off to hide their movements.
Why are oil prices still high?

Given the recovery in exports from the Middle East, why is the price of oil still so high? A barrel of dated Brent crude scheduled for delivery in the next month is trading at more than $130, while benchmark Brent futures have recently been above $100.
“Physical prices remain elevated because escalation threatens supply while near-record-low global inventories fuel strong restocking demand,” Struyven writes.
For example, Iran or the Houthis could target oil infrastructure in the region, including ports, pipelines, and oil fields. Struyven estimates that spot prices for Brent crude include a nearly $25 risk premium on top of their fair value because supply could be curtailed and inventories could be drawn down further if there is an escalation.
At the same time, the sensitivity of global stocks and bonds to oil prices has created increasing demand for oil as a hedge for portfolios. This is another factor helping keep prices high.
When will global oil supply recover from the war in Iran?

Helping to keep prices in check, on the other hand, is the base case expectation that the balance between supply and demand in the global market for crude oil and other liquid fuels will shift to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026 and in 2027, the researchers find. Struyven describes this as “the key driver” of his team’s forecast for crude prices to moderate.
In fact, the oil market was nearly balanced in September. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that demand exceeded supply by just 0.3 mb/d that month, a dramatic easing from the 7.2 mb/d supply deficit in March.
The market’s return to balance is likely the result of higher non-Gulf oil production and a decline in global oil demand, offsetting the remaining deficit in production from the Persian Gulf. Also, the crude oil market was operating with a surplus in 2025. Global demand for oil declined by roughly 1.3 mb/d in September 2026 compared with the 2025 average as oil prices climbed, Struyven writes.
The recovery of Persian Gulf oil shipments, as producers adapt to the conflict there, also supports the base case that the oil market will soon be back in balance, Struyven writes. His team expects the supply of oil from the Persian Gulf to “trend higher as continued adaptation and added transportation resources—especially pipelines and a larger tanker fleet—support further gains,” he adds.
How has the war in Iran impacted global oil demand?

Finally, our commodities analysts say that the shock to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz is likely to continue to weigh on the global demand for oil, bringing the market nearer to balance. Oil demand in the third quarter of 2026 was down by 3.3 mb/d year-over-year, “with much of the weakness concentrated in China, the Middle East, and OECD Asia,” Struyven writes.
Our analysts estimate that global oil demand in the third quarter was nearly 4 mb/d below its hypothetical path if there had been no oil shock from the war in Iran. They assume that 80% of this gap between actual global demand and the counterfactual will unwind by the fourth quarter of 2027, with the dropoff in demand narrowing to 0.7 mb/d as the availability and affordability of refined oil products gradually improve.
“This forecast that oil demand largely recovers is directionally consistent with the demand recovery from prior negative oil supply shocks in 2011 and 2022, and our view that the weakness in Chinese petrochemicals oil demand is largely unsustainable,” Struyven writes.
Still, the expected 0.7 mb/d hit to global oil demand that is forecast for the fourth quarter of 2027 reflects the team’s finding that the oil shock has accelerated behavioral changes, especially in the use of existing electric vehicles and trucks in China instead of oil-based equivalents and in electric vehicle sales.

articles.title: Seeking Out AI’s Next Winners
articles.text:
Seeking Out AI’s Next Winners

Artificial intelligence (AI) is driving one of the largest investment cycles in
decades. The companies building the infrastructure that underpins AI — from
semiconductors and manufacturing equipment to cloud platforms and data
centers

October 2026
Author: Jay McLeod, Walter Scott Investment Analyst

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The scale of AI investment is
unprecedented, with much of
the spending directed toward
AI infrastructure.
The companies building
AI infrastructure remain
essential to the ecosystem’s
development. However,
history shows that as new
technologies mature, value
creation often broadens
beyond the businesses
supplying the tools.
Some of the most compelling
opportunities may lie with
businesses that can use AI
to strengthen established
competitive advantages,
improve customer outcomes
and enhance productivity.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is driving one of the largest investment cycles in decades. The companies building the infrastructure that underpins AI — from semiconductors and manufacturing equipment to cloud platforms and data centers — are attracting significant attention as organizations invest heavily to develop and deploy the technology.
However, history suggests that the ultimate beneficiaries of transformative technologies are not always the businesses supplying the tools. Electrification created substantial opportunities for power providers, but its broader economic impact came from the companies that successfully applied it to improve productivity and strengthen their competitive positions. AI may prove no different.
For long-term investors, the key question is where AI will have the greatest economic impact. While the foundations remain essential, some of the most compelling opportunities may emerge among businesses using AI to improve customer outcomes, operate more efficiently and reinforce strengths built over many years.
Laying the Foundations
Understanding that opportunity begins with the infrastructure enabling AI today. The scale of investment is unprecedented, with the world’s leading technology companies expected to invest approximately US$730 billion in capital expenditure in 2026 alone,1 much of it directed toward AI infrastructure. Every dollar invested creates demand across a much broader ecosystem, from semiconductor manufacturing and cloud computing to data centers, cybersecurity, industrial automation and the businesses that will use AI to operate more efficiently.
Much of the market’s attention has focused on the companies developing the technology. These businesses are likely to remain important to AI’s development, but the opportunity may extend well beyond them.
AI adoption depends on a much wider network of physical and digital infrastructure. Every new data center requires substantial investment in the facilities and systems that support its operation. Networks must be secured. As AI moves beyond the data center, intelligence needs to be embedded into factories, vehicles and industrial equipment.
From Infrastructure to Adoption
The companies building AI infrastructure remain essential to the ecosystem’s development. However, history shows that as new technologies mature, value creation often broadens beyond the businesses supplying the tools. The ability to apply technology effectively can become just as important as the technology itself.
Businesses across industries are incorporating AI into products and existing operations, using machine learning and advanced analytics to automate routine tasks, improve decision-making and increase productivity.
These applications are emerging across a range of industries, from financial software and energy to utilities, manufacturing and transportation. By embedding AI into established products and processes, companies can build on their existing strengths while improving how they operate and serve customers.
What Makes a Long-Term AI Winner?
AI is often most powerful when combined with advantages that are difficult to replicate. These include proprietary data, deep operational expertise, strong customer relationships and established market positions. Rather than disrupting such companies, it may reinforce their competitive positions by improving decision-making and enhancing customer outcomes.
For long-term investors, this reinforces the importance of looking beyond today’s headlines. In our view, some of the most compelling opportunities may lie with businesses that can use AI to strengthen established competitive advantages, improve customer outcomes and enhance productivity. Where new technology meets enduring business quality, the potential for long-term growth may be greatest.

About Walter Scott
Walter Scott is the global equities-focused investment firm within BNY Investments.

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making, and language translation.

articles.title: Who is at high risk from climate hazards? A new map to explore exposure and vulnerability
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Who is at high risk from climate hazards? A new map to explore exposure and vulnerability

Minh Cong Nguyen

Christoph Lakner

Ben Brunckhorst

Nisan Gorgulu

Esther Naikal

Stéphane Hallegatte

October 15, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The People at Risk from Climate-Related Hazards map shows where exposure to floods, droughts, heatwaves, and cyclones overlaps with socioeconomic vulnerability. / Image: World Bank Group

In June 2026, the World Bank Group introduced a new Scorecard indicator that counts the people most at risk from climate hazards. Our recent research shows that, under current climate conditions, more than half of the world's population — over 4.5 billion people — are likely to face at least one major flood, drought, heatwave, or cyclone within their lifetime. Combining these exposure estimates with household vulnerability data, we estimate that about 1.2 billion people in countries with available data are at high risk, rising to 1.5 billion—nearly one in five people—when extrapolated to the global population. What does this mean? It means that these people live in harm's way and would struggle to recover because they are poor, lack basic services, or have no safety net to fall back on.
Our updated People at Risk from Climate-Related Hazards (PARCH) map, available through the World Bank Group’s Geospatial Poverty Portal on the Poverty and Inequality Platform, shows both sides of that picture: where people are exposed to climate hazards, and where they lack the resources and services that help them cope. Users can explore climate hazard exposure and socioeconomic vulnerability separately, or see where the two overlap.
The earlier post gave the global picture. The new page lets users go further: zoom in on a country, choose which hazards and dimension of vulnerability to count, and see how the numbers have changed over time.

What you can do with the map
The map offers an interactive way to explore where climate hazards and socioeconomic vulnerabilities overlap. It helps identify areas where people face both exposure to hazards and challenges such as poverty or limited access to basic services, highlighting where interventions such as cash transfers, resilient infrastructure, or early warning systems may be most needed. Users can explore different hazards and vulnerability measures, compare patterns across locations, and examine how the results change with different selections. The map also illustrates why exposure to a hazard does not necessarily mean being at risk. It provides estimates of how many people are exposed to specific hazards and how many of them also experience poverty or gaps in basic services.

Two questions: who is exposed, and who is vulnerable?
The map keeps two questions apart. The first is who is exposed: people living where a severe flood, drought, heatwave, or tropical cyclone is likely enough, and strong enough, to do real harm. For example, the population living in areas where there is at least a 1 percent chance that floods exceed 0.5 meters each year, or a tropical cyclone of at least Category 2 strength. This way, data users can focus on places where dangerous hazards occur more frequently by adjusting the frequency threshold.
The second is who is vulnerable: people who lack something that helps them cope or recover from exposure to climate hazards. The map looks at seven areas, asking, for example, whether a household lives below the international poverty line of US$3.00 a day, whether anyone in it has completed primary school, and whether it has access to a bank or mobile money account, electricity, and safe drinking water. These thresholds are deliberately set at basic minimum levels, in the same spirit as the extreme poverty line, to pick out the people least able to recover from a shock.
People who are both exposed and vulnerable are counted as at risk. Users can choose ‘only hazards’ and the map will show the share of people exposed; choose only ‘areas of hardship’ and it will show the share who are vulnerable; or choose both and it will expose the share at risk.

Choose what counts
Users can choose which hazards and areas of hardship to focus on, as well as how to combine them.
Using OR counts people affected by ANY of the selected categories — for example, exposure to floods or heatwaves — while using AND counts only people affected by ALL selected categories, such as exposure to floods, droughts, and heatwaves together. As users make their selections, the page explains in plain language exactly who is being counted.
The World Bank Group’s Scorecard Vision indicator uses the broadest setting: it counts people exposed to ANY hazard AND vulnerable in ANY area.

What the map reveals
Risk looks very different from one region to the next. Exposure is highest in South and East Asia, but vulnerability there is lower, thanks to broader access to social protection and financial services among the factors that can reduce vulnerability. In Sub-Saharan Africa, the picture flips: 90% of people are highly vulnerable on at least one dimension, so almost everyone who is exposed is also at risk.
Hazards differ, too. Globally, more people are exposed to heatwaves than to any other hazard, while most rural people face agricultural drought, often while vulnerable in more than one way. The map lets users check these patterns for any country and see which hazards and hardships drive the numbers there.

Looking back in time
Step forward and back between years to see how things have changed. Progress since 2010 has been mixed. The share of people at high risk fell from about one in three to one in five, driven largely by declining socioeconomic vulnerability, while exposure to climate hazards remained broadly similar as a share of the population. Yet the number of people exposed grew by 461 million, reflecting in part population growth.
Keep in mind that the map counts people living directly in a hazard's path, not those affected indirectly. Countries without recent household survey data are not included, and the latest numbers trail the present by a few years.
These findings are only part of the story. The forthcoming Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report (3PR) will provide a deeper look at the scale and distribution of climate risks, and how exposure and vulnerability intersect to shape the challenges facing people around the world.

More information
• Explore the People at Risk from Climate-Related Hazards (PARCH) map at [URL].
• Read Who is most at risk? A global vision indicator to measure climate vulnerability for the global findings and what they mean for policy.
• See the indicator on the World Bank Group Scorecard.
• The WBG Scorecard methods note explains how people at high risk are counted, step by step.
• The World Bank Policy Research Working Paper sets out the research behind the method.
• An earlier Data Blog post looks at which regions are most at risk and how that compares with their greenhouse gas emissions.
• How to Cite the PARCH Map: World Bank. (2026). People at Risk from Climate-Related Hazards (PARCH) [Data or Interactive map]. Poverty and Inequality Platform, World Bank. Retrieved [Month Day, Year], from https://pip.worldbank.org/map/climate-risk

articles.title: Weekly links October 15: what does a coach do, beyond services vs manufacturing, what DiD to use, migration and jobs, and more…
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

Weekly links October 15: what does a coach do, beyond services vs manufacturing, what DiD to use, migration and jobs, and more…

David McKenzie

October 15, 2026

This page in:

English

English

· What is the magic sauce in coaching? On the Agency Fund blog, Patricia Andrews Fearon and Mahreen Khan summarize four different roles that “coaching” can play in programs like graduation programs (aspirational, behavioral and skill building, relational, and administrative), and how some of them are more easily scaled or substituted by technology than others.
· Can we skip the factory? asks Francisco Amodio in In Development. “Countries can succeed in attracting modern factories, integrating into global value chains and expanding exports, but that no longer seems to generate the broad-based employment growth that characterized earlier episodes of industrialization…If factories no longer absorb labor on the scale they once did, perhaps they should no longer sit at the center of governments’ development strategies.” He argues what matters is increasing consumer demand and multiplier effects “Recent research has shown that productivity improvements in consumer services can generate self-reinforcing growth…[but] Manufacturing’s historical contribution was that, in raising the productivity of firms, it raised the productivity of ordinary workers, at scale. It took millions of people with limited formal education and placed them in organizations where technology, specialization and scale made them dramatically more productive. That was the foundation on which the broader multiplier was built. There are reasons to believe that, while present, non-tradable services cannot generate virtuous cycles that are sufficiently large, broad and predictable to anchor a national development strategy.” He then argues to look beyond sector “But if traditional manufacturing no longer works as the primary engine of development, and if labor-absorbing services are unlikely to become one, governments need to think differently about industrial policy. They should not ask which sectors employ the most workers today but start asking a different question: Which sectors create opportunities for everyone else? The sectors that matter most may not be creating jobs within themselves but can trigger a chain reaction of investment, production and consumption far beyond their own boundaries.”
· Migration and jobs: On the CGD blog, Dany Bahar argues that “Development institutions should acknowledge that many of those jobs they want to create already exist, except that in other countries” – “without migration, the rich democracies would lose 121 million working-age people between 2020 and 2050, while Africa and South Asia together would gain more than a billion. Connecting the two requires visas, language preparation and recognition of qualifications.”
· A searchable archive of all job market posts: In case you missed it, we launched our annual blog your job market paper call. Pierre Biscaye (who had a post in our 2023 series) has helpfully put together a searchable database of all 260 of our posts, along with those in the ETRM series – so you can search by topic, year, country, etc.
· What DiD estimator should you use? A dashboard and Stata command to tell you: Clement de Chaisemartin shared this very nice dashboard which helps you think through which design case you are in, which estimators you can use, the relevant Stata, R and python commands, and a link to the relevant section of his textbook. He also notes a Stata command whichDIDshouldIuse that will use your data to characterize your design and suggest estimators.
· Overeducated and underemployed – this JPAL piece on Egypt’s labor market mismatch is a useful summary of the issues around educated youth wanting only certain types of jobs. But the conclusions made in the piece are to change the type of training- when there also needs to be a focus on entrepreneurship, competition policy, and how to increase the demand for educated labor.
· Using AI to enhance your survey instrument/lab-in-the-field experiment: on the ETRM blog Francisco Flores shares his experiences using Claude Code to assist him in his data collection through a lab experiment.

David McKenzie
