The $93,452 figure reflects 2024 benefit levels—the version CRFB used for comparability with the international data—and is adjusted for purchasing-power parity. CRFB’s accompanying analysis, which argues that the maximum benefit now reaches into six figures, uses 2026 figures: roughly $99,600 for a couple both claiming at the full retirement age, about $101,000 at 67, and roughly $124,000 if both claim at age 70. The gap between the $93,452 shown here and the six-figure 2026 maximum is almost entirely two additional years of cost-of-living adjustments and wage-indexed benefit growth; the PPP adjustment rescales other countries’ benefits into U.S. purchasing-power terms and leaves the U.S. amount essentially unchanged.

For more on wage-indexing, see Charles Blahous, “An Analytical Framework for Strengthening Social Security” (Mercatus Center, October 28, 2020), pp. 22-26 at https://www.mercatus.org/research/research-papers/strengthening-social-security. Because the initial-benefit formula is indexed to the national Average Wage Index rather than to prices, and wages typically outpace inflation, real benefit levels rise for each successive cohort of retirees, causing program costs to grow faster than the tax base.

C. Eugene Steuerle and Karen E. Smith, Social Security and Medicare Lifetime Benefits and Taxes: 2025 (Urban Institute/Tax Policy Center, 2025), Table 15 (married couple with two average earners), First-year Social Security benefit column. Figures are in constant 2025 dollars; the report assumes claiming at age 65.

SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, “Benefit Examples for Workers with Maximum-Taxable Earnings,” https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/examplemax.html. The maximum monthly benefit of $5,181 (2026) equals $62,172 annually for an individual and $124,344 for a two-earner couple.

Barry Bosworth, Gary Burtless, and Kan Zhang, Later Retirement, Inequality in Old Age, and the Growing Gap in Longevity Between Rich and Poor (Brookings Institution, January 2016), Table IV-6, “Estimated Life Expectancies and Expected Years of Benefits by Equivalized Household Earnings Deciles, 1920 and 1940 Birth Years,” 93, https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/bosworthburtlesszhang_retirementinequalitylongevityfullpaper.pdf.

National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, The Growing Gap in Life Expectancy by Income: Implications for Federal Programs and Policy Responses (Washington, DC: National Academies Press, 2015), https://doi.org/10.17226/19015, Summary (Tables S-1–S-3, Figures S-1–S-2) and Chapters 4–5. The committee finds that “the overall progressivity of lifetime benefits … declines markedly for both males and females” (p.8): net benefits as a share of inclusive wealth rise 7 percentage points for the top quintile of male earners and 5.4 points for the top quintile of female earners, while falling for the lowest earners (Summary, Table S-3). Tables S-1 and S-2 combine all four programs (Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and SSI); the report attributes the growing gap “primarily” to Social Security and Medicare, with the program-by-program breakdown in Chapter 4 and the net-benefit simulation method in Chapter 5. See also Congressional Research Service, The Growing Gap in Life Expectancy by Income: Recent Evidence and Implications for the Social Security Retirement Age, R44846, https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R44846.

Dana P. Goldman and Peter R. Orszag, “The Growing Gap in Life Expectancy: Using the Future Elderly Model to Estimate Implications for Social Security and Medicare,” American Economic Review 104, no. 5 (2014): 230–233 (finding “significant reductions in [the] progressivity” of both programs as mortality gaps widen). By contrast, the Congressional Budget Office found Social Security still progressive on a lifetime basis—the ratio of lifetime benefits to taxes for the bottom fifth of earners was roughly three times that of the top fifth—in Is Social Security Progressive? (December 2006); the widening longevity gap erodes, but does not by itself eliminate, that lifetime progressivity when Social Security is considered alone.

Congressional Research Service, Social Security: Revisiting Benefits for Spouses and Survivors, R41479, https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R41479. See also C. Eugene Steuerle and Jon M. Bakija, Retooling Social Security for the 21st Century (Urban Institute Press, 1994), on the one-earner-couple advantage, at https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v60n2/v60n2p37.pdf.

Medicare Part B and Part D are financed roughly three-quarters by general federal revenues, with beneficiary premiums set to cover about 25 percent of Part B and 25.5 percent of standard Part D costs. Congressional Research Service, Medicare Financial Status: In Brief, R43122, https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R43122; 2025 Medicare Trustees Report, https://www.cms.gov/oact/tr/2025. Higher-income beneficiaries pay income-related premium surcharges (IRMAA) that reduce but do not eliminate this subsidy; for 2026 the surcharges begin at modified adjusted gross income above $218,000 for married couples filing jointly (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, 2026 Medicare Parts B and D premiums).

Author’s tabulations from Congressional Budget Office, The Distribution of Household Income, 2022 (January 2026), supplemental Table Builder data, https://www.cbo.gov/publication/62300—elderly-headed households ranked by market income (which excludes Social Security), 2022. The cutoffs are the 80th/90th-percentile market-income thresholds by household size ($110,000/$160,300 for one-person, $155,600/$226,700 for two-person households); 7.0 million seniors fall in the top quintile and 3.9 million in the top decile.

C. Eugene Steuerle and Karen E. Smith, Social Security and Medicare Lifetime Benefits and Taxes: 2025 (Urban Institute/Tax Policy Center, 2025), Table 15 (married couple with two average earners), https://www.urban.org/research/publication/social-security-and-medicare-lifetime-benefits-and-taxes-2025. All amounts are expected present values in 2025 dollars (discounted at a 2 percent real rate, assuming benefits are claimed at age 65). The net figures for higher earners cited here are from the same report’s single- and couple-earner tables (e.g., Tables 3, 4, 16, and 17).

This section’s figures represent author calculations. Population counts and Social Security benefits by income group are derived from Congressional Budget Office, The Distribution of Household Income, 2022, Pub. No. 61911 (Washington, DC: Congressional Budget Office, January 2026), https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61911, using data for elderly-headed households ranked by market income (income before Social Security and other transfers), interpolated to household-income thresholds of $100,000 and $200,000 expressed in 2026 dollars (≈ $87,700 and $175,400 in 2022 dollars); on this basis roughly 12.8 million seniors, and 4.7 million above $200,000, have six-figure incomes before counting Social Security. Each program’s estimated 2026 share of spending on the group is held constant and applied to CBO’s fiscal-year 2027–2036 baseline outlays for Social Security and for Medicare Supplementary Medical Insurance (Parts B and D); see Congressional Budget Office, Medicare—February 2026 Baseline, Pub. No. 51302, https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2026-02/51302-2026-02-medicare.pdf, and the companion Social Security baseline, Pub. No. 51301, https://www.cbo.gov/about/products/baseline-projections-selected-programs. Because the thresholds rise only with inflation while real incomes grow faster, holding the share constant understates later years and is therefore conservative. Medicare figures represent the federal general-revenue subsidy—about 75% of Part B and Part D costs, net of enrollee premiums and income-related surcharges (IRMAA)—based on Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, “2025 Medicare Parts A & B Premiums and Deductibles,” fact sheet, November 8, 2024, https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/2025-medicare-parts-b-premiums-and-deductibles, and the 2025 Medicare Trustees Report, https://www.cms.gov/oact/tr/2025; Social Security figures are full benefits received. The higher totals in the final paragraph redefine income to include Social Security, using CBO’s income-before-transfers ranking.

Jessica Riedl, Spending, Taxes, and Deficits: A Book of Charts (Brookings Institution, April 2026), 61, https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/BudgetChartBook-2026.pdf.

Andrew G. Biggs, “An Agenda for Retirement Security,” National Affairs, Spring 2017, https://nationalaffairs.com/publications/detail/an-agenda-for-retirement-security.

For such a proposal, see Jessica Riedl, “A Comprehensive Federal Budget Plan to Avert a Debt Crisis,” Manhattan Institute, June 27, 2024, https://manhattan.institute/article/a-comprehensive-federal-budget-plan-to-avert-a-debt-crisis-2024.

Author’s calculation. Under current law the basic Medicare premium is set at 25 percent of program costs and the income-related adjustments (IRMAA) at 35 to 85%; the ten-year savings from raising these shares are estimated against the Congressional Budget Office’s Medicare baseline for enrollment and program costs. See Social Security Administration, “Medicare Premiums: Rules for Higher-Income Beneficiaries,” Publication No. 05-10536, https://www.ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10536.pdf; and Congressional Budget Office, “Medicare—Baseline Projections,” https://www.cbo.gov/topics/health-care/medicare.

Author’s calculation based on Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary, “Provision A9” (chain-weighted C-CPI-U cost-of-living adjustment below the income thresholds and no adjustment above them), Provisions to Change the Cost-of-Living Adjustment, table run 129, 2025, https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/solvency/provisions/tables/table_run129.html.

Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, “A Six-Figure Limit for Social Security,” Trust Fund Solutions Initiative, March 24, 2026, https://www.crfb.org/sixfigurelimit.

Author’s calculation. The benefit-reduction schedule is applied to the distribution of Social Security beneficiaries by post-retirement income and to aggregate scheduled benefits projected in the 2025 Social Security Trustees Report; the income distribution is drawn from Internal Revenue Service Statistics of Income data on Social Security benefits by adjusted gross income. See Board of Trustees, “The 2025 Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the Federal OASI and DI Trust Funds,” https://www.ssa.gov/oact/tr/2025/; and Internal Revenue Service, “SOI Tax Stats—Individual Statistical Tables by Size of Adjusted Gross Income,” https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-individual-statistical-tables-by-size-of-adjusted-gross-income.

Wendell Primus, Tara Watson, and Jack A. Smalligan, “Fixing Social Security: Blueprint for a Bipartisan Solution,” Brookings Institution, February 11, 2025, https://www.brookings.edu/articles/fixing-social-security-blueprint-for-a-bipartisan-solution/. The report estimates $241 billion from 2025-2035, so shifting the window to 2026-2036 likely nudges up the fiscal impact.

Social Security Administration, “Primary Insurance Amount,” Office of the Chief Actuary, 2026, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/piaformula.html. The official SSA formula is expressed in monthly amounts; those figures are annualized here to make them more relatable to readers.

Author’s calculation based on Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary, “Provision B3.14” (reduce the 15% PIA factor to 5%), table run 122, 2025, https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/solvency/provisions_tr2025/tables/table_run122.html. SSA scores this provision at roughly 0.37% of taxable payroll over 75 years; the figure here is converted to a share of GDP and assumes an earlier implementation than SSA’s phase-in.

Author’s calculation based on Social Security Administration, Office of the Chief Actuary, “Provision B1.5” (progressive price indexing that protects earners at or below the 60th percentile), table run 115, 2025, https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/solvency/provisions_tr2025/tables/table_run115.html. Converted to a share of GDP; assumes an earlier implementation than SSA’s phase-in.

Jessica Riedl, Spending, Taxes, and Deficits: A Book of Charts (Brookings Institution, April 2026), 66, 67, https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/BudgetChartBook-2026.pdf. Between 2026 and 2056, the federal government is projected to spend $192.6 trillion on Social Security and Medicare benefits—plus $73.7 trillion in resulting interest on the debt, while taking in $109.3 trillion in dedicated tax revenues.

Penn Wharton Budget Model, “How Federal Spending Is Distributed by Age Group in FY2025,” April 1, 2026, https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2026-04-01-how-federal-spending-is-distributed-by-age-group-in-fy2025/.

“Budget Basics: Medicare,” Peter G. Peterson Foundation, last updated August 20, 2024, https://www.pgpf.org/article/medicare/.

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, “What’s Not Covered by Part A & Part B,” accessed August 3, 2026, https://www.medicare.gov/providers-services/original-medicare/not-covered.

Imani Telesford et al., “How Does Health Spending in the U.S. Compare to Other Countries?,” Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker, March 11, 2026, https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/chart-collection/health-spending-u-s-compare-countries/.

Jessica Riedl, “The Progressives’ Empty Policy Agenda: Utopian Promises Are Not Backed Up with Serious Legislation,” Manhattan Institute, December 8, 2022, https://manhattan.institute/article/the-progressives-empty-policy-agenda-utopian-promises-are-not-backed-up-with-serious-legislation.

See Linda J. Blumberg et al., “From Incremental to Comprehensive Health Insurance Reform: How Various Reform Options Compare on Coverage and Costs,” Urban Institute, October 2019, https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2019/10/15/from_incremental_to_comprehensive_health_insurance_reform-how_various_reform_options_compare_on_coverage_and_costs.pdf; Congressional Budget Office (CBO) Director Phillip L. Swagel, “A Single Payer Health Care System That Is Based on Medicare’s Fee-for-Service Program,” testimony before the Committee on the Budget, U.S. Senate, May 12, 2022, https://www.cbo.gov/publication/58103.

Virtually all Medicare-for-All legislative proposals are skeleton bills that lack even the most basic operational details. See Jessica Riedl, “The Progressives’ Empty Policy Agenda: Utopian Promises Are Not Backed Up with Serious Legislation,” Manhattan Institute, December 8, 2022, https://manhattan.institute/article/the-progressives-empty-policy-agenda-utopian-promises-are-not-backed-up-with-serious-legislation.

articles.title: Daily: Higher inflation need not derail US assets
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Market Playbook | Asia beyond the AI trade (6 mins)Video: The AI Show | Is the AI trade under strain? (4 mins)Thought of the dayUS equities fell on Wednesday after September inflation came in higher than expected, increasing expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes. Headline inflation accelerated to 0.6% month over month from 0.4% in August, driven largely by a 9.1% rise in gasoline prices. More importantly, core inflation rose 0.3%, above the 0.2% increase consensus forecast for a second consecutive month, while the annual rate rose to 2.6% from 2.4%.Price pressures also extended beyond energy, with increases in shelter, airfares, vehicles, apparel, and technology-related goods. Markets raised the probability of an October hike to around 40% from about 20% before the release.The breadth of the increase makes the latest inflation strength hard for the Fed to dismiss. We now expect the Fed to raise rates in December and March, following its September move. We have also raised our end-December forecast for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.9%, from 4.6% previously.But this remains below Wednesday's closing level of 5.19%, and we do not expect the revised rate and yield outlook to undermine the positive outlook for US assets.The economic strength driving the Fed to raise rates is also supportive for equities. US GDP growth was close to 2.5% annualized in the first half of the year and likely near 3% in the third quarter, underpinned by a healthy labor market. While September payroll growth slowed to 29,000, the three-month average of 51,000 remained broadly in line with estimates of the pace needed to keep unemployment stable. Initial unemployment claims also recently reached a 10-week low, with no broad increase in layoffs, while the ISM manufacturing index remained firmly in expansion at 54.5 in September. This combination gives policymakers greater scope to focus on inflation without creating a high near-term risk of recession. For investors, the same resilience should support household income, consumer spending, and company profits, helping equities absorb moderately higher rates.Markets are pricing a more aggressive rate path than we expect. Investors are pricing roughly 3.5 further hikes, in addition to the one in September, while we expect just two more increases. Recent Fed communication also supports a more measured path: New York Fed President John Williams has said there is “no need for urgency,” although back-to-back higher-than-expected core inflation readings make October a closer call. We expect hikes in December and March, and then for rates to remain on hold until late 2027. The gap between market pricing and our forecast leaves scope for Treasury yields to decline if the Fed waits in October and subsequent data indicate that inflation pressures are stabilizing.Another strong earnings season should help equities withstand moderately higher rates. We forecast S&P 500 earnings per share growth of 28% for the September quarter, supported by AI demand, improvement in cyclical industries, and resilient consumer spending. We expect AI-related capex to rise 84% this year to USD 900bn, while semiconductor profits are expected to account for about half of the S&P 500 earnings growth in the third quarter. The earnings contribution should also extend beyond technology: The new-orders component of the ISM manufacturing index has remained in expansion for nine consecutive months, supporting the outlook for industrial profits. Notably, equities have historically performed well after the start of Fed tightening cycles. Across the 16 Fed hiking cycles since 1954, the S&P 500 gained an average of 10.8% in the year following the first increase, although past performance is no guarantee of future returns.So, we remain positioned for further equity gains while emphasizing broad diversification across sectors and regions. Strong economic growth and earnings should help equities withstand moderately higher rates. We also continue to see value in fixed income: Higher starting yields provide attractive portfolio income, while our expectation for the 10-year Treasury yield to decline to 4.9% by the end of December leaves scope for capital gains. We continue to favor a combination of cyclical and secular equity exposure alongside quality fixed income.

articles.title: Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?
articles.text:
Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?

AJ Cortese

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy | 12 Oct 2026

China is the world’s biggest builder of nuclear power plants, but unlike in other energy sectors it has not become a significant exporter of reactors. The international market is still dominated by Russia, with South Korea beginning to pick up some projects in the Middle East and Europe with its low-cost models. So far China’s only overseas projects are in Pakistan, a close strategic ally. For the moment Chinese nuclear firms have their hands full satisfying domestic demand. And while they have figured out how to make reactors relatively cheaply, the complexity and safety needs of nuclear projects mean they will never be able to gobble up world markets through ultralow prices, as Chinese solar, EV and battery firms have done. But over the next decade it is likely China will become an important nuclear exporter, thanks to its ability to combine low cost, quick construction time, and state-backed financing support.Also in this issue of New Energy Insight:

What you need to know
We place restrictions on the use of physical and digital images of Bank of England banknotes. This is to stop the creation of banknote copies that could accidentally be used for, or accepted as, payment and to avoid banknote images being used in an offensive or inappropriate context, including distortion to the monarch's image.
We give you consent to reproduce our banknotes, or a part of one, if you comply with our reproduction conditions (you do not need to contact us for permission). These conditions apply whether you are using our approved images or creating your own.
If you do not comply with our conditions, this may result in legal action.
Banknotes and the law
It is an offence to:

reproduce banknotes issued by us, or part of banknotes issued by us, on any substance or to any scale without our consent. For the avoidance of doubt, consent for items marketed as ‘Movie’, ‘Prop’ or ‘Training’ items can only be obtained if such items meet our reproduction conditions. We have described these in more detail in the FAQ below.
deface Bank of England banknotes (including printing, writing or impressing words, letters or figures on them).
without the Bank’s consent knowingly and in the course of a business make for sale or hire, import, offer, exhibit in public, or distribute a copyright work. Copyright in Bank of England banknotes is owned by the Bank of England and also contains works which the Bank uses under licence from public and private sector bodies.
without the Bank’s consent apply to goods or packaging, to sell, expose or distribute goods with the Bank’s registered trade mark (or a sign likely to be mistaken for it) with a view to gain for himself or another, or with intent to cause loss to another.
commit fraud by false representation and misuse the Bank’s name as an instrument of fraud.

Counterfeit banknotes
It is also an offence to:

make a counterfeit banknote without lawful excuse or with the intention of passing or tendering it as genuine.
pass or tender or deliver to another a counterfeit banknote knowingly or believing it to be counterfeit.
have custody or control of a counterfeit banknote intending to pass or tender or deliver it as genuine or have in custody or control without lawful excuse.
have custody or control of anything intending to or allowing any person to use it to make a counterfeit banknote intending to pass it as genuine or make or have anything designed or adapted to make a counterfeit banknote without lawful excuse.

Find more about counterfeit banknotes

These offences are covered under sections 14-17 and 18 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981 Opens in a new window, section 12 of the Currency and Banknotes Act 1928 Opens in a new window, section 107 of the Copyright Designs and Patents Act 1988 Opens in a new window, section 92 of the Trade Marks Act 1994, and section 2 of the Fraud Act 2006.
In addition, civil liability attaches to infringement of the Bank’s copyright, moral rights, and trade mark rights.
The list is non-exhaustive. The content of this website is provided for general information purposes only and it does not constitute in any way legal advice. If you are seeking specific legal advice, you may wish to contact a qualified legal professional at your own expense.

Our banknote reproduction conditions
If you plan to use an image of one of our banknotes, you must meet our conditions. These are different depending on whether you plan to produce a physical or digital reproduction.
These conditions apply whether you are reproducing:

all or part of a banknote
the front or the back of a banknote
current or withdrawn Bank of England banknotes.

Conditions for physical and digital reproductions
For physical reproductions, conditions 1, 2, 3 and 4 must be met and at least one of 5a) to 5c).
For digital reproductions, which include photos and filming of genuine banknotes. Conditions 3 and 4 must be met and at least one of 5b) to 5c).

Reproduction condition

Physical reproductions eg books, newspapers, banners.
Digital reproductions eg on screen only.

Free banknote images you can use
You can download images of banknotes that meet our conditions from our current banknotes image library Opens in a new window and our withdrawn notes gallery.
Both physical and digital reproductions must be used in line with our reproduction conditions as outlined above. Use of these images that fall outside these conditions may result in prosecution under UK legislation: Forgery & Counterfeiting Act 1981 (Part II).

Inappropriate or novelty reproductions
We do not allow inappropriate or novelty reproductions because they could affect the integrity or public image of our banknotes, cause offence, or infringe copyright.
You must not produce or use images of our notes in a way that we consider offensive, inappropriate or that undermines the integrity of the currency. This includes reproductions that:

show the destruction of banknotes (eg banknote images being cut or burned) or producing products that will be destroyed (eg tissues)
associate banknotes with inappropriate content (eg sexually explicit images)
distort the image of the monarch or any of the people featured on banknotes in a way that we think is disrespectful.

You must not produce or use images of our notes in a way that they could be mistaken as genuine. This includes reproductions that are:

double-sided
the same size as the actual banknote
printed on a similar material to that used for current Bank of England notes, unless it includes the word ‘SPECIMEN’ or is only showing half of the banknote.

You must not produce novelty versions of our notes, for example ones that feature a celebrity. This is because some notes that have been altered in this way have been mistakenly accepted as genuine. This restriction also applies to digital images, including for social media purposes.

Banknote reproductions frequently asked questions (FAQs)

If your reproduction does not have any of our banknote features on it, this would be considered more of a ‘voucher’ rather than a banknote and would not need to meet our reproduction requirements.

You need to check with the Debt Management Office Opens in a new window to find out what you need to do if you want to use images of banknotes issued by the Treasury between 1914 and 1928.

You can find out when our current banknotes were issued from ‘How to check your banknotes’. Find out when our withdrawn banknotes were issued from ‘Withdrawn banknotes’.

Some likenesses of our banknotes are marketed as Movie, Prop or Training notes. These look like Bank of England banknotes, but are often printed onto paper without any security features such as windows or holograms and may have misspelt wording. Examples include POONDS instead of POUNDS, Bank of Lagland instead of Bank of England. They may also contain phrases such as ‘Money for Prank’, ‘This is not legal to be used for Motion props’, or ‘This is play money for video movie, it is a toy’. Training notes are similar and will often have Chinese characters printed on the front and back.
To be legal reproductions, they must meet our reproduction conditions. Please see above for the full conditions.
All other likenesses which do not meet our reproduction conditions are illegal.

You should contact your nearest police station or call their 101 non-emergency telephone number if you discovered you are in possession of such a note. If you have information about someone reproducing banknotes illegally, please contact the police or phone Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111. As well as there being a risk of a reproduction offence, there is also a risk that a such notes may be counterfeit banknotes if they are reasonably capable of passing for a currency note.

Counterfeit banknotes

No, these are not Bank of England banknotes and no exchange for a Bank of England banknote can be made. Fortunately, such occurrences are extremely rare but please report any such cases to your local police.

articles.title: Going Back To An Old Tool
articles.text:
Going Back To An Old Tool

Charles Gave

Gavekal Research | 16 Oct 2026

Those who were managing money in the 1970s and are still active today may remember a tool developed by economist Arthur Okun during that decade: the so-called “Misery index”.The idea was simply to add the unemployment rate to the inflation rate to produce the Misery index, shown by the blue line in the left-hand chart below. At the time of writing, the US Misery index, based on the consumer price index, stands at 7.88, well below the critical level of 10.

CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsHedge Funds Are Cautious on Stocks amid Rates and Energy VolatilityOct 9, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptHedge fund positioning in equities for long-short strategies is at historically low levels amid ongoing volatility in interest rates and oil prices, says Mark Wilson, head of European Equity Franchise Sales and Hedge Fund Coverage in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. And even as investor scrutiny of French government borrowing grows, Wilson points out that there are investment opportunities in Europe in defense stocks and the energy independence theme. In The Markets podcast, he also discusses his outlook for mega-capitalization technology companies, stocks that benefit from German government spending, and US third-quarter earnings.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Wednesday, October 7th, and I'm here in the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Mark Wilson, who is head of European Equities, Franchise Sales and Hedge Fund Coverage within our FICC and Equities Group. Mark, thanks so much for joining us.
Mark Wilson: Thanks for having me, Chris.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Mark always great to have you here. Let's kick it off with the two headwinds in the market today.
Rates have been going higher, oil's been going higher. Europe, of course, is exposed to both. What is Europe exposed to most, and what are clients caring about most here?
Mark Wilson: In Europe, we are more vulnerable to the energy shock, and so the inflationary pressure is higher. If you think about the feed through to the markets, on six-month correlations, Euro stocks and 10-year Bund yields are about negative 70% correlated right now. You haven't seen that degree of negative correlation since back to the 1990s, so this is really a bit of a regime shift.
You're right to ask the question though, because obviously over the last couple of weeks we've had a much more idiosyncratic event in Europe. OAT spreads versus Bunds have blown out, and some of the social, but mainly political issues focused around the upcoming budget in France have been a real problem.
And so that's a major European specific issue, which is now there, and I think will be an ongoing feature over the next few months as we get towards the presidential elections in France in the first half of next year.
Ultimately, here and now, the two things which clients are most focused on are the price behavior of that OAT-Bund spread, and also the energy and gas inventory stock situation as we head in towards winter.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Mark, I get it. Oil more important than rates in Europe, but we also know that rates matter a lot to stocks. What are you seeing from clients around how rates are impacting stock valuation and positioning?
Mark Wilson: In terms of equities specifically, and this isn't just common to Europe, you've seen a very logical de-rating in equity markets. So, S&P multiple has come down, same is true in Europe. If you look at the more rate sensitive parts of the market, if you look at European renewables, for example, they've de-rated at well over 20%, and so you've seen this quite logical re-rating, de-rating specifically, in equities in response to higher rates.
You mentioned positioning. I think the most standout piece of information that we've been thinking about the last couple of weeks is just how much this has caused investors to reappraise their equity exposure and their equity risk. So, to put a number on this, we look at our fundamental hedge funds and their net exposure to the markets, and if you look at US-specific fundamental long-short clients today, their net length is in the north percentile on a one-year look-back.
It's at a two and three percentile on a three-year and five-year look-back. I think globally, global fundamental long shorts, these are anywhere from nought to 9% in terms of their net length and exposure to the market. So positioning has been really cut in response to rates and a bunch of other uncertainties that are out there.
Chris Hussey: Yeah. That, that is, that is a fascinating number, and nought, for our audience, is zero in England. So, let me expand, though, onto your energy comment, cause you make an interesting energy comment around how Europe is so exposed here. What many people don't realize is nat gas is the exposure as much as oil, and there have been, our commodities team has written about the potential for nat gas to really spike maybe five, ten times what you have to pay for nat gas in the US.
Are you seeing that in the industrial complex of Europe yet? Are you seeing these in the numbers, or is this just something people are scared about and it's not something in the numbers yet?
Mark Wilson: So it is in the numbers. Europe has definite competitive issues related to higher energy price costs, but this isn't new news. Europe trades cheaper. Part of it is this phenomena. These competitive threats are impacting industry and impacting the market.
I do think, though, the starting point matters, and Europe is a lot cheaper than other global markets, especially the US, and so some of that is already in the price, and I don't think it's an impediment to performance. European banks have beaten Mag Seven on a one-year, three-year, four-year look-back, and so there's the opportunity for performance, but it's certainly a competitive headwind and issue for Europe.
Chris Hussey: All right, Mark. 25 years ago, you were brokering me as a US analyst in Europe, so I know you know the US markets well. I know now --
Mark Wilson: You're aging us both, Chris.
Chris Hussey: Well, I know that you now know the European markets really well. So, I want you to compare US versus Europe here. Talk to me. Is Europe a value trap here with all the headwinds that they're facing, or is Europe an opportunity because it's so cheap?
Mark Wilson: So part of the European discount is certainly because of the index composition. We have less tech, we have less high-growth companies, and so inevitably there is a value element to it. The European market has been holding its own. I mean, it's kept up with the US this year, and part of that is because there are some clear investment cycles within Europe, within industrials, within renewables, within defense.
And what I'd say is the last few years have had a series of ongoing challenges to Europe, and Europe is slow to respond, but Europe is responding. So when you go back to COVID, there was a very large fiscal mobilization. Pretty soon afterwards, you had the Russia-Ukraine conflict and a real acknowledgment of a need for energy independence domestically.
Not long after that, you had the challenge of the Iranian conflict and the obvious heightened energy issues, and the AI cycle in of itself is a challenge to Europe to respond, to have its own deployment. And so, within Europe, these forcing mechanisms have continued to compound and to drive action and to drive response.
And so what I'd say is there are real themes to invest behind. That industrial theme, the rearmament of Europe, the drive for energy independence. And demographics has been one of the key issues for Europe and one of the key bear theses and one of the key planks of this value trap argument. This argument around demographics is destiny, I think, is somewhat being debunked when we think about the real power of AI and the deployment of AI, which will be very prevalent soon.
Demographics times agents deployed in the economy could be a real uplift to demographically challenged areas. And so I think there's increasing hope that actually the European market offers real opportunity, and as the strategy to respond to these challenges becomes more evident.
Chris Hussey: Okay. Third quarter earnings season is right upon us. We're going to kick it off in the United States tomorrow. Europe and the US, and the world more generally, is this peak earnings, or is this another opportunity to buy the earnings growth?
Mark Wilson: So, I'm pretty sure in the US we have peak earnings growth for the third quarter.
I think 27% earnings growth in the US, which is topping an amazing run in terms of earnings growth. And that's a clean earnings number, not taking benefit for all these one-time gains. Europe has actually been similarly strong, so we're forecasting 22% earnings growth year on year for the second half of this year.
It's aided a little bit by the energy benefit, so there's a big composition within the index of energy companies. Clean of the energy stocks, we're still looking at 15% earnings growth. So yes, I think the second derivative is slowing, especially in the US, but the earnings growth environment speaks to that high nominal growth environment that we spoke about at the beginning.
And given that we're now transitioning, about to transition into a new calendar year, and you've seen this very significant multiple compression, I do think where you see high nominal growth, where you see high corporate earnings and a more reasonable multiple, the market setup is still pretty favorable.
Chris Hussey: All right, Mark, let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Mark Wilson: So I'm going to give you two, Chris.
Chris Hussey: I love it.
Mark Wilson: The first one is US-focused. There's been a lot of commentary around the narrowness of the US market performance, and the largest stocks in the index have been the largest spenders.
There's been a huge amount of focus on the ROIC and the returns in which these spenders may garner, and I think that the momentum around real AI adoption is beginning to come through, whether it's Muse and other products in the consumer hands, or whether it's some of the enterprise adoption that we're beginning to see, the numbers are clear.
And I do think that some of the hyperscaler revenue growth is really lagging by three, four, five, six quarters, the very strong CapEx spend north of 100% that we're seeing, the very, very strong cloud revenue backlog that we're seeing, again, north of 100%. And so, I think as we begin to see some of this ROIC and the real return on spend come through, I absolutely want to be long US mega cap tech.
The second one is German fiscal spend beneficiaries. We know how strong the US growth story has been. German manufacturing PMIs are actually outpacing the US right now. Part of that is because as the rest of the world worries about fiscal space, the Germans are able to fiscally expand, and that's driving significant investment across broad industrial complex in Germany.
Through this year, you've seen 13 to 14% estimates revisions for EPS, yet those stocks have derated over 20% as well. So right now you're paying low teens multiple for a group of companies that is going to grow earnings in line with the US market over the next 12 and 24 months, so I want to be long that basket of German fiscal spend beneficiaries.
Chris Hussey: I love it. US mega cap tech, the harvesters, and the German fiscal beneficiaries. Great.
Okay, Mark, last question. What are you watching for next week?
Mark Wilson: So, first order I think is going to be CPI next Wednesday. It's going to be all important when we think about what might break this trend of, higher yields. Good news on the inflation front is going to be key.
I do think there's a window of opportunity for some news and a break in the Iran conflict given the timing now ahead of the midterms. And then I think all importantly, you mentioned it before, we're going to go into third quarter earnings. We've been in this unique period where really the micro is driving the macro, and I think as we learn more about the state of the AI trade as we go through corporate earnings, that's going to be all important.
Chris Hussey: Mark Wilson, you are always a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us.
Mark Wilson: Great to see you, Chris. Thank you.
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.

CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesChairman and CEO David Solomon Joins CNBC from Our Builders and Innovators SummitOct 15, 2026ShareDownload TranscriptDavid Solomon discussed the firm’s third-quarter earnings, his outlook for near-term dealmaking activity, and continued confidence in the IPO market. He also shared his views on AI innovation, and the need for human and enterprise accountability and risk controls.
Transcript:
Kelly Evans: Let’s begin with one of the standout bank names so far this earnings season. Increasingly so, as we see the raft of results today: Goldman Sachs. Yes, it’s down 2% in sympathy with other financials, but they reported their second-highest quarterly revenue ever yesterday. Earnings per share were $2 higher than the highest Wall Street estimates. Equities trading, investment banking, and wealth management all posting big year-over-year gains. Joining us now to weigh in on that, on what’s happening with AI financing, perhaps inflation, and so much else, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. And amid some speculation about his potential replacement, by the way, he’s out at Goldman’s Builders and Innovators Conference in San Francisco with that lady right there, Kate Rooney. Kate, over to you.
Kate Rooney: Kelly, thank you so much. We are here with David Solomon. It’s great to see you in person. Thanks for having us. We’re at the Builders and Innovators Summit. You were just saying, 15 years now. Is this the 15th year?
David Solomon: Well, first of all, Kate, thanks for being here. And this is a pretty great spot. It’s a nice place for you and I to have a day to be here and do this. But a little more than 15 years ago, we created this conference. The idea was to bring together really interesting entrepreneurs that were doing fascinating things and building interesting companies. I go back 15 years and I think about Travis Kalanick from Uber. I think about Dropbox. I think about Matthew Prince from Cloudflare. Drew Houston from Dropbox. These were some of the early entrepreneurs. They built great big companies. And here’s another class of 150 that are coming today. Some of these will be companies that, 10 years or 15 years from now, we’ll talk about. It’s been a fascinating place to see innovation and kind of the real engine of the U.S. economy and U.S. innovation.
Kate Rooney: We want to get your take on the pipeline. It’s a great setup. But Kelly mentioned earnings. You guys are coming off one of your strongest earnings reports in the firm’s history. I wonder about durability, though. You talked on the analyst call about volatility helping you guys, this tech supercycle as you described it. What is the earnings engine going forward for Goldman if things start to change or rates really start to take a bite here?
David Solomon: I think one of the things that’s missed in the narrative of day-to-day reporting and trading is that we’ve been working for eight years to really grow our franchise and increase the durability of our revenues and the diversity of our business. When we started eight years ago, we had a little less than $5 billion in management fees in our asset and wealth management business. We had $3.6 billion this quarter. We’re on a run rate of $15 billion in management fees. We have built now a firm where 45% of revenues are considered durable, recurring revenues.
Now, of course, when you look at IPOs and M&A activity, there’s a little more cyclicality around those activities. But go look at M&A revenues for the last 15 years. Every year there’s M&A revenue, some years more than others.
So we have a big, durable, diverse business in global banking and markets and asset and wealth management. And what we’ve done strategically as a firm is we’ve significantly lifted the floor of our business, both in terms of the revenue base and also the returns. I think investors are seeing that and rewarding that, and we feel very good about it.
I can’t tell you what’s going to happen in the next three months or six months. I actually look out and see some very big equity deals coming. I see some potentially very big IPOs coming. I look at our M&A backlog. We said on the call yesterday our backlog is still at very, very robust levels. I feel very good about revenue accruals we have coming in M&A. I also see the strategic activity and dialogues that are going on, and I feel pretty good about it.
Counter to that, we saw a slightly hot inflation print today. There are obviously four interest-rate hikes baked in. When you look forward, the 10-year Treasury has moved kind of 75 basis points in the last quarter and people are concerned about that. But we can operate in this environment pretty well, and we are operating well. We’ll just have to keep, quarter after quarter after quarter, showing people that our firm is a big, diverse, durable firm.
Kate Rooney: Well, one of the things you said on the call was that 5% on the 10-year didn’t scare you. What is the number that would make you nervous?
David Solomon: It’s all got to be put in context. But my point was, if you step back, the anomaly is the last 15 years after the financial crisis.
Kate Rooney: The record low.
David Solomon: Interest rates. That’s the anomaly. I mean, I’ve been around for 64 years. The anomaly is zero interest rates, not a 5% 10-year Treasury. Obviously, significant moves when they happen quickly upset markets and can have an impact. But you’re seeing the world absorb this move in the 10-year Treasury reasonably well.
Now, if you continue to have pressure because of deficits, the fact that there is big demand for capital, I think one of the things that’s going on is there’s a lot of demand for capital for this AI cycle, and that’s also competing with the fact that governments have borrowed very aggressively. There’s a lot of demand for capital for government. So there is some pressure around that that affects rates.
But I’m not scared about all this. This is the environment we live in and we operate in.
Kate Rooney: Well, one of the things that is different, I mean, you look back 20 years and sure, rates were the same, but the amount of AI capex that is now reliant on debt is very different than what we’ve seen in the past. We had Broadcom’s CEO recently saying that he thinks capital could be the biggest constraint and really a potential choke point for this entire buildout. What do you make of that?
David Solomon: I saw his comments. I have a different point of view. My point of view is there’s a lot of capital in the world. Think of the size of the market cap of public equities in the world. Think about all the savings that exist in the world. Think about the wealth that exists in the world. There’s a lot of wealth in the world.
That doesn’t mean that everybody that has an idea, everybody that has a data center, everybody that has a chip, can have unlimited capital at a very, very low cost to pursue their aspirations.
At the end of the day, capital is disciplined. It looks for returns. It goes to the best opportunities.
I would just say there’s a lot of capital out there. The financing markets, particularly in this country, the capital markets are extraordinary and developing new ways to access capital and package capital. I think some of the things we’re talking about doing right now, and our partnership with NVIDIA around compute, are super interesting.
Is there a crowding-out effect that at the margin affects the cost of capital a little bit? Absolutely. But that doesn’t mean the capital is not available. For good projects and good returns and good opportunities, there’s plenty of capital in the world.

articles.title: Daily: Quality bonds for income and diversification
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Investors Club: Managing inflation, UST yields and tech pressure (6 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Asia beyond the AI trade (6 mins)Video: The AI Show | Is the AI trade under strain? (4 mins)Thought of the dayUS bond and equity markets have remained volatile over the past 24 hours as investors weigh mixed signals on the outlook for AI alongside further evidence of persistent US inflation. Chipmaker TSMC offered a more cautious outlook, while the producer price index in the US rose 1.3% in September, its largest monthly increase in four and a half years and well above the 0.5% consensus forecast. Although energy accounted for much of the rise, prices also increased across a broader range of goods and services, adding to concerns that inflation pressures remain in the pipeline. The data followed a higher-than-expected consumer price index print in the US earlier in the week.But US Treasury yields declined, with the 10-year yield trading at around 5.09% and close to its lowest level in three weeks. Equity market volatility increased risk aversion and supported demand for high-quality bonds. While further yield volatility cannot be ruled out amid elevated inflation, heavy debt supply, and persistent fiscal concerns, we continue to rate fixed income as Attractive.Current market pricing of Federal Reserve tightening remains too hawkish. We now expect the Fed to raise interest rates by another 50 basis points over the next 12 months, but this remains more dovish than the current market pricing of nearly 90 basis points more. Recent comments from several Fed officials support a more gradual tightening, with Vice Chair Philip Jefferson stating there is no immediate urgency to hike again, and New York Fed President John Williams saying he sees no need for further rate increases in 2027. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly has also signaled little urgency in adjusting policy rates. This suggests to us that Treasury yields should decline from their current levels as markets scale back their expectations, leaving scope for capital gains in bonds.Elevated starting yields offer an attractive income cushion. Elevated starting yields provide a stronger income base and have historically been a good indication of subsequent total returns. This income can also cushion portfolios against further increases in yields. Our analysis indicates that 2-, 5-, and 10-year US Treasury yields would need to rise by around 257, 113, and 65 basis points, respectively, for capital losses to offset the income earned. We therefore believe investors can benefit from attractive portfolio income even if yields remain volatile.Quality bonds offer diversification and stability in a portfolio. The latest Treasury rally underscores how high-quality bonds can help stabilize portfolios by providing diversification when risk assets come under pressure. Our analysis of US stock and bond portfolios found that a conventional 60/40 portfolio had a maximum recovery period of 4.2 years from bear market drawdowns since 1945, compared with 6.2 years for an all-equity portfolio. Medium- to long-duration quality bonds may also appreciate if tighter monetary policy slows growth or reduces longer-term inflation expectations, helping to offset weakness elsewhere in a portfolio. This combination of income, potential price appreciation, and diversification can help smooth overall portfolio returns across different market environments.So, fixed income should remain a key component in a well-diversified portfolio, and we see opportunities across regions and market segments. Investors should calibrate both credit risk and duration to their objective and investment horizons. More income-focused investors may turn to short-maturity bonds to reduce duration risk, while those who are willing to tolerate volatility may consider select tactical opportunities in medium- to long-duration high-quality bonds. We remain cautious on the longest maturities given fiscal concerns and rising AI-related issuance.

articles.title: Commodity prices to hit record highs before easing through 2027
articles.text:
Blog

14 Oct 2026

Commodity prices to hit record highs before easing through 2027

Global commodity prices are set to reach an all-time high in Q4 2026 as disruption to Middle Eastern energy supplies continues to push prices higher. While we expect prices to ease through 2027, the recovery will be uneven, with significant differences across energy, metals and agricultural markets.

We forecast the S&P GSCI spot index to rise by 28% in annual-average terms in 2026, reaching a record high in Q4. The increase is driven primarily by higher energy prices, although the impact is spreading across commodity markets as rising fuel, electricity and transport costs feed into production.

There are parallels with the supply shocks following the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, when disruption to production, trade and logistics affected multiple markets simultaneously. However, the current shock is particularly concentrated in energy, and the outlook for individual commodities differs considerably.

Our central forecast is for aggregate prices to decline gradually through 2027 as Middle Eastern exports recover and supply constraints ease. But the pace of that adjustment will depend on how quickly physical supply is restored and whether geopolitical risks subside.

Chart 1: The GSCI is forecast to hit its highest level in Q4 2026 due to energy supply

Oil prices to remain above $100 until mid-2027

Oil remains at the centre of the current commodity price shock. We now expect Brent crude to average above $100 per barrel through Q2 2027, following attacks on Red Sea export infrastructure and a more persistent geopolitical risk premium.

September’s attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline highlighted the vulnerability of alternative export routes. The pipeline had been carrying around 4 million barrels per day, allowing Saudi exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Although operations have partially resumed, the risk of renewed disruption continues to support prices.

Importantly, as export capacity recovers, the main obstacle to price normalisation is increasingly the geopolitical risk premium rather than physical crude availability. Even with sufficient supply reaching the market, continued uncertainty over regional security could keep prices elevated.

We still expect Brent to converge towards its long-run equilibrium of around $60 per barrel, but now anticipate this adjustment will be completed in 2029 rather than 2028.

The impact also extends beyond crude oil. Tight refined-product markets have pushed European diesel refining spreads close to $100 per barrel, amplifying transport and production cost pressures. Higher fuel costs affect diesel-intensive mining operations, agricultural machinery and freight, transmitting the energy shock into other commodity markets.

Natural gas faces a winter squeeze, with significant uncertainty

Natural gas remains particularly exposed to Middle Eastern disruption because LNG exports are harder to reroute than crude oil.

Qatar and the UAE accounted for around 20% of global LNG trade before the conflict, but exports have effectively been trapped inside the Strait of Hormuz since March. LNG-linked gas prices in Europe and Asia are consequently around 130% above pre-conflict levels, compared with a 45% increase in Brent.

We expect gas prices to remain elevated through winter 2026–27 before easing as global LNG supply expands. However, the outlook is particularly sensitive to weather, storage levels and further supply disruption.

European gas inventories are at their lowest for this time of year in over a decade. Our baseline assumes storage will fall to just 17% of capacity by 1 April 2027, leaving the market exposed to a colder-than-expected winter.

A cold spell combined with disruption to US LNG or Norwegian pipeline supplies could push prices towards $35/MMBtu. Conversely, mild weather and continued growth in global LNG supply could limit the winter peak to around $21/MMBtu.

Europe is nevertheless better positioned than during the 2021–22 energy crisis. Gas demand is around a fifth below its 2021 level, while expanded LNG import capacity provides greater flexibility.

These contrasting outcomes illustrate why the trajectory of gas prices depends not just on Middle Eastern exports, but also on Europe’s ability to manage winter demand and secure alternative supplies.

Chart 2: A cold winter could squeeze EU natural gas inventories

Gold prices to rise as investment demand remains strong

Gold has not benefited from the Middle East shock as much as might have been expected. Higher oil prices have revived inflation concerns and reinforced expectations of tighter US monetary policy, supporting bond yields and the dollar and partly offsetting safe-haven demand.

Nevertheless, central-bank purchases and investor demand continue to underpin prices. We expect gold to average around $4,515 per ounce in 2026, rising to $4,840 in 2027 and $5,140 in 2028.

We anticipate fewer Federal Reserve rate increases than financial markets currently expect, reducing upward pressure on yields and the dollar. Meanwhile, emerging-market central banks should continue diversifying their reserves, providing sustained support to demand.

The outlook elsewhere in the precious-metals complex is more mixed. High silver prices are encouraging recycling and substitution, particularly in solar applications, while constrained mine supply supports platinum. Palladium faces weaker structural demand as internal-combustion-engine vehicles gradually lose market share.

Copper and aluminium to correct before strengthening again

Copper and aluminium prices should decline in early 2027 as supply disruptions ease and trade distortions unwind. However, prices are expected to remain close to historically high levels.

For aluminium, Gulf production and exports are recovering, while additional output from China and Indonesia has helped offset earlier losses. Nevertheless, China’s proximity to its effective capacity ceiling should limit further supply growth.

Copper presents a different picture. Despite weak mine production, stronger refined output and recycling have kept the global refined market in surplus. Yet regional availability remains distorted by US trade policy uncertainty.

Around 80% of exchange copper inventories are concentrated in the US, as expectations of import tariffs have encouraged metal to flow into the American market. Greater clarity over tariff policy could reduce the incentive to hold inventories there, easing tightness elsewhere and putting downward pressure on prices.

This distinction between global supply conditions and regional trade distortions is important in understanding the near-term outlook.

Further ahead, structural demand provides support. Investment in electricity grids, electrification and data centres should underpin copper consumption, while aluminium benefits from transport, aerospace and power infrastructure investment.

Combined with constraints on aluminium capacity expansion and persistent challenges increasing copper mine supply, these demand drivers should allow prices to strengthen again later in 2027.

Grain inventories cushion geopolitical and weather risks

Agricultural markets face a different balance of risks. Higher energy and fertiliser costs, Black Sea disruption and adverse weather could support prices, but relatively comfortable inventories should limit the impact.

We expect grain prices to remain broadly stable through 2027, following strong previous harvests that left sufficient stocks to absorb moderate supply disruptions.

Attacks on Black Sea ports and shipping continue to disrupt exports and raise freight costs. Meanwhile, a strong El Niño could threaten rice production in Asia and wheat yields in Australia.

However, fertiliser prices have eased as Gulf exports recovered and China relaxed some export restrictions, reducing agricultural input cost pressures.

Supply recovery will determine the pace of the correction

The aggregate commodity price cycle is approaching a peak, but the adjustment will vary significantly across markets.

Oil and gas prices should decline as disrupted supply recovers, while base metals face a near-term correction before structural demand and supply constraints become more supportive. Gold is expected to move higher, whereas comfortable inventories should limit grain price increases.

The key uncertainty is the pace of supply normalisation. A faster recovery in Middle Eastern exports could accelerate the decline in energy prices, reducing transport and production costs across other commodities. Conversely, renewed attacks on regional infrastructure could keep prices elevated and delay the correction.

For businesses exposed to commodity markets, understanding these differences will be critical. The challenge is not simply anticipating when prices will peak, but identifying which pressures are temporary, which may persist and how alternative supply scenarios could change the outlook.
