articles.title: A divided southern flank faces Trump 2.0 and NATO 3.0 | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

A divided southern flank faces Trump 2.0 and NATO 3.0

Bruno Cardoso Reis

Bruno Cardoso Reis

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Center on the United States and Europe

October 12, 2026

A focus on how much NATO members on the southern flank are spending on defense obscures the question of whether they are effectively contributing to strengthening the alliance.
Southern NATO member states too often focus on what divides them rather than what they might do better together.
By expanding their engagement through minilateral arrangements, southern members could contribute more to NATO 3.0.

9 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The Trump administration and some Northern and Eastern European allies have criticized southern NATO members for not taking the Russian threat—and the demands of alliance solidarity—seriously. This criticism matters more as NATO becomes, in Secretary General Mark Rutte’s words, “more European”: a “NATO 3.0” in which European allies are expected to do more while the United States does less. Yet every NATO member on the southern flank has increased defense spending since 2016, and even more since 2022. Even Spain, the only member to resist NATO’s new target of spending at least 5% on defense and defense-related investments, has nearly doubled defense spending as a share of GDP since 2022, despite Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s public defiance of U.S. President Donald Trump. The focus on how much southern NATO members spend, however, risks obscuring a more important question: how effectively are they contributing to regional security?
Southern NATO members—Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, Albania, Greece and Turkey—perceive the Russian threat differently than their northern and eastern counterparts. Public opinion polls suggest that while majorities in most countries on the southern flank reject Russia’s war of aggression and therefore support aiding Ukraine, they do not see Russia as an imminent threat to their own security. This helps explain why most Southern Europeans do not seem to support massive and rapid increases in defense spending. The more critical issue is the southern NATO members’ inability or unwillingness to coordinate their strategic assets. Currently, southern NATO member states are too often focused on what divides them rather than what they might do better together.
A divided southern flank
The integration of Europe’s southern states into the Atlantic alliance was never problem-free. Italy and Portugal were both founding members of NATO in 1949, but Italian membership was opposed by those who wanted an exclusively Atlantic-facing alliance. Portugal, because of the Azores Islands, was vital for control of the Atlantic, but the authoritarian Estado Novo government was an awkward fit in an alliance of liberal democracies. NATO’s 1952 enlargement to Greece and Turkey was seen by critics as importing an unresolved conflict into the alliance and as moving it too close to the Middle East. Spain joined NATO in 1982, but its continued membership required a national referendum four years later, in which 52.5% voted in favor and 39.8% against. Indeed, resistance to NATO membership has arisen also from within the south: in Spain, Portugal, France, Italy, Greece, and Turkey, there have been political movements, chiefly on the far left or right, arguing that neutrality serves the national interest better. They may grow, fueled by a global wave of nativist populism.
While it’s apparent that Europe’s southern alliance members have to quickly catch up after years of relatively low defense spending, this is not due to their lack of commitment to NATO. Instead, it is explained by these countries’ low threat perceptions combined with pressure from key allies (like Germany) during the 2011 fiscal crisis to enact draconian spending cuts. Greece was the exception; ironically, at the time, Athens was harshly criticized for “overspending” on defense, despite its location in the conflict-prone Eastern Mediterranean. Now the South is catching up with a degree of fiscal caution that may be excessive, but its recent experience with budgetary crises makes it understandable. Domestic politics also matters: right-of-center governments tend to spend more on defense. But what matters most, given tight budgets, is threat perception: proximity to an aggressive Russia correlates well with how much of GDP European states are spending on defense.
Although Russia’s gray-zone warfare in Europe is intensifying, Southern Europe has seen significantly fewer serious incidents than Northern or Eastern Europe. Portugal, for instance, has recorded Russian cyberattacks, while Spanish authorities believe Russian operatives carried out a targeted assassination. Nonetheless, the southern flank faces growing risks: Moscow backs anti-Western military juntas across the Sahel, whose violence has previously triggered refugee flows northward, while increased Russian naval activity in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean threatens critical subsea cables. According to reporting by El Mundo, the CIA has alerted European governments of the risk of drones being launched against Spain, France, and Italy from the Russian shadow fleet operating in the Mediterranean.
Working around Southern Europe’s divisions
Of course, Southern Europe is not homogeneous. This is where the flexibility of minilateralism becomes so useful. For instance, bilateral relations with Washington vary across NATO’s southern flank. They have visibly improved with Turkey and Greece in recent years but have deteriorated markedly with Spain and, more recently and to a lesser extent, Italy. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is ideologically close to Trump, has made clear that “being your friend has certainly not helped” her popularity.
Smaller powers such as Portugal and Greece have too much to lose from a rupture with the United States, while medium powers such as France, Spain, Italy, and Turkey appear to believe they have more room to hedge or criticize the current administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Greece and Portugal in October 2026 publicly displayed appreciation for allies that had allowed the United States access to military bases denied by other countries. The visits also sought to reinforce these partnerships, including through weapons procurement.
From spending to strategy
Where does this leave the southern flank as the Trump administration compels NATO 3.0 to take on the burden of Europe’s conventional defense? Many Southern Europeans hope that this is an episode in the alliance’s long history, rather than a period of permanent U.S. unreliability or hostility. But hope is not a strategy. There will be no return to the past. Europe will need to do more than increase investment in additional capabilities: It will need to develop independent strategic thinking and conceive of a European way of warfare that does not rely on or attempt to replicate U.S. weapons systems and doctrines. Finally, Europe’s collective action problem in foreign and defense policy means that coalitions of the willing are the most realistic shortcut to reordering regional security without significant U.S. involvement. Unfortunately, this is precisely where Southern Europe is weakest.
Turning capabilities into collective strength
What could be done to improve security coordination in Southern Europe? One existing minilateral format already covers most of it: the so-called Med9, inaugurated as the Med7 in 2016. It brings together all of the European Union’s (EU) southern states, from Portugal to Cyprus, and held its latest annual summit of heads of government in October 2026 in Split, Croatia. Turkey, as well as other NATO members not in the EU, are not part of this grouping, whose original purpose was to offer a counterpoint to the “Frugal Four” (Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Sweden) on EU economic governance. Its scope, however, has since widened, with recent agendas and final statements increasingly alluding to security challenges.
Regular meetings of Med9 defense ministers would be the next logical step. They could provide an opening for political dialogue to bridge differences in threat perceptions across the south, particularly between the Eastern and Western Mediterranean, and to identify shared security concerns. These should include maritime security, from port and coastal defense to securing key routes; air defense, including counter-drone capabilities; threats from the Sahel and North Africa; migration management; and the protection of critical infrastructure.
If a Europeanized NATO is to be more than a slogan, southern NATO commands and brigades must be revised, turning capabilities that exist largely on paper into fighting forces that can operate with European assets and troops. Some of the most relevant challenges are discussed by Carlo Masala and Michael O’Hanlon.
Subregional groupings could help. The 5+5 Defense Initiative brings together 10 littoral nations in the Western Mediterranean—five European and five North African—to discuss soft security and confidence-building. Its four NATO members—Portugal, Spain, France, and Italy—could and should build on that experience by coordinating regular staff talks, exercises, and planning for regional deterrence and defense. Ideally, a similar arrangement would be created for the Adriatic and the Eastern Mediterranean, if Greece and Turkey could be convinced to work together.
So far, though, new developments have been limited and bilateral. Portugal and Greece, for example, have decided to buy new frigates from Italy and to hold defense consultations with Rome. Some Southern Europeans, sensitive to the negative perceptions often associated with the south, seem to fear being associated with any southern grouping. This represents a significant missed opportunity.
Southern European countries could contribute more to NATO 3.0. They could provide strategic depth for reserves, production, and logistics against threats to the east or north; play a key role in providing maritime security and securing routes for critical raw materials; and act as a barrier against threats from the south. It would require not just more investment but a degree of regional coordination that Southern Europe has not even begun to pursue. At a time of proliferating tensions and conflicts—and an explosion of minilateralism elsewhere in Europe—this inertia is baffling. The alternative is stark: Southern Europe will continue to be strategically defined by others and potentially defended by no one. Southern Europeans should stop complaining about being misrepresented and misunderstood by others and start getting their own house in order.

Author

Bruno Cardoso Reis

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Center on the United States and Europe

articles.title: Supporting the growth of the West Midlands as a UK transport hub | Macquarie Group
articles.text:
Supporting the growth of the West Midlands as a UK transport hub

Link copied to clipboard

Macquarie is supporting Birmingham Airport's next phase of growth and strengthening the West Midlands' role as a global gateway for trade, investment and connectivity

Swipe for more

SectorInfrastructureSub-sectorTransportLocationUnited Kingdom

Opportunity

The UK’s West Midlands region is home to more than four million people and a £117 billion economy.1
Its central location, strong transport links and manufacturing heritage make it a key gateway for business, trade and investment across the UK. The region accounts for approximately 9 per cent of the UK’s goods exports2 and is one of the leading destinations for foreign direct investment outside London.3
Birmingham Airport directly connects customers and cargo to over 140 destinations in over 40 countries and is accessible to over half of the population of England and Wales within a two-hour rail or road journey. The airport helps attract global investment, supports the region's advanced manufacturing, aerospace and automotive sectors, and connects UK exporters with international markets.
It is also a major contributor to the regional economy, supporting thousands of jobs and helping drive long-term prosperity across the region.

Approach

In November 2025, Macquarie Asset Management (MAM), through its managed funds, acquired a stake in Birmingham Airport as part of a wider transaction that also included investments in Bristol Airport and London City Airport.
MAM brings more than 20 years of experience investing in and managing airports globally, and more than 35 years of experience investing in infrastructure in the UK. This includes a decade of ownership of AGS Airports, comprising Aberdeen, Glasgow and Southampton airports.4
Partnering with Birmingham Airport's management team, MAM will support the next phase of its development and long-term growth ambitions. A key focus is the airport’s draft 2041 Master Plan, which sets out its vision for the next 15 years.
Developed in collaboration with key stakeholders, including local government and regional partners, the Master Plan defines how the airport will evolve to serve an increasing number of passengers and airlines while focusing on sustainability, operational efficiency, and an enhanced passenger experience.
Through its investment, MAM is supporting the airport's sustainability ambitions, including its target of achieving net zero carbon emissions from direct operations by 2033. The airport's Sustainability Strategy 2026-2030 sets out a roadmap to achieve this target through initiatives being undertaken across airport operations, alongside collaboration with suppliers and partners and local communities.5

Outcome

In October 2026, the airport released its draft 2041 Master Plan for public consultation. It sets out how the airport proposes to serve up to 30 million passengers a year by 2041 and grow its economic benefit to the West Midlands and UK more widely.6
Under its proposed investment of more than £2 billion, the airport is forecast to support approximately 107,400 jobs across the West Midlands and contribute around £7.2 billion annually to the regional economy by 2041, roughly doubling the current levels.7
Alongside more than 13,000 on-site roles by 2041 across airport operations, airlines, retail, hospitality, cargo and other areas, wider employment will be supported through the airport's supply chain, business connectivity, freight activity and inbound tourism.
By increasing capacity and strengthening connectivity, Birmingham Airport is positioned to play an even greater role in supporting the long-term growth of the West Midlands.
As a strategic regional asset and critical piece of national infrastructure, the airport will continue to connect people, businesses and markets, fostering employment, investment and economic activity in local communities and across the region.

articles.title: Inflation-linked bonds: protection in a more volatile inflation world - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Geopolitics, energy security, changing supply chains, fiscal policy, climate investment and increased infrastructure and AI spending could all contribute to a structurally more volatile inflation environment.

Andy Craig, Co-head of the Investment Insights Centre, talks with Elida Rhenals, Co-head of Inflation and Senior Portfolio Manager within the Global Fixed Income team, about the role inflation-linked bonds can play in today’s investment landscape.

For investors, inflation-linked bonds can provide inflation protection within a fixed income or multi-asset portfolio. Their cash flows are linked to realised inflation, while their performance is also driven by real yields and changes in inflation expectations.

Elida highlights that real yields are now significantly more attractive than during much of the past decade so investors may be able to earn a positive real yield while retaining protection against higher-than-expected inflation.

“With inflation outcomes becoming less predictable, we believe a global, actively managed approach can help investors navigate different markets, maturities and inflation dynamics.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast to discover the role inflation-linked bonds can play in an investment allocation.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Elida Rhenals

Andy Craig: Hello and welcome to this week’s BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing inflation-linked bonds and the role they can play for investors in view of the current macroeconomic environment and outlook. I’m Andy Craig, Co-head of the Investment Insights Centre. I’m joined today by Elida Rhenals, Co-head of Inflation and a Senior Portfolio Manager within the Global Fixed Income team. Welcome, Elida, and thank you for joining me today.

Elida Rhenals: Hi, thank you for having me.

AC: Let’s start by talking about the macroeconomic picture – on why, in our view, this is an environment which is favourable for inflation-linked bonds. Inflation has reappeared on investors’ radars. We have the situation in the Middle east, the crucial choke points for the delivery of petrol, but there’s still a lot of uncertainty. How do you see the current environment for inflation? And why do you think investors should consider inflation-linked bonds in this context? Isn’t it getting a bit late for the trade into inflation-linked bonds? We’ve been here for some time now.

ER: Inflation has clearly come back into investors’ radar but I would argue that the story goes beyond the latest energy shock. For a couple of years now, markets have been debating whether inflation was just a temporary consequence of the pandemic and the subsequent supply chain disruptions, or whether we have moved into a structurally more volatile inflation environment.

Our view has consistently been closer to the second option, and what has happened recently is a good illustration of why. The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has once again shown how quickly an external shock can change [the] inflation outlook. Energy prices moved sharply higher and central banks suddenly had to reassess a policy path that at the beginning of the year looked much more straightforward.

The lesson for investors is not necessarily that inflation will remain permanently high, it’s that the distribution of inflation outcomes has become much wider; volatility is higher.

That distinction is very important, in our view. We have moved away from the environment we experienced during the decade before the pandemic when inflation was persistently below target and investors could almost take price stability for granted.

Today there are several forces that can generate more inflation volatility – geopolitics, energy security, changing supply chains, climate-related investment, fiscal policy and of course significant infrastructure and AI related investment.

So, late or not to invest in inflation in bonds? I would say this is the wrong way to frame the question. Inflation in bonds should only be considered when you expect the next inflation print to surprise to the upside. They are an asset class that allows investors to build inflation protection into a fixed income or multi asset allocation.

The other important point today is valuation. Real yields are significantly more attractive than they were for much of the last decade, so investors are no longer necessarily sacrificing yield to obtain inflation. You can earn a positive real yield while retaining that protection if inflation turns out to be higher than expected.

And that creates a much more interesting starting point to go into the asset class.

AC: You’ve mentioned real yields and that brings us into the functioning of inflation-linked bonds. Can you talk us through how inflation-linked bonds work? They’re obviously very different from nominal bonds. They provide inflation protection. How do they actually function?

ER: The first thing to clarify is a very common misconception. Inflation in bonds do[es] not simply go up whenever inflation goes up. At their core, they are still bonds. The difference is that their cash flows are linked to an inflation index. This means the principal or the coupons are adjusted according to realised inflation. That’s what we call inflation accrual. So, over the life of the bond, the investor receives compensation for the inflation that actually occurs. But the market price is also driven by interest rates, just like any other bond.

A useful way to understand the market is to split a nominal government bond yield in[to] two components – a real yield and expected inflation. That’s what we call breakeven inflation. If you compare a nominal government bond with an inflationary bond of similar maturity, the difference between the two yields give you an approximation of the inflation rate that the market is pricing over that period.

That means there are really two engines of performance.

The first is the real yield component. If these real yields fall, the price of an inflation bond rises like any other bond. If [the] real yield rises, its price falls, and then sensitivity to those movements depends on duration, exactly as it does for a nominal bond.

The second one is the inflation component. If inflation rises relative to what was previously priced by the market, inflation bonds tend to outperform nominal bonds. If inflation falls versus market expectations, the opposite will happen.

This is why saying “I think inflation is going to be 2.5% or 3%, therefore I should buy an inflationary bond” is not enough. The question that an investor should ask is “what inflation is already priced by the market?” Today, the market pricing for future inflation is slightly above 2%.

If you believe realised inflation will be persistently higher, that can create an opportunity. And we think it does today.

That is precisely where active management becomes interesting. Because once you understand that performance come from the interaction between real yields, inflation expectations, duration and realised inflation, you realise that there isn’t simply one inflation trait. There are potentially very different opportunities across maturities and across countries. And the asset class allows you to explore all of this.

AC: Okay, so today we’ve got an environment where we think inflation is going to be higher than what the market’s pricing. Real yields are at what we think are attractive levels. They’ve risen, they’re perhaps at a level that makes sense for investors. Let’s talk about the different sorts of instrument we have for investing [in] inflation-linked bonds, and what sort of approach would you consider at the moment?

ER: For us, there are two important dimensions to this question. The first is global versus single country exposure or currency. The second is active versus passive management.

Let’s start with the global versus single dimension. Inflation is a global phenomenon, but it is certainly not synchronised. The US, the Euro and the UK, which are the main markets, can be at very different stages of their inflation and monetary policy cycles, so the sources of inflation can also be different. At one point the opportunity may be in US TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) – like last year with Liberation Day – and another point in Euro inflation or UK, like this year with the energy shock.

That makes differently attractive markets. Why limit yourself structurally to a single market when a global universe give you a much broader opportunity set and allows you to diversify the sources of inflation exposure?

The second point is active management versus passive. Inflation bonds are particularly well suited to an active approach because the asset class has many performance drivers.

Passive indices or passive benchmarking are built according to issuance of market capitalisation. That does not necessarily mean they give you the exposure that is most attractive from an investment perspective. They can also have significant duration exposure depending on what you’re choosing.

For an investor looking primarily for inflation protection, taking a very large amount of long duration interest-rate risk may not always be desirable, [as] was the case in 2022. That’s one of the reasons why we prefer the short part of the curve. It allows us to capture inflation exposure while limiting some of the volatility associated with very long duration bonds. And within that universe, active management allows us to make several decisions.

We can decide which markets we want to favour, where on the curve we want to be positioned. We can actively manage real duration exposure, and can assess where inflation expectations, so called breakevens, look cheap or expensive relative to our macroeconomic view.

So again, rather than simply buying the global inflation in bond markets as it exists, we’re trying to identify where we believe investors are being best compensated for the risk they are taking. In the end, for the investor, the objective is therefore quite simple. You don’t have to decide yourself where you buy TIPS, euro area linkers, or just one country in the EU, or UK linkers. Which maturity should you own or when you should adjust that exposure? That is the role of active management.

If I had to summarise in one sentence, I would say inflation protection should not necessarily be a tactical trait. On the next CPI (consumer price index) print, it can be a structural component of a fixed income or multi asset portfolio and we believe that a global actively managed approach is a particularly efficient way of accessing it.
